x: Introduction Crow is a programming language for people who work with data and ship what they find. It looks like Python, compiles to Rust, and makes three promises: Parallel by default. A for loop runs its iterations concurrently. You never write threads, async, or locks — you write loops. Errors are values. No exceptions, no try / catch , no null. A failed operation returns a value that carries its own story ( .ok , .reason ), propagates safely, and refuses to be silently misread. One way to do things. One call syntax ( f[x] ), one string quote ( ' ), one loop, one way to build a map. When Crow rejects a feature you expect, a Design Note in the specification explains why — and the compile error tells you what to write instead. The language ships as a single binary containing an interpreter (for immediate feedback), a compiler to Rust (for production speed; the Rust toolchain it needs is fetched once, on the first native build), tensors, data frames, a database layer, and a reactive web framework. The final chapter of this book builds a live dashboard using all of them. The same binary talks to language models: a model is a connection, a program's own functions are its tools, and an agent loop runs them ( use llm , use mcp ; Crow by Example shows both). Crow is in alpha: the language still changes between releases, the changelog in the repository says what moved, and this book is rebuilt for every change, so what you read matches the release you install. Who This Book Is For You've written some Python, R, MATLAB, or JavaScript. You don't need to know Rust — Crow compiles to Rust, you never read the output. How to Read It Two parts, one language. Part I is the book: read it in order. Getting Started installs Crow and meets the toolchain, the guessing game builds a small program before any theory, and the chapters that follow build the language up one idea at a time — concepts, functions and scope, collections, parallelism, errors, modules, testing — each using only what came before it. Then the applied layers: a hands-on data project, databases, web UIs, and a final project that uses everything. Crow by Example closes Part I with one runnable program per area of the language. Whatever language you're arriving from — Python, JavaScript, R, MATLAB, Julia, Go, Rust, Elixir, Ruby, Swift, Zig — Appendix B lists the habits to unlearn, and Appendix A is the language on one page. Part II is the reference: the standard library module by module, every function linked to the example that shows it, and the language specification — the source of truth ( docs/language-spec.md in the repository), with a Design Note for every feature Crow deliberately leaves out. Consult it whenever the book says "the spec covers the rest", and read its Design Notes whenever you wonder "why can't I…". The book teaches; the spec specifies. Every Block Runs Every code block in this book is executed by crow test --book in both of Crow's execution modes on every change: what you read is what runs. And every block can be run where it stands. From a checkout of the repository run crow book and open the printed address: each block gets ▶ Run (the interpreter), ⚙ Compile (the native binary), ✓ Test (its test blocks), ↺ Reset, and ■ Stop. The block itself is editable — change it and run again. The same binary that verifies the book serves it.

Getting Started Let's install Crow, meet the toolchain, and run your first program. By the end of this chapter you'll have both execution modes working and a project directory ready for the rest of the book. Installation You need a Mac or a Linux machine (on Windows, run everything inside WSL). One line installs Crow: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/agncrow/crow/main/install.sh | bash It puts one prebuilt binary in ~/.crow/bin , checks it against its published hash, runs a hello program, and prints the line that puts ~/.crow/bin on your PATH . Add that line to your shell profile, open a new terminal, then verify: crow -v You should see the version. crow on its own starts the REPL, crow help lists the main commands, and The Toolchain, next, has the rest. Nothing else is installed: the interpreter, the tests, crow check , the language server and a served app need only that binary. Crow compiles your programs to Rust, so a native build needs a Rust toolchain too: crow setup fetches a pinned one into ~/.crow , with Crow's runtime, once (about 175 MB), and the first crow build does the same if you have not; crow setup --check says what is present. Until then crow run says so and interprets, which answers the same, only slower. Building from a checkout On a machine the release has no binary for, build crow from its source: git clone https://github.com/agncrow/crow.git cd crow ./install.sh --source The script installs whatever is missing and skips whatever is present, in order: A C toolchain. The Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS (a dialog opens; accept it), gcc through your package manager on Linux. Rust , through rustup — stable, no prompts. Crow needs 1.85 or newer. A permanent home. The source is copied to ~/.crow/src . Compiled programs link against the runtime crates there, so the clone can go once the script is done, and re-running the script on a newer checkout is the upgrade. The binary , built in release mode into ~/.cargo/bin/crow . The first build takes a few minutes. Proof. A hello project is created, compiled, and run. ./install.sh --dev builds the checkout in place instead — for working on Crow itself, since compiled programs then link against your working tree. --quick skips the proof; --uninstall removes the binary and ~/.crow and leaves Rust alone. If this was your first Rust install, open a new terminal (rustup put ~/.cargo/bin on your PATH through your shell profile) before crow -v . If something goes wrong crow: command not found right after the install: the binary is in ~/.crow/bin . Add the PATH line the installer printed to your shell profile and open a new terminal. A build from a checkout is in ~/.cargo/bin , which a fresh Rust install adds to your shell profile: open a new terminal, or run source "$HOME/.cargo/env" in this one. No binary for this machine. The release carries crow for macOS on Apple silicon and Linux on x86_64; anywhere else, build it from a checkout with ./install.sh --source . A dialog appeared on macOS while building from a checkout. That is the Command Line Tools installer; accept it. The script waits for it to finish. Linux asked for a password while building from a checkout. Installing the C compiler goes through your package manager with sudo . Nothing else in the script needs it. It seems stuck on "building crow". A release build of the compiler takes a few minutes the first time and is quiet while it runs. Later runs reuse the cache in ~/.crow/target . Upgrading: crow upgrade replaces the binary in ~/.crow/bin with the latest release, verified; a crow built from a checkout upgrades by git pull , then ./install.sh --source (or --dev ) again. Removing: delete ~/.crow and the PATH line; in a checkout, ./install.sh --uninstall removes both binaries and ~/.crow . Editor Support Crow ships its own language server — diagnostics as you type, completions with inferred signatures, hover types, go-to-definition — as a subcommand of the same binary you just installed: crow lsp You never run that yourself; your editor does. For VS Code and the editors built on it, install the extension "Crow" by crow-lang : Cursor and VSCodium find it on Open VSX, and each release carries its .vsix for VS Code, which code --install-extension crow-lang-<version>.vsix installs. It starts crow lsp with the crow on your PATH ; the setting crow.serverPath names another. Neovim, Helix, and Zed speak LSP natively — copy the snippet for your editor from docs/crow-lsp.md . Everything the editor shows comes from the real compiler pipeline, so the squiggles never disagree with crow run .

The Toolchain One binary, a handful of verbs. Every one of them runs the same compiler pipeline the editor uses, so nothing you see in one place disagrees with another. crow the REPL, interpreted crow new name [--web --ml --db] scaffold a project (a crowfile, main.co, a .gitignore) crow run [-i] [file] execute: compiled when the compiler is here, else interpreted and told; -i interprets crow file the short form of crow run file crow run --opt N file the program at optimization level N (0 to 3; 0 unless said, crow build is 3 with LTO) crow dev [file] serve with the interpreter, reloading as files change (sessions kept) crow stop stop the app this project runs (crow run, crow run -i, crow dev) crow build [file] compile to a native binary here, named after the file (./main in a project) crow test [file] run the test blocks crow check [file] verify: tests, generated edge cases, contracts, and the app baseline — what changed since the accepted one crow fix file apply the fixes the error messages name, and those crow check offers crow fmt [file] format the files named, or the project's entry; --check only says crow install fetch the crowfile's deps into crow_modules/, pinned by crow.lock crow db diff [file] the SQL that makes each database hold the tables the program declares crow db apply dir url run the migrations in dir that the database has not applied yet crow setup [--check] fetch the Rust toolchain and the runtime for compiled builds, once; --check says what is present crow upgrade [--check] replace this crow with the latest release, verified; --version X installs that one; --check says what is newer crow book [--port N] in the crow repository, serve this book with every block runnable; inside an app, the app's own book crow lsp the language server (your editor runs it) crow launch N [file] run the program as N processes, each reading its rank from CROW_RANK crow test --parity | --book in the crow repository: the two execution modes must agree crow test --docs [--write] in the crow repository: the documentation must cover the compiler crow help lists every command and flag, one line each, and the toolchain guide ( docs/usage.md ) says what each does at length. Two execution modes, one behaviour. crow run -i interprets: instant start, the mode to use while you explore. crow run transpiles to Rust and builds a native binary: the mode to ship. The binary you installed holds the interpreter and needs nothing else; the compiler is a Rust toolchain that crow setup , or the first crow build , fetches into ~/.crow once, and until it is there crow run says so and interprets. They are held to identical output by crow test --parity over a corpus of programs and by crow test --book over every code block in this book. Interpret while you explore; compile when you ship. That is the whole workflow. crow upgrade keeps the binary current: it replaces the one the install line put in ~/.crow/bin with the latest release, held to its published hash, and the new version fetches its own compiler the same way, on its first compiled build. A crow built from a checkout upgrades by git pull and ./install.sh --dev or --source again; crow upgrade says so rather than replace it. A project's crowfile names the entry point and the resources: keys name , entry , db , schema , cpu , gpu , deps , jobs . The next page makes one.

Hello, World! Create a file named hello.co : log['hello, world'] Two things already differ from the languages you know: calls use square brackets ( log[...] , never log(...) ) and strings use single quotes . These are the two most common reflexes to retrain, and the compiler will remind you if you slip. Run it compiled — Crow transpiles to Rust, builds a native binary, and executes it: crow run hello.co hello, world Or run it interpreted for instant startup while you're iterating: crow run -i hello.co The two modes are guaranteed to agree — the project's test suite diffs their outputs on a growing corpus of programs, including every code block in this book. Interpret while you explore; compile when you ship. That's the whole workflow. One more taste of what's ahead — interpolation uses paired backticks, and a for loop is an expression that runs in parallel: name = 'crow' log['hello, `name`'] squares = for x in [1, 2, 3, 4] x * x log[squares] hello, crow [1, 4, 9, 16]

Hello, Crowfile! Single files are fine for scripts; projects get a directory. crow new scaffolds one: crow new hello_crow cd hello_crow Look at what it made — two files, and a .gitignore that keeps the build and the installed packages out of version control: hello_crow/ crowfile main.co .gitignore The crowfile is the project manifest. It is itself a Crow file — one assignment for now: name = 'hello_crow' Later you'll add keys to it: db = '...' so the checker can read your database schema (chapter 11), jobs = map[...] for batch tasks, deps for packages. main.co is the entry point, and it already runs: crow run # compile and run main.co crow run -i # the same program, interpreted — instant start crow build # compile only; the binary lands in the project directory crow run writes the generated Rust into .crow_build/ inside the project. You never need to look at it, and it's safe to delete — the next run recreates it. The first compile builds Crow's runtime along with your program, which takes a while (about half a minute on a fast machine); after that only what changed is rebuilt. Two more commands you'll use in every chapter from here on: crow check # verify the project: your tests plus everything automatic crow fmt # format the project's entry, or the files you name For a web project, crow new myapp --web adds a views/ directory wired into the server (chapter 12); --db adds db/schema.co , the tables main.co declares on a SQLite database (chapter 11), and --ml a training job that crow run train runs. crow run works the moment crow new finishes. You now have everything the rest of this book needs. Next: build a real program before learning any more theory.

Programming a Guessing Game Let's write a real program before any more theory. This chapter builds the classic first project: the computer picks a number between 1 and 100, you guess, and it tells you too low or too high until you find it. Small as it is, this game touches most of what makes Crow itself: reading input, converting types, meeting your first error value , comparing with word operators, and looping. Everything it introduces gets a full chapter later — here we just use it all. Setting Up crow new guessing_game cd guessing_game Open main.co and replace its contents as we go. Run at any point with crow run (compiled) or crow run -i (instant, interpreted). Processing a Guess First, ask for input: raw = input['your guess: '] log['you guessed: `raw`'] input[prompt] prints the prompt, reads a line from the keyboard, and returns it as a string. The backticks in 'you guessed: `raw`' are Crow's string interpolation — any expression between paired backticks is evaluated into the string. A Value That Might Have Failed The player typed a string ; we need a number . int[...] converts: n = int['42'] log[n] log[n + 8] bad = int['abc'] log[bad.ok] log[bad.reason] 42 50 false cannot convert 'abc' to int Look closely at the second half — this is your first encounter with Crow's error model, and there is no try , no catch , no exception. int['abc'] simply returns a value that knows it failed . Every value in Crow carries .ok and .reason ; for successful values .ok is true and you never think about it (notice n + 8 just works — values auto-unwrap). For a failure, .ok is false and .reason says why. What if you ignore the failure and use bad anyway? Crow refuses to guess: an error value has no truth value — compared with something, it answers the error again — so a branch on it stops the program (or returns the error from a function) rather than silently picking a wrong path. Chapter 7 is entirely about this; for the game, all we need is .ok . Generating the Secret Number secret = rand[1, 100] rand[min, max] returns a random integer in the range, inclusive. Comparing Crow's comparison operators are words — eq , ne , lt , gt , lte , gte — no shift key, no == -vs- = bugs: secret = 62 guess = 50 if guess eq secret log['you got it!'] else if guess lt secret log['too low'] else log['too high'] too low (There is no elif keyword — else if is just an if in the else branch, and it reads the same way.) Looping Until They Get It while true with break and continue gives the game loop. Here is the complete program: secret = rand[1, 100] log['I am thinking of a number between 1 and 100.'] while true raw = input['your guess: '] n = int[raw] if not n.ok log['`raw` is not a number — try again'] continue if n eq secret log['you got it — `secret`!'] break if n lt secret log['too low'] else log['too high'] A session looks like this: I am thinking of a number between 1 and 100. your guess: fifty fifty is not a number — try again your guess: 50 too low your guess: 75 too high your guess: 62 you got it — 62! Walk the error path once more, because it's the most Crow-shaped part: when the player types fifty , int[raw] returns a failed value. We check .ok , explain, and continue . If we hadn't checked, the very next line — if n eq secret — would have refused to run on an error value and stopped the program with the reason. Wrong input can never masquerade as a wrong guess. Summary You've used: input and interpolation, int conversion, error values and .ok , rand , word comparisons, if / else , and while / break / continue . Chapter 3 now walks the everyday material properly, and chapter 7 returns to error values in depth.

Common Programming Concepts This chapter covers the material every program uses: variables, the basic types, strings, comments, and control flow. None of it will surprise a Python or JavaScript programmer for long — but each section notes where Crow deliberately differs, and why.

Variables A variable is created by assigning to it. No keyword, no type annotation: count = 10 name = 'crow' ready = true log[count] 10 Reassignment is fine — but a variable's type cannot change: items = [1, 2, 3] items = 'three things' --- error: cannot reassign from array to string The one deliberate loosening: a variable ever assigned a float is a float for its whole scope, because numeric code mixes 10 and 3.14 constantly: x = 10 x = 3.14 log[x] 3.14 Multiple assignment and swap work as you'd hope: a, b = 1, 2 a, b = b, a log[a] log[b] 2 1 Each name takes a value of its own, as many values as names. A list is never taken apart into names — that is a compile error, which shows the form to write instead: fn pair[] return [3, 4] c, d = pair[] --- error: Crow takes no list apart into names Hold the list, then read its items by position: fn pair[] return [3, 4] r = pair[] c = r[0] d = r[1] log[c + d] 7 One rule you'll meet early: names you define can't collide with names the language owns . range = [1, 2] is a compile error ( range is a core builtin), and after use math , so is sum = 0 . The error always says what to do — rename, or import the module under an alias. Chapter 8 covers the full story.

Data Types The scalar types are int , float , bool , and str (text). Arithmetic is familiar, with two things worth pinning down. Division between ints rounds toward zero; a float anywhere makes it float: log[3 / 2] log[3 / 2.0] 1 1.5 Exponentiation is ^ (not ** ), and % is remainder: log[2 ^ 10] log[7 % 3] 1024 1 An int is a whole number of any size. It grows as far as its value needs, so int arithmetic is exact, as Python's is — nothing is written to ask for it: log[2 ^ 100] top = 9223372036854775807 log[top + 1] fn fact[n] r = 1 for i in range[2, n + 1] r = r * i return r log[len[str[fact[100]]]] 1267650600228229401496703205376 9223372036854775808 158 The compiled program keeps an int in 64 bits wherever it can show the int stays within them — a loop's counter, a position, a count — so a program pays for the size only where a number can have it. A number past 64 bits handed where 64 bits are taken, a position or a count, is refused there: range[2 ^ 70] stops with a whole number past 64 bits where range[] takes an int of 64 bits: 1180591620717411303424 . Exact numbers. A float is a nearby binary number — 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 — which is right for measurement and wrong for money. A decimal is an exact base-ten number that keeps its places, and a fraction an exact ratio in lowest terms: a = decimal['0.1'] log[a + decimal['0.2']] price = decimal['12.30'] log[price * 3] log[decimal[1] / decimal[3]] log[fraction[1, 3] + fraction[1, 6]] 0.3 36.90 0.3333333333333333333333333333 1/2 + , - and * of decimals are exact; a quotient has 28 significant digits, rounded half away from zero, unless a decimal was given more with decimal[x, digits = n] — which makes it the language's big float: log[sqrt[decimal[2, digits = 30]]] log[round[decimal['2.345'], 2]] 1.41421356237309504880168872421 2.35 An int meeting a decimal is the decimal it is, and a literal with a point is the number it writes ( price * 1.1 is exactly 13.530). A float computed elsewhere meeting a decimal is refused before the program runs, with both conversions named — decimal[rate] or float[price] — since the exact answer would be a guess. Convert between types with int[...] , float[...] , str[...] . Converting a string can fail — which returns an error value , not an exception (you met this in the guessing game; chapter 7 goes deep): log[int[3.9]] log[float['2.5']] log[str[42]] 3 2.5 42 Collections — arrays, tensors, maps, structs — get their own chapter (5).

Strings and Interpolation Strings use single quotes, only . There is no double-quote form — one way to write a string, no style debates. Escape a quote with \' : msg = 'he said \'hi\'' log[msg] he said 'hi' Interpolation Any expression between paired backticks is evaluated into the string: name = 'crow' n = 4 log['hello, `name`'] log['`n` squared is `n * n`'] hello, crow 4 squared is 16 Outside backticks, strings are completely inert — braces, JSON, and regex punctuation need no escaping. For a literal backtick, write \` . A backslash before any other character stays as it is, so a regular expression is written as it is: '\d+' , '\|' . Length and slicing count characters len[] , slice[] , and indexing all work in characters, never bytes, so accented letters and dashes are one step each in both execution modes: s = 'naïve — café' log[len[s]] log[slice[s, 6, 7]] log[s[-1]] log[s[2]] 12 — é ï Counting and mapping characters occurs counts how many times a part occurs, not overlapping (as Python's str.count counts), and translate maps each character of one text to the character at its place in another, all in one pass — the complement of a strand of DNA: dna = 'GATTACA' log[occurs[dna, 'A']] log[occurs['aaaa', 'aa']] log[translate[dna, 'ACGT', 'TGCA']] 3 2 CTAATGT No + on strings + is for numbers. To combine strings, interpolate; to build from many pieces, collect and join : parts = split['a,b,c', ','] log[parts] log[join[parts, '-']] log[upper['crow']] ['a', 'b', 'c'] a-b-c CROW s = 'a' + 'b' --- error: cannot use '+' with strings The error message itself tells you the two idioms above. For value formatting (decimals, widths, percents) there's fmt[...] with named arguments — chapter 10 uses it to report.

Comments A comment runs from --- to the end of the line. There is no closing delimiter, so an unclosed comment can never swallow code: --- this whole line is a comment x = 5 --- and this trails a statement log[x] 5 Multi-line commentary is just multiple --- lines. A line that holds only a comment opens and closes no block, whatever its indentation, as a blank line does: a comment that goes on from a trailing one can sit aligned under it, and a note at the margin inside a function leaves the function open: fn hello[name] words = 'hi `name`' --- the greeting, as the --- page shows it --- a note at the margin, inside the function return words log[hello['ada']] hi ada That's the entire comment system.

Control Flow if / else Conditions use word operators — eq , ne , lt , gt , lte , gte , combined with and , or , not . Blocks are indentation, no colons: age = 20 if age gte 18 and age lt 65 log['working age'] else log['not working age'] working age Chain conditions with else if (there is no elif keyword — it's just an if in the else branch): score = 72 if score gte 90 log['A'] else if score gte 70 log['B'] else log['C'] B There is no ternary expression: use an if / else statement, and set the variable before it. A variable set inside a branch belongs to that branch and ends with it, so a value the rest of the program reads is set first and changed inside: n = 42 size = 'small' if n gt 10 size = 'big' log[size] big Reading a variable after the branch that set it ended is refused before the program runs, with the line and this fix. while i = 0 while i lt 3 i = i + 1 log[i] 3 (No += in Crow — write i = i + 1 . The compiler optimizes it the same.) for for iterates arrays and ranges: total = 0 for n in [1, 2, 3, 4] total = total + n log[total] 10 But for is bigger than this in Crow: it's an expression that collects values, and when its body only computes, it runs its iterations in parallel on every core. That story deserves its own chapter, and it's chapter 6. doubled = for n in [1, 2, 3] n * 2 log[doubled] [2, 4, 6]

Functions and Scope Functions are where Crow makes its first big bet. The syntax will take you thirty seconds; the scope rule — what a function can and cannot see — is where Crow deliberately parts company with Python, and it's the foundation that makes chapter 6's automatic parallelism possible. We take them in that order.

Defining and Calling Functions fn , a name, parameters in square brackets, an indented body: fn area[w, h] return w * h log[area[3, 4]] 12 The last expression in a body is the return value, so return on the final line is optional: fn cube[x] x * x * x log[cube[3]] 27 Functions Are Values A function name without brackets is the function — store it, pass it, call it later. This is how Crow does everything other languages use lambdas for (Crow has no lambdas — a deliberate choice; named functions keep every callsite greppable and every behavior testable): fn cube[x] x * x * x op = cube log[op[2]] fn apply_twice[f, x] return f[f[x]] log[apply_twice[cube, 2]] 8 512

Named Arguments Trailing parameters can declare defaults, which makes them optional and nameable at the call site: fn greet[name, greeting = 'hello'] return '`greeting`, `name`' log[greet['crow']] log[greet['crow', 'hey']] log[greet['crow', greeting = 'welcome']] hello, crow hey, crow welcome, crow The rules are exactly four: Named parameters come after all positional ones A named parameter must have a default — that's what makes it optional A default is a literal — a number, text, a bool — or an empty [] or map[] , never an expression, so when and where it is computed never comes up Callers may use position or name for those slots — both are fine You'll use this constantly with builtins: fmt[x, decimals = 2] , sort[df, 'age', desc = true] , sum[m, axis = 0] . It's the same mechanism everywhere — there is no separate "keyword argument" system for builtins versus your functions.

Function Scope Isolation Here is the rule, and it is stricter than Python's: Module variables are invisible inside functions. A function sees its parameters, its own locals, other functions, structs, and imported vocabulary — nothing else. Data enters through parameters and leaves through the return value. count = 5 fn bad[] --- error: 'count' is a module variable, which a function does not --- see — pass it as a parameter return count + 1 The fix is always the same shape: count = 5 fn bump[n] return n + 1 log[bump[count]] 6 A local that happens to reuse a module name shadows nothing — module variables were never visible, so it's simply a fresh binding. No global keyword, no nonlocal , no scope-resolution table to memorize. Why So Strict? Two reasons, and they're both load-bearing: A signature that tells the whole truth. If a function can secretly read ambient state, its behavior depends on things not in its signature — refactoring, testing, and crow check all get harder. Parameters-in, return-out means every dependency is visible at the call site. Parallelism needs it. Chapter 6's parallel loops work because every read and write in the loop body is visible at the call site. Hidden reads would turn "parallel by default" into "data races by default." Crow chose the scope rule that makes the loop rule sound. The one sanctioned exception is the state of a program that serves (chapter 12): view blocks, event handlers and derivations read a page's reactive state, and a route's handler reads the derivations its app holds — a managed channel, synchronized by the runtime, not ambient mutation.

Collections Crow has exactly three shapes for grouping data, with a clean division of labor: arrays for ordered values of one type (numeric arrays are tensors and get real math), maps for uniform lookup tables, and structs for records with mixed, named fields. If you're wondering which to reach for, the section titles are the rule: maps are dictionaries, structs are records.

Arrays and Tensors Arrays are ordered and homogeneous. Indexing is zero-based; negative indices count from the end: nums = [10, 20, 30] log[nums[0]] log[nums[-1]] log[len[nums]] more = push[nums, 40] log[more] log[concat[[1, 2], [3, 4]]] 10 30 3 [10, 20, 30, 40] [1, 2, 3, 4] push and concat return new arrays — Crow collections are immutable-by-rebuild, which is part of what keeps parallel loops safe. Numeric Arrays Are Tensors An all-numeric array literal is backed by a real tensor, so math works on it wholesale — + adds element-wise against another tensor or broadcasts a scalar; the dotted operators .* , ./ , .^ are explicit element-wise multiply/divide/power: a = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0] b = [10.0, 20.0, 30.0] log[a .* b] log[a + b] log[a * 2.0] [10, 40, 90] [11, 22, 33] [2, 4, 6] Nest literals and you have a matrix — m[0] is a row, .shape tells you the dimensions, * of two matrices multiplies them, and use math unlocks the full toolkit ( zeros , eye , transpose , reductions along axes — chapter 10 puts it to work): m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] log[m[0]] log[m.shape] [1, 2] [2, 2]

Maps Are Dictionaries A map is a lookup table: keys of one kind — text, or ints ( map[1 = 'a'] ) — and values of one type. Build one with the map[...] constructor; read with dot or bracket; set returns an updated copy: scores = map[alice = 10, bob = 7] log[scores.alice] log[scores['bob']] s2 = set[scores, 'carol', 9] log[s2] log[keys[s2]] log['alice' in scores] 10 7 [alice = 10, bob = 7, carol = 9] ['alice', 'bob', 'carol'] true The one-type rule is enforced — a map of ints won't accept a string. If you're tempted to mix types under named keys, what you want is not a map. It's the next section.

Structs Are Records A struct declares named fields of any mix of types: struct Trade [symbol, qty, price] t = Trade['AAPL', 100, 191.5] log[t.symbol] log[t.qty * t.price] log[t] AAPL 19150 Trade[price = 191.5, qty = 100, symbol = 'AAPL'] Construct positionally (or with names — Trade[symbol = 'AAPL', ...] ), access with dots. Structs pass to functions efficiently and print themselves readably. Field names are free — schema names like type , sum , or count are fine as fields ( t.type ) even where they'd be reserved as variables. The only names a field can't take are the four error-metadata names every value already carries: ok , reason , kind , trace . The decision rule, one line: same type under many keys → map; mixed types under fixed names → struct; a column of records → chapter 10's data frames. Next: the loop that processes all of these at once.

Parallel by Default This is the chapter where Crow stops resembling Python. In most languages, parallelism is something you add — threads, pools, async , locks. In Crow it's what for already does: iterations run concurrently, on all your cores, and you never wrote a thread. The design has consequences, and this chapter is honest about them: what the loop gives you, what it asks of you, and the three search builtins that cover the patterns a parallel loop can't. One boundary to keep in mind as you read: for is about throughput — finishing a computation faster by using every core. Keeping an app responsive while something slow happens is a different job with its own verb, later , which you'll meet in the web chapter ( Slow Work and the Live Loop ).

for as an Expression Assign a for loop and it collects — the last expression of each iteration becomes an element of the result: squares = for x in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] x * x log[squares] [1, 4, 9, 16, 25] A trailing if filters — iterations that produce no value contribute nothing: evens = for x in range[10] if x % 2 eq 0 x log[evens] [0, 2, 4, 6, 8] This one construct is Crow's map , filter , and list comprehension — none of which exist separately, because they'd all be second ways to write this. The Parallel Part Those iterations did not run in order. Crow reads what the loop's body does, and when its rounds are independent it runs them concurrently — a for over ten thousand rows uses every core, for free: celsius = [0.0, 21.5, 100.0] fahrenheit = for c in celsius c * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 log[fahrenheit] [32, 70.7, 212] The results arrive in input order — collection is deterministic. The iterations run in parallel only when nothing in the body can show the order they ran in. A body that prints, writes a file or a fact, draws a random number, renders a view, or accumulates into an outer variable ( total = total + n ) runs in order, so it stays correct and just forfeits the parallelism. A function you call counts by what it does, however deep: a loop over a function that only computes runs on every core, one over a function that logs runs in order. crow build --ir shows which loops run in parallel. The idiom that keeps a loop parallel is the one you've been seeing all book: compute in the loop, collect the values, print after. cpu[8] before a loop caps its thread count; cpu[1] runs every loop on one core.

t: Searching with any, all, and find
x: Searching with any, all, and find There is no break in a for loop — deliberately. A break-driven search forces sequential execution, exactly what Crow's loops exist to avoid. In its place, three builtins ask the three questions searches actually ask — and because Crow implements the early exit, they stop across all cores at once: fn is_big[x] return x gt 1000 nums = [3, 12, 4021, 55] log[any[nums, is_big]] log[all[nums, is_big]] log[find[nums, is_big]] true false 4021 Predicates are named functions — the same functions-as-values idea from chapter 4, and every predicate is independently testable. find returns the first matching element . And when nothing matches? It returns the value you already know how to read — an error value: fn is_big[x] return x gt 1000 fn is_negative[x] return x lt 0 nums = [3, 12, 4021, 55] missing = find[nums, is_negative] log[missing.ok] log[missing.reason] false no match No sentinel -1 , no null, no exception — a miss is a value carrying its own explanation, checked with .ok like every other fallible result.

Controlling Resources Parallelism defaults to all cores; two builtins adjust it when you need to: cpu[8] --- cap the next loops at 8 threads cpu[1] --- one core: every loop in order gpu[] --- enable GPU execution for tensor work Running a program as several processes is the launch's, not the program's: crow launch 4 train.co runs four, and each reads its rank with env['CROW_RANK', '0'] . That's the entire concurrency API. There are no threads to spawn, no futures to await, no locks to take — the scope rule (chapter 4) plus the read/write analysis make the safe thing the only thing. Next: what happens when an operation fails — Crow's other big idea.

Errors Are Values Every language must answer: what happens when an operation fails? Exceptions answer with a jump — control teleports to the nearest handler, and every function between is silently interruptible. Null answers with a landmine — a value that detonates somewhere far from where it was made. Crow's answer: failure is data. A failed operation returns a value that knows it failed and can say why. That value flows through your program like any other — until something tries to act on it, at which point Crow refuses to guess. No try , no catch , no null, no unwinding. You've been using this model since chapter 2. This chapter makes it precise, in four steps: what every value carries, how failures travel, why an error can never decide a branch, and how to handle one on purpose.

Every Value Has Status All values — not a special error type, all of them — carry four pieces of metadata: .ok , .reason , .kind , and .trace . A successful value answers boringly, and auto-unwraps so you never think about the wrapper: n = int['42'] log[n] log[n.ok] log[n + 8] 42 true 50 A failure is the same shape with a different story: bad = int['oops'] log[bad.ok] log[bad.reason] false cannot convert 'oops' to int You can also make one deliberately — this is Crow's raise , except nothing is thrown; you just return it: down = error['price feed is down', 'network'] log[down.ok] log[down.reason] log[down.kind] false price feed is down network .kind is a category for programmatic handling ( 'parse' , 'io' , 'network' ); .trace accumulates the path a failure traveled, for debugging.

Propagation What happens when a failed value meets an operator? The failure wins, and keeps its story: bad = int['oops'] worse = bad + 10 log[worse.ok] log[worse.reason] false cannot convert 'oops' to int No crash, no exception — bad + 10 is simply another error value with the original reason. Arithmetic, interpolation, function calls: pass a failure through any of them and it propagates unchanged, appending to .trace as it crosses function boundaries. This is the quiet radicalism of the model: the code between where a failure happens and where it's handled doesn't participate. No ? on every call, no try blocks around every section, no exception specifications. Intermediate code stays written for the happy path, and failures flow through it inert — they only matter when something tries to make a decision with one. Which is the next section.

Errors Have No Truth Value Here is the rule that completes the model: An error value cannot be compared and cannot decide a branch. It is not falsy. It is not truthy. It is unanswerable , and Crow treats it that way. Consider if bad gt 5 where bad is a failed int[...] . Exceptions would have crashed earlier; truthy/falsy languages would silently pick a branch — misclassifying corrupt input as a small number. Crow does neither: bad = int['x'] if bad gt 5 log['big'] runtime error: line 2: cannot branch on an error value — cannot convert 'x' to int At top level, the program halts with the original reason. Inside a function, something better happens: the function returns the error to its caller — the decision that couldn't be made becomes the caller's failure to inspect: fn size_of[s] n = int[s] if n gt 100 return 'big' return 'small' r1 = size_of['150'] log[r1] r2 = size_of['xyz'] log[r2.ok] log[r2.reason] big false cannot convert 'xyz' to int size_of contains no error handling at all — it's written purely for the happy path. Feed it garbage and it returns the garbage's story, at the exact moment the garbage mattered. The failure detonates at the decision, not at the origin, and never silently. A loop is a decision too. An error has no items to walk, so a for over a list that failed is refused the same way: for i in range[len[r]] inside a function hands r 's error back when r failed, and at the top level it halts with cannot loop over an error value . An error could also slip past in a variable. A variable whose first value could not fail never holds an error: a later value that fails is refused right where it is assigned, the same way a decision refuses one. fn add_up[items] acc = 0.0 for s in items acc = acc + float[s] return acc log[add_up[['1.5', '2']]] bad = add_up[['1.5', 'two']] log[bad.ok] log[bad.reason] 3.5 false cannot convert 'two' to float acc began as a plain number, so the failed item never lands in it: add_up hands the error back at that line. At the top level the program halts there with cannot assign an error value to 'acc' . When you want to keep a failure and look at it, give it a name of its own whose first value can fail: r = float[s] , then if not r.ok . A failure nothing reads A line made of one call is usually there for what the call does: write[path, text] , query[conn, sql] , rm[path] . Each answers a value that can fail, and on a line of its own nothing reads it. If that failure simply went by, a program could lose its work without a word. So Crow treats the line as a decision, like a branch: a function hands the failure to its caller, and the top level halts. fn save_note[path, note] write[path, note] return 'saved' r = save_note['/no/such/folder/note.txt', 'hello'] log[r.ok] log[r.reason] kept = rm['/no/such/folder/old.txt'] log[kept.ok] false cannot write '/no/such/folder/note.txt': No such file or directory (os error 2) false save_note never reached its return : the write failed, and the function handed that failure back. The rm failed too, but its value was given a name, so it is an ordinary value the program may look at or ignore; naming it is how you say a failure is fine. At the top level, a dropped failure stops the program on its line: write['/no/such/folder/note.txt', 'hello'] log['not reached'] runtime error: line 1: cannot drop an error value — cannot write '/no/such/folder/note.txt': No such file or directory (os error 2) A collecting loop's last line hands its value on, so it is not dropped, and neither is a test's truth: len[xs] eq 3 on a line of a test block is asserted. What no value can carry A few failures have no error value to become. xs[i] reads an element and a / b of two ints makes an int, and neither an element nor an int can say it failed. So an index outside its array, a key the map lacks, or an int divided by zero stops the program on the line it happened on — as does an int grown past 64 bits where only 64 bits are taken, a position or a size (an int itself grows as far as it needs: chapter 3): fn pick[xs, i] return xs[i] log[pick[[10, 20, 30], -1]] log[pick[[10, 20, 30], 5]] 30 runtime error: line 2: index 5 is out of range for an array of 3 items A negative index counts from the end, so -1 is the last item. The stop names line 2, inside pick , where the index was read. The words are the same in crow run -i and crow run , and in a handler the click stops with nothing it did landing. When an index might be outside, check len first, as you would guard any decision.

Handling Errors Explicitly Reading metadata ( .ok , .reason , .kind ) never propagates — that's the one bridge from a failed value back to normal control flow. The guard is the whole pattern: raw = '42x' n = int[raw] if not n.ok log['bad input: `n.reason`'] else log['parsed `n`'] bad input: cannot convert '42x' to int Branch by category when it matters: fail = error['connection refused', 'network'] if not fail.ok if fail.kind eq 'network' log['will retry'] else log['giving up: `fail.reason`'] will retry A guard can be its own if , telling each case apart: text = read['no_such_file.txt'] if not text.ok log['unreadable'] else if len[text] eq 0 log['empty'] else log['`len[text]` characters'] unreadable Or one condition, where the cases are handled alike: and and or decide from the left, so the right side runs only where the left has not already decided — len[text] is never asked of a read that failed: text = read['no_such_file.txt'] if not text.ok or len[text] eq 0 log['nothing to read'] else log['`len[text]` characters'] nothing to read Inside a function, a guard whose branch leaves also narrows : after if not text.ok ending in return , text is known good for the rest of the block, so len[text] there is a plain number, and the function is not typed as able to fail: fn size_of[path] text = read[path] if not text.ok return 0 return len[text] log[size_of['no_such_file.txt']] 0 When to Check The idiom that falls out of this chapter: check .ok at boundaries — user input, files, network, database — and let everything between flow. Interior code stays happy-path; a failure entering it comes back out carrying its story; the boundary that cares inspects it. It's the discipline exceptions promise ("handle errors at the right level") made mechanical: you can't forget an unhandled failure, because the moment one reaches a decision, it stops the show with its reason attached. That's the whole error system. No other constructs exist to learn.

Modules and Names Crow's module system is small — one keyword, use — but it sits on a rule most languages don't have: a bare name means exactly one thing, and collisions are compile errors, never silent . This chapter covers importing, aliasing, the reservation rule, and writing modules of your own.

Importing with use use brings a standard-library module's vocabulary into your file, bare: use math xs = [3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0] log[sum[xs]] log[mean[xs]] log[math.sum[xs]] log[pi] 14 2.8 14 3.141592653589793 After use math , its functions ( sum , mean , exp , zeros , transpose , …) and constants ( pi , e , inf , nan ) work without a prefix — and the prefixed form math.sum[...] always works too, if you prefer to read the source of a name at its callsite. Import several modules in one line: use web, ui . Submodules opt in separately: use math.stats adds median and friends without bloating plain use math . The standard modules are math (+ .stats , .nn ), frame , io , db , doc , bits , chart , llm , mcp , web (+ feature submodules), and ui ; the standard library's pages in Part II list each one's names. Only these get the bare-name privilege — everything else you import lives behind a prefix, as you'll see in the last section.

Aliased Imports Any import can take an alias — and an aliased import is qualified-only , exactly like Python's import pandas as pd . Nothing enters your bare namespace except the alias itself: use math as m sum = 0 for x in [1, 2, 3] sum = sum + x log[sum] log[m.sum[[10.0, 20.0]]] 6 30 Look at what happened there: with use math as m , the name sum stayed yours — the accumulator is an ordinary variable — while math's sum is reached as m.sum . The alias is the escape valve for exactly the moment when you and a module want the same word. Calling sum[...] bare in that file is a compile error that names the fix: use math as m --- error: 'sum' comes from math which was imported as 'm' — call m.sum[...] log[sum[[1.0, 2.0]]]

Names Are Never Ambiguous The rule behind everything in this chapter: a definition may not take a name the language or an import already owns. Not shadowing, not precedence — an error, at the definition line, with the fix included. --- error: 'range' is a core builtin — pick another name for this variable range = [10, 20, 30] use math --- error: 'sum' is provided by math (imported on line 1) — rename the --- variable, or import qualified: use math as m sum = 0 Why so strict? Because Crow's brackets serve both calling and indexing. In a language where range[0] could mean index my variable or call the builtin , silent shadowing produces silently wrong answers — delete the variable during a refactor and the same expression changes meaning without an error. Crow refuses the ambiguity at the source. What this costs you: an occasional rename ( total instead of sum , kind instead of type ) — the error always suggests one, and the alias form is there when you'd rather keep your word. What it buys: any bare name in any Crow file means one thing, for you, for readers, and for every AI assistant generating Crow. Four softenings keep it livable: Core is held — the ~75 always-reserved names grow only as a breaking change the changelog lists first, until 1.0, and not at all after it, so code that compiles on 1.0 can't be broken by a future builtin. Fields are exempt — row.type , account.sum , df.mean are always fine; reservation governs bare definitions, not the insides of your records. (Only ok / reason / kind / trace are off-limits as struct fields — every value already carries those.) Modules reserve only where imported — no use math , no reserved sum . Inside a view, the element wins. With use frame, math loaded, stack[...] in a view is the layout container, not frame.stack or math.stack ; the prefix ( frame.stack[a, b] ) still reaches the module version from inside a view.

Writing Your Own Modules A module is a .co file of functions, structs, and constants. Your modules are always qualified — importing one reserves a single bare name (the prefix), and everything inside is reached through it: --- geometry.co --- struct Circle [r] fn circle_area[c] return 3.14159 * c.r * c.r --- main.co --- use geometry c = geometry.Circle[2.0] log[geometry.circle_area[c]] Subdirectories map through slashes ( use myapp/utils → utils.helper[...] ) or dots, the same way ( use views.home loads views/home.co ), and aliases apply as everywhere ( use geometry as g → g.circle_area[...] ). The asymmetry with the standard library is deliberate: the bare namespace belongs to the language. Stdlib names are hand-curated and frozen-or-slow-moving; your module can export a thousand names and take none of anyone's vocabulary — the import costs exactly one word, the prefix. That's also why two modules can never collide: same trailing name, different aliases, done. The one name your module cannot take is a standard module's. A math.co beside a program that says use math would make the import mean two modules, so it is refused at the import, naming the file: rename it ( arith.co , then use arith ), or move it out of the project to import the standard math . Next: saying what a function must do — and having Crow prove it.

Testing In most languages, testing is a second discipline: a framework to install, a directory to arrange, fixtures to learn. In Crow, verification is part of writing a function. A test block right under a fn states what that function does — and what it can never do. Everything in it is ordinary Crow you already know: comparisons, if , error values, maps, structs. fn fee[notional] if notional lt 0 return error['negative notional', 'validation'] return max[1.0, notional * 0.001] test[n] fee[50000.0] eq 50.0 fee[100.0] eq 1.0 fee[-5.0].kind eq 'validation' if n gte 0.0 fee[n] gte 1.0 log['fee is defined'] fee is defined Notice what running that program printed: just the log line. Test blocks never execute when a program runs — crow run skips them, crow build strips them from the binary entirely. They run when you ask for verification: $ crow test pricing.co ✓ 1 block pass — 4 truths, 1 law, 5 inputs run Truths: bare booleans Each plain boolean line in a test block is a truth — something that must be so. The first three lines above are examples : exact facts at inputs you chose. fee[100.0] eq 1.0 records a decision (the fee floor is one dollar), and the .kind line pins the error path — error values are ordinary values (chapter 7), so verifying them needs nothing special. A truth under a precondition ( if n gte 0.0 , and the comparison inside it) is checked where the precondition holds. A block has to reach at least one truth or assert , in its body or in a function it calls. One that reaches none fails with asserts nothing : a test that cannot fail tests nothing, and a line that was meant as a truth but is not one (a call whose value nobody compares) would pass forever. When a truth fails, you see both sides: ⚠ 1 failing of 1 block pricing.co:5 fee tests — line 7: assert failed: eq left: 0.1 right: 1 Someone "simplified" fee and dropped the floor; the truth caught it with the actual values, not just a red X. A failing law — a line that reads the generated input — also names the input it failed at: (at n = -1) . Laws: generated inputs The block's parameter — test[n] — is not an argument anyone passes. It declares a generated input : the checker invents many values for n , boundary cases first, and checks the lines that use it against every one. fee[n] gte 1.0 is a law : true not at a point, but everywhere. The if n gte 0.0 line is doing honest work. Without it, the checker finds n = -1.0 — where fee returns an error, and errors have no truth value, so the law fails loudly. That failure is correct: the law as first written claimed too much. A precondition in a test block is just an if . Examples pin decisions; laws pin relationships. Most functions only need examples. Write a law when your domain hands you one — "doubling the quantity doubles the price", "encoding then decoding returns the original." Named tests: scenarios A test with a name stands alone — it isn't about one function, it's about functions working together. Setup, a sequence of calls, and assert at each step: fn restock[stock, item, n] if item in stock return set[stock, item, stock[item] + n] return set[stock, item, n] fn take[stock, item, n] if item not in stock return error['no `item` in stock', 'stock'] if stock[item] lt n return error['only `stock[item]` `item` left', 'stock'] return set[stock, item, stock[item] - n] test restock_then_take[] s = restock[map[], 'apples', 10] after = take[s, 'apples', 4] assert[after.apples eq 6] short = take[after, 'apples', 100] assert[not short.ok] assert[short.kind eq 'stock'] log['module loaded'] module loaded Inside scenarios you use assert for each step. assert is the one verification word that also ships in production — a runtime guard — which is exactly why the block keyword is test , not assert : one word runs in your program, the other never does. A scenario can open a database or a headless web session too; chapters 11 and 12 show both. A named test with parameters is a stateful law — test webhook_twice[fill] reads as "for any fill…" and the checker generates the fills. The one rule about where things live Verification never creates methods. A test body calls your real functions — that is what testing is — but you never define a function for a test. Bindings, sequences, conditions: they all live inside the block. If it's in the program's namespace, it's the program; if it's under test , it's the rules. The boundary is the syntax, so nobody has to police it. The verbs crow test runs the blocks you wrote. crow check runs those plus everything you didn't write: automatically generated edge cases for your pure functions, determinism contracts, and — with a database url — the concurrency hazard checks from the databases chapter. Tests are the part of verification you author; check is all of it. Next: put the last seven chapters to work on real data.

Project: Analyzing Data Time to put chapters 3–9 to work on Crow's home turf: tabular data. We'll take a small file of trades from raw CSV to a grouped summary — the whole loop of load, inspect, filter, sort, aggregate, report. The star is the frame : a column-oriented table with named, typed columns. Maps hold one type; structs hold one record; frames hold many records — the third point of the collections triangle from chapter 5. The Data We'll generate our data file right in the program so the example is self-contained (in real life this arrives from disk or a database): use frame, math csv = 'symbol,qty,price AAPL,100,191.5 MSFT,50,415.2 AAPL,40,193.1 NVDA,20,875.0 MSFT,25,411.9' write['trades.csv', csv] trades = frame.load['trades.csv'] log[trades.shape] log[trades.columns] rm['trades.csv'] [5, 3] ['symbol', 'qty', 'price'] One detail worth pausing on: we wrote frame.load , not bare load — because with both frame and math imported, two modules provide a load (frames from CSV; numeric tensors from CSV). Crow refuses the ambiguity, exactly as chapter 8 promised: use frame, math --- error: 'load' is ambiguous — provided by frame and math; use --- frame.load[...] or math.load[...] df = load['trades.csv'] Other Formats, Other Places A file's extension names its format. save writes a frame as CSV, as JSON records or as Parquet — the columnar format data tools share — and load reads each one back: use frame prices = frame.new[] prices.symbol = ['AAPL', 'MSFT'] prices.price = [191.5, 415.2] save[prices, 'ch10_prices.parquet'] back = frame.load['ch10_prices.parquet'] log[back.columns] log[back.symbol] save[prices, 'ch10_prices.json'] log[read['ch10_prices.json']] rm['ch10_prices.parquet'] rm['ch10_prices.json'] ['symbol', 'price'] ['AAPL', 'MSFT'] [{"price":191.5,"symbol":"AAPL"},{"price":415.2,"symbol":"MSFT"}] A path can also be a URL or an S3 object — wherever a program reads a file, it reads those the same way. A JSON API's answer that holds its rows in one list ( {"status": "OK", "results": [...]} ) loads as those rows, and an S3 bucket is reached with the credentials in the environment ( AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID , AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY , AWS_REGION ): use frame day = frame.load['https://data.example.com/aapl/2026-07-14.parquet'] archive = frame.load['s3://market-archive/2026/07/14/trades.csv'] save[day, 's3://reports/aapl-2026-07-14.parquet'] Filtering and Sorting Column access ( trades.qty ) plus a comparison gives a mask , and the frame's index applies it: trades[trades.qty gte 40] is the rows where it is true, as xs[mask] is a list's items. sort takes a column name, with desc as a named argument: use frame csv = 'symbol,qty,price AAPL,100,191.5 MSFT,50,415.2 AAPL,40,193.1 NVDA,20,875.0 MSFT,25,411.9' write['trades.csv', csv] trades = frame.load['trades.csv'] big = trades[trades.qty gte 40] log[len[big]] by_price = sort[trades, 'price', desc = true] log[by_price] rm['trades.csv'] 3 symbol qty price str int float ------ --- ----- NVDA 20 875 MSFT 50 415.2 MSFT 25 411.9 AAPL 40 193.1 AAPL 100 191.5 [5 rows x 3 cols] Frames print themselves as aligned tables with their column types — no formatting code required. Aggregating and Reporting Math reductions accept columns directly, fmt handles presentation, and group aggregates by key: use frame, math csv = 'symbol,qty,price AAPL,100,191.5 MSFT,50,415.2 AAPL,40,193.1 NVDA,20,875.0 MSFT,25,411.9' write['trades.csv', csv] trades = frame.load['trades.csv'] log['total shares: `sum[trades.qty]`'] avg_price = sum[trades.price] / 5.0 log['avg price: `fmt[avg_price, decimals = 2]`'] by_symbol = group[trades, 'symbol', ['qty', 'sum']] log[by_symbol] rm['trades.csv'] total shares: 235 avg price: 417.34 symbol qty_sum str int ------ ------- AAPL 140 MSFT 75 NVDA 20 [3 rows x 2 cols] Twenty-odd lines: load, validate shape, filter, sort, aggregate, format. Every piece was a chapter you've already read — frames just give the pieces something worth doing. Several Keys, Pivots and Windows group takes a list of keys for a row per combination; pivot lays one column's cells out as columns; and window computes a column over each row's partition — a running sum per symbol, the previous row's price — written into the frame under a name: use frame csv = 'symbol,day,qty,price AAPL,1,100,191.5 MSFT,1,50,415.2 AAPL,2,40,193.1 NVDA,1,20,875.0 MSFT,2,25,411.9' write['trades.csv', csv] trades = frame.load['trades.csv'] by_day = group[trades, ['symbol', 'day'], ['qty', 'sum']] log[by_day] wide = pivot[trades, 'symbol', 'day', 'qty'] log[wide] trades.so_far = window[trades, 'qty', 'sum', by = 'symbol'] trades.prev = window[trades, 'price', 'lag', n = 1, by = 'symbol'] log[trades] rm['trades.csv'] symbol day qty_sum str int int ------ --- ------- AAPL 1 100 MSFT 1 50 AAPL 2 40 NVDA 1 20 MSFT 2 25 [5 rows x 3 cols] symbol 1 2 str int int ------ --- ------- AAPL 100 40 MSFT 50 25 NVDA 20 missing [3 rows x 3 cols] symbol day qty price so_far prev str int int float int float ------ --- --- ----- ------ ------- AAPL 1 100 191.5 100 missing MSFT 1 50 415.2 50 missing AAPL 2 40 193.1 140 191.5 NVDA 1 20 875 20 missing MSFT 2 25 411.9 75 415.2 [5 rows x 6 cols] A pivot's cell is missing where no row has the pair (NVDA on day 2), and a pair two rows share stops the program, naming the group that would aggregate it first. A window's n is the trailing rows ( n = 3 for a three-row mean; 0, the default, for every row so far), and how is an aggregate group takes — sum , mean , min , max , count and the ones below — or lag , lead or rank . Keys, Time and Text The same verbs reach further: bucket floors each moment to a span, so a group over the bucket makes bars; group and window take median , a percentile, std , first , last and distinct beside sum and mean ; sort and join take several keys; where picks a cell by a mask; complete keeps the rows with no missing cell; unpivot makes a wide frame long; in tests a text column ( 'AA' in ticks.symbol ), and .hour reads a moment column's field — each over the whole column at once: use frame csv = 'symbol,at,qty,price AAPL,2026-07-14T09:30:00-04:00,100,191.5 MSFT,2026-07-14T09:31:00-04:00,50,415.2 AAPL,2026-07-14T09:35:00-04:00,,193.1 AAPL,2026-07-14T10:36:30-04:00,40,190.0 MSFT,2026-07-14T10:40:00-04:00,70,410.0' write['ticks.csv', csv] ticks = Working with Databases use db gives you SQL — real SQL, no ORM, no query builder. Connections are pooled handles, results come back as the frames you learned in chapter 10, and failures are the error values you learned in chapter 7. Nothing in this chapter is a new concept; it's the existing concepts meeting a database. Connect, Create, Insert use db conn = connect['sqlite://:memory:'] query[conn, 'CREATE TABLE trades (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, symbol TEXT, qty INTEGER, price REAL)'] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, ?, ?, ?)', ['AAPL', 100, 191.5]] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (2, ?, ?, ?)', ['MSFT', 50, 415.2]] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (3, ?, ?, ?)', ['AAPL', 40, 193.1]] rows = query[conn, 'SELECT symbol, qty FROM trades WHERE qty >= 50 ORDER BY id'] log[rows] symbol qty str int ------ --- AAPL 100 MSFT 50 [2 rows x 2 cols] Three things to notice: The connection string picks the backend — sqlite://:memory: here; a file path or postgres://user:pass@host/dbname in production. Your code doesn't change. ? placeholders bind values from an array — never interpolate user input into SQL text. The bind array is positional open data , one of the few places a mixed-type array literal is exactly right. SQL strings are SQL. Crow strings are inert, so >= , quotes, and % wildcards need no escaping — and it's >= in there, not gte ; the database speaks its own language. query returns a frame — everything from chapter 10 (masks, sort, columns, sum ) applies to results directly. It is the one verb for every statement: a CREATE or an UPDATE answers an empty frame, and a write that must say what it touched reads it back with RETURNING . Whether a call reads or writes is the statement's to say, not the name's: use db conn = connect['sqlite://:memory:'] query[conn, 'CREATE TABLE trades (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, symbol TEXT, qty INTEGER)'] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, ?, ?)', ['AAPL', 100]] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (2, ?, ?)', ['MSFT', 50]] touched = query[conn, 'UPDATE trades SET qty = qty + 10 WHERE symbol = ? RETURNING id', ['AAPL']] log[len[touched]] 1 Failure Is a Value Here Too A bad query doesn't crash and doesn't throw — it hands you chapter 7: use db conn = connect['sqlite://:memory:'] bad = query[conn, 'SELECT nope FROM missing_table'] log[bad.ok] log[bad.reason] log[bad.kind] false no such table: missing_table db Check .ok at this boundary (databases are exactly the kind of boundary chapter 7 meant), branch on .kind eq 'db' if you handle database failures specially, and let success flow. Transactions transact[conn, fn] runs a named function inside a transaction — commit if it completes, roll back everything if it fails. All-or-nothing transfers, the classic: use db conn = connect['sqlite://:memory:'] query[conn, 'CREATE TABLE accounts (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, balance INTEGER)'] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (?, ?)', ['alice', 100]] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (?, ?)', ['bob', 50]] fn transfer[tx] query[tx, 'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE name = ?', ['alice']] query[tx, 'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 30 WHERE name = ?', ['bob']] transact[conn, transfer] log[query[conn, 'SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY name']] name balance str int ----- ------- alice 70 bob 80 [2 rows x 2 cols] The function receives a transaction handle tx and uses the same query on it — passed by name, like every callback in Crow. That's the whole database API: connect , query , insert , transact and describe . Migrations are the tool's: crow db apply <dir> <url> runs the .sql files a directory holds that the database has not seen. Letting the Checker Read Your Schema There's a class of database bug that no amount of testing on your laptop will find, because it only exists when two copies of your program run at once. Here's the classic — enforcing "at most one active trade per symbol" with an if : use db conn = connect['sqlite://:memory:'] query[conn, 'CREATE TABLE trades (symbol TEXT, qty INT, status TEXT)'] sym = 'AAPL' open_trades = query[conn, 'SELECT symbol FROM trades WHERE symbol = ? AND status = ?', [sym, 'active']] if len[open_trades] eq 0 query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades (symbol, qty, status) VALUES (?, ?, ?)', [sym, 100, 'active']] after = query[conn, 'SELECT symbol FROM trades'] log[len[after]] 1 Runs perfectly. Ships. Then one day two copies run at the same moment: both query, both see zero rows, both insert — two active trades, and the if never lied, it just couldn't hold between two programs. Point crow check at your development database and it reads both sides of the story — your code's assumptions and the schema's actual guarantees: crow check trading.co --db 'sqlite://dev.db' trading.co:7-9 — two programs can pass this check at the same time what can happen: 1. program A runs the query (line 7) — the check passes 2. program B runs the same query — the check passes too (A hasn't written yet) 3. A writes (line 9). 4. B writes. 5. the rule the check was protecting is now broken the database has no rule saying 'at most one active trades row per symbol', so this if is the only guard — and an if cannot hold between two programs. fixes, safest first: [1] let the database enforce it — generates migrations/one_active_per_symbol.sql: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_per_symbol ON trades(symbol) WHERE status = 'active'; crow fix trading.co --hazard 1 --option 1 --db 'sqlite://dev.db' applies the first option: writes the migration, applies it to the dev database, and re-checks to confirm the hazard is gone (with the database in the crowfile, below, --db can go). After that, the losing program's insert comes back as an ordinary error value with kind = 'conflict' — loud, at the moment it matters, instead of a silent duplicate. The catalog goes well beyond this one shape — lost updates, one-way status flags, single-row reads on non-unique columns, un-transacted write pairs, plus schema verification (column typos get did-you-mean suggestions). Put db = 'sqlite://dev.db' in your crowfile and every crow check — and the editor, through crow lsp — runs them. The full reference is docs/crow-check.md . A list is a parameter too An array bound as a parameter expands to a list, so WHERE id IN ? takes [[1, 3]] and never needs the ids pasted into the query text: use db conn = db.connect['sqlite://:memory:'] query[conn, 'CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, name TEXT)'] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, ?)', ['ann']] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO t VALUES (2, ?)', ['bob']] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO t VALUES (3, ?)', ['cat']] picked = query[conn, 'SELECT name FROM t WHERE id IN ? ORDER BY id', [[1, 3]]] log[picked.name] ['ann', 'cat'] Your tables are the ones your program makes The CREATE TABLE statements your program runs are its schema. Each literal one it hands a connection declares that table, and opening the connection checks the tables the database already has against them: use db book = connect['sqlite://board.db'] query[book, 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cards (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, due TEXT)'] Add due to that statement after board.db was made without it, and CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS alone would do nothing: the first query that reads due would fail. Run from its source ( crow run , crow run -i , crow test ), the program reconciles instead: the connection opens, finds cards without due , and adds it, under a lock so two processes starting at once add it once. What it cannot add without guessing — a NOT NULL column with no default on a table that has rows, a column of another kind than the database holds — stops the program with the SQL that would make it. A program crow build makes verifies : it changes nothing, reads the catalog, and stops at connect if a table lacks a column the program declares, printing the statement that would mend it — the database in production is someone else's to change. crow db diff prints every such statement as a migration to review, with what reconciling would not make commented out: $ crow db diff app.co -- sqlite://board.db (book) -- table 'cards' lacks column 'due' ALTER TABLE "cards" ADD COLUMN due TEXT; schema = 'verify' in the crowfile (or 'reconcile' , or 'trust' , which checks nothing and says so at every start) changes the mode for both; CROW_SCHEMA=trust changes it for one run. A table your program does not make is not its to check. The compiler asks your database A query's result is a frame, and a frame's cells are typed by the database: an integer column reads as an int, a numeric one as a float, and a column that can hold NULL has cells that can be missing. Before the program runs — under crow run , crow run -i , crow build , crow test and crow check alike — Crow asks the databases your program connects to what each literal query returns — a prepared statement on Postgres, a DESCRIBE on ClickHouse — and types the cells the same way in both modes. A ? placeholder and an interpolated span stand in as NULL for the question. What each database answers is kept in the project's .crow/schema , so when a database cannot be reached — a server down, a machine without the data — the build says so once and types the cells from that record; with no record, that query's cells are dynamic, read with int[…] , float[…] or str[…] . CROW_NO_DESCRIBE=1 skips the question: the record types the cells, and nothing is written. Next: the web layer, where these frames become pages.

Building Web UIs Crow's web story is the LiveView model: your UI logic lives on the server, in Crow; the browser renders HTML and streams events back over a WebSocket; state changes re-render automatically. No JavaScript build step, no client framework, no API layer between your data and your page — the dashboard in chapter 13 is one file. Three pieces: view blocks describe the page, reactive state makes it live, components make it composable. Then what every real app needs — slow work that doesn't freeze the page, tests that drive the page without a browser, and charts and styling that look right without writing CSS — and last the rest of the element vocabulary and derivations, the values a page computes from what it holds.

View Blocks A view is a declaration — fn 's sibling — whose body builds a UI tree. Inside a view, the standard HTML vocabulary is active as functions: use web, ui view render[] return div[ h1['Market Overview'], p['All systems operational.'], ul[ li['AAPL'], li['MSFT'], li['NVDA'] ] ] serve[3000] page['/', render] Run it and open localhost:3000 — a server, a page, no other files. page[path, view] serves the view at that path; serve[port] starts the app (the runtime manages the app object; you never thread one through). Elements nest by nesting calls — the tree you write is the tree you get. Attributes are named arguments: a['docs', href = '/docs'] , div[..., class = 'card'] . Tables that respond table[frame] shows a frame. Give it a handler and it becomes a control: click = focus sends the clicked row's key column to fn focus[symbol] , key = 'symbol' says which column that is, and mark = 'gate' tints the rows whose gate cell is true. A list of records usually wants a button or two per row: actions = map[Replay = replay, Delete = ask_delete] puts them in a trailing cell, each sending the row's key to its handler, and hide = ['id'] keeps the key column in the frame but out of the table. The scanner and the session history in the final project are these. A view renders wherever it is called A view is not tied to page[] . Call it from a test block, from a loop that writes pages to disk, or from another view, and it returns its markup. Hand that markup to document[] from use doc (Crow by Example, and the standard library reference in Part II) and you have a complete page without a server — the book you are reading is built exactly this way. Two rules make this safe: Text is text. Markup is what a view, an element or doc makes, and it stays markup however it travels — held in a local, collected by a for , handed to another view. Every other string is text and is escaped, whatever it holds: a reader who types into a field sees those characters, on their page and on everyone else's, and nothing runs. A failed argument renders, it does not propagate. Elements render what they are given (chapter 12.5), and so does a view: an error value handed to a view shows as error: the server's log has why, as in place of the tree — the reader is told an id, the server's log has the reason. A page with one unreadable chapter is still a page. use web, ui, doc view card[title, body] return stack[h3[title], p[body], surface = 'card'] markup = doc.document['Card', card['Hello', 'a paragraph']] log['

Reactive State and Events Top-level variables in a ui program are reactive state , and every reader's page holds its own copy. Views read them; event handlers change them; every change re-renders that reader's page. Here is the whole loop: use web, ui count = 0 fn inc[] count = count + 1 fn dec[] count = count - 1 view render[] return div[ h1['Count: `count`'], button['+', click = inc], button['-', click = dec] ] serve[3000] page['/', render] Click + : inc runs on the server , count changes, and the page shows the new value. A second tab has a count of its own — each page is its own session, and what pages share is the database (the two-users example in the testing chapter shows both). You wrote no JavaScript, no fetch calls, no socket code. Events bind by name — click = inc — the functions-as-values idea from chapter 4, never a lambda. And notice what count is: the one sanctioned exception to scope isolation. Ordinary functions still can't touch it; views and handlers can, because the runtime owns it, synchronizes it, and knows when it changed. It's not ambient mutation — it's a managed channel. Data sources compose the same way: prices = poll['/api/prices', 5] declares state that refreshes every five seconds and re-renders whatever reads it. The records arrive as a frame with the columns the page reads of them — prices.px added up is a column of numbers — and are checked where they arrive, in both modes: a column missing or of another kind stops the session with the column, what it holds and the read that asked. State gets its value once, where it is declared: count = 0 is what every session starts from, and handlers move it from there. The top level does not change it afterwards — a second count = 1 , or a loop at the top level that pushes into a list of state, is refused and told why, since no session and no test would see the change. Give the state its whole value where it is declared (a function can loop to build it), or make it a derive . A script that imports a ui part but not ui itself keeps its own top-level variables plain, and runs top to bottom. The page and its connection The browser holds a socket to the server, and the server holds your session. Several things follow. A dropped connection says so, and your session waits for you. When the socket closes — the laptop slept, the network dropped — the page dims, shows reconnecting… and takes no clicks until it is back. The server keeps your session for ten minutes: when the tab reconnects (or you reload it) you are back where you were, a replay still running, sent the page's render first so you never click on a page the server no longer holds. A second tab is a session of its own. serve[…, keep = true] keeps sessions across a restart of the program too — what a rebuild would otherwise throw away. crow dev reloads the program as you edit it. It serves the program with the interpreter, checks each change you save, and restarts it when the change is good: every open tab reconnects and resumes its session, drawn by the new code, so the page you were testing stays where it was. A change that breaks the program leaves the last good one serving, and the page shows the refusal with its file and line until you mend it. A change to css/app.css reloads the tabs. Ctrl+Shift+D opens the dev panel: the session's facts, each event with the facts it changed and how long its render took, and the renders' timing. A render sends what changed. After the first page, the server sends the page only what a render changed — a text, an attribute, a row added or gone — not the page again. A chart whose play-head moves is sent the play-head, a few bytes, not the drawing; a list whose items carry an id gains one row when one item is added at its top. The server sends the whole page when that is smaller, and when your markup is one the browser would have to repair — a div inside a p , a row outside a table — and it says so in the log, once, so you can fix the markup. A field you are typing in keeps what you typed while the page around it changes. A click shows it was taken. The element you press is marked busy ( data-crow-busy ) the instant you press it, and unmarked when the server's answer to that click arrives — over a slow network the page still shows the click in the same frame. A page can send only what it was offered. The server accepts a click only when a render it sent carried that handler with exactly those arguments — button['10x', click = set_speed[10.0]] offers set_speed with 10.0 and nothing else — and a bound value only for an input it drew. A handler no button names, a helper, a variable no input binds, and the button of a closed modal are refused and logged, so a confirmation's second step cannot be sent without its first. The socket opens only from the app's own page, and a served app listens on this machine only; set CROW_HOST=0.0.0.0 when a server must be reachable from the network. A click is one transaction A handler's writes land together when it ends, or not at all. It works on its own copy of the session's facts — a render never sees it halfway — and its database writes are one transaction, committed with it. When an error reaches a decision, a fact or a database write, the handler stops : nothing it did lands, and the reader is told so through the session's notice — that it stopped, that nothing changed, and an id.
