Why is in the server's log beside that id, and is the click's value in a test: use web, ui saved = 0 fn save[] saved = saved + 1 notice['saved `saved`'] fn broken[] saved = saved + 100 px = float['no quote'] if px gt 1.0 saved = 0 view panel[] return stack[ p['saved `saved`'], p['`notice.text`'], button['Save', click = save], button['Broken', click = broken] ] test one_transaction[] a = app[panel] click[a, save] assert[a.saved eq 1] assert['saved 1' in html[a]] r = click[a, broken] assert[not r.ok] assert[a.saved eq 1] assert['cannot convert' in r.reason] assert['broken stopped, and nothing changed' in html[a]] page['/', panel] log['panel defined'] panel defined notice[text] waits for the commit, so a handler that stops never says it succeeded. notice.text and notice.at read the latest one; a page that shows no notice of its own gets the runtime's toast, which fades by itself. While a handler runs, the button that started it is disabled and marked busy, and running[save] is true — the page shows the work without a flag in your program. Inside one click now[] is one moment, however many times it is read. The address and the questions Two things every app ends up building by hand come with the page. The address can carry facts — page['/', render, url = ['day']] starts a session from /?day=2026-09-04 and keeps the address in step as day changes, so a reload or a shared link opens the same view. And a click can ask first: use web, ui ended = 0 fn end_session[] ended = ended + 1 view panel[] return stack[ p['ended `ended`'], button['End session', click = end_session, confirm = 'End this session?'] ] test the_button_asks_first[] a = app[panel] b = elements[a, 'button'][0] assert[b['data-crow-click'] eq '__ask'] click[a, end_session] assert[a.ended eq 1] page['/', panel, url = ['ended']] log['panel defined'] panel defined The button offers the question, not the handler: the runtime shows the dialog, and only its Confirm button reaches end_session , so the step cannot be skipped by sending the click directly. On a table the questions sit beside the actions: actions = map[Delete = delete_session], confirm = map[Delete = 'Delete this session?'] . In a test click[a, end_session] runs the handler itself — the question is the page's, not the program's. Keys and forms A key presses a button. shortcut names the keys, and the button keeps its one handler: use web, ui saved = 0 added = 0 helping = false note = '' fn save[] saved = saved + 1 fn show[] helping = true fn hide[] helping = false fn add[] added = added + 1 view desk[] return stack[ p['saved `saved` added `added`'], button['Save', click = save, shortcut = 'ctrl+s meta+s'], button['Help', click = show, shortcut = '?'], modal[stack[p['Press ? for this help.'], button['Close', click = hide, shortcut = 'escape']], open = helping], form[field['Note', note, type = 'text'], button['Add'], submit = add] ] test the_keys_are_the_buttons[] a = app[desk] b = elements[a, 'button'][0] assert[b['aria-keyshortcuts'] eq 'Control+S Meta+S'] click[a, add] assert[a.added eq 1] page['/', desk] log['desk defined'] desk defined Ctrl+S, or Command+S on a Mac, presses Save as a click would; ? opens the help and Escape closes it. A key works only while its button is on the page and can be pressed, so it reaches nothing the reader could not click. While the reader types in the Note field the keys are theirs: a ? typed there is a question mark. Enter in the field presses the form's first button, and the form's submit = add runs add once; a form never reloads the page. A shortcut that names no key, or sits on something a press does nothing to, is refused before the program runs. The keyboard reaches everything a click does. A card or a table row with a click is a tab stop that Enter presses; when the help opens, focus moves into it and Tab stays inside, and when it closes focus goes back to the Help button. A field's label names its input for a screen reader, and an img must say what it shows ( alt = 'the logo' , or alt = '' when it only decorates). Pages, their addresses and their titles An app serves every page it registers, in both modes, and each page is a session of its own. A :name segment of a page's path is a fact in its address, the way url = […] puts facts in the query string: use web, ui card = 1 fn next_card[] card = card + 1 view board[] return stack[ title['Cards'], nav[a['Card 1', href = '/card/1'], a['Card 2', href = '/card/2']] ] view card_page[] return stack[ title['Card `card`'], meta[name = 'description', content = 'The card numbered `card`'], p['card `card`'], button['Next', click = next_card] ] test a_card_names_itself[] a = app[card_page] click[a, next_card] assert[elements[a, 'title'][0].text eq 'Card 2'] page['/', board] page['/card/:card', card_page] log['two pages'] two pages /card/7 opens a session with card set to 7 , read in the fact's shape, and when Next makes it 8 the address becomes /card/8 , so a reload or a shared link opens that card. A value the fact cannot hold, /card/x , is no page: a 404, as is an address no page or route answers. The path says which thing the page shows; the query string ( url = […] ) tunes how, and a page can have both. A :name must name a fact, or the program is refused before it runs. A link is an a with an href , alone or in a nav . Following one opens the session of the address it names, even to the page you are on: a link to /?day=tue from /?day=mon starts from Tuesday. Reloading the tab, or coming back with the browser's back button, resumes the tab's own session. title and meta are the page's head. They take no room on the page: the tab shows the title, and a render that changes it changes the tab. The last title a page places wins, so a layout's default gives way to the page's own, and a page that places none is titled Crow App . In a test they are elements of the render, as above. Who the reader is A page knows who is reading it through reader : a map of strings, empty until someone signs in. A handler signs the reader in with sign_in[record] and out with sign_out[] . Passwords are stored with hash[password, 'password'] — salted and deliberately slow — and checked by hashing the attempt the way the stored one was made: use web, ui, db book = db.connect['sqlite://:memory:'] name = '' password = '' fn setup[] query[book, 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS people (name TEXT, role TEXT, hash TEXT)'] query[book, 'INSERT INTO people VALUES (?, ?, ?)', ['ada', 'admin', hash['lovelace', 'password']]] fn log_in[] found = query[book, 'SELECT role, hash FROM people WHERE name = ?', [name]] if len[found] eq 0 notice['no one called `name`'] return if hash[password, found.hash[0]] ne found.hash[0] notice['wrong password'] return sign_in[map[name = name, role = found.role[0]]] fn log_out[] sign_out[] derive greeting if 'name' in reader return 'hello `reader.name`' return 'hello stranger' view door[] return stack[ p[greeting], field['Name', name, type = 'text'], field['Password', password, type = 'password'], button['Log in', click = log_in], button['Log out', click = log_out] ] test ada_signs_in_and_out[] a = app[door] click[a, setup] change[a, 'name', 'ada'] change[a, 'password', 'lovelace'] click[a, log_in] assert[reader.role eq 'admin'] assert[elements[a, 'p'][0].text eq 'hello ada'] click[a, log_out] assert[len[reader] eq 0] page['/', door] log['door defined'] door defined Signing in gives the browser a cookie, so the reader is signed in on every page and tab they open next, and after a restart, for thirty days. Signing out clears it and ends that sign-in everywhere: another tab still open is signed out at once, and the old cookie is refused if it ever comes back. The program never touches the cookie, and nothing on the page can write reader — no field binds it, no handler assigns it. Deciding who may do what is ordinary code in the handler: if reader.role ne 'admin' . A signed-out reader has no role , and reading it is an error that stops the handler, so a forgotten check fails closed. In a test, change[a, 'reader', map[name = 'bob', role = 'member']] stands for someone who signed in, without a password. The cookie is signed with the app's secret — CROW_SECRET , or a key the runtime writes to .crow/keys/ the first time it needs one. A page only signed-in readers may see checks reader in its view, and draws the sign-in form until someone signs in: use web, ui name = '' refunded = 0 fn log_in[] sign_in[map[name = name]] fn refund[] refunded = refunded + 1 view sign_in_form[] return stack[ field['Name', name, type = 'text'], button['Log in', click = log_in] ] view orders[] if 'name' not in reader return sign_in_form[] return stack[ p['orders for `reader.name`, `refunded` refunded'], button['Refund', click = refund] ] test the_orders_wait_for_a_sign_in[] a = app[orders] assert[len[elements[a, 'button']] eq 1] change[a, 'reader', map[name = 'ada']] assert[elements[a, 'p'][0].text eq 'orders for ada, 0 refunded'] page['/orders', orders] log['orders defined'] orders defined Nothing else of the page reaches a signed-out reader. The page answers only the buttons its render drew, so refund can't be pressed, not even by a message written by hand, and a query the orders view reads never runs for them. When log_in succeeds, the same page, at the same address, shows the orders. Files, and tables too big to show A file is an input: field['Trades', upload, type = 'file'] binds upload , declared upload = map[] . When the reader picks a file the page sends it, and upload holds its name , type , size and the path of the server's copy — read it like any file. The other way, download[value, name] hands the reader's browser a file when the handler commits: a frame as CSV, a string as text. And a table that could grow past a screen pages: table[frame, page = 50] draws fifty rows at a time, with the count and the previous and next pages under it. sort = true lets the reader sort it: each header becomes a button that orders the rows by its column, ascending and then descending. use web, ui, frame upload = map[] derive trades if 'path' in upload return frame.load[upload.path] return frame.new[] fn export[] download[trades, 'trades.csv'] view desk[] return stack[ field['Trades', upload, type = 'file'], table[trades, page = 50, sort = true], button['Export', click = export] ] test a_file_in_and_out[] write['desk_trades.csv', 'symbol,qty
IMRN,100
FFIE,300
'] a = app[desk] change[a, 'upload', map[name = 'trades.csv', type = 'text/csv', size = '29', path = 'desk_trades.csv']] assert[len[elements[a, 'tbody tr']] eq 2] assert[elements[a, 'th button'][0].text eq 'symbol'] click[a, export] assert[downloads[a][0].name eq 'trades.csv'] assert['IMRN,100' in downloads[a][0].text] page['/', desk] log['desk defined'] desk defined The file travels beside the page's connection, never through it, and a file bigger than the app allows — 10 MB, or serve[…, uploads = 50] in megabytes — is refused before it is sent, with the limit named. The server's copy belongs to the session and goes when the session does; a handler that wants to keep it copies it. A table of more than 1,000 rows without page is refused in place, as an over-budget chart is: the page says how many rows there are and how to page them, rather than quietly cutting some off. The session keeps each table's page and its order, and the frame stays as it was: sorting the program's own data is sort[df, 'col'] . Mail mail[mailer, to, subject, body] sends a plain-text message through a mailer that smtp[host, port, user, pass] makes once for the whole program, as a connection is made. Like notice and download it is an effect held to the handler's commit, so a handler that stops sends nothing, and a function a handler calls holds its messages for that handler. A handler that must know whether the server took a message reads the answer: sent = mail[…] is sent at once, and sent.ok says. A test sends nothing: mails[a] is what the session sent. use web, ui use web.mail mailer = smtp['smtp.example.com', 587, 'desk@example.com', 'app-password'] email = '' fn subscribe[] mail[mailer, email, 'Subscribed', 'You will hear from the desk.'] notice['subscribed `email`'] view signup[] return stack[field['Email', email], button['Subscribe', click = subscribe]] test a_subscription_sends_one_message[] a = app[signup] change[a, 'email', 'ada@example.com'] click[a, subscribe] assert[len[mails[a]] eq 1] assert[mails[a][0].to eq 'ada@example.com'] page['/', signup] log['signup defined'] signup defined A mailer prints as its host, never its password. Sliders, helpers, and bigger state slider['Seek %', seek_pct, min = 0, max = 100, step = 1] binds a range input to seek_pct the way field binds a text input; a Seek button's handler then reads it. Bound inputs keep the variable's type: the browser sends text, and an integer variable receives an integer. When a handler assigns to a bound variable (a row click that sets sym ), the field shows the new value on the next render. A handler may call a helper that assigns module state — fn restart[] calling fn rewind_to[t] — and the helper joins the handler class in both renderers, so its write lands in state. And state is not only numbers and strings: an array, a map, a record, or a whole frame can be reactive, each kept as the value it is, and written as JSON only where it leaves the program — a test's harness, a bound input, a session kept across a restart. The following block is verified by the book's tests: use web, ui, frame seek_pct = 50 focus = '' universe = frame.new[] fn pick[symbol] focus = symbol fn keep[u] universe = u fn load_universe[] u = frame.new[symbol = ['IMRN', 'AOUT', 'CHPT']] u.gate = [1, 0, 1] keep[u] view render[] return stack[ slider['Seek', seek_pct, min = 0, max = 100, step = 5], p['focus: `focus`'], table[universe, click = pick, key = 'symbol', mark = 'gate'], button['Load', click = load_universe], gap = 'm' ] test rows[] s = app[render, width = 1280] click[s, load_universe] h = html[s] assert['type="range"' in h] assert['data-crow-click="pick"' in h] assert['class="marked"' in h] assert[len[elements[s, 'tr']] eq 4] click[s, pick['AOUT']] assert[s.focus eq 'AOUT'] assert[fits[s, 390]] page['/', render] log['reactive page defined'] reactive page defined

Components A view that takes parameters is a component. Views call views; the tree composes: use web, ui view stat_card[label, value] return div[ h3[label], p['`value`'], class = 'card' ] view render[] return div[ h1['Dashboard'], stat_card['Trades today', 128], stat_card['Open positions', 7] ] serve[3000] page['/', render] Package components in a module and they arrive qualified, like every module export ( use cards as c → c.stat_card[...] ) — your component library takes one name from the file that imports it, exactly per chapter 8's rules. The lowercase element vocabulary itself never grows and never varies: elements are the language's, components are yours, and a reader can always tell which is which at a glance. That's the whole UI model. What remains is to use it on something real.

t: Slow Work and the Live Loop
x: Slow Work and the Live Loop A live Crow app serves every reader's page from the server, and each page has its own loop: a click runs a handler, then the page renders again. Two kinds of slow work can get in its way — a query a view needs, and a handler that takes a while — and Crow treats them differently. Slow data is the runtime's job A derivation that queries a database is computed off the render. When its value is stale, the page renders at once with the value it has, and renders again when the new value lands; a view still catching up with something the reader did is dimmed after a moment, so the reader can see that part is catching up. One that is only behind a moving clock is not dimmed: it is always one query behind while the clock plays. A click never waits for a query it did not cause. A query it did cause — the rows its own handler just inserted — is part of its answer: use web, ui, db book = db.connect['sqlite://book.db'] sym = 'IMRN' derive trades return query[book, 'SELECT id, px FROM trades WHERE symbol = ?', [sym]] fn buy[] query[book, 'INSERT INTO trades (symbol, px) VALUES (?, ?)', [sym, 1.79]] view render[] return stack[table[trades], button['Buy', click = buy]] page['/', render] serve[3000] Pressing Buy answers with the new row already in the table: the handler wrote trades , so the derivation over it is recomputed before that render. Changing sym answers at once with the old rows, dimmed, and the new ones arrive a query later. You wrote nothing for either. Before its first value, a derivation that queries reads as an error of kind 'pending' with the reason loading — a view that renders a failed read in place shows error: loading , and the page appears at once instead of waiting for its slowest query. running[trades] is true while it recomputes, for a spinner of your own. Nothing one reader does holds another. Handlers and renders run on worker threads, never on the threads that carry the sockets; database handles are pools; a derivation shared by every page is computed once, however many pages ask for it together. And a write reaches every reader: when one page inserts a row, every other page that read that table renders again with it. Slow handlers A handler runs off the page's loop too. While it works the page stays live — the clock ticks, landed values render — and the button that started it shows it is working, disabled, with nothing written in the program for it: use web, ui status = 'ready' fn load_book[] sleep[2] --- stand-in for the slow part: a remote query, status = 'updated' --- a model load, a shell call… fn refresh[] load_book[] view render[] return div[h1['Live book'], p['`status`'], button['refresh', click = refresh]] page['/', render] serve[3000] Click refresh: for two seconds the button is disabled and marked busy, and the rest of the page carries on. What waits is the session's other clicks — events are applied one at a time, in order, so a second click lands after the first handler ends, and a second click on the running handler is dropped as the double-click it is. crow check points this out — the blocking in view finding — because when the reader should be free to keep clicking while the work runs, there is a verb for it. later: the kitchen later[fn] runs a named fn off the loop and returns immediately. The fn does its slow work in the background; the reactive state it writes is applied back on the loop, one schedule at a time, and the page re-renders when the results land: fn refresh[] status = 'loading' later[load_book] The click now takes a millisecond: refresh sets status , schedules load_book , and returns — your screen shows "loading" instantly, and the reader can go on clicking. Two seconds later the work finishes, status updates, and the page re-renders. Think of the loop as a waiter and later as handing the slow order to the kitchen: the waiter keeps waiting tables, and the dish comes out when it's ready. The schedule is made when refresh commits — a handler that stops never leaves work running. Three rules make this safe, and you get all of them without writing anything: State is the only mailbox. The background fn communicates by writing reactive state — no return values, no callbacks, no await . Its writes are applied between renders, serially, so a view never sees half-finished state. Impatience is harmless. A second later[load_book] while the first is still running is not stacked: load_book runs once more when the first ends, from the state as it then stands, however many asked meanwhile. Hammering the refresh button cannot stack five queries, and the last ask is never lost. Failure stops it cleanly. If a query inside the fn fails at a decision, the fn stops as a handler does: nothing it wrote lands, the page keeps its last good values, and the notice says why. For the impatient-user experience there's running[fn] , true while a schedule is in flight — disable the button, show a spinner: view render[] label = 'refresh' if running[load_book] label = 'loading…' return div[p['`status`'], button[label, click = refresh]] later in scripts The same verb works outside the web layer, because scripts have loops too — a poll loop that must tick on schedule shouldn't stall while one slow batch processes. In a script, extra arguments are captured by value and passed to the fn, and the program waits for background work to finish before exiting: fn announce[msg] log[msg] later[announce, 'report ready'] report ready One honest subtlety: in the interpreter ( crow run -i , crow test ), later runs the work immediately, inline . That's not a parity break — later promises the work happens eventually and its writes apply atomically , and "immediately" is a perfectly legal schedule. Tests get deterministic behavior; the compiled app gets true background threads. Periodic freshness Some pages shouldn't wait for a click at all — a dashboard should just stay current. That's not a loop you write; it's a property you declare on serve : use web, ui status = 'ready' view render[] return div[h1['Board'], p['`status`']] page['/', render] serve[3000, refresh = 5, budget = 50] refresh = 5 re-renders every connected session every five seconds — a derivation over the clock, or over a table something else writes, is computed again (chapter 12.8), so the page tracks the database with zero lines of update code. If a render is slow, missed ticks are skipped , never stacked. And budget = 50 is the loop's own heartbeat: any handler or render over 50ms gets logged with its name, so a freezing loop is loud in development instead of mysterious in production. There is no every[] and no timer in Crow, deliberately: hand-rolled poll loops always end up needing an overlap guard, backoff, and shutdown handling, and every codebase writes them badly once first. The runtime owns the clock. What later is not later is for responsiveness ; for is for throughput . Crunching a million rows is already parallel — that's chapter 6. later exists so an interaction never waits on slow work: remote queries, shell calls, model loads. And later is in-process, best-effort: if the process dies mid-flight, that work is gone. Refreshing a panel can be redone; placing an order cannot. Work that must survive a crash belongs in a durable queue — a design on Crow's roadmap, not a property of later . The checker knows this chapter crow check detects the frozen version statically — a handler that reaches a call that waits ( sleep , shell , input , a socket's recv ) through any chain of calls gets flagged with the path, and the interactive loop can apply the fix for you (a view that reaches one is refused before the program runs): [1/1] scanner.co:14 in refresh 'refresh' holds the session's other clicks until it ends — sleep[] blocks it (refresh → score_board → sleep) fix: schedule it off the loop: later[score_board] enter = recheck, s = skip, f = fix (later[]), q = quit > f rewrote scanner.co: score_board[] → later[score_board] — rechecking... ✓ all good Slow work scheduled through later is the sanctioned home for blocking calls — the checker never flags it.

Testing a Live App A view is a function from reactive state to a tree. That one fact is why Crow's UI tests need no browser, no driver, and no fixtures: render the tree, run a handler, render again, and state truths about what you see. UI tests are ordinary named test blocks (chapter 9), run by crow test , stripped from every build. Both crow run app.co (compiled) and crow run -i app.co (the interpreter, with no compile between an edit and the page) serve it, and they serve the same page: crow test --served drives a set of pages in both modes with the same clicks and compares what they settle on. The harness Its verbs, valid only inside test blocks: Verb What it does s = app[view] opens a headless session that renders view against the program's reactive state click[s, handler] runs an event handler on the session — the same thing a button click does (deferred calls too: click[s, set_speed[10.0]] ) change[s, 'var', value] what typing into a bound field does: sets the reactive variable, so the next render and the next handler see it html[s] the rendered view as one HTML string — for "does the page say ready " elements[s, selector] the rendered elements matching a selector, in document order, as records — for where and what things are box[s, selector] the layout engine's boxes for matching elements — x y width height overflow — at the session's viewport ( app[view, width = 390] ) style[s, selector] resolved colour and type tokens — background color size weight fits[s, width] true when nothing overflows at that width Reactive state reads as fields of the session: s.status , s.min_qty , and a derivation as that session sees it: len[s.orders] . A selector is a tag ( 'button' ), a class ( '.card' ), both ( 'div.stats' ), or a space-separated chain that must nest ( 'div.controls button' ). Each record has tag , text , and class , plus every attribute the element carries — href , name , src — as a key. Behaviour: a click changes state use web, ui status = 'ready' count = 0 fn slow_refresh[] count = count + 1 status = 'updated' fn go[] status = 'loading' later[slow_refresh] view render[] return div[h1['Live book'], p['status: `status` count: `count`'], button['refresh', click = go]] test refresh_flow[] s = app[render] assert['ready' in html[s]] click[s, go] assert[s.status eq 'updated'] assert['count: 1' in html[s]] page['/', render] serve[3000] The later[] call is the interesting part. In production it schedules slow_refresh off the live loop; in a test it runs inline, so the line after click already sees the final state. Background work is deterministic in tests and concurrent in production — the same code, verified without waiting or flakiness. Structure, attributes, and two-way binding html[s] is one string. For where things are — the button inside the controls panel, two cards in the stats row, the heading first — ask for elements. For what a link points at, read its attribute. For typing into a bound field, change the variable it is bound to: use web, ui min_qty = 0 fn reset[] min_qty = 0 view panel[] return div[ h1['Trades'], a['docs', href = '/docs'], div[field['Min qty', min_qty], button['Reset', click = reset], class = 'controls'], div[div['P&L', class = 'card'], div['Count', class = 'card'], class = 'stats'], p['showing trades with qty above `min_qty`'] ] test layout[] s = app[panel] assert[len[elements[s, 'div.controls button']] eq 1] assert[elements[s, 'button'][0].text eq 'Reset'] assert[len[elements[s, '.stats .card']] eq 2] assert[len[elements[s, '.stats button']] eq 0] assert[elements[s, 'h1'][0].text eq 'Trades'] assert[elements[s, 'a'][0].href eq '/docs'] test typing_into_the_field[] s = app[panel] change[s, 'min_qty', 50] assert[elements[s, 'p'][0].text eq 'showing trades with qty above 50'] click[s, reset] assert[s.min_qty eq 0] page['/', panel] log['panel defined'] panel defined Read the layout block as a set of claims about the tree: one button in the controls panel, none in the stats panel, two cards, the heading text, the link target. Move the Reset button into the stats panel and the fourth line fails in crow test with both sides shown — the kind of mistake that otherwise survives until someone looks at the page. The second block is two-way binding end to end: the field's variable changes, the paragraph re-renders with it, the handler puts it back. What a test block sees A test block sees declarations: functions, views, structs, imports. Of the top-level assignments only two kinds ride along — literal values, which are reactive-state defaults the harness reads and handlers write, and connections ( db.connect[...] ), which are resources the derivations and handlers under test need to exist at all. Everything computed at the top level is invisible, exactly as it is inside a function, so a view under test cannot depend on work the program did before page[] . Failure renders, it doesn't crash A view renders what it is given, and what it is given may be an error value (chapter 7). The page shows the failure as error: the server's log has why, as <id> — a reader is told an id, never the reason, which names what the program reaches — and the server's log has the reason beside the id. Feed a view one on purpose and check that the failure reaches the page; the reason itself is yours to check on the value: use web, ui fn latest_price[] return error['price feed is down', 'network'] view quote[] px = latest_price[] return div[h1['AAPL'], p['last: `px`'], class = 'card'] test feed_down_is_visible[] s = app[quote] assert['the server\'s log has why' in elements[s, 'p'][0].text] assert[latest_price[].reason eq 'price feed is down'] page['/', quote] log['quote defined'] quote defined Time is an input Inside a test the clock is yours: it starts when the first app[…] opens and moves only when you move it, the way a field changes when you type in it. A handler that stamps now[] stamps the moment you set, and the fact holds a moment — moment[0.0] , the epoch, until a handler moves it: use web, ui stamped = moment[0.0] fn stamp[] stamped = now[] view clock[] return p['stamped `stamped`'] test the_test_sets_the_clock[] a = app[clock] change[a, 'now', 1000.0] click[a, stamp] assert[a.stamped eq moment[1000.0]] change[a, 'now', moment['2026-07-14T09:30:00Z']] click[a, stamp] assert[str[a.stamped] eq '2026-07-14T09:30:00Z'] page['/', clock] log['clock defined'] clock defined A click that stops — an error at a decision, a fact, a database write — evaluates to that error, and the session is exactly as it was before the click: r = click[a, apply] , then assert[not r.ok] . Two users at once Two sessions are two independent pages, each with its own reactive state — exactly what two browser tabs get from the server. That is how you test the awkward orderings — one person resets while another is still typing — with no threads to wrangle: use web, ui, db book = db.connect['sqlite://:memory:'] min_qty = 0 fn setup[] query[book, 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER)'] derive orders return query[book, 'SELECT qty FROM orders ORDER BY id'] fn reset[] min_qty = 0 fn order[] query[book, 'INSERT INTO orders (qty) VALUES (?)', [min_qty]] view panel[] return stack[ p['min `min_qty`'], p['orders: `len[orders]`'], button['Reset', click = reset], button['Order', click = order] ] test two_people[] alice = app[panel] bob = app[panel] click[alice, setup] change[alice, 'min_qty', 25] click[bob, reset] assert[alice.min_qty eq 25] change[bob, 'min_qty', 10] click[bob, order] assert[elements[alice, 'p'][1].text eq 'orders: 1'] page['/', panel] log['panel defined'] panel defined Bob's reset is his own: Alice still has 25. What the two share is the database — the order Bob places is in Alice's list the next time her page renders. Per-user state is the default; shared state is a table. What kind of mistake, which truth The mistake How you catch it Wrong structure — a button in the wrong panel, a missing heading elements[s, sel] with a nested selector Wrong content or formatting elements[...].text , or … in html[s] A click doesn't change state, or changes the wrong thing click[s, handler] then s.field Typing into a bound field doesn't propagate change[s, 'var', value] , then render again Wrong href , missing name , wrong class attribute keys on element records A failed query crashes instead of rendering in place render with an error value, assert on the tree Two users' events interleave badly two app[] sessions in one test Background work never lands later[] runs inline in tests — observable on the next line A handler blocks the live loop, or a view serves a stale snapshot crow check , statically — no test needed A chart draws the wrong thing elements[s, 'rect'] walks the SVG too What this cannot see Pixels beyond the layout model. Positions, sizes, and colours are testable now — box[] , style[] , fits[] in the next section — for everything built from the layout vocabulary. What they can't see is whatever lives in css/app.css outside that vocabulary, and glyph rendering, which stays the platform's. The design and its limits: docs/ui-engine-design.md . Routing. That a page is registered on the right path is not testable through a session today. Remote data. fetch and poll sources cannot be stubbed inside a test yet; put the logic that depends on them in a function that takes the data as a parameter, and test that. Against the compiled program crow test runs a block in the interpreter, and the apps it opens with it. crow test --compiled app.co runs the same blocks with every app they open compiled: the program is built once, each run that opens an app starts it fresh, and click , change , html , elements , box , a session's facts and derivations all reach the compiled program. The block itself, its truths and the functions it calls directly, still runs in the interpreter. So a handler the compiled program runs differently fails the test that exercises it, with the same message. A handler a test clicks with arguments ( click[a, begin[1000.0, 100.0, 1050.0]] ) is typed by them when nothing in the program types it. Blocks that open no app run as they always do, and nothing is built for them. $ crow test --compiled sim/clock.co ✓ 3 blocks pass, the apps they opened compiled (2 runs) — 2 truths, 1 law, 52 inputs run A test that reaches a database server or a model needs it running — unless it was recorded. crow check --record-fixtures runs the tests against the real servers and keeps what each statement and each request answered under .crow/fixtures ; crow test --fixtures runs them from what was kept, in both modes, and names a statement or a request nothing recorded. A request's fixture is named by its method, its URL and what it sends, so a changed prompt to a model is a changed request; its headers, and the key in them, are no part of it. crow test runs these blocks; crow check runs them plus the live-loop hazards; crow run and crow build ignore them. The baseline: what changed, without writing a test Every crow check derives what the program does and keeps it beside the source, under .crow/baseline/ : for each handler, every path through it as a condition over facts and inputs with the facts it writes; for each view, its tree of elements, controls and sub-views under their guards; for each fact, who writes it and who reads it. The first check records it. Every check after diffs against it. $ crow check baseline — 95 unchanged, 1 changed (.crow/baseline/main) [1/1] sim/session.co in start_session handler start_session changed (sim/session.co, in what you edited): ~ …when (not (v2 «lte» → «lt» v1)) and v1.ok and v2.ok: fix: if intended, accept with a and the baseline moves; otherwise fix the cause — reaches page / Locals and temporaries are substituted and paths are sorted, so a rename, a reordering or a helper moved to another part changes nothing. A guard, a write, an effect or a wiring that changed shows as a diff, with the file it came from and the views and pages it reaches; a diff reached from a file you did not edit is the headline. Accept with a and the baseline travels with your change; without a terminal, an unaccepted change fails the check, so CI blocks on it. Nothing runs and nothing is written: the artifacts come from the source alone. Each page also has its states : every state the handlers can bring it to, from the declared facts, with each control said once with when it is offered. states / (board_page_render) button 'Sign in' → board_door_log_in: when reader = 'nobody' button 'Attach' → board_cards_attach: when board_cards_card_id = * · reader = 'someone' ... A fact takes the few values the program gives it — a literal, or * for some other — and reader is the signed-in reader. A button that becomes reachable where it was not, a field left on screen after its session ended, is that control's line changing. And each page has its layout : every state laid out by the engine at desktop and phone widths, with its height and anything that runs past the width ( 390: 185 high, past the width: button 'Sign in' by 181 ), so a row that no longer fits a phone shows in the check. The app's book crow book , run inside the app, serves a book derived from the source on every start: the app and its parts, each page as a composition tree with a wireframe per state at desktop and phone widths, a chapter per part with its facts, derivations, handlers as paths, views with their trees and wireframes, and tests as steps, then the data wiring and the changes since the accepted baseline. The wireframes are the layout engine's boxes over the view's tree with placeholders, so nothing runs and no database is touched. $ crow book crow book: the app's book is written to .crow/book/site crow book: http://localhost:3101/ — the app's book (Ctrl-C or `crow stop book` to stop) The book serves next to the app, on its serve port plus one; --port chooses another. crow stop book stops it from anywhere in the project. Next: the two things every dashboard needs that you haven't written yet — a chart, and a page that looks right.

Charts and Styling Two things every real dashboard needs, and neither costs you a line of CSS or JavaScript: a chart over your data, and a page that looks right. chart: a view over a frame chart is an element like table — valid inside views, it takes a frame and named arguments naming the columns to draw, and renders as SVG on the server: use web, ui, db, frame conn = db.connect['sqlite://bars.db'] derive bars return query[conn, 'SELECT ts, o, hi, lo, c, vol FROM bars ORDER BY ts'] view render[] return div[ h1['AAPL — 1 minute'], chart[bars, candles = ['o', 'hi', 'lo', 'c'], bars_y = 'vol', tz = 'America/New_York', height = 240], class = 'card' ] page['/', render] serve[3000] The named arguments are the whole vocabulary: Argument Default Draws x 'ts' the column of moments on the x axis candles [] open, high, low, close columns as candlesticks lines [] columns as line series ( lines = ['vwap', 'ema'] ) bars_y '' a column as a volume pane marker 0 a moment marked with a vertical play-head tz 'UTC' the timezone the axis ticks are labeled in height 320 height in pixels panes [] lists of columns, each drawn in its own strip with its own scale ( [['rsi'], ['cvd']] ) levels 0 dashed reference lines keyed by column ( map[rsi = [30, 70], cvd = [0]] ) points 0 a frame of markers: ts , y , and optionally label and kind ( 'buy' , 'sell' ) seek 0 a handler that receives the moment of whichever bucket is clicked Three properties follow from "a chart is a view over a frame": It re-renders like everything else. Derive the frame, or read a reactive variable, and the chart tracks the data — the derivation recomputes when its table is written or a refresh tick passes, so serve[3000, refresh = 5] from the live-loop section keeps it moving. Empty is not an error. A frame with no rows renders a placeholder, so a chart before the first tick doesn't blank the page. Too much is an error. A frame over 1000 points refuses with an error that names the fix — aggregate to what a screen can show, with a coarser GROUP BY in the query or head[frame, n] — because a chart that repaints ten thousand points every refresh would freeze the live loop the last section warned about. It never downsamples silently. The colors come from the style tokens below, so a chart is theme-correct in light and dark mode without any color plumbing. Indicators and panes A chart draws columns, so an indicator is a column. use chart brings the usual ones — sma , ema , rsi , macd , vwap , rolling_sum , cvd — as functions over series that return a series of the same length, with NaN where the value is not defined yet, so the line starts where the math does instead of guessing: use chart, frame bars = frame.new[] bars.ts = [0.0, 60.0, 120.0, 180.0, 240.0, 300.0] bars.c = [10.0, 11.0, 10.5, 11.5, 12.0, 11.0] bars.vol = [100.0, 200.0, 150.0, 300.0, 250.0, 100.0] bars.sma3 = sma[bars.c, 3] bars.ema3 = ema[bars.c, 3] bars.rsi3 = rsi[bars.c, 3] bars.vwap = vwap[bars.c, bars.vol] bars.vol_2m = rolling_sum[bars.ts, bars.vol, 120.0] bars.cvd = cvd[bars.c, bars.vol] m = macd[bars.c, 2, 4, 2] log[bars.sma3[5]] log[bars.ema3[5]] log[bars.rsi3[5]] log[bars.vwap[1]] log[bars.vol_2m[5]] log[bars.cvd[5]] log[m.columns] 11.5 11.25 50 10.666666666666666 650 500 ['line', 'signal', 'hist'] The same function computed the same numbers in both execution modes — the indicators live in the kernel, next to the chart geometry. Two forms take moments: rsi[ts, values, n, secs] computes on clock-aligned buckets of secs seconds (a 14-period RSI on 3-minute candles, drawn over 1-second bars, whose history never changes as the tape advances), and vwap[ts, price, vol, secs] is the trailing-window VWAP. Derived once per change, each indicator column names a pane, a level, or a line in the view: use web, ui, db, frame, chart conn = db.connect['sqlite://bars.db'] clock = 0.0 fn jump[t] clock = t derive bars raw = query[conn, 'SELECT ts, o, hi, lo, c, vol FROM bars ORDER BY ts'] raw.rsi = rsi[raw.c, 14] raw.cvd = cvd[raw.c, raw.vol] return raw derive fills return query[conn, 'SELECT ts, px AS y, side AS kind FROM fills'] view render[] return chart[bars, candles = ['o', 'hi', 'lo', 'c'], bars_y = 'vol', panes = [['rsi'], ['cvd']], levels = map[rsi = [30, 70], cvd = [0]], points = fills, seek = jump, marker = clock, tz = 'America/New_York', height = 400] page['/', render] serve[3000] panes stacks strips under the volume, each with its own scale and a legend; levels draws dashed lines in whichever pane holds the column; points marks trades on the price pane ( kind = 'buy' is an up triangle in the up color, 'sell' a down triangle); seek = jump makes every bucket a click target that sends its moment to the handler — a replay's scrubber in one line, with the play-head as reactive state the way the live-loop section described. Layout: compose boxes, don't write CSS A page is composed from five containers — stack , row , grid , overlay , scroll — and a fixed set of layout attributes that any element accepts: spacing from a scale ( gap = 'm' , pad = 'l' ), sizes ( width = '240px' , '50%' , 'fill' ), type ( size = 'xl' , weight = 'bold' ), surfaces ( surface = 'card' , radius , shadow ), colours as tokens ( color = 'up' ), and responsive rules at named widths ( below = 'phone', columns_then = 1 ). There is no CSS to write, and a wrong value is a compile error that names the scale. Because the vocabulary is closed, Crow ships a layout engine — written in Crow — that computes where everything goes. Tests read it through box[] , style[] , and fits[] : use web, ui min_qty = 0 fn reset[] min_qty = 0 view stat_card[label, value] return stack[h3[label], p['`value`', size = 'xl', weight = 'bold', font = 'mono'], surface = 'card'] view render[] return stack[ h1['Trading Dashboard'], grid[stat_card['P&L', '1,116.10'], stat_card['Trades', '4'], columns = 2, below = 'phone', columns_then = 1], row[field['Min qty', min_qty], button['Reset', click = reset], gap = 'm'], overlay[scroll[p['the tape'], height = '120px'], span['LIVE', color = 'up', anchor = 'top_right']], gap = 'l', pad = 'l' ] test layout[] s = app[render, width = 1280] cards = box[s, 'grid .card'] assert[len[cards] eq 2] assert[cards[0].y eq cards[1].y] --- side by side on a desktop controls = box[s, 'row'][0] assert[controls.y gt cards[0].y + cards[0].height] assert[fits[s, 1280]] assert[style[s, '.card'][0].background eq '--crow-surface'] assert[style[s, '.card p'][0].size eq 'xl'] phone = app[render, width = 390] stacked = box[phone, 'grid .card'] assert[stacked[1].y gte stacked[0].y + stacked[0].height] --- one under the other assert[stacked[0].width eq stacked[1].width] assert[fits[phone, 390]] page['/', render] log['dashboard defined'] dashboard defined Read the test block as claims about the page at two widths: two cards side by side at 1280 pixels and stacked at 390, the controls under them, the card on the surface colour, the big number at the xl step, and nothing overflowing at either width. Every claim is checked by the same engine that determined the page's layout, and the browser lays out the emitted CSS by the same rules — see docs/ui-engine-design.md for how that agreement is kept. The whole vocabulary Every attribute is a literal, and a value the table does not know is refused before the program runs, naming the values it takes. On Attribute Values any container gap , pad , margin 'xs' 's' 'm' 'l' 'xl' (4, 8, 16, 24, 32px); pad = 'm l' is vertical then horizontal row align , justify , wrap 'start' 'center' 'end' 'stretch' ; 'start' 'center' 'end' 'between' 'around' ; wrap = 'true' grid columns a count; cells share the width equally scroll height a size such as '96px' overlay children anchor 'top_left' 'top_right' 'bottom_left' 'bottom_right' 'center' any element width , height , min_width , max_width , fill , aspect '240px' , '50%' (a width), 'fill' ; fill = 'true' takes the remaining space in a row; aspect = '16/9' any element size , weight , font , lines 'xs' 's' 'm' 'l' 'xl' 'xxl' ; 'regular' 'medium' 'bold' ; font = 'mono' , the monospace face with tabular digits; a line clamp any element surface , radius , border , shadow surface = 'card' ; radius = 'none' 's' 'm' 'l' 'round' ; border = 'true' ; shadow = 's' 'm' 'l' any element color , background a token name: 'text' 'muted' 'accent' 'up' 'down' 'surface' 'bg' any container below + becomes , below + columns_then , hidden_below below = 'phone' (under 600px) or 'tablet' (under 1024px); becomes = 'stack' turns a row into a stack; columns_then = 1 reflows a grid; hidden_below hides the element Anything else ( class , href , title , placeholder ) passes through as an ordinary HTML attribute. Run the layout example yourself The full version of that dashboard — three cards, an alert badge in an overlay , a control row that turns into a stack on phones, a scrolling tape — lives in the repository as examples/layout_dashboard.co . Three commands, in the order you'd use them: crow test examples/layout_dashboard.co # the layout truths, no browser crow run examples/layout_dashboard.co # serve it on http://localhost:3000 crow stop # from the same directory crow test runs three blocks: structure clicks and changes state, layout_desktop checks that the cards share a line at 1280px and that the P&L is green and the drawdown red, layout_phone checks that the same cards stack one per row at 390px and that nothing pokes out. Break a rule — drop becomes = 'stack' from the header row — and the phone block fails before you've opened a browser, because at 390px a heading and a badge no longer fit side by side. crow run compiles the same file and serves it; the page you see is laid out by the same rules the test just checked, emitted as CSS. Change a number in a test block, or an attribute in the view, and run again. On this page, the shorter example above has the same buttons: with crow book running, press ▶ Run for the interpreter, ⚙ Compile for the native build, ✓ Test for its test layout[] block — the file is served and tested from the book without leaving it. Styling: seven classes, eight tokens Every page ships with a default stylesheet — cards, tables, buttons, forms, light and dark following the system theme. The entire styling vocabulary you write in Crow is a handful of class names, passed as an ordinary attribute: classes card stats controls primary up down stale tokens --crow-bg --crow-surface --crow-text --crow-muted --crow-border --crow-accent --crow-up --crow-down You've used card , stats , and controls in the dashboard already. up / down color a value by sign, stale dims data past its freshness window, primary marks the one button that matters. When the defaults aren't enough, write plain CSS in css/app.css in the project — it's inlined after the defaults on every page. Override a token there and every element and chart that uses it follows: :root { --crow-accent: #c60; } crow check flags a misspelled --crow-* token with a did-you-mean. CSS never appears inside a .co file: the view says what , the stylesheet says how it looks , and the boundary is the file extension. That's all of it. Next: the rest of the element vocabulary.

The Element Vocabulary A page is composed from a closed vocabulary: the containers you met in the layout section, the HTML elements, and a set of primitives that each add a capability nothing else composes — an input bound to state, a disclosure, a layer, an icon. Anything else you want is a view you write from these. This chapter walks the primitives with the test harness, so every claim is checked without a browser. Inputs are state A bound input has no value of its own. The reader's change lands in the variable, handlers read the variable, and the next render draws it. Every kind of input binds the same way: use web, ui name = 'Ann' qty = 100 notes = '' agree = false notify = true side = 'buy' mode = 'Practice' pct = 0.4 view form[] return stack[ tabs[['Scanner Replay', 'Practice'], mode], row[field['Name', name], field['Qty', qty], gap = 'm'], field['Notes', notes, lines = 3], row[checkbox['I agree', agree], toggle['Notify', notify], radio[['buy', 'sell'], side], gap = 'l'], progress[pct], gap = 'm' ] test inputs_bind_to_state[] a = app[form] h = html[a] assert['aria-selected="true" role="tab"' in h] assert['<input aria-label="Qty" data-crow-input="__field:qty" type="number" value="100">' in h] assert['<textarea aria-label="Notes" data-crow-input="__field:notes" rows="3">' in h] assert['crow-toggle"><input checked="" data-crow-input="__field:notify" type="checkbox">' in h] assert['<progress class="crow-progress" max="1" value="0.4">' in h] page['/', form] field looks at the variable: an int or float gets a number input, and type = 'date' or 'time' asks for the browser's picker. lines = 3 makes a textarea. tabs and radio hold one of several strings, checkbox and toggle a bool — the same binding drawn two ways. Revealing: disclosure, dropdowns, and the three layers details shows its summary always and its body when open. A dropdown is a button whose second child floats under it. The three layers — modal , drawer , toast — sit outside the flow and show while open is true. Open is state, so a handler opens and closes them: use web, ui show_help = false saved = false fn open_help[] show_help = true fn close_help[] show_help = false fn save[] saved = true view layers[] return stack[ details[summary['More filters'], p['Min price, max float'], open = true], dropdown[summary['Actions'], stack[button['Help', click = open_help], button['Save', click = save]]], modal[stack[h3['Help'], p['Click a bar to seek.'], button['Close', click = close_help]], open = show_help], toast[p['Saved'], open = saved, color = 'up'], divider[], gap = 'm' ] test layers_follow_state[] a = app[layers] assert['class="modal" data-open="false"' in html[a]] click[a, open_help] assert['class="modal" data-open="true"' in html[a]] click[a, close_help] click[a, save] assert['class="toast" data-open="true"' in html[a]] page['/', layers] Framing and detail nav marks the current page, icon draws from a closed set in the text colour, tip puts the browser's tooltip on anything, and divider rules between siblings: use web, ui view top_bar[] return stack[ nav[a['Home', href = '/'], a['Scanner', href = '/scanner'], active = '/scanner'], row[icon['search'], span['Search the tape', tip = 'type a symbol'], icon['star', color = 'accent'], gap = 's'], gap = 'm' ] test the_shell[] a = app[top_bar] h = html[a] assert['<a aria-current="page" href="/scanner">' in h] assert['<svg aria-hidden="true" class="icon icon-search"' in h] assert['title="type a symbol"' in h] assert[len[box[a, 'nav a']] eq 2] page['/', top_bar] Lists of things A page shows many of something: past, bookmarks, trades. A for expression over a view gives a list of nodes, and a child that is a list contributes each item. That is the whole rule — no loop element, no template syntax: use web, ui past = ['HSCS 2026-06-23', 'EZGO 2026-06-17', 'ANY 2026-06-01'] starting = true fn forget[] past = ['HSCS 2026-06-23'] starting = false view session_row[s] return row[span[s], button[icon['x', size = 's'], click = forget, tip = 'delete'], justify = 'between'] view past_sessions[] rows = for s in past session_row[s] return stack[h2['Past past'], rows, button['Start', disabled = starting, class = 'primary'], gap = 's'] test a_list_is_its_items[] a = app[past_sessions] assert[len[elements[a, 'row']] eq 3] assert['disabled=""' in html[a]] click[a, forget] assert[len[elements[a, 'row']] eq 1] assert['disabled=""' not in html[a]] page['/', past_sessions] The same rule gives every row its own controls — a delete icon, a pin, a link — which table[frame] cannot, since a frame's cells are values. Use the table for data and a list of views for rows that act. disabled = starting shows the other half: a boolean attribute follows state. HTML reads presence, not the word, so the renderers write disabled="" when the value is true and nothing when it is false — the same for hidden , readonly , required , checked and selected . The look of the app Theme, density, accent and width are settings of the app, not of the elements. They go on serve : use web, ui view render[] return stack[h1['Terminal'], p['dense, dark, full width']] page['/', render] serve[3000, theme = 'dark', density = 'compact', accent = '#3b82f6', wide = true] theme is 'light' , 'dark' , or 'system' (the default). density = 'compact' tightens every element's defaults for a screen full of numbers. accent replaces the one colour the tokens leave to you. wide drops the reading column so a dashboard uses the whole window. Nothing in the views changes: the same tree renders under every look, and the layout engine places it the same way. Records with actions A list of records usually wants a button or two per row. table takes them as actions , a map from label to handler; each button sends the row's key to its handler, as a row click does. hide keeps a helper column in the frame but out of the table, and a header bar is header . use web, ui, frame deleted = 0 opened = 0 fn open_row[id] opened = id fn delete_row[id] deleted = id view records[] rows = frame.new[] rows.id = [3, 4] rows.name = ['alpha', 'beta'] return stack[ header[h1['records', size = 'm'], nav[a['Home', href = '/'], active = '/'], gap = 'm'], table[rows, click = open_row, key = 'id', actions = map[Delete = delete_row], hide = ['id']] ] test each_row_carries_its_actions[] a = app[records] h = html[a] assert['<header' in h] assert['<button data-crow-args="[3]" data-crow-click="delete_row">Delete</button>' in h] assert['<th class="num">id</th>' not in h] click[a, delete_row[4]] assert[deleted eq 4] page['/', records] One way out: widgets The vocabulary is closed on purpose, which means a map, a rich-text editor or a calendar cannot be written with it. Those are widgets: a piece of the page your own JavaScript draws. widget['map', props = …, on = map[pick = choose]] draws the module widgets/map.js in your program's folder. The module exports two functions: // widgets/map.js export function mount(el, props, send) { const b = document.createElement('button'); b.textContent = 'Pick Paris (showing ' + props.city + ')'; b.onclick = () => send('pick', 'Paris'); el.appendChild(b); } export function update(el, props) { el.querySelector('button').textContent = 'Pick Paris (showing ' + props.city + ')'; } The page loads the module once and calls mount with the element and the props, as JSON. Whenever a render changes the props it calls update , and the element's insides stay the module's. send('pick', value) runs the handler that on names for pick , the way a click would: the page offers exactly the events its widgets name, and the handler receives the value, so it checks what it is given. In a test a widget is its element, and a click on the handler stands for what the widget would send: use web, ui place = 'London' fn choose[city] place = city view atlas[] return stack[ p['showing `place`'], widget['map', props = map[city = place], on = map[pick = choose]] ] test the_map_s_pick_moves_the_page[] a = app[atlas] click[a, choose['Paris']] assert[elements[a, 'p'][0].text eq 'showing Paris'] assert[elements[a, 'div.crow-widget'][0]['data-crow-props'] eq '{"city":"Paris"}'] page['/', atlas] log['atlas defined'] atlas defined There is no other way to put code on a page: no script tags, no inline handlers.

Derivations Facts are stored; beliefs are derived. A live page holds a few facts — the symbol, the day, where the play-head was anchored — and shows many things computed from them: the bars for that symbol, the rows at the play-head, the trades of this session. In most frameworks the view fetches and computes those on every render, or an effect fetches them and stores a copy that goes stale. Crow has a form for them. A value that follows what it reads use web, ui qty = 100 price = 1.79 derive cost return qty * price fn more[] qty = qty + 100 view render[] return stack[p['`qty` shares cost `cost`'], button['More', click = more]] test cost_follows_qty[] a = app[render] assert['cost 179' in html[a]] click[a, more] assert['cost 358' in html[a]] page['/', render] derive cost is read like a fact and never assigned — cost = 5 in a handler is an error that tells you to change qty or price instead. It is recomputed only when something it read changed: the handler wrote qty , so the next render recomputes cost ; a render where nothing changed serves the cached value. A helper that only reads state is a derivation too. A fn band[] that returns the config's price band is refused — a function sees its parameters and nothing else — and derive band is what it was all along: a value that follows the config, read by the handlers as band . What a derivation reads is decided from the source Both execution modes obey the same read sets: the facts and other derivations a body names, transitively through the functions it calls and inside interpolated strings; now[] ; and the tables its queries read. There is nothing to declare. use web, ui, db conn = db.connect['sqlite://:memory:'] sym = 'IMRN' fn setup[] query[conn, 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS trades (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, symbol TEXT, px REAL)'] derive trades return query[conn, 'SELECT id, symbol, px FROM trades WHERE symbol = ?', [sym]] derive summary return '`sym`: `len[trades]` trades' fn buy[] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades (symbol, px) VALUES (?, ?)', [sym, 1.79]] view render[] return stack[p[summary], button['Buy', click = buy]] test a_write_recomputes_the_query[] a = app[render] click[a, setup] assert['IMRN: 0 trades' in html[a]] click[a, buy] assert['IMRN: 1 trades' in html[a]] page['/', render] trades reads the table trades ; the handler buy writes it, so the derivation is recomputed on the next read and summary , which reads trades , follows. A derivation whose value did not change — an equal number, string or bool — cuts the chain: nothing downstream recomputes. Freshness for sources you don't write A table another system writes — a day's bars in ClickHouse — cannot be invalidated by anything in your program. A derivation over it says how old it may be: use web, ui, db ch = db.connect['clickhouse://clickhouse.example:8123/market'] sym = 'IMRN' day = '2026-09-04' derive bars[fresh = 300] return query[ch, 'SELECT ts, o, hi, lo, c, vol FROM bars WHERE symbol = ? AND date = ?', [sym, day]] view render[] return table[bars] page['/', render] serve[3000, refresh = 1] The default is fresh = 0 : as fresh as the loop , recomputed every refresh tick, which is exactly what a query inside a view did before. Declaring fresh is the relaxation, never the other way round. A derivation that reads now[] recomputes every tick too, which is how a play-head derived from the clock stays honest. A recompute never holds the page. A derivation that queries is computed off the render: the tick renders at once with the value it has, and again when the new value lands, and until its first value it reads as "loading" (chapter 12.4 has the rules). In crow test every event settles before the next line, so a test always reads the landed value. One value for the app, or one per session Who holds a derivation is inferred from what it reads. A fact a session writes belongs to it — assigned by a handler, bound to an input the reader types into, or carried in the page's address: their own symbol, their play-head, the card the URL names — so a derivation that reads one is computed per session, and so is one over a data source ( fetch / poll ), whose answers land in each session that asks. A derivation over constants, tables and the clock alone is the same for everyone, so it is computed once for the app and every session reads it: the day's universe, the latest bar in a table, a scanner's config. Database handles are not facts, so query[conn, …] over a table nobody's handler touches is shared. A table write in any session reaches every session's derivations over that table: when one reader buys, the blotter of another reader watching the same book follows at once — the write wakes every page that read the table, with no refresh tick and no code. A derivation that reads only a slice of a table is recomputed only when a write may have touched that slice. Every one of its queries of the table has to fix one column by a fact, as WHERE board = ? with [board_id] does. A local that is only the fact also counts, including the fact as text ( b = ' board_id ' ). A card added to board 2 then leaves every page showing board 1 as it was. A write says which rows it touched when its WHERE is equalities joined by AND , or an INSERT names its values. A write that does not say ( WHERE qty > ? , a card moved by its id alone, which does not say its board) reaches every reader of the table, as before. crow check prints the read set and the holder of each derivation, and a slice by its column, so the split is never a guess: derivations — what each reads, and who holds it: bars: reads day, sym · tables bars (external, fresh 300s) — held by each session (it reads 'sym', which a session writes) cards: reads board_id · tables cards where board = board_id — held by each session (it reads 'board_id', which a session writes) universe: reads day · tables datasets — held by the app Routes read what the app holds A route has no session, so what its handler reads is what the app holds: a derivation over tables, the clock and facts no session moves. That is the cache a web service keeps — the rows it would otherwise ask the database for on every request: use web, db book = db.connect['sqlite://notes.db'] made = query[book, 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT)'] derive notes return query[book, 'SELECT id, body FROM notes ORDER BY id'] fn list_h[req] return json[notes] fn add_h[req] conn = db.connect['sqlite://notes.db'] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES (?)', [req.body]] return text['added'] route['/notes', list_h] route['/add', 'POST', add_h] serve[8080] The handler reads notes once, as its request begins: the app's value, computed by the first request and kept until this program writes the table. /add 's write lands as its handler ends, so the next request reads the new rows — no key to clear, no copy to refresh. Requests that arrive together while the rows are computed wait for that one query. A table something else writes is read through fresh : derive notes[fresh = 60] keeps its rows a minute, and at fresh = 0 , as over the clock, each request computes its own. A web program that declares a derivation holds state as a page program does, so each of its top-level names gets one value, which its derivations read; a route's handler still sees none of them, and opens its own connection to write. A route that reads a derivation a session holds is refused before the program runs, with what makes it the session's: 'band' is held by each session, and a route's handler has no session — it reads 'picked', which a session writes: a route reads a derivation the app holds, one over tables, the clock and facts no session moves Rows that keep their place A list rendered from data is patched by position unless its rows say who they are. Give a row's root an id built from its item's key and the live client matches it to the same row in the previous render: a deletion in the middle removes one node, a reorder moves nodes, and nothing else on the page is rebuilt. Elements without an id still match by position. use web, ui items = [1, 2, 3] view item_row[i] return p['item `i`', id = 'r-`i`'] derive rows out = for i in items item_row[i] return out fn drop_middle[] items = [1, 3] view render[] return stack[stack[rows], button['Drop', click = drop_middle]] test rows_carry_their_identity[] a = app[render] assert['id="r-2"' in html[a]] click[a, drop_middle] assert['id="r-2"' not in html[a]] assert['id="r-3"' in html[a]] page['/', render] Because nodes survive a render, so does everything the browser keeps on them: the field a reader is typing in keeps its focus and caret while the rest of the page updates around it. Where the queries went Before derive , the finch simulation's view ran four queries a second, three of which changed a few times an hour. crow check warned about it — remote-query-in-view — and could only warn. With derive , no view queries anything: the bars are a derivation over the symbol and the day, the rows at the play-head over the day and the clock, the trades over the session. A tick recomputes the play-head and the rows; a symbol change recomputes the bars; a buy recomputes the trades. Nothing else moves, and nobody wrote a line about caching. The checker now teaches the form instead of warning about its absence. A top-level variable assigned from a query and read by a view — a launch-time snapshot served forever — is an error in crow check , with a one-key rewrite: d turns trades = query[…] into derive trades . A query inside a view is refused before the program runs: a view shows the page's state, and a derivation is where a page reads a table. Derivations are state, so they live in a program that serves: a use ui program with a page, or a use web program whose routes read them. In the test harness html[a] is a tick and click[a, h] marks what the handler wrote, so a test can watch a derivation follow its inputs the way these blocks do.

Final Project: A Live Dashboard Everything in one program: a trading dashboard that reads a real SQLite database, computes stats with frames and math, renders with views, and updates live in the browser. About sixty lines of Crow, one binary, no JavaScript, no ORM, no framework configuration. We build it in four steps: the data, the database layer, the live views, and shipping it. The finished program is examples/dashboard.co in the Crow repository — every step here is the path to exactly that file.

Loading and Shaping the Data Real apps get data from outside; ours needs a database to exist first. A seed script is a plain Crow program — chapter 11, nothing more: use db conn = connect['sqlite://trades.db'] query[conn, 'DROP TABLE IF EXISTS trades'] query[conn, 'CREATE TABLE trades (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, symbol TEXT, qty INTEGER, price REAL, pnl REAL)'] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, ?, ?, ?, ?)', ['AAPL', 100, 191.5, 250.0]] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (2, ?, ?, ?, ?)', ['MSFT', 50, 415.2, -120.5]] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (3, ?, ?, ?, ?)', ['NVDA', 20, 875.0, 890.2]] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (4, ?, ?, ?, ?)', ['AAPL', 40, 193.1, 96.4]] counts = query[conn, 'SELECT count(*) AS n FROM trades'] log['seeded `counts.n[0]` trades'] rm['trades.db'] seeded 4 trades (The final line removes the file only so this book's test runner stays tidy — the real seed script, examples/dashboard_seed.co , keeps it.) sqlite://trades.db is a file this time, not :memory: — the data survives between runs, and the dashboard process will open the same file. Swap in a postgres://... URL later and nothing else changes.

The Database Layer The dashboard's data needs are three queries' worth of chapter 11 and chapter 10 — run against the seeded file, straight into frames: use db, frame, math conn = connect['sqlite://ch12demo.db'] query[conn, 'CREATE TABLE trades (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, symbol TEXT, qty INTEGER, price REAL, pnl REAL)'] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (1, ?, ?, ?, ?)', ['AAPL', 100, 191.5, 250.0]] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (2, ?, ?, ?, ?)', ['MSFT', 50, 415.2, -120.5]] query[conn, 'INSERT INTO trades VALUES (3, ?, ?, ?, ?)', ['NVDA', 20, 875.0, 890.2]] trades = query[conn, 'SELECT symbol, qty, price, pnl FROM trades ORDER BY id'] total_pnl = sum[trades.pnl] log['P&L: `fmt[total_pnl, decimals = 2, commas = true]`'] by_symbol = group[trades, 'symbol', ['pnl', 'sum']] log[by_symbol] rm['ch12demo.db'] P&L: 1,019.70 symbol pnl_sum str float ------ ------- AAPL 250 MSFT -120.5 NVDA 890.2 [3 rows x 2 cols] Query results are frames, frames feed sum / group / sort and masks, and fmt dresses the numbers. This is the entire "backend" of the dashboard — there is no separate API layer to write, because the views run in the same process as the data.

Views and Live Updates Now the full program — the seed script's sibling, and the payoff of every chapter in this book: --- Live trading dashboard: SQLite -> frames -> views --- Seed first: crow run dashboard_seed.co Then: crow run dashboard.co use web, ui, db, frame, math conn = db.connect['sqlite://trades.db'] --- Reactive UI state min_qty = 0 --- Event handlers fn reset_filters[] min_qty = 0 view stat_card[label, value] return div[ h3[label], p['`value`'], class = 'card' ] derive trades return query[conn, 'SELECT symbol, qty, price, pnl FROM trades ORDER BY id'] view render[] total_pnl = sum[trades.pnl] shown = trades if min_qty gt 0 shown = trades[trades.qty gte min_qty] shown = sort[shown, 'pnl', desc = true] by_symbol = group[trades, 'symbol', ['pnl', 'sum'], ['pnl', 'count']] return div[ h1['Trading Dashboard'], div[ stat_card['P&L', fmt[total_pnl, decimals = 2, commas = true]], stat_card['Trades', len[trades]], class = 'stats' ], div[ field['Min qty', min_qty], button['Reset', click = reset_filters], class = 'controls' ], h2['Trades'], table[shown], h2['P&L by Symbol'], table[by_symbol] ] serve[3000] page['/', render] Walk it top to bottom and count the chapters: db.connect — written with its module's prefix, which always reaches a module's name (chapter 8); bare connect would do as well, since db alone provides it. The connection is infrastructure, not UI state — Crow keeps it as a process-wide handle, never serialized. min_qty / reset_filters — chapter 12's reactive loop: edit the field, the state changes, the page re-renders; click Reset, same. stat_card — a parameterized component, used at two types (string and int values). A function or a view called with two kinds is compiled once for each, which quietly makes both work. trades — a derivation, chapter 12's other half: the query runs off the render, and runs again when a handler writes the table or a refresh tick passes, so every page shows the database as it is now without a query per render. A view reads it like a fact; a view that queried itself would be refused, since a view is a function of the state it is given. Frames flow from the derivation through masks, sort and group into table[...] untouched. A failed query renders in place — a view renders what it's given, and what it's given is chapter 7's error value. Stop the database and the page shows the failure where the data would be, with an id the server's log explains, instead of crashing. Seed, run, open localhost:3000 — the page below is real output, served by this program during this book's own verification: Trading Dashboard P&L: 1,116.10 Trades: 4 [Min qty ____] [Reset] Trades: symbol qty price pnl ... P&L by Symbol: AAPL 346.4 · MSFT -120.5 · NVDA 890.2

Polish and Deployment One Binary crow build dashboard.co The output is a single native executable containing the web server, the LiveView runtime, the SQLite driver, and your compiled logic. Deployment is copying one file (plus trades.db ) to a machine and running it. There is no interpreter to install, no node_modules , no Python environment — the binary is the app. Running It for Others The binary reads a few settings from its environment: CROW_PORT — the port, over the one serve names. CROW_HOST — 0.0.0.0 to listen beyond this machine; a served app listens on this machine only until told otherwise. CROW_SECRET — at least 32 characters, the key sign-in cookies are sealed with. Without it the app writes a key of its own to .crow/keys/ ; changing the key signs everyone out. Beside the binary it keeps .crow/ : keys/ (that key, and the sign-ins signed out), sessions/ (with serve[…, keep = true] ) and uploads/ (files in flight). The directory must be writable, and keys/ must outlive a restart — on a machine whose disk starts fresh each time, set CROW_SECRET . An app others reach sits behind a proxy, which holds the certificate and limits connections and slow clients. The proxy hands on the page's socket and says who asked: location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade"; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; } Each line has a reason. Upgrade and Connection carry the page's socket. Host keeps the address the reader typed: a page's socket opens only from the app's own page, so a proxy that rewrites it — nginx does unless told — leaves every page dim, reconnecting. X-Forwarded-Proto makes the sign-in cookie Secure over https, and X-Forwarded-For lets a route's limit count each client rather than the proxy (the app believes it only from a proxy on its own machine). How Far One Process Goes A Crow app is one process: its sessions, its derivations' values and its tables' versions live in it, and that is a decision, not a limit you discover later (session-layer-design.md §6). How far one goes is measured, not guessed. tests/capacity.rs serves a compiled app — a route that queries, a route that answers JSON, a live page — and measures it: cargo test --release --test capacity -- --ignored --nocapture On a laptop (an M-series Mac, over loopback, eight clients), one process: sessions: 2007 opened in 0.1s (24903 a second), 0 failed, p50 0.29 ms, p99 0.57 ms memory: 30784 KB before, 39184 KB after: 4.2 KB a session tabs: 500 sockets opened and held in 2.1s, each sent its render; 142.0 KB a connected session a route answering JSON (/status): 34418 a second, 0 failed, p50 0.21 ms, p99 0.30 ms a route that queries (/count): 29972 a second, 0 failed, p50 0.25 ms, p99 0.34 ms a page load (/): 27260 a second, 0 failed, p50 0.27 ms, p99 0.37 ms Read it as: a tab that is open costs about 140 KB while it is open, so a gigabyte holds some seven thousand open tabs of a page like this one (a bigger page holds a bigger render); a page loaded and left costs a few kilobytes until its grace period ends; and the routes themselves are not where the time goes — a real route is as fast as its query. The soak test ( tests/soak.rs ) holds an app at a steady load for as long as you ask and watches that memory and latency stay flat. What bounds a process in practice: the file descriptors it may hold (one per open tab — raise ulimit -n on a server), the proxy's own limits on connections, the memory the open tabs' renders take, and the database behind the routes. When an app outgrows that, a second process is a second app: run one per port behind a proxy that sends each tab back to the process it started on (a sticky route by cookie or address), and let the database be what they share. A write one process makes shows in another's derivations when their fresh = N window elapses, as an external source's does — the table's version that wakes a derivation at once lives in the process that wrote it. Sessions that any process could resume, and a change that wakes every process, are not built: not before an app needs them. Growing It Every direction from here is a chapter you've already read: More data — the seed script becomes a real ingest job; poll a price feed into reactive state for tick updates More pages — page['/positions', positions_view] ; components shared through a module ( use widgets as w ) A real database — change one connection string to postgres://… Auth, sessions, JSON APIs — use web.auth , route['/api/pnl', pnl_json] What You've Built A data application with live UI, in one language, one file, one binary — parallel where it helps, sequential where it matters, with failures that never lose their reasons. That's Crow's whole bet. The reference ( docs/language-spec.md ) covers what this book didn't; the Design Notes there explain every "why can't I…" you'll hit next. Welcome aboard.

JSON data = json['[1, 2, 3]'] log[data[0]] obj = json['{"name": "crow", "n": 3}'] log[obj.name] log[int[obj.n] + 1] log[encode[[1, 2, 3]]] bad = json['not json'] log[bad.ok] log[bad.kind] 1 crow 4 [1,2,3] false parse Strings are inert outside backtick interpolation, so JSON braces and double quotes need no escaping. A parsed field is open-schema data, read as the kind its use implies: obj.n + 1 reads n as a number, upper[obj.name] reads name as text, and a field that holds another kind stops the program, naming what it holds and the read that asked. int[] , float[] and str[] read one by hand, as int[obj.n] does here, and that conversion is an error value where the field isn't what you expected. Text for a header or a URL pair = 'ada:secret' coded = encode[pair, 'base64'] log['Basic `coded`'] log[decode[coded, 'base64']] log[encode['crow & more', 'url']] bad = decode['not base64!', 'base64'] log[bad.kind] Basic YWRhOnNlY3JldA== ada:secret crow%20%26%20more parse Given a scheme, encode writes text so something else can carry it — base64 for an authorization: Basic … header, 'url' for one piece of a URL — and decode reads it back. request and the readers encode a query and a form themselves. Automatic differentiation fn f[x] return x * x + 3.0 * x df = grad[f] log[df[2.0]] fn g[x, y] return x * y dg = grad[g] log[dg[3.0, 4.0]] 7 [4, 3] A function of numbers may use arithmetic and ^ , and abs , sign , sqrt , exp , ln , log2 , log10 , sin , cos , tan , asin , acos , atan , sinh , cosh , tanh , erf , floor , ceil and round : use math fn h[x] return sin[x] * exp[x] dh = grad[h] log[dh[0.0]] 1 A function of tensors is differentiated backward: it runs once on traced tensors, and every parameter's gradient comes from that one run. true true Setup Run this first. true Six names, all pure: chapters[] turns a summary into a frame, markdown[] turns a chapter into HTML, menu[] turns the frame into navigation with collapsible groups and the current page marked, pager[] gives the previous and next links, plain[] gives a chapter's words for a search index, and document[] wraps a body in a complete page with the kernel stylesheet, the runner, the sidebar behaviour, and search. The Crow Book itself is rendered this way by docs/book/site.co , whose one view puts the menu and the chapter side by side with the layout vocabulary and whose test layout[] checks that arrangement at two widths without a browser. Because both renderers call the same kernel, crow run -i and the compiled binary write byte-identical pages. Markdown code spans use backticks, which are interpolation inside a Crow string. Read chapter text from files, as the book does, rather than writing it inline. Reference: spec section 13 (doc).
