A set of small numbers fits in one int's bits — here the columns an n-queens search may still use, cut to the board's width with bitand after each shift so the numbers stay small: use bits fn queens[n, mask, row, cols, d1, d2] if row eq n return 1 count = 0 free = bitand[bitxor[bitor[bitor[cols, d1], d2], -1], mask] while free ne 0 bit = bitand[free, -free] free = bitxor[free, bit] count = count + queens[n, mask, row + 1, bitor[cols, bit], bitand[shift[bitor[d1, bit], 1], mask], shift[bitor[d2, bit], -1]] return count log[queens[8, shift[1, 8] - 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]] 92 A character's code and back, for a parser or a hash that works on codes: use bits fn fnv[s] h = 2166136261 for c in split[s, ''] h = bitxor[h, code[c]] h = h * 16777619 % 4294967296 return h log[fnv['crow']] word = '' for n in [99, 114, 111, 119] word = '`word``char[n]`' log[word] 2472741726 crow Reference: spec section 13 (bits).

[2 rows x 2 cols] false not today 3 2 5 query runs every statement — a CREATE , an INSERT , a SELECT — and answers a frame: the rows the statement reads, or none; a write that must say what it touched reads it back with RETURNING . describe answers the columns a statement would, without running it, as the compiler reads them: a kind marked ? where the column can hold NULL (neither k nor v is declared NOT NULL ). transact answers what its function answers, committed — or the error of a function that failed, its transaction rolled back. insert uses each backend's bulk path (COPY, RowBinary, batched statements) and returns the row count, or the database's refusal — a key two rows share — as an error value. Migrations are the tool's: crow db apply <dir> <url> . Reference: spec section 13 (db) and book chapter 11.

Web: a JSON route use web fn health[req] return json[map[status = 'ok']] route['/health', health] serve[3000] route[path, handler] registers a plain HTTP handler — a function that receives the request and returns a response; page[path, view] registers a live page (chapter 12). Responses come from json , html , text , respond[status, body] , and redirect[url] . The handler is handed the request: req.params holds the path's :name s, req.query the query string's values, req.body the body, and req.method , req.path and req.headers the rest; route['/items', 'POST', add] answers a method other than GET. Reference: spec section 13 (web) and book chapter 12.

Web: responses and submodules The blocks that start a server or reach another host are built by the book's verification but not run; the others run. Every kind of response a route can return: use web, frame fn plain[req] return text['ok'] fn markup[req] return html['ok'] fn moved[req] return redirect['/'] fn missing[req] return respond[404, 'not here'] fn packed[req] return msgpack[map[status = 'ok']] fn table_out[req] return arrow[frame.load['data.csv']] fn raw[req] return bytes['raw'] fn numbered[put, n] for i in range[n] if not put['line `i`\n'] return fn flow[req] return stream[numbered, int[req.query.n]] route['/plain', plain] route['/markup', markup] route['/moved', moved] route['/missing', missing] route['/packed', packed] route['/table', table_out] route['/raw', raw] route['/flow', flow] serve[3000] stream[numbered, n] answers at once and then calls numbered[put, n] as the response is sent: each put sends a chunk as it is put, and answers whether the reader still listens, so numbered stops when they have gone. Both modes answer every one of these alike, to the byte. A server's options are serve 's and a route's: the sites whose pages may call the app, a directory of files for the addresses no route answers, and how often each client may call a route: use web fn api[req] return json[map[ok = 'yes']] route['/api', api, limit = 60] serve[3000, cors = ['https://app.example.com'], files = 'public'] A route's handler is handed its request and nothing else, so it opens what it needs itself. Every connect to one URL in a program is one handle, so the handlers share its pool — and a query that fails while the database is away is the handler's to answer: use web, db fn count[req] conn = connect[env['DATABASE_URL', 'sqlite://app.db']] q = query[conn, 'SELECT count(*) AS n FROM trades'] if not q.ok return respond[503, q.reason] return text['trades: `q.n[0]`'] route['/count', count] serve[3000] A form's fields arrive in req.form and its files in req.files , each a copy the handler reads by its path . An API has no page session, so it says who calls it with a token: sign gives one, and verify reads its claims back — or says why not: use web, web.auth secret = 'a-secret-of-at-least-thirty-two-chars' token = sign[map[user = 'alice'], secret] claims = verify[token, secret] log[str[claims.user]] log[verify[token, 'another-secret-of-thirty-two-chars!!'].reason] alice the token's signature does not match A mailer is made from web.mail , once for the whole program as a connection is, and its messages come from its user, an address; mail[mailer, to, subject, body] sends one, held to a handler's commit (chapter 12): use web, web.mail smtp['smtp.example.com', 587, 'ops@example.com', 'pass'] serve[3000] A socket reads a live feed. Each failure is the call's error value — here, a server that does not answer — so a program decides what to do about it: use web, web.ws feed = socket['ws://127.0.0.1:1/stocks'] if feed.ok send[feed, 'subscribe'] log[recv[feed, 5]] close[feed] else log['no feed: `feed.kind`'] no feed: socket A program asks another server with request — a GET, or any method with a body. Its answer is a record, whatever the status: status , body and headers . Only a request that got no answer is an error value, as here: order = map[symbol = 'AAPL', side = 'buy'] r = request['http://127.0.0.1:1/orders', 'POST', encode[order]] if not r.ok log['not placed: `r.kind`'] else if r.status eq 201 log['placed: `r.body`'] not placed: http A key goes in its headers, and a body that is JSON is sent as JSON: token = env['API_TOKEN'] key = map[authorization = 'Bearer `token`'] r = request['https://api.example.com/orders/7', 'DELETE', headers = key] log[r.status] A query, a form, files and a timeout are options too, and save keeps a download's bytes in a file: pw = 'not this one' found = request['https://api.example.com/search', query = map[q = 'crow lang'], timeout = 5] signed = request['https://example.com/login', 'POST', form = map[user = 'ada', password = pw]] sent = request['https://example.com/upload', 'POST', form = map[title = 'July'], files = map[report = 'july.csv']] logo = request['https://example.com/logo.png', save = 'logo.png'] log[logo.status] Reference: spec section 13 (web), and Requests.

Views: the whole element vocabulary Every HTML element Crow knows, in one view. Built by the book's verification, not served. A driver written in Crow keeps a connection and sends statements on it (docs/db-in-crow-design.md): notes on the connection by key — a query's id for a cancel later — and one request on the connection already open, kept alive for the next. use sys s = open['db.example.com', 8123, false, 5.0] note[s, 'query', 'crow-local-4242-1a2b'] log[noted[s, 'query']] a = exchange_on[s, 'db.example.com:8123', 'POST', '/?default_format=TabSeparated', [], bytes['SELECT 1'], now[] + 30.0, true] log[a.status] A standard module that hands functions to a model, or runs one by its name, has two operations over functions (spec section 13, sys; the compiler lowers each to what inference knows, so both modes agree): describe answers a function's description — its name, the comment above it, its parameters with the word errors use for each kind and its default, what it answers — and apply calls a function with its arguments read by name from a parsed value, answering the value encoded as text, or an error of kind call where an argument is missing or of another kind. A list literal of functions is a group, each held by its name, so a loop over it describes and calls each. use sys --- the forecast for a city fn forecast[city, days = 2] return '`days` days of sun in `upper[city]`' --- the time somewhere fn clock[zone] return 'noon in `upper[zone]`' d = describe[forecast] log[str[d.name]] log[str[d.doc]] log[str[d.params[1].name]] log[str[d.params[1].takes]] log[int[d.params[1].default]] log[apply[forecast, json['{"city": "Oslo", "days": 3}']]] missing = apply[forecast, json['{"city": "Oslo"}']] log[missing.kind] for tool in [forecast, clock] log[str[describe[tool].name]] log[apply[clock, json['{"zone": "Rome"}']]] forecast the forecast for a city days an int 2 "3 days of sun in OSLO" call forecast clock "noon in ROME"

t: A language model as a connection: `use llm`

A language model as a connection: use llm reach makes a model a connection — anthropic://<model> , or openai://<host>/<model> for any server speaking the OpenAI chat completions (Ollama, vLLM, OpenRouter, LiteLLM). The key is read from the environment when a call is made; a local host needs none. What reach answers is a description the program can read: use llm m = reach['openai://localhost:11434/llama3.2'] log[m.provider] log[m.model] log[m.base] log[m.key] bad = reach['ftp://somewhere'] log[bad.ok] log[bad.reason] openai llama3.2 http://localhost:11434 OPENAI_API_KEY false cannot reach 'ftp://somewhere': a model's URL is anthropic://<model> or openai://<host>/<model> A conversation is a parsed value, a list of turns, built a turn at a time: ask begins one with the user's turn, asked adds the user's next, said the model's reply, told a tool's result. A reply is a parsed value too — its text , its calls , its usage and its stop — so the builders take what chat answers: use llm talk = ask['What is the capital of Mongolia?'] log[len[talk]] log[talk[0].role] talk = asked[talk, 'And its population?'] log[len[talk]] r = json['{"text": "Let me check.", "calls": [{"id": "c1", "name": "lookup", "args": {"city": "Ulaanbaatar"}}], "usage": {"input": 12, "output": 7}, "stop": "tool"}'] talk = said[talk, r] log[talk[2].role] log[talk[2].calls[0].name] talk = told[talk, r.calls[0], '1.6 million'] log[talk[3].role] log[talk[3].id] 1 user 2 assistant lookup tool c1 chat asks the model; a server nobody answers is the call's error value, of kind llm , and so is a stream that cannot be opened ( follow ), whose pieces ( next ) and whole ( reply ) then fail with it. embed answers a matrix of embeddings from an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which Anthropic does not serve: use llm m = reach['openai://127.0.0.1:1/llama3.2'] talk = ask['Hello?'] r = chat[m, talk, system = 'Answer in one word.', tokens = 16] log[r.ok] log[r.kind] s = follow[m, talk] log[s.ok] piece = next[s] log[piece.ok] whole = reply[s] log[whole.ok] e = embed[m, ['one', 'two']] log[e.ok] a = reach['anthropic://claude-sonnet-5-5?key=CROW_BOOK_NO_SUCH_KEY'] log[a.reason] false llm false false false false cannot reach 'anthropic://claude-sonnet-5-5?key=CROW_BOOK_NO_SUCH_KEY': the key's variable CROW_BOOK_NO_SUCH_KEY is not set Tools are the functions themselves: tools = [weather] hands the function, and the module writes its schema from the function's description — the name, the parameters with the kinds inference found (what the program's calls hand them, or what the body reads them as), and the comment above the function as the description. The program dispatches the model's calls and hands each result back with told : use llm --- the current weather in a city, in °C fn weather[city] return 'sunny in `upper[city]`' m = reach['openai://127.0.0.1:1/llama3.2'] talk = ask['How warm is it in Lisbon right now?'] r = chat[m, talk, tools = [weather]] while r.ok and r.stop eq 'tool' talk = said[talk, r] for call in r.calls if call.name eq 'weather' talk = told[talk, call, weather[call.args.city]] r = chat[m, talk, tools = [weather]] log[r.ok] log[weather['Lisbon']] false sunny in LISBON act is that loop, written once in the module: the model runs its tools until it answers or a limit stops it. Each reply's calls are answered by the tools' own functions, every call answered — a name no tool has, an argument of the wrong kind and a tool's own failure are each told to the model as a failed result that says why — and the run comes back as a record: text , stop ( end , length , other , rounds , budget ), rounds , usage , talk and steps , a frame with a row per model call and per tool call. allow = [g] names the program's gates, functions of the call asked before a tool runs: a call one refuses is told to the model as a failed result rather than run, and a function that is no gate — one that takes another count of parameters or answers another kind — is the call's error. told[…, failed = true] is how a failure is told by hand; the loop is held to its limits before any model is asked: use llm --- the current weather in a city fn weather[city] return 'sunny in `upper[city]`' --- the weather may be asked for Lisbon alone fn only_lisbon[call] if str[call.name] ne 'weather' return true return str[call.args.city] eq 'Lisbon' m = reach['openai://127.0.0.1:1/llama3.2'] done = act[m, ask['Is it warmer in Lisbon or Porto?'], tools = [weather], allow = [only_lisbon], rounds = 4] log[done.ok] log[done.kind] none = act[m, ask['hi'], tools = [weather], rounds = 0] log[none.reason] ungated = act[m, ask['hi'], tools = [weather], allow = [weather]] log[ungated.reason] r = json['{"text": "", "calls": [{"id": "c1", "name": "weather", "args": {"city": "Nowhere"}}], "usage": {"input": 3, "output": 4}, "stop": "tool"}'] talk = told[said[ask['hi'], r], r.calls[0], 'no station in Nowhere', failed = true] log[talk[2].failed] false llm act[…] runs at least one round: rounds = 0 a gate takes the call and answers a bool: weather takes 1 and answers text true A subagent is a tool that runs the loop: a function the parent model calls, whose body runs act with a model and tools of its own and answers what the inner run found. A function sees no top-level name, so it reaches its model itself; trim[question] reads the question as text ( ask takes any value and types nothing); and a run that failed fails the tool, so the parent model hears a failed result that says why. The parent's steps show the delegation as one tool row; the inner run's steps are the tool's own to read: use llm --- the current weather in a city fn weather[city] return 'sunny in `upper[city]`' --- what a smaller agent finds out about a question, with the weather as --- its only tool fn research[question] small = reach['openai://127.0.0.1:1/llama3.2'] inner = act[small, ask[trim[question]], tools = [weather], rounds = 4] return inner.text m = reach['openai://127.0.0.1:1/llama3.2'] done = act[m, ask['Is it warm in Lisbon today?'], tools = [research]] log[done.ok] found = research['Is it warm in Lisbon today?'] log[found.ok] log[found.kind] false false llm The run's context and know-how are options too. keep = n cuts the tool results of rounds older than the last n to a stub naming their size, compact = n asks the model for a summary once a reply has read n tokens and goes on from the summary alone, and budget = n stops the run once it has spent n tokens, after the reply's calls are answered. skills = folder reads a folder of skills in the Agent Skills format — each a folder holding a SKILL.md : a frontmatter with its name (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, the folder's own name) and its description , then the instructions — names each in the system prompt, and lets the model load one, and the files it refers to, through the tools skill and skill_file . servers = [s] adds the tools MCP servers offer ( use mcp ), each called on its server. A skill that breaks the format's rules is the call's error, before any model is asked: use llm mkdir['ex_skills/refunds'] write['ex_skills/refunds/SKILL.md', '---
name: Refunds
description: How the shop decides a refund, and what to ask first.
---
Ask for the order number, then read its status.
'] m = reach['openai://127.0.0.1:1/llama3.2'] r = act[m, ask['May I have a refund?'], skills = 'ex_skills', keep = 2, compact = 8000, budget = 20000] log[r.reason] rm['ex_skills'] the skill refunds's name 'Refunds' does not match its folder refunds A whole agent — three tools over a shop's orders in SQLite, the refund behind a gate, every run's steps frame written to the database as a trace beside a row per run, a page over the traces with their tokens and latency charted, evals as test blocks replayed from recorded fixtures with a model as the judge, and a page that asks the agent — is examples/agent , the fourth reference app: from its folder, crow run main.co serves it, and crow test --fixtures agent/support.co runs its evals with no model (docs/agents-design.md, Traces, evals and a page). Reference: spec section 13 (llm).

Tools from other programs: use mcp The Model Context Protocol is how a harness gets tools from another program: a server offers tools, each a name, a description and an input schema, and a client lists and calls them over one HTTP endpoint, or over the standard streams of a process it starts. server names an endpoint, or by name the command that starts one (below); what it answers is a description the program can read: use mcp s = server['http://127.0.0.1:1/mcp'] log[s.url] log[s.token] t = server['https://tools.example.com/mcp', token = 'secret'] log[t.token] bad = server['localhost:8000/mcp'] log[bad.ok] log[bad.reason] http://127.0.0.1:1/mcp secret false an MCP server is reached at its endpoint's URL: localhost:8000/mcp is none — http://localhost:8000/mcp — or started as a command: server[command = 'npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-everything'] discover asks a server what it is and supports, catalog lists its tools and tool calls one by name with its arguments, a map or a parsed value, answering the text its result carries. A server nobody answers is the call's error value, of kind mcp , and so is a result the server marks an error: use mcp s = server['http://127.0.0.1:1/mcp'] d = discover[s] log[d.ok] log[d.kind] ts = catalog[s] log[ts.ok] r = tool[s, 'weather', map[city = 'Lisbon']] log[r.ok] log[starts[r.reason, 'cannot reach the MCP server']] false mcp false false true A server named by a command runs over its standard streams — the stdio transport: the process starts at the first message and stays while the thread that started it lives, each request one line on its input, the response the line on its output carrying the request's id. The same discover , catalog and tool serve it. /bin/cat echoes the request, which is a message with no result; a command the shell does not find ends before answering (and is started again at the next message); a shell loop that answers by method is a server: use mcp cat = server[command = '/bin/cat'] log[cat.command] log[cat.url] got = catalog[cat] log[got.ok] log[got.reason] gone = server[command = 'no-such-mcp-server'] log[catalog[gone].reason] log[server[command = '/bin/cat', token = 't'].reason] loop = server[command = 'while read -r line; do id=${line#*\"id\":}; id=${id# }; id=${id%%,*}; case $line in *tools/list*) echo "{\"jsonrpc\": \"2.0\", \"id\": $id, \"result\": {\"tools\": [{\"name\": \"echo\", \"description\": \"says its words back\", \"inputSchema\": {\"type\": \"object\", \"properties\": {\"words\": {\"type\": \"string\"}}, \"required\": [\"words\"]}}]}}";; *tools/call*) w=${line#*\"words\":}; w=${w# }; w=${w#\"}; w=${w%%\"*}; echo "{\"jsonrpc\": \"2.0\", \"id\": $id, \"result\": {\"content\": [{\"type\": \"text\", \"text\": \"echo: $w\"}], \"isError\": false}}";; *) echo "{\"jsonrpc\": \"2.0\", \"id\": $id, \"error\": {\"code\": -32601, \"message\": \"Method not found\"}}";; esac; done'] log[catalog[loop][0].name] log[tool[loop, 'echo', map[words = 'hi there']]] log[discover[loop].reason] /bin/cat false the MCP server answered no result cannot reach the MCP server no-such-mcp-server: the process ended a bearer token goes to an endpoint's URL: a server started as a command takes none echo echo: hi there the MCP server answered an error -32601: Method not found A Crow program becomes an MCP server with one route: answer reads the request a POST route was handed and answers server/discover , tools/list and tools/call over the functions themselves — each tool's schema from the comment above it and the kinds its parameters take, each call applied by name, a failure marked an error the model can read: use web, mcp --- the current weather in a city, in °C fn weather[city] r = request['https://wttr.in/`trim[city]`?format=j1'] return str[json[r.body].current_condition[0].temp_C] fn served[req] return answer[req, tools = [weather], name = 'weather-server'] route['/mcp', 'POST', served] serve[8000] The same program serves over its standard streams with listen in place of the route — a client starts it as a command, server[command = 'crow run weather.co'] , and reads its answers line by line; it ends when its input does: use mcp --- the current weather in a city, in °C fn weather[city] r = request['https://wttr.in/`trim[city]`?format=j1'] return str[json[r.body].current_condition[0].temp_C] listen[tools = [weather], name = 'weather-server'] An agent takes a server's tools beside the program's own: act[m, talk, tools = [f], servers = [s]] ( use llm ) adds every tool s offers, each called on the server, and a name a server's tool shares with another tool is refused before any model is asked. tests/mcp.rs drives a Crow client against a stand-in server, a stand-in client against a Crow server like the first one, and a Crow client against a Crow program serving over stdio like the second, in both modes. Reference: spec section 13 (mcp).

t: Appendix A: The Language at a Glance
x: Appendix A: The Language at a Glance The language on one page: every keyword, every operator, every form, and the four names every value carries. The names of the standard library — core builtins, module functions, elements, and layout attributes — are in The Standard Library , one page per module, generated from the compiler's own tables with an example for each. The commands are in The Toolchain . Keywords fn view struct use test declarations if else for in while control flow return break continue flow exits true false literals eq ne gt lt gte lte comparison (words, not symbols) and or not then logic and chaining in not in membership: an item, a part, a key, a mask over a column There is no class , lambda , async , await , try , catch , match , elif , null , or import — each reflex has a Crow form (Appendix B). Operators + - * / % ^ arithmetic (/ floors between ints; ^ is power) .* ./ .^ element-wise on tensors x then f[a] pipe: f[x, a], chains left to right then g[x] a chain as lines: x = …, then one step a line; a step that names x reads it where it says `expr` interpolation (inside 'single-quoted strings') --- comment to end of line No == != < > && || ! += or ternary — every one is a teaching error naming the Crow spelling. Parallel assignment exists: a, b = x, y . Forms One line for every shape the parser knows. x: Appendix B: Coming from Another Language Every language you already know has habits that Crow deliberately breaks. Most wrong reflexes below produce a compile error that names the fix, so you would find those out anyway — this appendix saves you the round-trips, and warns of the few that run and mean something else: ^ is the power, not exclusive or, and an index counts from 0. Read the six facts, then the section for your language. The six facts that cover most of it Calls use square brackets. f[x] , sqrt[9] , log['hi'] . Parentheses only group arithmetic. One string quote, and interpolation is paired backticks. 'hello name ' . No + on strings: interpolate, or join[parts, sep] . Comparison and logic are words. eq ne gt lt gte lte , and or not . No == , < , && , ! , and no += . Blocks are indentation; there is no : , {} , end , or ; . fn f[x] , if x gt 0 , else if , while , for x in xs . No lambdas, no null, no exceptions. Behavior is a named fn passed by name; failure is a value with .ok and .reason that propagates through use and refuses to decide a branch. for is an expression that runs in parallel. ys = for x in xs … x * 2 is your map ; a trailing if is your filter ; any / all / find with a named predicate are your early-exit searches. A loop whose body prints, writes or draws keeps its order, decided for you. There are no threads to write. A seventh, for anyone with a data background: an all-numeric array is a tensor ( * is matmul, .* is element-wise), and a table is a frame ( use frame ), not a matrix. (The same material, phrased for pasting into an AI assistant, lives in docs/crow-for-llms.md .) The Standard Library Every module ships with the compiler: use it and its names are there in both execution modes. Each page lists the module's functions with the book examples that use them, generated from the language specification so the two cannot drift. Core builtins need no import. Core builtins Always available, no import. The tables below are the spec's, with the book pages whose verified code uses each name. The functions available in every file without an import. These names are reserved — a definition may not reuse them (see Design Note: Names Are Never Ambiguous). Module functions ( use math , use frame , …) are in section 13. A builtin handed a number of arguments, or a kind of argument, it does not take is refused before the program runs, in both modes, naming what it takes: min['a', 'b'] is min[] takes an int and an int or a number and a number, got text and text . (The interpreter had stopped on the value while the compiled program did not build — or, for min of text, compared it.) A module's function is refused alike: mean['a'] is mean[] takes numbers, got text . A parsed JSON value is read as one type before a builtin computes with it (see JSON). An argument whose kind shows only as the program runs — an item of a list of parsed values, a cell no description typed — is read then, by the same rule. Core Function Description Example log[value] Print a value to stdout, as it shows: text bare, a number as it displays (a whole float as an int), a list as [1, 'a'] with its text quoted, a map as [key = value] , a record as Point[x = 1, y = 2] (its fields in name order; a module's record by the name it was declared by, as type names it), a value that failed as error: reason — the same in both modes, through one display ( crow_runtime::display ). To a terminal, each line as it is logged; a script whose output goes to a file or a pipe writes it in blocks — before the program sleeps, at least every tenth of a second whatever else it is doing (so a reader watching it sees each line within that), at the end, before a stop is reported, at exit and before input reads (a line at a time had been a write to the system per line); a text of 64 KB or more goes out where it lies, after what is held, never copied into the block (fasta's 125 MB section had been held twice). A parameter the body never assigns (nor an item of), never binds anew and never hands on — it is indexed, measured, walked, compared, given to a builtin that reads it, or handed to a function that only reads it in turn — reads the caller's list, map or text where the caller holds it, in both modes; any other parameter gets its own copy, so what the function does to it the caller never sees. (A call had copied every list it was handed: a long list given to a function called once per item was quadratic — revcomp's lines ran 130 times slower than the same loop without the call.) A value read for the last time moves; one read again is copied. A variable's last read — returned, pushed, assigned, handed to a function or a builtin that keeps it — hands its value on without a copy, in both modes, and so does a local of a loop's body, or the loop's variable, at its last read in a round (the next round binds it anew: spec, Scope). A text nothing else holds is changed where it lies: s = replace[s, old, new] of one ASCII character by another, and upper , lower and reverse of a text read for the last time or of another call's answer. Any other read copies, so a name still holds what it held. A value that can fail, held by a name, is read where it lies to be checked and handed on. (A function's return out had copied the list it returned — lines copied every line it read — a loop body's local was copied into the list that kept it, a file's lines held at the top level were copied whole twice by every call they were handed to, and each of twelve replace calls made a new text.) A text read by position costs what is read. A slice, a character and a length count characters, and a text holds UTF-8, where a character is one to four bytes. A text a function reads by position — a parameter, or a local it does not give a new text while the call runs — keeps, in both modes, how far its start is known to be ASCII, checked only as far as a read has needed: within that start a character is a byte, so slice[seq, i, i + k] reads k characters wherever i is, and a loop over a long text's windows is linear (each read had walked the text from its start, and counting k-mers by slices was quadratic). Past the ASCII start, a read walks only from where it ends. A slice compared with a text ( slice[seq, i, i + k] eq pat ) is compared where it lies. A width is fmt 's to give: pad is no name of the language, so a program may give it to a function of its own. Design Note: No Format Mini-Language What was considered: Python-style format specs inside interpolation ( {pnl:,.2f} ) or as spec strings ( fmt[x, '.2f'] ). Why rejected: format codes are a second grammar — cryptic single-character commands with their own parser, embedded in strings. That violates the no-DSL rule and requires memorization; nobody writes %-+8.2e without a lookup. Named arguments are ordinary Crow: self-documenting, validated at compile time (unknown names and arity are lowering errors), and guessable without docs. The trade: one-off formatting is wordier than {pnl:,.2f} . The sanctioned recovery is the named formatter ( money[x] ), which is shorter than the Python spec at the call site, has a domain name, and keeps every money field in the project formatted identically — the consistency that per-slot codes never provide. A collection builtin walks a tensor as a loop does and an index reads it: a vector's numbers, a matrix's rows. len , slice , reverse , pop and push count and keep rows, so a matrix stays a matrix — slice[m, -1, len[m]] is its last row, reverse[m] its rows backwards, pop[m] all but its last row, and a slice that holds nothing is a matrix of no rows. ( slice , reverse and pop had counted a matrix's numbers: slice[m, -1, 3] of three rows was empty, slice[m, 0, 5] stopped, reverse[m] answered its numbers backwards as one axis, which its type did not say, and the next read of a row stopped; sort[m] had sorted its numbers, 2.0 in m asked them, and join[m, sep] joined them.) A collection builtin takes the kinds its forms above say — a list, a map, text, a tensor — and any other is refused before the program runs, in both modes, naming the forms it takes: 1 in [1, 2] is has[] takes a map and text, got numbers and an int , and len[5] , keys[[1, 2]] and 'a' in m of a map are refused alike. A JSON value's kind shows only as the program runs, so len of one that is a number or a bool stops the program with the same words. (Compiled, those calls did not build, where the interpreter stopped as it ran; and len of a JSON number was 0.) All builtins are immutable. No builtin modifies its arguments. To update a variable, reassign: nums = push[nums, 4] . Both modes turn x = push[x, v] (and pop , sort , reverse , concat , set , del in the same shape) into an in-place update: the collection is moved into the operation, not copied, when the right-hand side reads x exactly once. A value goes after its last read. A variable's last read moves its value where the read can take it — into a call, out of a function — and a variable last read where nothing takes it (indexed, body[0] ; walked by a loop; measured, len[body] ) is let go after the statement that reads it, in both modes, rather than at the end of its block. A collecting loop over a list it reads for the last time takes the list's items into its body, none copied, and a list cut by slice there is cut where it lies, the list it came from let go with what it leaves. So a program that turns a big input into a series of lists holds the lists it still reads: revcomp's 254 MB input had been held beside five of its intermediate lists, each one's last read long past (1.25 GB at the peak, 0.92 GB after), and k-nucleotide's slice of the lines beside every line (645 MB, 356 MB after). Nothing a program prints changes: a value let go is one nothing reads again. Files, URLs and S3 A path is a file on this machine, a URL ( http://… , https://… ), or an S3 object ( s3://bucket/key ) wherever the program reads one — read , use io 's csv and lines , and both modules' load — and a file or an S3 object wherever it writes one ( write , use frame 's save ): bars = load['https://data.example.com/aapl/2026-07-14.parquet'] trades = load['s3://market-archive/2026/07/14/trades.csv'] r = save[bars, 's3://reports/aapl.parquet'] token = env['API_TOKEN'] fills = load['https://api.example.com/fills.json', headers = map[authorization = 'Bearer `token`']] day = load['https://api.example.com/bars.csv', query = map[symbol = 'AAPL', day = '2026-07-14'], timeout = 20] Every reader takes three options for a URL, in both modes: headers = map[…] , sent with its request — an API's key, a token; query = map[…] , its pairs added to the URL, each name and value URL-encoded ( query = map[q = 'crow lang'] asks ?q=crow%20lang , after the URL's own ?… if it has one); and timeout = seconds , how long the read waits for its answer (unless told, thirty seconds to connect and ten minutes in all; 0 is as none). A map's values go as text, each as it shows, so a map of numbers is one too ( query = map[page = 2] ). Without the key a server's refusal is the read's error ( cannot read 'https://…': the server answered 401 Unauthorized ), and so is a server that does not answer in time ( cannot read 'https://…': no answer in 20 s ). A file has none to send and an S3 object is signed with the environment's credentials, so either given an option is refused: cannot read 'trades.csv' with headers, a query or a timeout: they go with an http:// or https:// URL ; a timeout below 0 is refused too ( a timeout is a number of seconds, 0 or more — not -1 ). A table's format is its extension: .csv , .json or .parquet . A URL with none is read as the media type its server names ( application/json , text/csv , Parquet's), and failing that as its bytes show — Parquet's PAR1 , JSON's opening bracket, CSV otherwise. A JSON table is a list of records, a row each, or an object holding exactly one list of records, as an API's answer {"status": "OK", "results": [...]} does; an object holding two is refused, naming them, and json[read[url]] reads it whole. An S3 object is read and written with the environment's credentials — AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID , AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY , AWS_SESSION_TOKEN when there is one, AWS_REGION ( us-east-1 when unset) — signed as AWS's Signature Version 4 says; AWS_ENDPOINT_URL points it at an S3-compatible store (MinIO, R2) by path. Without credentials an object is read unsigned, as a public bucket's is. A URL is read, never written. What goes wrong is the read's error value, as a missing file's is, its reason naming the path: a server that answers an error ( cannot read 'https://…': the server answered 404 Not Found , and S3's own words after it), one that does not answer within 30 seconds (or its timeout ), a transfer longer than ten minutes (or its timeout ), more than 4 GB. A program's own URL, built from what a reader typed, reaches wherever it names: a served program checks it as it checks any input. The readers are written in Crow (design rule 20): the protocol is sys 's own, in src/modules/sys.co — a URL got with the options and its redirects followed, an S3 object signed with the environment's credentials as Signature Version 4 says and reached by path at an endpoint — and each reader is a few lines in its module's source ( src/modules/core.co , io.co , frame.co , math.co ) over the layer's parsers; every row above keeps its contract in both modes. Their tests are their own ( crow test src/modules/sys.co checks the signature against AWS's documented example), and tests/reader_headers.rs and tests/s3_endpoint.rs run them against servers of their own in both modes. Design Note: one load , wherever the data is. Considered: an HTTP client ( get , post ), an s3 module and a parquet module, each with its own readers. Decided: where the data is and what shape it is in are the path's, not the program's, so every reader takes a URL or an S3 object as it takes a file, and the extension names the format — one way, which a new source or format joins without a new name. A key an API asks for is part of where the data is, so a reader sends headers with its URL ( headers = map[…] , Vijay, 2026-10-01), and so is the question a URL asks ( query = map[…] , 2026-10-01); other methods, a body, a form and files are request 's (### Requests). A rehearsal ( crow check ) records a request instead of sending it. Both modes send it through the one client the readers use ( crow_runtime::sources ). read and load stay the readers: they want data, so a server's refusal is their error, where a request's record says it. request is written in Crow ( src/modules/core.co ) on the sys layer — the second standard module moved (design rule 20) and the first that reaches the operating system: its row keeps the contract above, in both modes, and its own tests ( crow test src/modules/core.co ) read a URL apart, add a query, name a part's type, decode a chunk's size and spell a timeout; tests/http_request.rs runs it against a server in both modes. The Rust client it replaced ( crow_runtime::sources::request , over ureq ) is gone, and so is ureq : the readers' remote branch ( read[url] , load[url] , S3) moved after it (Files, URLs and S3). A request's answer is kept and replayed as a statement's is ( crow test --fixtures ): crow check --record-fixtures sends the request and keeps what it answered under .crow/fixtures/<hash>.json ( {"kind": "request", "method", "url", "body", "reply": {"status", "headers", "body"}} ), and crow test --fixtures answers the request from that and sends nothing, in both modes — request and every call standing on it ( llm 's chat and embed , a reader of a URL). The fixture is named by the request as made — its method, its URL with the query, and what it sends: a body as written, a form as its encoded pairs, files by their field and path — so a changed prompt is a changed request; its headers are no part of it, and a key sent in one lands in no fixture. A request no fixture holds is, in a replay, the request's error value of kind 'http' ( no fixture holds `POST https://…` — `crow check --record-fixtures` records it where the server is ), which the test run names. In a recording a request already kept is answered from its fixture, as a statement is — delete the file to ask again. A save = path request's fixture holds the answer as the program saw it, its body empty; the file is the recording's. A reply followed piece by piece ( llm 's follow ) is not kept. A rehearsal ( crow check ) answers a request from its fixture too, where a recording kept one, and any other as a request that landed with nothing to say (crow-check.md). The fixture is asked for and kept by request 's own body, through sys 's replaying , recording , rehearsing , replayed and recorded , so the two modes cannot differ on it. Design Note: a request's fixture, keyed by what it sends. Considered: a fixture by the URL alone (rejected: every question to a model would replay the first answer); a name the program gives the request (rejected: a second way to say what the request already says); the fixtures consulted by each backend where it runs the effect (rejected: two places, two chances to differ — the body that both modes run is the one place). Considered: a word for each method — get , post , put , delete — as many HTTP clients spell them. Decided: one request with its method as text, as route['/up', 'POST', handler] names the server's (Vijay, 2026-10-01): get would be a second read , put is the name a stream's feed is handed ( fn numbered[put, n] ), and delete would stand beside the map's del ; a method as text reaches PATCH, HEAD and OPTIONS with no more names. A duration is a number of seconds, as sleep , later and every timeout take one; there is no duration kind. A list of moments is a list. A moment written as a column ( df.at = moments ) makes a moment column ( datetime , as .dtypes names it), fill fills one with a moment, a moment column's cell read one at a time is a moment — from a file, a query or a column written alike — and a moment column compares with a moment: df[df.at gt open_bell] . One moment per event. In a script now[] is the clock at the call. In a live program it is the moment the current event began — a click or a change from the page, a render, a refresh tick, a later schedule — everywhere inside it: a handler and every helper it calls, a render and every view and derivation in it. Time advances between events, never inside one, so base, anchor = head, now[] reads one clock twice and gets one answer, and two rows a handler stamps with now[] share a stamp. In the test harness the clock is the test's: it starts at the moment the first app[…] opened and moves only when the test moves it with change[a, 'now', t] . Zones are IANA names ( 'America/New_York' , 'Europe/London' ) or offsets ( '+09:00' , 'UTC' ) and are always explicit — the default everywhere is UTC. Invalid dates, unknown zones, DST gaps and text that is no time are error values of kind 'time' . Design Note: a moment is one kind. Considered: the three moments Crow had grown — the core's, a float of epoch seconds with calendar , parse_time and fmt[t, time = …] ; the frame module's, ISO text with datetime , tz and fields read from the text; and a database column's, a float again — so that df.at[0] was text from a file and a float from a query, and the functions of one refused the other. Decided (Vijay, 2026-10-06): one kind, carrying its instant and the offset it was written in, so t.year is the year it was written in and moment[t, tz = …] moves it; one name for each thing a program does with a moment — now , moment , the fields, str , fmt and the operators — and the rest parameters. So calendar , parse_time , datetime , tz and the duplicate time[] are gone, outright, and fmt 's time = option is style = : the one renderer's option for one more kind, not a renderer per kind. Rejected: a float everywhere, which loses the zone a text was written in; text everywhere, on which nothing computes; a duration kind, where seconds already serve. float[t] and moment[seconds] are the bridges for a program that keeps a time as a number, as finch's simulated clock does. Freshness: captured Values read from the outside world remember when they arrived: Function Description Example captured[x] The moment x was read from outside (a moment, so ordinary arithmetic applies). A value computed here has no capture moment: the answer is an error value with kind = 'no_capture' Moments and freshness px = query[conn, 'SELECT last FROM ticks WHERE symbol = ?', [sym]] if now[] - captured[px] gt 10.0 return error['price is stale — not trading on it', 'stale'] place_order[sym, px.last[0]] Readers stamp: query , read , input , ls , env , shell , csv , lines , load (frame and math), fetch , recv . Only a successful read is stamped — captured[] of a failed read propagates the read's own error. Reading a field of a captured value keeps the capture ( px.last is as old as px ); arithmetic does not — a computed number is a new value, not a remembered one. crow check covers that gap statically: a reader value that flows through computation into a decision without any freshness guard is reported (see crow-check.md ). Design Note: Freshness Lives at the Boundary What was considered: propagating capture time through every operation so a derived value is as old as its oldest input — provenance as a sibling of the error system. Why it was rejected: compiled Crow stores plain numbers as bare machine values with nowhere to keep a header; carrying age through arithmetic would mean boxing every scalar, forfeiting exactly what compiled mode is for. The interpreter could do it (measured: ~4-5% on a scalar-heavy loop), but the two modes must agree, so the feature would have been interpreter-only. Why this design: freshness is tracked where data enters and checked before it is trusted — which is what every system that got burned by stale data already does: HTTP's Age header, ROS message stamps, dbt source freshness, stream-processing watermarks. The flow-through-computation case moves to crow check , which is the same answer compiled languages reached for taint tracking: runtime labels stayed in interpreted languages, while compiled ones (Java's Checker Framework, FlowDroid) moved propagation into static analysis. Deferred: declarative thresholds on the reader itself (dbt's warn_after shape), which would fit a future store declaration. Design Note: Adopting External Ground Truth A remote system's state cannot be made atomic by any language. Observations of it are delayed and transiently wrong — a position row reads flat for a moment while a fill settles, an order looks missing before it appears. The doctrine: never act on an external absence until it has been stably absent. A grace window is freshness inverted — where captured asks "is this recent enough to trust?", adopting an absence asks "has this been true long enough to believe?": if flat[position] and now[] - first_seen_flat gt 15.0 mark_closed[sym] The authoritative source is the external system, not a cached row derived from it: derive closure from order status and fills, not from a position snapshot. No primitive can enforce this — it is a modeling rule, and the reason it is written down here is that every system that skipped it rediscovered it as an incident. Design Note: A Moment Was a Number Superseded on 2026-10-06 by "a moment is one kind" (Moments, above): a moment is a kind of its own, an instant and the offset it was written in. This note is kept for what it decided first and what still holds. What was considered: the design before it — now[] / date[] returning component maps and elapsed[a, b] returning a duration map. It could not express a named timezone, parse a timestamp, add a duration, or compare two moments directly; worse, now[] built its components in machine-local time while date[] timestamped at UTC midnight, so mixed arithmetic was already silently wrong by hours. What it decided: a moment as epoch seconds, so that comparison, subtraction and "ten seconds before the bell" were ordinary arithmetic on floats, with calendars and zones as named-argument functions. What still holds: a duration is a number of seconds, with no duration kind; zones are always explicit and the default is UTC — machine-local time is absent by design, since "correct on my laptop, wrong on the UTC server" is the classic deploy-day bug, and a language that makes the timezone explicit never has it. elapsed , date and today went with the component maps: a moment subtracted from a moment is the seconds between, moment[…] makes a date, and fmt[now[], style = 'date'] is today's. math.stats Descriptive statistics, correlation, tests, and fitting over tensors and frame columns. Import with use math.stats . Functions become top-level after import. Function Description Example median[x] Median of a 1D array Statistics: use math.stats std[x] Population standard deviation Statistics: use math.stats var[x] Population variance Statistics: use math.stats percentile[x, p] p-th percentile (0-100) with linear interpolation Statistics: use math.stats zscore[x] Z-score normalization: (x - mean) / std → returns array Statistics: use math.stats corr[x, y] Pearson correlation coefficient between two arrays Statistics: use math.stats cov[x, y] Population covariance between two arrays Statistics: use math.stats ttest[x, y] Welch's two-sample t-test → returns map with t and p Statistics: use math.stats linreg[x, y] Simple linear regression → returns map with slope , intercept , r2 Statistics: use math.stats chisq[observed, expected] Chi-square goodness-of-fit test → map with chi2 , p Statistics: use math.stats anova[g1, g2, ...] One-way ANOVA → map with f , p Statistics: use math.stats kstest[data, dist_name] Kolmogorov-Smirnov test → map with d , p . Distributions: "normal" , "uniform" Statistics: use math.stats fit[data, dist_name] Distribution fitting (MLE) → map of parameters. Distributions: "normal" → {mu, sigma} , "exponential" → {lambda} , "uniform" → {a, b} , "poisson" → {lambda} Statistics: use math.stats A statistic of no values is NaN . The series a function pairs up ( corr , cov , linreg , chisq ) are one length, percentile 's p is from 0 to 100, anova compares two groups or more, and kstest and fit know the distributions above; anything else stops the program with the reason (see When a Program Stops). They had answered NaN , 0.5 or an empty map. The module is written in Crow ( src/modules/stats.co , design rule 20): each statistic is a formula over the math builtins — a median the middle of sort , a variance the mean of squared distances, a regression its sums of products — and the tests' p-values are the t, F and chi-square distributions written over the sys layer's betainc and gammainc , which stay validated kernels. Its functions are its declaration (section 13's opening; anova , whose arguments are the groups, keeps its row), typed by their use in both modes; its tests are the module's own ( crow test src/modules/stats.co ): each statistic at known values, and its laws over a spread of inputs (a median is the 50th percentile, a series' covariance with itself is its variance, a correlation is symmetric and within −1 and 1, a z-score keeps nothing of the scale, a line through its own points has r² 1). use math use math.stats x = linspace[1, 10, 10] log[median[x]] --- 5.5 log[std[x]] --- 2.872... log[var[x]] --- 8.25 log[percentile[x, 25]] --- 3.25 z = zscore[x] --- mean=0, std=1 y = linspace[2, 20, 10] log[corr[x, y]] --- 1.0 (perfect correlation) log[cov[x, y]] --- 16.5 result = ttest[x, y] log[result.t] --- t-statistic log[result.p] --- p-value Generated by crow test --docs --write from the language specification, section 11 and 13. math.nn Activation functions, losses, and a linear layer for small networks with autograd. Import with use math.nn . Functions become top-level after import. Activations: Function Description Example relu[x] Rectified linear unit: max(0, x) element-wise (NumArray) Neural-network building blocks: use math.nn sigmoid[x] Sigmoid: 1/(1+exp(-x)) element-wise (NumArray) Neural-network building blocks: use math.nn softmax[x] Softmax: exp(x)/sum(exp(x)) with numerical stability (NumArray) Neural-network building blocks: use math.nn gelu[x] Gaussian error linear unit element-wise (NumArray) Neural-network building blocks: use math.nn Loss functions: Function Description Example mse[pred, target] Mean squared error (Float) Automatic differentiation · Neural-network building blocks: use math.nn crossentropy[logits, targets] Cross-entropy loss with log-sum-exp stability (Float): logits [classes] with one target, or [batch, classes] with a target per row, each a class from 0 up to classes − 1 Neural-network building blocks: use math.nn bce[pred, target] Binary cross-entropy with clamping (Float) Neural-network building blocks: use math.nn Layers: Function Description Example linear[x, w, b] Linear layer: x @ w + b (NumArray) Neural-network building blocks: use math.nn math.nn is written in Crow ( src/modules/nn.co ) over the math builtins, the first of the standard modules that are (design rule 20): each function is the formula the table above states — relu is clip[x, 0.0, inf] , sigmoid is 1.0 / (1.0 + exp[-x]) , crossentropy the mean over the rows of log(sum(exp(row))) − row[target] with the row's largest score taken out of the exponentials first — and each is its own declaration (section 13's opening): what it takes is what its formula takes (a tensor, which a list of numbers becomes where the formula computes with it), what it answers its formula's, how it fails its formula's words, on the program's line. The module is inlined into every program that imports it and runs in both modes as the program's own functions do; under grad its formulas are differentiated as any function is, so no rule of their own exists to disagree with them (Automatic Differentiation). Its tests are its own: crow test src/modules/nn.co runs the formulas at known values, their laws over a spread of inputs, and a gradient through every one against central differences. Shapes mse cannot broadcast or linear cannot multiply ( x and w matrices, x 's columns as many as w 's rows), two lengths given to bce , and a crossentropy target that is no class (or not a whole number, or one too few or too many for the rows of logits) stop the program with the reason, on the line of the call in the program (see When a Program Stops): linear: x has 3 columns and w 2 rows — x * w needs them equal , crossentropy: target 7 is not a class of 3 (0 to 2) . Design Note: a module written in Crow declares its functions by writing them. Considered (decided 2026-10-04, undone 2026-10-18): the builtin table stating every builtin's contract whether its body is Rust or Crow — a row per Crow-written function, the arguments read as the row's parameters take them (a list of numbers converted to a tensor), a misuse refused with the row's own words ( relu[] takes numbers, got an int ), a value JSON can hold handed to the function as its JSON text and read back with json[…] . Rejected now: the compiler then names every module's function (design rule 24), a module cannot be written without a row written in Rust beside it, and the row was a second signature that drifted from the function's. Decided (2026-10-18): a module's exported functions are its declaration (section 13's opening) — inlined where the program reaches them, by a bare name, the module's path, an alias, or as a value, and typed by their use, a copy per signature; a helper begins with an underscore. A misuse is refused where the formula first cannot take the kind, the refusal naming the function the program called and the program's line ( in relu: clip[] takes numbers, got an int ); the body's own stops name that line too, never a line of the module's source. A module's function is read in the module's own scope: the program's functions, imports, aliases and elements are invisible in it — the protocol's local lines , indexed lines[0] , stays its local in a program with a lines of its own, and a program names its functions as it likes (parity 162) — and a module's functions are inlined only where the program reaches them: a program that uses math without load carries none of the protocol. A function that reads a value JSON can hold ( sign 's claims, msgpack 's value) takes the value the program holds and reads it as its JSON inside ( json[encode[claims]] ). The rows left (an effect's, a rest parameter's, a driver's) keep the earlier rule until their phases; the IR verifier holds each one's function to its row. use math use math.nn x = linspace[-2, 2, 5] log[relu[x]] --- [0, 0, 0, 1, 2] log[sigmoid[x]] --- [0.119..., 0.269..., 0.5, 0.731..., 0.881...] log[softmax[x]] --- probabilities summing to 1 pred = linspace[0.1, 0.9, 3] target = linspace[0, 1, 3] log[mse[pred, target]] --- 0.00667 input = reshape[linspace[1, 4, 4], 2, 2] w = eye[2] b = ones[2] log[linear[input, w, b]] --- input + bias Generated by crow test --docs --write from the language specification, section 11 and 13. The frame is whatever holds it — a variable, a record's field ( book.prices.doubled = … ), a list's item — and a function writes the frame it was handed, its caller's copy untouched. A column written through a record's field or a list's item is read as the program runs: the field's type is every record's and the item's every item's, so neither can carry the column, and the frame there is open from that line on (as a frame whose columns show only as it runs is). After a dot, a column's name reads as text does: a backtick inside it is an interpolation, so df.lag_ k = … writes the column named by the text lag_ and k , and df. name = … the column a variable names; read the same three ways ( df.lag_ k , `df.`name ). A name no dot can write — a header with a space, a keyword — is reached through the marks, df. 'in px' , and that is the escape, not the idiom. A computed name is a frame's alone: a record's fields are fixed before the program runs (`.`f of a record is refused), and a map's key is m[key] . Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-20): the dot writes, as it reads; after a dot a name reads as text does, a backtick inside it an interpolation; with is removed from the language (an unknown name, as every removed builtin is). A column handed to sum , mean , min or max holds numbers, and a missing cell stops the program as it does where numbers are taken. The same in both modes. Design Note: pivot reshapes, group aggregates. Considered: pivot[df, rows, cols, values, how = 'sum'] , a pivot table that aggregates the rows sharing a pair, as a spreadsheet's does and pandas's pivot_table . Decided (2026-10-02, with the frame work): one way to aggregate — group — and one way to reshape; a pair two rows share stops the program, naming the group that aggregates it. Rows and columns come in ascending order of their cells, where group keeps the order first seen: a pivot is read as a table, and its days and symbols are looked for by their order. Design Note: percentiles are words, keys are lists, and the other names are the old ones. Considered, for a percentile, ['px', 'quantile', 0.9] — a list holds one kind, and 'quantile 0.9' as text — a name with a space in it. Decided: 'p90' , one word for the 90th percentile, as a column is named by it ( px_p90 ); 'median' is 'p50' by its own name. Considered, for a join on several keys with an as-of clock, pandas's and polars's by = beside on = . Decided: one list of keys, the last the clock — join[bars, signals, ['symbol', 'at'], 'asof'] reads as the match it is. Considered, for a conditional column, a new word ( pick , choose ); decided: where , math's word for the same operation over tensors — one name, the kinds picking the row. Considered, for the reverse of pivot , pandas's melt and polars's unpivot ; decided: unpivot , naming its two new columns variable and value as both do, so a program ported from either keeps its names. Considered, for rows without a missing cell, dropna ; decided: complete , the word the masks section already used for them. A bucket's edge is the local midnight of the moment's own offset (a day in New York starts at 04:00Z), where pandas floors a zone-aware moment in UTC: a bar is drawn on the exchange's clock, and a moment carries the offset it was written in for this. A fill by direction is fill[df, col, how = 'forward'] , since fill[df, col, 'forward'] would be the text in a column of text. A text function over a column keeps its name, as the arithmetic operators keep theirs; len of a column stays its row count. Design Note: the frame module is held to pandas. tests/parity/185_frames_held_to_pandas.co computes 59 cases over four tables ( tests/frames/data/ ) and compares each with what pandas 3.0 answered ( tests/frames/expected/ , written once by tests/frames/reference.py ): loading and its kinds, select , six filters, five sorts, head and tail , four groups, a pivot, running, trailing, shifted and ranked windows, the four joins, stack , three fills, unique , rename , a computed column, reductions, moments moved between offsets, and quoted cells read and written back — every column, kind and cell the same, in both modes (2026-10-06); and, since 2026-10-07, the other aggregates (a median, percentiles, the deviation, first and last, distinct), windows of them trailing and running and over a span of six hours, sorts on two and three keys, joins on two keys of every kind, distinct rows, an as-of join, six-hour buckets and the bars over them, text and a moment's fields over a column, an unpivot, fills by direction, complete rows, a conditional column and casts. What that round found: pandas's rolling kernels compile to fused multiply-adds, so a deviation or a percentile agreed to twelve digits and not the last — the runtime's mul_add now computes the same rounding, and a window whose squared sum collapsed is computed afresh as pandas's is. What it found and changed: a CSV column of true / false had loaded as text (so save then load lost the kind) and a quoted cell had been split at its comma; the sort was unstable and a missing int cell sorted as 0 — now stable, missing cells last either way, as pandas sorts them (polars puts them first, Postgres first or last by direction: one rule was needed, and the one that keeps the present cells together was taken); every aggregate of group was a float and a sum over text silently 0; a window's sum over ints was a float; unique answered text for every column, and gave up scanning after a long stretch without a new cell; a right or outer join's unmatched row had lost its key; a sum over floats differed from pandas and numpy in the last digit — a group or window total is now compensated as pandas keeps one (Kahan, with pandas's separate compensations for the cells added and taken off, and its exact answer for a window whose cells are all one value), and sum[t] adds as numpy does, pairwise; and, in the compiled program alone, a moment cell read one at a time was seconds where the interpreter read its text, a field of a moment that can fail ( tz 's answer) did not build, [1, 2] written as a column made a column of floats, a list a function started empty and pushed onto did not build, and a list of a loaded file's cells, read one at a time, did not join . And in crow test alone, window[…, by = …] and request[…, timeout = …] were refused in every test block: the runner desugared the program twice, and the options filled in once were too many arguments the second time. Where pandas has a choice, the spec's is taken, and the script says so: groups in the order first seen ( sort=False ), a trailing window over the rows there are ( min_periods=1 ), rank sharing a rank between equal cells ( method='min' ), the population deviation ( ddof=0 ), a right frame's duplicate column named _right , and a right or outer join compared sorted, since pandas orders those rows by the right frame or by key where Crow keeps the left frame's order and appends the unmatched. Not compared: stats , a display, and fill of a moment column, which neither side needed. Design Note: a window is a frame's, an indicator a series's. Considered: leaving trailing aggregates to the market package's indicators ( sma[bars.c, 3] is a trailing mean over one series), so that a frame has no second way to a moving average. Decided: window computes within a frame's partitions, in its order — one column holding a series per symbol, each windowed on its own — where an indicator takes one series; over one series, sma[df.close, 3] and window[df, 'close', 'mean', n = 3] agree. A trailing window's first rows are the rows there are, as SQL's window frames give them (pandas leaves them empty until the window fills). A frame's type is its columns. A frame built in the program ( frame.new[] , a column written under a name the program writes), a query a database described (see db, Typed cells), and a frame derived from either through select , a mask ( df[mask] ), sort , head , tail , fill , stack , join , rename , group or pivot carries its columns in its type, each with its cells' type (a column written from another keeps its cells' type; a pivot's rows column, and its others as they show). A column written under a name the program computes ( df. name = xs ) leaves the columns the type knows and makes the frame open : a column it cannot name may be there. A column written binds the frame anew: after df.x = xs , df has x from that line on, and before it the frame it was. Where branches, or a loop's rounds, meet, a frame has the columns they all give it; a column only some add may be there, and is read as the program runs. A function handed frames of different columns is a copy per set of columns, so it reads the columns each call hands it. Where a frame's columns are all known, a column it lacks — read as df.x , named where select , sort , fill , rename , group or join takes a column, or named by a table ( key , mark , delta , hide ) or a chart ( candles , lines , bars_y ) — is refused before the program runs, in both modes, with the columns the frame has ( frame has no property or column 'cost' — its columns are 'price' , and, read in a function, the parameter the frame was handed as); the stop above is for a frame whose columns show only as it runs (a file load reads then, a query no database described, a column a variable names). A frame loaded from a file has the columns the program reads. frame.load cannot see a file's columns before the program runs, and neither can the program state them: the reads of the frame's cells say what they are. A cell walked and handed to upper , or to a function that reads it as text, is text; one met as a number — compared with one, added to one, halved — is a number, held as floats whichever the file wrote, so q gt 20 holds for a file's 20.5 and q / 2 of its 7 is 3.5 , as a variable that may hold a float divides (§1); one handed to what takes nothing but an int — a position, xs[q] , or head , repeat , slice — is an int; one decided on is a bool; one met beside a moment is a moment. A function the cell is handed to says what its own body reads the parameter as. The frame is held to that shape where it is bound, before any cell is read: a column missing, or holding another kind — numbers where the program reads text, text where it reads numbers, floats where a position reads ints — stops the program there with the column, what it holds, what the program reads and the read that asked ( column 'slot' holds floats where the program reads ints (a position in labels at line 12) ), the same words in both modes. A column of whole numbers the program reads as numbers is widened to floats at the load, exactly: a whole number beyond 2^53 stops the load there rather than lose digits (read it with int[…] where it is compared). From then on the frame's cells are typed, in both modes, and nothing is read first — each a cell that can be missing, since a file's cell can be empty and a record's field null: read one at a time, a missing one is an error value of reason missing (below; the reads had typed the cells plain, and a missing one had been read as '' or NaN with .ok true, in both modes). A column the program writes on the frame ( df.when = … ) is the program's from then on: what it reads of it after the write — on the frame, on one a verb derives from it, in a function it is handed to — says nothing of the file, which need not have it (a column of moments written and compared had been asked of the file, and the load had stopped: the frame has no column 'when' ). A column no read says anything of stays as it comes, a parsed value read as its use implies where it is used (see JSON). A column read as two kinds — text here, a number there — is refused before the program runs, naming both reads. A page's data source ( fetch[url] , poll[url, seconds] , ui) is such a frame too: its reads say its columns, the fact carries them to the session, and the answer is held to them where it arrives — its records a frame, a column of whole numbers read as numbers floats, an answer of no records the table with no rows yet — before the page shows; what is not what the page reads (no answer, no JSON, a column missing or of another kind) stops the session there, told to the reader as a handler's stop is, the reason in the server's log with the column, what it holds, what the program reads and the read that asked — the same in both modes. fn label[t] return upper[t] df = frame.load['orders.csv'] --- sym is text, qty a number: the reads below say so labels = for t in df.sym label[t] for q in df.qty if q gt 20 log[q] Design Note: a loaded frame's columns are what the program reads, not what it writes. Considered: the program stating a column's type ( columns = map[sym = 'str'] , in the words type answers) or showing it by a sample value ( map[sym = '', qty = 0] ). Rejected: each is a second way of saying what a value already says, and the sample asks the programmer to invent one. Considered: reading every cell first, as a parsed value's (the way until 2026-10-08). Rejected: the program did nothing wrong, and the compiled program had not held a function handed such a cell. Decided: the reads say the columns, the file is held to them where it is loaded, and a column no read types stays as it comes. Considered, and built for a day: a cell compared with an int held as ints, so a file's 20.5 stopped the load where the program wrote q gt 20 . Only a use that takes nothing but an int asks the file for ints, and the stop names that use. A page's data source is held the same way where its answer arrives, in the session both modes share (2026-10-08: the interpreter had answered an empty map and registered no source at all, and the compiled program had turned the records into a frame of its own at every render). Design Note: a frame's reassignment is a new binding. Considered: one type per variable, as every other variable has, the frame's columns joined over its assignments — which loses exactly the columns a program adds ( df.x = xs , then df.x ); and a name per shape ( df2 = … for every column added), which asks the program to rename what it changes, and makes a loop that adds columns impossible to write. Decided (Vijay, 2026-09-29): a frame variable's type is its last assignment's — a new binding where its columns change, as a Rust let shadows one — and where ways through meet it has the columns they share. Design Note: a frame operation's misuse stops the program. Considered: error values of kind 'frame' , which the table of kinds listed for filter , sort , group and join , and which the interpreter answered. Rejected: the operations are typed as giving a frame, which cannot fail, and the compiled program stopped — so a program that checked .ok worked in one mode only — and the same column the frame lacks, read as df.col , stops the program. A misuse is the program's mistake, not something it reads: an error value would carry it to wherever a decision first met it. Reading a file, load , stays an error value; a column written with values of another length than the rows stops, as a write at a position that is not there does. (Every other value's .ok is its own status: a list that did not fail is ok.) A frame shows a missing cell as missing , and a column shown as a list shows it as the error it is read as, error: missing ; a NaN a number column holds is a value, and shows as nan (until 2026-10-08 a missing cell had shown as nan too, in a text column as well). Read one at a time ( df.age[3] ), a cell of a column that can have missing cells is fallible: a missing one is an error value of reason missing , which computes and cannot be decided on (§10), so .ok guards it and a guard narrows it to its value. The columns that can are a loaded file's and a page's data source's, whose columns the program's reads type (A frame loaded from a file, above: an empty cell, a null or absent field), a database column that can hold NULL (see db, Typed cells) and the side of a join a row can have no match on — a left join's right columns, a right join's left ones, all of an outer join's. fill[df, 'age', 0] gives a column a value where it had none, and its cells are plain again, as are a column's that cannot have missing cells. A mask decides every row, so a list of values that can fail — built from such cells — is refused as one, in both modes: fill the column first, or guard each value with .ok . Handed whole to a function that takes numbers — mean[df.age] , median , sma[bars.c, 3] — or used in arithmetic — df.price * 2 , df.a + df.b — a column is its numbers, as a list of numbers is, and the answer is a tensor; a missing cell stops the program ( row 3 of the column is missing — fill the column first: fill[frame, 'column', value] ), and so does a column of text or of bools, in both modes. (Compiled, a missing cell had been read as 0 and a column of text parsed, where the interpreter stopped — or, for df.a + df.b , refused the sum.) A comparison is a mask, as above. A column written from another ( df.b = df.a ) keeps its kind and its missing cells, even when every cell is missing. Design Note: a missing cell is an error, not a placeholder. Considered: reading a missing cell as its column's placeholder in both modes — NaN in a number column, 0 in an int one, false in a bool one, nan in text — as a filter reads it, which both modes did. Honest for a number, since NaN compares as false; for an int or a bool it is a guess the program cannot tell from a value, of the kind §10 refuses elsewhere (an unmatched row's count read as 0 ). Decided (Vijay, 2026-09-25, typed frames decision 3): where the schema says a column can have missing cells its cells are fallible, and where it says it cannot they are plain, so no cell is a guess. Dynamic column names need no special syntax — a string variable works everywhere a column name does: col = 'age' sorted = sort[df, col] Design Note: No Bare-Name Column References What was considered (and originally shipped): Bare identifiers as column names — sort[df, age] , group[df, dept, [salary, mean]] — where an identifier that isn't a defined variable is treated as a column-name string. Why it was removed: Scope-dependent meaning. Adding a local variable named age silently changed sort[df, age] from a column reference into a value argument. Code broke at a distance with no error. Interpreter–transpiler divergence. The interpreter preferred the variable when one existed; the transpiler force-converted certain argument positions to strings regardless. The same program meant different things in the two modes, violating the parity rule. Violates rule 19 (no DSL). A second evaluation rule inside frame calls means a line of Crow can't be read without knowing which builtin it appears in. What to use instead: Strings for column names, expressions for computation — as specified above. One mechanism, no sugar, dynamic columns free.
