db Databases as connections: every statement through query, bulk insert, transactions, the tables a program declares, and pooling (migrations are the tool's: crow db apply). The db module provides database connectivity. Import with use db . Supports SQLite, PostgreSQL, and ClickHouse via URL-scheme dispatch. See docs/db-module.md for full architecture details. Connection use db --- SQLite conn = connect['sqlite://data.db'] --- PostgreSQL (default pool: 10 connections) conn = connect['postgres://user:pass@host/mydb'] --- ClickHouse (its HTTP interface: port 8123 when none is given) conn = connect['clickhouse://default@localhost:8123/default'] --- Custom pool size conn = connect['postgres://user:pass@host/mydb', 20] Function Description Example connect[url] Open a database connection (pool) with default pool size, checking its database holds the tables the program declares on it (The schema a program declares, below) Databases: use db · Web: responses and submodules · Working with Databases · Reactive State and Events · Slow Work and the Live Loop · Testing a Live App · Charts and Styling · Derivations · Loading and Shaping the Data · The Database Layer · Views and Live Updates connect[url, pool_size] Open a database connection (pool) with custom pool size; a pool size of 0 is the default Databases: use db · Web: responses and submodules · Working with Databases · Reactive State and Events · Slow Work and the Live Loop · Testing a Live App · Charts and Styling · Derivations · Loading and Shaping the Data · The Database Layer · Views and Live Updates describe[conn, sql] The columns a statement answers, without running it: a frame of name and type ( int , float , str , bool , datetime , with ? after a kind where the column can hold NULL); a ? placeholder stands in as NULL, and a list parameter ( IN ? ) as a list of one. What the compiler asks at build time (Typed cells, below), asked by the program: the same answer, a computed column typed and a column that can hold NULL marked, in both modes (it had answered the database's word alone — no ? on SQLite or Postgres, and on SQLite unknown for a computed column no row typed and an error for IN ? ) Databases: use db · The standard library's layer: use sys The ClickHouse driver is written in Crow ( src/modules/clickhouse.co , design rule 20, docs/db-in-crow-design.md), over its HTTP interface: clickhouse://user:pass@host:port/database names that interface, port 8123 when none is given; the native protocol's port, 9000, is no longer spoken, and a URL that names it is read as the HTTP port, which the log says once. Each statement is sent with an id ( crow-<machine>-<process>-<draw> ), its rows come back as RowBinary and are decoded by the frame_of_rowbinary kernel, typed as the server names each column; an insert goes as RowBinary encoded by the table's types; a statement a stop abandoned is killed by its id (tests/query_cancel.rs); at connect, the statements a dead run of this machine left running are swept. The server says how long it keeps a connection open (its Keep-Alive header), and the driver notes it: an idle connection past that is let go before the server closes it, not found closed under the next statement. The handle, its pool of kept connections (four, since ClickHouse runs one query on every core already), the reconnect and the cancel are crow_db 's, which calls the driver through a table of calls the program registers (the compiled program's generated functions; the interpreter's child over the program's functions). A program never imports the driver: use db carries the drivers its connection URLs name. The Postgres driver is written in Crow too ( src/modules/postgres.co ), speaking the wire protocol over sys : a connection started and authenticated — trust, a clear password, md5, or SCRAM-SHA-256 as RFC 7677 says, its proof held to the RFC's own example in the module's tests — and its backend's process and key noted for a cancel; a statement without parameters as a simple query, one with parameters through the extended protocol, each parameter typed by its kind (text, int8, float8, bool; a cast like ?::date is a cast from text) and bound as text; the answer decoded by the frame_of_postgres kernel, typed as the server names each column; a command's count from its completion; insert as COPY … FROM STDIN in the text format ( copy_of_frame ); describe from Parse and Describe without an Execute; a statement a stop abandoned cancelled by a CancelRequest on a connection of its own. tokio-postgres and deadpool are gone; the pool (ten), a handler's transaction on one connection, transact , the advisory lock around reconciling a schema and the reconnect are crow_db 's. A connection is not the program's lifetime. When the server closes it — a restart drops every one — the next query reopens it and runs, and the server log says so; a program told to stop stops the statements it had in flight on their servers (ClickHouse by the statement's id, Postgres by a CancelRequest) and waits for that, three seconds at most, before it ends: a restarted app does not leave its predecessor's queries running; Postgres and ClickHouse connections are pooled, so queries from different sessions run side by side, and sqlite is a file. Every connect to one Postgres or ClickHouse URL in a program is one handle: parts that each connect to the same server share its pool. A query nobody waits for is stopped. A background recompute whose session has gone, or whose inputs moved while it ran, stops its query on the server (ClickHouse and Postgres); so does every query in flight when a served program is told to stop — crow stop , a rebuild, Ctrl-C. A program killed outright cannot stop anything; the next run that connects to a ClickHouse server on the same machine stops the queries the dead run left behind, and the log says so. Each ClickHouse statement carries a leading comment naming the machine, the process and a number, which is how it is found again. Statements Function Description Example query[conn, sql] Run a statement; the rows it answers, as a frame Databases: use db · Web: responses and submodules · Working with Databases · Reactive State and Events · Slow Work and the Live Loop · Testing a Live App · Charts and Styling · Derivations · Loading and Shaping the Data · The Database Layer · Views and Live Updates query[conn, sql, params] The same, with a list of bind values for its ? s Databases: use db · Web: responses and submodules · Working with Databases · Reactive State and Events · Slow Work and the Live Loop · Testing a Live App · Charts and Styling · Derivations · Loading and Shaping the Data · The Database Layer · Views and Live Updates One verb runs every statement. query answers a frame: the rows a SELECT answers, the rows a RETURNING clause reads back, and an empty frame for a statement that answers none — a CREATE , an UPDATE , a DELETE . No count of rows affected is answered: a write that must say what it touched reads it back with RETURNING . The statement says whether it reads or writes, not the name. A literal statement is read by the compiler: a SELECT (without INTO ), VALUES , SHOW , EXPLAIN , DESCRIBE and a PRAGMA asked are reads ( db.read ); anything else is a write ( db.write ), RETURNING included, so a derivation may hold a literal read and a handler's writes are held to its commit (Effects Have Kinds). A statement built as the program runs — a string joined from pieces, a parameter — writes for all the compiler can tell: a derivation that hands one is refused, naming the fix, which is the literal with ? for its parameters. use db conn = connect['postgres://user:pass@host/mydb'] users = query[conn, 'SELECT * FROM users'] log[len[users]] filtered = users[users.age gt 25] query[conn, 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (id INT, name TEXT)'] gone = query[conn, 'DELETE FROM users WHERE age < ? RETURNING id', [18]] log[len[gone]] Design Note: one statement verb. Considered: exec beside query , two names carrying what the compiler needs before the program runs — the answer's kind (a count or a frame) and the effect's (a write or a read) — which every typed client has (Go's Exec and Query , sqlx, JDBC); a flag on the call. Rejected: the statement already says both, and the compiler reads literal statements anyway; the count was read in one program of the corpus; and a SELECT through exec failed on SQLite with the library's words while Postgres and ClickHouse ran it and threw the rows away. Decided (Vijay, 2026-10-19): one verb, query , a frame for every statement, the literal's first word deciding its kind, a computed statement a write. List parameters. An array bound as a parameter stands for a list: its ? becomes (?, ?, …) with one placeholder per element, on every backend. Write WHERE id IN ? and pass [[1, 3]] ; an empty list matches nothing. A list goes after IN and nowhere else: handed to another ? — x = ANY(?) — it would be sent as a row where the database wants an array, so a literal statement that does so is refused, in both modes, before it runs. The compiler asks a database about IN ? as the list of one it is sent as, IN (?) . A parameter that failed is the statement's answer. A bind value that failed — [float[entry]] where the entry is no number, or an item of a list parameter — is what query answers, with its reason, kind and trace, and the statement is not run, as any call handed a failed argument answers it (Auto-Propagation); a transaction whose function meets one is rolled back. In a handler, a write handed one stops the handler, as every effect held to its commit does (Errors in Conditions), and a read answers it. (The interpreter had stopped — cannot bind done as SQL param — where the compiled program answered the failure; compiled, a handler's read had stopped too, and a list parameter holding an item that failed had not built.) Typed cells in compiled programs. The compiler asks the program's databases what each literal query returns — a prepare on Postgres, DESCRIBE on ClickHouse — and types every column: rows.price[0] is a float, rows.n[0] an int, in the compiled program as it always was in the interpreter. A column that can hold NULL has fallible cells, in both modes: a NULL one is an error value of reason missing (see frame). The compiler reads which can from the statement and the tables' declarations — a column read from a table can hold NULL unless it is declared NOT NULL (or is SQLite's INTEGER PRIMARY KEY ); every column of the side of an outer join a row can have no match on can; an expression can where what it reads can, except count , coalesce with an argument that cannot, IS NULL and a literal, and an aggregate over no rows (no GROUP BY ) can; a function it does not know can; and a column the WHERE clause compares or asks IS NOT NULL of cannot, in the rows it keeps. ClickHouse says it itself, by a Nullable type. A statement it cannot read that way can hold NULL in every column. Connections bound to a literal URL ( pg = db.connect['postgres://…'] ) are asked in declaration order; ? placeholders and interpolated spans stand in as NULL. A database that cannot be reached at compile time is skipped. What each database answers is kept in the project's .crow/schema — a file per statement and the connection it was asked on, holding the statement and its columns' types, a column that can hold NULL marked ? ( float? ) — and when no database answers a statement its cells are typed from that record, and the build says so once; with no record they are dynamic, as below. A project may keep .crow/schema in version control, so a machine without the databases — CI, a laptop without the data — builds the program typed as it was. The frames the standard modules build are typed as they are built: doc.chapters ' title , path and part are text and its depth an int, and chart.macd 's columns are floats. Frames derived through select , a mask, sort , head , tail , fill , stack , and join keep their column types; group gives its key columns as they were and a float per aggregate ( group[df, 'dept', ['salary', 'mean']] has dept and salary_mean ); pivot gives its rows column as it was, the rest as they show; a window is typed by what it computes (frame). A frame handed to a function keeps its column types there — each call's, the function a copy per set of columns (see frame, A frame's type is its columns) — so a function reads its cells as the numbers or text they are. A cell of a column whose type nothing tells the compiler — a file loaded as it runs, a query no database answered and no record holds — is dynamic, as a value json[] parsed is, in both modes: int[c] , float[c] and str[c] read it as one type (and fail as they do on text), arithmetic or a comparison with a number reads it as a number, and giving one to a variable that holds another type reads it as that type, as a parsed value's field is read (Parsed values: read as its use implies) — a cell that is not what the use reads stops the program and says where ( a parsed value holds text 'abc' where the program reads a number (met in mul at line 6) ) — and a missing one is JSON's null , an error value of reason null . (Compiled, such a cell was read as text while the interpreter read the number: the same line meant two things.) On sqlite, a computed column ( count(*) , round(...) ) is typed by stepping the SELECT once with null parameters; when no row comes back — WHERE session_id = ? , an empty table — it is typed from the statement itself, by the declared types of the columns it reads and SQLite's rules ( round , avg and arithmetic on a REAL are floats, count and comparisons ints, || and datetime text; a parameter or NULL alone stays text). The cells of a RETURNING clause — query[book, 'INSERT ... RETURNING id', [...]] , the way to read back a row the database numbered — are typed from the table's declared columns; asking never runs a write, and never creates a sqlite file that is not there yet. Every command asks the same way — crow run , crow run -i , crow test , crow check and the app's book — so a program refused for its columns' types (a local given an int cell, then text) is refused by all of them. Set CROW_NO_DESCRIBE=1 to build without asking: no database answers then, so the records type the cells, and nothing is written. Bulk Insert Function Description Example insert[conn, table, frame] Bulk insert a frame into a table using native fast paths: the count of rows written, or, when the database refuses them — a constraint they break, a column the table lacks — an error value of kind 'db' with the database's reason, as a refused statement is (compiled, it had stopped on a Rust unwrap) Databases: use db Uses backend-specific protocols for maximum performance: PostgreSQL: COPY … FROM STDIN , the text format ClickHouse: RowBinary over the HTTP interface, encoded by the table's types ( DESCRIBE first) SQLite: Batched prepared statements in a transaction use db conn = connect['clickhouse://localhost/default'] insert[conn, 'events', events_frame] Transactions Function Description Example transact[conn, fn] The function run inside a transaction: its value, committed; or its error, rolled back Databases: use db · Working with Databases One connection is checked out, BEGIN run on it, and the function handed it as its one parameter; its statements through that parameter are the transaction's. transact answers what the function answers. A function that fails — its value an error ( return error['no', 'db'] , or a failed value it returns), or a stop inside it — rolls the transaction back, and transact answers that error (a stop stops, as a stop does); a function that succeeds commits, and a commit the server refuses answers an error of kind 'db' with the server's words. Inside a handler, whose writes through a connection are one transaction already (A handler is a transaction), transact is a savepoint on it: released when the function succeeds, rolled back to when it fails, the handler's other writes untouched. The same in both modes (parity 167). No begin / commit / rollback builtins — one way to do transactions. use db conn = connect['postgres://user:pass@host/mydb'] fn transfer[t] query[t, 'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1'] query[t, 'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2'] transact[conn, transfer] Migrations Migrations are the tool's, not a program's: crow db apply <dir> <url> runs the .sql files of a directory not yet applied on the database, in name order, recording each in a _crow_migrations table, and says how many were new. It is the apply half of crow db diff , which drafts the statements a schema change needs (below). The schema a program declares A program's tables are the ones its own statements make. Every literal CREATE TABLE a program hands a connection — query[book, 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cards (…)'] , directly or through a function the connection is handed to ( setup[book] ) — declares that table, with its columns, on that connection. A table the program also drops there ( DROP TABLE IF EXISTS scratch ) is one it remakes each run, and declares nothing. A connection the program declares no table on is one it does not own: nothing below reads or changes it, and the tables and columns a database has beyond the declared ones are its own. Opening a connection checks that the tables the database has hold what the program declares , in one of three modes, the same in both modes of running. A declared table the database does not have yet is not a difference: the program's own statement makes it as it runs, so a fresh database starts as it always has. Mode At connect Example reconcile What a table lacks is made: a declared column it does not have is added ( ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN , as the statement declares it), under the database's lock (Postgres: an advisory lock, in one transaction; SQLite: an immediate transaction), so two processes starting at once make it once. A column SQLite cannot add in place — a key, or NOT NULL without a default — is made by making a table with no rows anew. A difference reconciling cannot make without losing data or guessing — a column of another kind than declared, a NOT NULL column without a default for a table that has rows — stops the program with each difference and the statements that would make it, and nothing is made. verify Nothing is changed. The database's catalog is read (reading it needs no right beyond reading), and every declared column of every table the database has must be there, of the declared kind; a difference stops the program at connect with each difference and the statements that would mend it. Web: responses and submodules trust Nothing is read, and every start says so: schema not verified — schema = 'trust' . A column's kind is the kind Crow reads its cells as (int, float, str, bool, datetime): TEXT and VARCHAR(20) are one kind, INTEGER and TEXT two. A column declared without a type is of any kind. A program run from its source — crow run , crow run -i , crow test — reconciles: it is being developed, against a database of its own. A program crow build makes verifies: it runs where the database is someone else's to change. The crowfile's schema = 'verify' (or 'reconcile' , 'trust' ) says otherwise for both, and is what a built program starts with; the environment's CROW_SCHEMA says otherwise for one run ( CROW_SCHEMA=trust ./app ). crow db diff [file.co] prints, for each connection a program declares tables on and opens with a url it writes, the SQL that would make its database hold what the program declares: the CREATE TABLE of each declared table it lacks, the ADD COLUMN statements reconciling would run and, commented out, the changes reconciling will not make (a column of another kind, a NOT NULL column a table with rows cannot take without a default) — a draft for a migration to review. It only reads the catalog; a SQLite file that is not there is not made. $ crow db diff app.co -- sqlite://board.db (book) -- table 'cards' lacks column 'due' ALTER TABLE "cards" ADD COLUMN due TEXT; -- table 'labels' is missing CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS labels (card INTEGER, name TEXT); Design Note: schema modes. Considered: migrations alone, applied by hand, which leave a table the program changed — a new column — to fail at the first query that reads it, in development and in production alike; making the schema everywhere (Prisma's db push , Django's old syncdb ), which alters production databases the program's user has no right to alter and must not; and a check only in production. Decided (Vijay, July 2026; approved September 2026): a program's CREATE statements declare its tables; development makes what is missing under a lock, a built program checks it at connect, and crow db diff drafts the migration for what making would lose (as Terraform's plan drafts before an apply , and Prisma's db push in development meets migrate deploy in production). At connect a missing table is left to the program's own CREATE , which runs moments later: checking it there stopped every built program on its first run against a fresh database, and making it there broke a program whose own CREATE TABLE (without IF NOT EXISTS ) then found it made — the drift worth stopping for is the table that exists with other columns, which CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS silently keeps. bits An int's bits — read as two's complement of any width — and a character's code. Import with use bits . An int's bits and a character's code, for the algorithms that work on them — a set of small numbers held as one int's bits, a hash, a parser that reads character codes. An int is a whole number of any size, read as two's complement with as many bits as it needs (as Python reads one): bitand[n, -1] is n , a negative number's high bits are ones, and a shift right rounds down. Every function works identically in both modes ( crow_runtime::bits ). An int stays in 64 bits where the width rules show it fits (Numbers That Keep Every Digit); a shift left by a count nothing bounds grows, so a mask meant to stay a width is cut to it with bitand after the shift. Function Description Example bitand[a, b] The bits both have Bits and character codes: use bits bitor[a, b] The bits either has Bits and character codes: use bits bitxor[a, b] The bits one has and the other has not; bitxor[a, -1] flips every bit ( -a - 1 ) Bits and character codes: use bits bitcount[a] How many ones the bits of abs[a] hold Bits and character codes: use bits shift[a, n] a times 2^n; for a negative n , a divided by 2^-n and rounded down ( shift[-7, -1] is -4). A number past 2^32 bits stops Bits and character codes: use bits code[ch] The code of a one-character text, its Unicode scalar value ( code['A'] is 65); any other length stops: code takes one character, got "ab" (2 characters) Bits and character codes: use bits · Views: the whole element vocabulary char[n] The character whose code is n ( char[233] is 'é' ); a number that is no character's code stops Bits and character codes: use bits use bits fn queens[n, mask, row, cols, d1, d2] if row eq n return 1 count = 0 free = bitand[bitxor[bitor[bitor[cols, d1], d2], -1], mask] while free ne 0 bit = bitand[free, -free] --- the lowest free column free = bitxor[free, bit] count = count + queens[n, mask, row + 1, bitor[cols, bit], bitand[shift[bitor[d1, bit], 1], mask], shift[bitor[d2, bit], -1]] return count log[queens[8, shift[1, 8] - 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]] --- 92 Design Note: bits by name, in a module. Considered: the operators most languages write — & , | , ^ , << , >> — or the functions in the core. Decided (Vijay, 2026-10-11): named functions in a module a program imports. ^ is already the power, and symbols are shift-key syntax whose cost needs a reason a few algorithms do not give; the core is frozen by the budget rule, and code is a variable's name in many programs, so the names are taken only where a program asks for them. Before the module, a program had no way to read a character's code at all ( sys has one, and a program may not import sys ). ui Views and the element vocabulary, reactive state and inputs, the layout vocabulary, charts, and styling. Import sub-modules with use web.X . Each sub-module enables only its feature — minimal binary, minimal compile time. A sub-module's names are its own: mail and smtp are web.mail's, socket , send , recv and close web.ws's, sign and verify web.auth's — under use web alone each is refused where it is written, with the line that brings it ( smtp[] and mail[] are web.mail's: add `use web.mail` ; the interpreter had stopped as it ran, and the compiled program had not built), and each takes the kinds its rows do ( mail[] handed a column where it takes text is refused). See docs/web-framework.md for full architecture details. View Blocks — the UI Vocabulary Zone UI trees are built in view blocks — a declaration form, sibling of fn : use web, ui count = 0 fn inc[] count = count + 1 view render[] return div[ h1['Count: `count`'], button['+', click = inc] ] serve[3000] page['/', render] Inside a view, the standard HTML element vocabulary is active — plus the vocabulary's own elements: the containers stack , row , grid , overlay , scroll , the layers modal , drawer , toast , and details , summary , dropdown , divider (Revealing and framing, below) — div , span , p , h1 , h2 , h3 , h4 , h5 , h6 , button , ul , ol , li , form , a , nav , header , footer , section , tr , td , th , thead , tbody , option , textarea , label , pre , code , input , img , table — with their exact HTML names. Outside a view, those names don't exist : p = 0.95 , fn add[a, b] , and form = req.body are ordinary code in any ui program, and use ui reserves nothing in your file. Calling an element outside a view is an error that points at the fix. A child that is a list contributes each item. Markup a view or an element made is markup, anything else is text — so rows = for s in sessions over a view, then stack[h2['Sessions'], rows] , renders one row per session. Text is what log writes for the value — a number, a moment, a map, a record or a tensor as it shows, a parsed value as display shows it — and a frame's column contributes each cell, as a list does; a value that failed, a missing cell among them, shows as error: the server's log has why, as <id> with its reason in the log. A function is no child ( log shows none either), refused in both modes. Text is escaped as HTML needs, & , < and > , and an attribute's value its quotes too, by one escape both modes write with; a class joins the element's own ( stack[…, class = 'wide'] is class="stack wide" ), and one that holds no class adds none. A view called outside views — at the top level, by a derivation, handed to doc.document — answers its markup, the HTML a page would draw, in both modes (compiled, log[card[…]] and a name given a view's markup had not built). This is how a page shows many of something with their own controls; table[frame] is for cells that are values. A click can ask first : button['End session', click = end_session, confirm = 'End this session?'] shows the question in a dialog the runtime draws, and runs the handler only when the reader says yes. The server enforces it — the button offers the question, not the handler, and the dialog's own button offers the handler while the dialog is open — so the handler cannot be reached without the answer. On a table the question is a map from action to text: actions = map[Delete = delete_session], confirm = map[Delete = 'Delete this session?'] . A key presses an element : button['Save', click = save, shortcut = 'ctrl+s'] is pressed by Ctrl+S as a click presses it — the same handler with the same arguments, the question first when it asks one — and only while the page draws it and it can be pressed (shown, not disabled, not busy), so a key reaches only what the reader could click. A shortcut names its modifiers, ctrl , alt , shift and meta , then a key: a character ( '?' , '/' , 'g' ) or one of enter , escape , tab , space , backspace , delete , up , down , left , right , home , end , pageup , pagedown and f1 to f12 . Alternatives are separated by a space ( 'ctrl+s meta+s' , for the Mac's Command key), and a character shift makes is written as that character ( '?' , not 'shift+/' ). It is drawn as the browser's aria-keyshortcuts , which a screen reader announces. A key without ctrl , alt or meta is the reader's while they type in a field, Escape excepted, and Enter and Space are the focused control's; of two elements that take the same key, the one in an open dialog is pressed, else the first. The element must do something when pressed — a click , or it is a button or a link — or the program is refused, as a shortcut that names no key is, in both modes. A dialog's Close says shortcut = 'escape' , and the runtime's own question cancels on Escape. A form submits once and never reloads the page : Enter in a field presses the form's first button, and form[field['Name', name], button['Add'], submit = add] runs add when the form is submitted, by its button or by Enter, with the fields' facts already bound. Boolean attributes follow state : button['Start', disabled = starting] writes disabled="" when true and nothing when false, for disabled , hidden , readonly , required , checked , selected , multiple , autofocus . Design Note: keys press elements. Considered: keydown = h on an element or the page, the handler handed the key's name to decide what it means (ui-framework.md, Keyboard Events). Rejected: every shortcut would be an if-chain over key names, in a second kind of handler with arguments of its own, and a key could reach work no button offers, where a session accepts only what a render offered. A key that presses a drawn element keeps one handler, one set of arguments, and the reader's view of what they can do. Views compose: a view calls other views (components) and ordinary functions freely. A module can export views — importers reach them qualified, like any module name: --- cards.co view card[title, body_text] div[h2[title], p[body_text]] --- main.co use cards as c view render[] div[h1['Home'], c.card['Status', 'All good']] This is the JSX/SwiftUI boundary: the lowercase vocabulary is fixed and language-owned; your components are module-exported views. There is no way to add elements or define new vocabulary zones — see the Design Note "Names Are Never Ambiguous". Views and event handlers are the only functions that see reactive state (see Function Scope). crow fmt --fix-views migrates pre-view code ( fn declarations that build ui trees) automatically. The view tree is target-independent. A view describes a tree; what renders it is a build target. Web today; a desktop or mobile shell renders the same tree without a language change. Platforms are build targets, never dialects — there will never be a screen or window vocabulary fork. Reactive Data and Inputs ( use ui ) Top-level variables in a ui program are reactive state (see Function Scope). Three builtins declare state that the runtime keeps current, and bind inputs to it: Function Description Example fetch[url] A frame loaded once by HTTP GET when the page connects — from a URL, or from a path of this app's own ( fetch['/api/rows'] ) — held where it arrives to the columns the page reads of it (Frames: a frame loaded from a file has the columns the program reads) The standard library's layer: use sys · Views: the whole element vocabulary poll[url, seconds] The same, re-fetched every seconds ; every reader re-renders when it changes Views: the whole element vocabulary field[label, var, type = '', lines = 0] A labeled input two-way bound to reactive variable var (inside a view). type is the input's kind — 'text' , 'number' , 'date' , 'time' , 'password' , 'file' — and defaults to 'number' for an int or float variable; lines = 3 makes it a textarea Views: the whole element vocabulary · Reactive State and Events · Testing a Live App · Charts and Styling · The Element Vocabulary · Views and Live Updates slider[label, var, min = 0, max = 100, step = 1] A range input bound to a number Views: the whole element vocabulary · Reactive State and Events checkbox[label, var] A checkbox bound to a bool The Element Vocabulary toggle[label, var] A switch bound to a bool — the same binding as checkbox , drawn as a toggle The Element Vocabulary radio[options, var] One of several strings, as radio buttons: radio[['buy', 'sell'], side] The Element Vocabulary tabs[options, var] One of several strings, as a tab strip; the view shows the selected tab's content with if mode eq 'Practice' The Element Vocabulary select[options, var] One of several strings, as a dropdown list Frames: use frame · Project: Analyzing Data progress[value, max = 1.0] A progress bar The Element Vocabulary icon[name, size = 'm', color = ''] An icon from the closed set (below), sized by the type scale, colored by a token The Element Vocabulary Inputs are state: the reader's change lands in the variable, the handlers read it, and the next render draws it. There is no "value of the input" apart from the variable. Files in and out. A file is an input like any other: field['Trades', upload, type = 'file'] binds upload , declared upload = map[] . When the reader picks a file the page sends it to the server, and upload becomes a map of strings — name (the file's name on the reader's computer), type (its media type), size (its bytes, as text) and path , where the server keeps the copy — so a handler reads it as it reads any file: csv[upload.path] , read[upload.path] . The copy is the session's, kept under .crow/uploads/ (a directory that ignores itself in version control) and removed when the session ends; a handler that keeps a file copies it ( cp[upload.path, …] ). A file bigger than the app allows — 10 MB, or serve[…, uploads = 50] in megabytes — is refused before it is sent, and the reader is told the limit. The other way, download[value, name] hands the reader's browser a file: a frame as CSV, a string as text, or a picked file (a map with a path ) as that file's bytes, saved under name . It is an effect held to the handler's commit, as notice is, so a handler that stops sends nothing. In a test, change[a, 'upload', map[name = 'trades.csv', type = 'text/csv', size = '120', path = 'fixtures/trades.csv']] stands for a file the reader picked, and downloads[a] is the list of what the session was handed, each a map of name and text . Derivations — derive Facts are stored; beliefs are derived. A derivation is a value computed from facts and data sources, read like a fact, never assigned, and recomputed only when something it read changed: qty = 100 sym = 'IMRN' derive total return qty * 2 derive trades[fresh = 300] return query[book, 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE symbol = ?', [sym]] view render[] return stack[p['total `total`'], table[trades]] derive name opens a block with a return , like a view; it never takes parameters. The name reads as a variable anywhere a fact can be read — views, handlers, tests, other derivations, and the program's top level, once, as it starts, over the facts as declared (parity 168) — and in a route's handler when the app holds it (below); assigning it is an error that says what to change instead. A derivation writes no fact: only handlers write. What it reads is decided once, from the source , and both execution modes obey the same sets: the facts and derivations it names (transitively through the functions it calls, and inside interpolated strings), now[] if it or a callee reads the clock, and the tables its query literals read. A derivation recomputes, on its next read, when a handler wrote a fact it reads; a derivation it reads recomputed and its value changed — an equal number, string or bool cuts the chain (frames always propagate); a statement in this program wrote a table it reads — an insert , or a query whose statement writes ( INSERT … RETURNING id reads back the row it wrote, and the table is written all the same); it reads now[] and a tick of serve refresh passed — a click's render is not a tick, so a click recomputes only what it moved; it reads a table this program never writes — an external source — and its freshness window elapsed. fresh = N is seconds; the default fresh = 0 means as fresh as the loop : recomputed every tick, which is what a query inside a view did before. Declaring fresh is the relaxation. A derivation that fails — a query error — holds the error value; readers see .ok and .reason , and a view shows the failure in place as an id, its reason in the server's log beside the id. captured[x] on a derivation is the moment it last ran. Derivations live in a program that serves: a use ui program with a page, whose views and handlers read them, or a use web program whose routes read them — derive x needs a program that serves — … in a script, which computes a value where it needs it. In the test harness html[a] is a tick and click[a, h] marks what the handler wrote. Design: derive-design.md . Who holds a derivation is inferred from what it reads. A fact is a top-level variable; a database or socket handle is not one, and neither is a fetch / poll binding. A derivation that reads a fact a session writes — assigned by a handler or a helper a handler calls, bound to an input like field or select , or carried in a page's address (a :name of its path, a name of its url = […] ) — or a data source, whose answers land in each session that asks, or another derivation held per session, is computed per session. One that reads only constants, tables and the clock — the day's universe, the latest bar in a table — is computed once for the app and shared by every session and route, and a table write in any session, or any route, reaches every derivation over that table. (A derivation over a fact of the address, or over a source, had been counted the app's: one session's address, or the source's first answer, served to all.) crow check prints each derivation's read set and who holds it — held by the app , or held by each session (it reads 'picked', which a session writes) . A render never waits for a query it does not need. A derivation that reaches out — its read set includes a table or an external source — is computed off the render in a served page: a render reads its latest value, and when that value is stale the runtime starts a recompute on a worker thread and the render goes ahead with what it has; the page renders again when the new value lands. Staleness has a cause, and the cause decides what waits. A derivation over a table the current event wrote is recomputed before that event's render, so a click's own writes are on the page in its answer — after buy , the blotter shows the trade. One that is stale because time moved, because a fact it reads changed, or because another session wrote its table shows its last value until the recompute lands. A handler that reads a derivation always gets the recomputed value; a derivation over facts and the clock alone is computed where it is read. Before its first value, a derivation whose value can be an error — a query's frame, anything that can fail — reads as an error of kind 'pending' with the reason loading , which a view renders in place like any failed read; one that cannot fail is computed where it is first read. One recompute of a derivation is in flight at a time for each holder — the session, or the app for a shared one, so readers arriving together run a shared query once — and a value whose inputs moved while it was computed is dropped and computed once more with the latest inputs. running[x] is true while a recompute of x is in flight. The root element of a view that read a value still being recomputed carries data-crow-stale while the value is behind something the reader did — it was computed before their last change (a click or an input that moved a fact), or there is none yet — and the default stylesheet dims it after 300 ms, so a fast recompute never flashes. A value behind only the clock is not marked: a query over a playing replay's play-head recomputes each tick and is always one query behind, where marking it dimmed every pane it feeds once a second. In the test harness every event settles before the next line runs: the handler's writes, then every recompute they made stale, so a test reads the page a reader sees once the data is in. A write reaches every reader. When a handler writes a table, every session whose page read a derivation over that table renders again, recomputing it off the render: a reader sees another reader's change without waiting for a refresh tick, and without a line of code to publish it. A route's write is the same: it lands as the route's handler ends — a handler that stops too, since a store without transactions kept what it was given — and the pages over the table render again. A write made outside the program — another service, a person at a SQL prompt — is seen through fresh and the ticks, as above. A route reads what the app holds. A route has no session, so its handler reads, by name, the derivations the app holds — the one value every session reads too — and the cached rows a web service keeps in memory are a derivation: use web, db world_db = connect['postgres://app@127.0.0.1/hello_world'] derive worlds return query[world_db, 'SELECT id, randomnumber FROM world ORDER BY id'] fn cached_h[req] picked = for i in range[20] k = rand[0, len[worlds] - 1] map[id = worlds.id[k], randomNumber = worlds.randomnumber[k]] return json[picked] fn update_h[req] conn = connect['postgres://app@127.0.0.1/hello_world'] query[conn, 'UPDATE world SET randomnumber = ? WHERE id = ?', [rand[1, 10000], rand[1, 10000]]] return text['ok'] route['/cached-queries', cached_h] route['/update', update_h] serve[8080] A route's handler reads each derivation it names once, as its request begins — the app's value, computed then when there is none yet or something it reads moved — and reads that value wherever the body names it after, so a loop over the rows reads them where they lie; the same request reading it twice reads one value. A value is computed once for the requests that arrive together: a burst of requests after a write runs one query, and the rest wait for its answer. The rules above decide when it is computed again, with each request a moment of its own: a derivation over tables this program writes is kept until it writes one — worlds above until /update runs, whose write lands as its handler ends, so the next request reads the new rows — one over the clock, or over a table outside the program at fresh = 0 , is computed for each request that reads it, and fresh = N keeps one over an outside table N seconds. A route that reads a derivation a session holds is refused, with what makes it the session's: 'band' is held by each session, and a route's handler has no session — it reads 'picked', which a session writes: … . Both modes keep the app's values in the one runtime ( crow_web::live ) and read them by the same rule. Design Note: a route's cache is a derivation. Considered: a cache of its own for routes — cache[key, secs, compute] , or a module-level value a route may write — as web frameworks offer beside their database layer, and an external cache (Redis) as part of the language. Rejected: a derivation already says what a value is computed from, so the runtime knows when it is stale — the part a cache by hand gets wrong (a key forgotten at a write, a value served after the row changed). A second form would hold the same rows with the invalidation written out, and a value a route writes would be state a route can move, which routes do not have. A store shared by several processes is a database the program reads, and comes as a driver: what it holds is a table a derivation reads. Decided too: a route's handler reads a derivation once, as its request begins, as a view does, where a page's handler reads it where it uses it — a route writes no fact, so nothing it does moves the value under it, and a loop over the rows reads one value instead of asking the cache each round. Design Note: no channels. Considered: channel.join[name] , channel.send[name, message] and an on_channel handler, so that a route, a job or another process could push to the pages that joined a channel (ui-framework.md, Server Push). Rejected: a write already reaches every reader. The database is the channel, and a page learns of another's change the way it learns of its own, by reading a derivation over the table; a channel would be a second way to say that something changed, and a message pushed past the database could say what the database does not. A process outside the program is seen through fresh . Rows keep their identity through id . The live client patches the page in place: an element with an id is matched to the element with that id in the previous render, so a row rendered from data — p[' s.name ', id = 's- s.id '] — moves when its list is reordered and is dropped when its item is gone, while its neighbours are untouched. Elements without an id match by position. A node that survives a render keeps its focus, caret and scroll, so the field a reader is typing in is never rebuilt under them. The checker teaches the form. A top-level variable assigned from a query and read by a view (a launch-time snapshot) is an error in crow check ; d in the check loop rewrites it into derive x . A query inside a view never gets that far: a view reaches no database (Effects Have Kinds), so it is refused before the program runs, and the query's place is a derive above the view ( derive rows[fresh = 60] for a remote database). Tables over frames A big table pages. table[frame, page = 50] shows fifty rows at a time, says which ( 1–50 of 12000 ) and offers the previous and the next page; the frame stays on the server and only the page shown is drawn, so a hundred thousand rows cost the reader one page. Each paged table keeps its place for its session: new rows arriving keep the reader on their page, and a frame that shrinks brings them to its last one. A table of more than 1,000 rows without page is refused, as a chart over its point budget is — in its place the view shows table: 12000 rows — a table shows at most 1000 at a time: table[frame, page = 50] , never a silent cut. A test sees the first page. table[frame] renders a frame's rows. Numeric columns are typed: their cells carry the class num and the stylesheet right-aligns them with tabular figures. Six named arguments make it interactive and legible: click = handler sends the row's key to the handler when a row is clicked ( fn focus[symbol] ), key = 'col' names the column whose cell is sent (the first column by default; a numeric key travels as a number, a text key as a string), mark = 'col' names a column whose truthy cells put the class marked on their row, tinted by the stylesheet, delta = ['pnl', 'pct'] names columns whose cells are colored by sign ( up / down ), actions = map[Replay = replay, Delete = ask_delete] adds a trailing cell of buttons to every row, each sending the row's key to its handler, and hide = ['id'] keeps columns out of the table that stay in the frame — the key column, a helper. In the test harness click[a, ask_delete[3]] presses a row's button. A reader can sort a table. table[frame, sort = true] makes each header a button: pressing it shows the rows in the order of its column, ascending, and pressing it again, descending. Numbers sort as numbers and text alphabetically; missing cells come last either way, and equal cells keep the frame's order. The session keeps each sorted table's order, as it keeps a paged table's page, and a sorted table that pages pages through the sorted rows. The frame itself is untouched: sort[df, 'col'] orders the program's data, and the table's sort orders only what the reader sees. The sorted header carries aria-sort and an arrow. sort is written true or false , and a test sees the frame's own order. Design Note: no filter on a table. Considered: table[frame, find = true] , a search box that keeps the rows holding the typed text in any shown column (ui-framework.md, Table Features). Rejected: filtering is the program's, over its frame — a field bound to a fact and a derivation that filters by it — which says which columns to search and how to match, where a table's own box would decide both for every table and be a second way to filter a frame. Sorting is the table's because its headers are: nothing in the program draws them. Sliders slider[label, var, min = 0, max = 100, step = 1] is a range input bound to a reactive variable, exactly as field binds a text input. A handler reads the variable when the reader acts (a Seek button beside the scrubber). A bound input keeps its variable's type: text typed into a field bound to an integer becomes an integer (a float is truncated), a float variable gets a float, a bool variable gets a bool, and text that does not parse leaves a number alone. When a handler assigns to a bound variable, every field bound to it shows the new value on the next render; only the input the reader is typing in keeps its draft. Handlers and their helpers A view sees reactive state, a handler moves it, and a function a handler calls that assigns a module-level variable is a handler too — its own part's, or one of a part it uses ( session.picked = symbol in the scanner's part) — it joins the handler class in both renderers, so fn restart[] may call fn rewind_to[t] and the write lands in state. So does one that acts for the session — says a notice , signs the reader in or out, hands a download , sends mail — itself or through a function it calls, so what it does waits for its handler's commit. A pure helper (one that assigns no module variable) keeps its own scope. A helper a handler calls sees what the handler has written so far, and the handler sees what the helper wrote when it returns, in both modes — derivations included: a derivation the handler reads after a write to what it reads, its own or a helper's, is the recomputed one ( clock.jump[t] , then clock.head is t ). A helper that reads state and assigns none is a derivation, not a function: derive band computes the price band from the scanner's config, and the handlers read band . A function reading a derivation is refused with that advice — by crow run , crow test and crow check alike, which pass every program through the same checks before doing anything else. Reactive state may be an array, a map, a record or a list of records, or a frame; the compiled program keeps each fact in a typed field of its own, which its handlers, helpers, views and derivations read and write in place — one copy, so a helper reads what its caller wrote — and writes a fact as JSON only where it leaves the program: the harness, a bound input, the dev panel, a session kept across a restart. A handler is a transaction. It runs on a working copy of the session's facts, sees its own writes at once — as a helper it calls does — and when it ends its writes land as one; a render never sees a handler halfway, and two sessions never see each other's copies. Effects follow one rule, decided from the text: an effect whose answer the handler uses runs when asked; one whose answer it does not use runs when the handler commits, in program order. r = query[…] , n = shell['wc -l x'] and row = query[book, 'INSERT … RETURNING id'] answer at once; notice['saved'] and later[reload] wait for the commit, and a stop drops them. A function's last line is its value, but a handler's value goes to nobody, so an effect on a handler's last line waits for the commit too, as does one a helper returns to a caller that calls it as a statement; a caller that reads the helper's answer ( r = notify[…] ) has it at once. Database writes run in a transaction: the first write a handler makes through a connection begins one on it, every later read and write on that connection is inside it, and it commits when the handler does and rolls back when it stops — RETURNING answers inside it. A handler that writes two databases commits them in program order; the language promises no atomicity across stores, and ClickHouse, which has no transactions, keeps a write the moment it is made. The notice. notice[text] tells the reader something: an effect held to the commit, so a handler that stops never leaves a message saying it succeeded. The session keeps one notice, with the moment it landed; notice reads as a record with text and at , provided by the runtime like a derivation, so a view writes toast[notice.text] . A handler's stop is delivered the same way, as what a reader can act on — skip_symbol stopped, and nothing changed — the server's log has why, as 3f9a1c07 — its reason in the server's log beside the id, never on the page (A handler stops, §10). A page that reads no notice gets the runtime's own toast, which fades after a few seconds; the program keeps no flag and clears nothing. Who the reader is. reader is the page's signed-in reader: a map of strings, empty until someone signs in. A handler signs the reader in with sign_in[record] and out with sign_out[] — effects held to the handler's commit, like notice , so a handler that stops signs nobody in: fn log_in[] found = query[book, 'SELECT id, role, hash FROM people WHERE name = ?', [name]] if len[found] eq 0 notice['no one called `name`'] return if hash[password, found.hash[0]] ne found.hash[0] notice['wrong password'] return sign_in[map[id = str[found.id[0]], name = name, role = found.role[0]]] fn log_out[] sign_out[] Signing in sets reader for the session and gives the browser a cookie, so the reader is signed in on every page and tab they open next — after a restart too — for thirty days, or until they sign out. Signing out clears reader and the cookie, and ends that sign-in everywhere: every session holding it, another tab included, is signed out and redrawn at once, and the cookie is refused if it is ever sent again. A tab already open when someone signs in shows it the next time it opens the page. The program never sees the cookie: the runtime reads it when a page opens and fills reader . Nothing on the page can write reader — no input binds it and no handler assigns it; in a test, change[a, 'reader', record] stands for a reader who signed in. Authorization is ordinary code in the handler that needs it: if reader.role ne 'admin' . A signed-out reader has no role : reading it is an error, and a handler that meets one stops — nothing it did lands, and the reader is told it stopped — so the check fails closed (in a test, click reports the error); 'role' in reader asks first. A derivation that reads reader is computed per session; a plain function is handed the reader as a parameter ( is_admin[reader] ), as it is handed a module variable. The record travels in the cookie, so it stays small: at most 1 KB — an id, a name, a role; look the rest up. The cookie is HttpOnly , SameSite=Lax , and Secure when the page came over https through a proxy ( X-Forwarded-Proto: https ). It is signed with the app's secret: CROW_SECRET (at least 32 characters) when set, otherwise a key the runtime writes to .crow/keys/ on first use, a directory that ignores itself in version control. Changing the secret signs everyone out. Passwords are stored as hash[password, 'password'] and checked with hash[attempt, stored] eq stored (### Hashing). A page for signed-in readers checks reader in its view: view orders[] if 'id' not in reader return sign_in_form[] return stack[ table[open_orders, actions = map[Refund = refund]], button['Log out', click = log_out] ] While the reader is signed out the page draws the sign-in form, and nothing else of the page reaches them: a session accepts only the events a render it sent offered, so refund is refused even in a message written by hand, and a derivation is computed only where it is read, so open_orders is never queried for them. When log_in commits, the same session draws the orders, at the same address, so nothing has to send the reader back. A page for one role checks the role the same way ( reader.role ne 'admin' , after 'role' in reader ). Design Note: no auth on a page. Considered: page['/admin', admin, auth = true] , sending a signed-out reader to a login page and back once they sign in (ui-framework.md, Authentication). Rejected: the view's check already does all of it and fails closed. It draws the sign-in form in place, offers none of the page's handlers and runs none of its queries, and a second way to guard a page would leave two places to look for why a page is shown. The page keeps its address while the reader signs in, so there is nowhere to send them back to. A handler runs off the page's loop. While it runs the page stays live — refresh ticks render and landed values render, from the committed facts — and running[h] , true while a later schedule of h is in flight, is also true while h runs as a handler: every element that offers h renders disabled with aria-busy="true" , so a button shows it is working with no flag in the program. Events are applied one at a time, in arrival order, bound inputs included: a change that arrives while a handler runs waits its turn, and the browser keeps showing what the reader typed. A second click on the handler that is running is dropped: the button already shows it is working. later[f] is the one way to say the session's other clicks need not wait for this work (Design Note: Handlers and later ). Design Note: no debounce. Considered: debounce = ms on an input or a button, holding its events in the browser until the reader pauses (ui-framework.md, Debounce). Rejected: what it guards against is already kept small where it happens. A derivation over a field's fact has one recompute in flight, and a value its inputs moved past is dropped for the latest, so a search typed a key at a time runs at most one query at a time, always for the latest text; a second click on a handler that is running is dropped; and the events that arrive while a render runs are answered by one render. A delay the program chose would slow every reader to spare a server the runtime already spares. Views render wherever they are called A view returns its markup from any call site — a page[] , the test harness, another view, or a program writing pages to disk ( doc.document[title, chapter[...]] ). Text is text. Markup is what a view, an element, a chart, an icon, a bound input, or doc 's markdown , menu and pager make; it stays markup however it travels — held in a local, collected by a for , put in a list, handed to another view as an argument. Every other string is text and is escaped, whatever it holds: a reader who types <img src=x onerror=…> into a field sees those characters on every page that shows them, never an image and never a script. A view given markup in one call and text in another is compiled once for each. Both renderers apply the same rule. Layout — the vocabulary Pages are composed from layout primitives, never styled with CSS. Five containers join the element vocabulary inside views, and a fixed set of layout attributes applies to any element. Each has one written rule; the kernel table ( crow_runtime::layout ) turns it into the CSS a browser lays out with, and the layout engine — written in Crow, shipped inside the compiler — implements the same rule for tests and the desktop shell. Design and rationale: ui-engine-design.md . The page loads the module once, calls mount with the element and the props (the value, as JSON), and calls update with the same element whenever a render changes them; the element's contents are the module's, and no render touches them. send('pick', value) runs the handler on names for pick — fn choose[place] receives value — through the offers like any click: a page offers exactly the events its widgets name, and a handler takes a widget's value as it takes a field's, so it checks what it is given. A module name is letters, digits, _ and - ; the server serves only widgets/*.js . In a test a widget is its element, and click[a, choose['Paris']] stands for what it would send. There is no other client code. An unknown name is an error that lists them. Icons are inline SVG in the current text color, so color = 'muted' and the theme both apply. Charts — chart[frame, ...] A chart is a view over a frame. chart is an element like table : valid only inside views, it takes a frame plus named arguments that say which columns to draw, and renders server-side as SVG: derive bars return query[conn, 'SELECT ts, o, hi, lo, c, vol FROM bars ORDER BY ts'] view render[] return div[ chart[bars, candles = ['o', 'hi', 'lo', 'c'], bars_y = 'vol', marker = open_bell, tz = 'America/New_York', height = 200] ] Named argument Default Meaning Example x 'ts' Column of moments for the x axis Math: reductions and linear algebra · Math: tensors candles [] Four column names — open, high, low, close — drawn as candlesticks lines [] Column names drawn as line series Structured files: use io bars_y '' Column drawn as a volume pane under the chart marker 0 A moment marked with a vertical play-head tz 'UTC' Timezone for the axis ticks height 320 Height in pixels panes [] Lists of column names, each list drawn as its own strip under the volume with its own scale: [['rsi'], ['cvd']] levels 0 Reference lines keyed by column, drawn dashed in the pane that holds the column: map[rsi = [30, 70], cvd = [0]] points 0 A frame of markers on the main pane — columns ts , y , and optionally label and kind ( 'buy' an up triangle in the up color, 'sell' a down triangle in the down color, anything else a dot) seek 0 A handler: every bucket becomes a click target and the handler receives the bucket's moment — seek = jump with fn jump[t] Colors come from the style tokens ( --crow-up , --crow-down , --crow-accent , and --crow-series-2 … --crow-series-6 for the second line onward, counted across the whole chart), so every chart is theme-correct with no color plumbing. Every line series is named in a legend at the top of its pane. The indicators a pane usually draws come from use chart ( ### chart ). An empty frame renders a placeholder rather than an error; a frame over the point budget (1000 points) refuses with an error that says to aggregate first — coarser rows from the query, or head[frame, n] — never a silent downsample. The geometry and the SVG assembly live in crow_runtime::chart , so both modes emit identical markup. Design and roadmap: chart-module-design.md . Styling — the default stylesheet Pages look right with zero CSS: every page shell carries a default stylesheet (light and dark, following the system theme). The whole styling vocabulary is seven classes and eight tokens: classes card stats controls primary up down stale tokens --crow-bg --crow-surface --crow-text --crow-muted --crow-border --crow-accent --crow-up --crow-down Use the classes as ordinary attributes — div[..., class = 'card'] . To restyle, put plain CSS in css/app.css in the project; it is inlined after the defaults, and overriding a token ( :root { --crow-accent: #c60; } ) recolors every element and chart that uses it. crow check flags unknown --crow-* names with a did-you-mean. CSS never appears inside .co files. Design: style-module-design.md . Where this is going — a closed layout vocabulary with an engine written in Crow, so tests can state where things are and what colour they have without a browser — is ui-engine-design.md . Accessibility A page works for a reader on a keyboard or with a screen reader without a line of the program saying so, the same in both modes: A field's label names its input ( aria-label ), as a checkbox's and a radio's label wraps its input. A select is named by a label[...] around it: label['Symbol', select[symbols, sym]] . An element with a click that the browser does not press itself — a div , a card, a table row — is a tab stop with a button's role (a row keeps its own), and Enter and Space press it. A modal is a dialog ( role="dialog" , aria-modal ): when it opens, focus moves into it and Tab stays inside, and when it closes, focus goes back where it was. The runtime's question behaves the same way. A drawer is a dialog that does not hold focus, and a toast is a status a screen reader announces, as the runtime's own notice is. A chart is an image with a name that says what it draws ( a chart of candles, vwap and volume, 390 points ); an icon is hidden from screen readers, since words go beside it. While the page is reconnecting it takes no input from the mouse or the keyboard, and a screen reader is told. A key presses only what a click could (see Keys press elements), and a shortcut is announced ( aria-keyshortcuts ). An img says what it shows, alt = 'the logo' , or that it only decorates, alt = '' ; one that says neither is refused before the program runs, in both modes. The default stylesheet's text meets WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) in both themes, focus is always visible, and a drawer's motion stops for a reader who asks for less ( prefers-reduced-motion ). The page's language is English ( lang="en" ). What stays the program's: headings in order, a main for the page's content, and words on every button — a button that shows only an icon names itself with tip . chart Technical indicators for the chart element, computed by the kernel so both execution modes draw the same numbers. Import with use chart . Technical indicators for the chart element, computed by the runtime ( crow_runtime::indicators , over the kernels in crow_runtime::ta ) so the interpreter and compiled programs draw the same numbers. Every function takes series — frame columns or arrays of numbers — and returns a series of the same length, NaN where the value is not yet defined (a 14-period RSI has no value on row 3), so a chart draws a gap instead of a guess. Write a result into the frame ( df.name = series ) and name the column in lines = [...] or panes = [...] . Function Description Example sma[values, n] Simple moving average over the last n rows Charts and Styling ema[values, n] Exponential moving average, smoothing 2/(n+1) , seeded by the first n rows' mean Charts and Styling rsi[values, n] Wilder's relative strength index over n deltas (0–100), from the second row on: until n deltas have come, of the mean gain and the mean loss of those there are (the line shows from the open, as a scanner reading the first minutes needs); from the n th, each new delta smoothed in by (n−1)/n, as Wilder's is. 100 where there are gains and no losses, 0 where there are losses and no gains, 50 where there are neither (a flat series); a row that is no number is NaN and passed over Charts and Styling rsi[ts, values, n, secs] RSI on clock-aligned buckets of secs seconds over finer rows — a 14-period RSI on 3-minute candles drawn over 1-second bars: completed buckets feed the smoothing once, and rows inside the forming bucket see a provisional value from the latest close, so history never changes and the newest value moves with the tape Charts and Styling macd[values, fast, slow, signal] A frame with columns line (fast EMA − slow EMA), signal (its EMA), hist (their difference) Charts and Styling vwap[price, vol] Cumulative volume-weighted average price from the first row Charts and Styling vwap[ts, price, vol, secs] VWAP over the trailing secs seconds (rows with ts >= t − secs ) Charts and Styling rolling_sum[ts, values, secs] Sum over the trailing secs seconds Charts and Styling A trailing window — rolling_sum , vwap over seconds, rsi on buckets — reads its times in order, each at least the one before, and its seconds are 0 or more: a time that goes back stops the program, saying where ( rolling_sum: the times go back at row 1 (1 after 3) ), as a negative window does. | cvd[close, vol] | Cumulative volume delta: volume counted positive when the close rose, negative when it fell | Charts and Styling | ts is a column of moments (seconds). A window is 1 row or more, a trailing window 0 seconds or more and a bucket more than 0, and the series an indicator reads row by row are one length; anything else stops the program with the reason (see When a Program Stops), as does a wrong number of arguments, naming the counts the function takes ( rsi[] takes 2 or 4 arguments, got 3 ). web The server: routes and responses, auth, CORS, sessions, templates, cache, rate limits, uploads, SSE, sockets, pages, static files, mail, queues, API docs, and the HTTP client. Core (Server) use web, ui use views.home serve[3000] page['/', home.render] Crow manages the application instance implicitly — no app variable needed. page[path, view] registers a LiveView page rendered by a view; event handlers are bound inside the view ( click = inc ), so there is no separate handler argument. serve[port] starts the server ( serve[port, refresh = N, budget = M] adds periodic re-rendering and a latency budget — see Background Work). page[path, view, url = ['day', 'sym']] puts those facts in the page's address: a session starts from the values in the query string ( /?day=2026-09-04&sym=IMRN ), each read in its fact's shape, and the address follows them as they change ( history.replaceState ), so a reload or a shared link opens the same view — a fact of a part is named by its path, url = ['session.day'] , and appears by its last name. A :name segment of a page's path is a fact in its address too: page['/card/:card', card_page] opens a session with the fact card read from the path ( /card/7 is 7 , in the fact's shape; a value the fact cannot hold, /card/x , is no page — a 404, where a query value that does not fit is passed over), and the address follows the fact as it changes ( /card/8 ) — the path holds the facts that say which thing the page shows, the query string ( url = […] ) the facts that tune how. A path's name, like a url name, must name a fact (a part's by its last name, :day ), or the program is refused before it runs, in both modes. A program serves every page it registers, and a page is a session of its own: a link to another page ( a['Card 7', href = '/card/7'] , or a nav of them) opens that page's session, and what pages share is the database, the signed-in reader, and the address. ( crow run -i had served only the last page a program registered.) The look of the whole app is set there too: serve[port, theme = 'dark', density = 'compact', accent = '#3b82f6', wide = true] — theme is 'light' , 'dark' , or 'system' (the default, following the reader's setting), density = 'compact' tightens the element defaults for dense screens, accent overrides the accent token with a hex colour, and wide = true lets the page use the full window instead of the reading column. A wrong value is a startup error naming the choices. The order in source doesn't matter: the server starts only after every route is registered. If no routes are registered, serve[] shows a default welcome page so the user always sees something; once a route or a page is, an address none of them answers is a 404, no page at /cards (the welcome page had answered it). If the port is already in use, the server prints a friendly error: error: port 3000 is already in use . What it needs it opens itself — conn = connect[env['DATABASE_URL']] — and every connect to one URL in a program is one handle, so the handlers that connect share one pool (### db). The request's req.method , req.path and req.body are text, and req.headers (their names in lower case), req.query and req.params are maps of text, so /hello/:name reads its name as req.params.name and /find?q=crow its query as req.query.q — decoded, so ?q=hello%20world is hello world (a query had reached the program still encoded). A form's fields are req.form , a map of text, from an urlencoded body or a multipart one, and a multipart body's files are req.files , a list of maps of text as a page's picked file is — field (the form's name for it), name , type , size and path , where the server keeps a copy under .crow/uploads/ while the handler runs and removes it once the handler has answered ( cp[f.path, …] keeps one). A body bigger than the app takes — 10 MB, or serve[…, uploads = N] megabytes, the limit a page's uploads keep — is answered 413 Payload Too Large before the handler sees it (a body had been read whatever its size), and a multipart body that does not parse 400 Bad Request . serve[port, cors = ['https://app.example.com'], files = 'public'] sets the server's options. cors names the sites whose pages may call the app — '*' any — and answers their preflights; a page on any other site is told nothing, so its browser refuses the answer. files is a directory whose files answer the addresses no route or page does — /logo.png is public/logo.png , / its index.html — and a file it does not hold is the app's 404, as is one whose name, or a directory's on its path, starts with a dot: .env , .git/ , .crow/ , however the address spells the dot ( files = '.' had handed out .crow/keys/ , whose key seals the sign-in cookies); .well-known , where a certificate authority looks, is served. A route's limit = n answers each client at most n times a minute, a client being its address (a proxy's on this machine, the first address its X-Forwarded-For names); a request over it is 429 Too Many Requests , its Retry-After the seconds to wait. All three are the server's, the same in both modes. A route that names a method answers only it, and another method at its path is 405 Method Not Allowed . Both modes serve routes and make every response below through the same functions, so they answer alike, to the byte of a msgpack or an arrow body. A handler whose value fails — int[req.query.n] of a query that is no number, a frame that did not load — answers 500 and an id, the request could not be answered — the server's log has why, as 3f9a1c07 , and the server's log names the handler and the reason beside it, crow: flow stopped [3f9a1c07]: cannot convert 'x' to int ; so does one that stops ( boom stopped [91c0d2e4]: line 5: index 9 is out of range for an array of 2 items ). The client is told no more, since a reason names what the program reaches — a database's address, a file's path (it had been told the reason; Vijay, 2026-10-01) — in both modes, and the server goes on. A response HTTP cannot carry — a status outside 100 to 999, a header whose value holds a line break or another control character, as one a handler built from what a request sent may — answers 500 and an id as a failed handler does, the log saying why beside it ( a response could not be sent [5e07aa1b]: the header 'x-name' holds a line break or another control character ); text beyond ASCII in a header's value is sent as its bytes. (It had answered internal error , saying nothing, and refused text beyond ASCII the same way.) A route's handler that cannot wait on anything — no query, no read, no log, no loop, nothing it calls that does one — is answered on the server's own thread as its request is read (a hop to another thread and back had cost more than answering text['Hello, World!'] ); any other runs off the server's threads, as a page's does, so a slow one delays only its own request, on at most four threads a core (64 at least) at once: a request past them waits its turn, as one past a database's pool waits for a connection. Both modes decide which handlers cannot wait by the same rule. A route and its responses are web's: a program that calls one without use web is refused before it runs. (The interpreter had served no route at all, and then none of msgpack , arrow and stream ; a compiled route that read a param or named a method had not built, nor one whose handler's value can fail, and the compiled stream had not built either; a compiled handler that stopped had dropped the connection, saying nothing.)
