stream[feed, a, …] hands feed the rest Web: responses and submodules A response's body is text, its status HTTP's. text , html , redirect , bytes and respond 's body take text — a value of another kind is written into text first, text['`n`'] , and refused before the program runs; a parsed value is read as text, as any builtin reads one. respond 's status is an int from 100 to 999: one written in the program is refused ( respond[] takes an HTTP status, from 100 to 999, got 1000 ), and one computed as it runs stops the handler in the same words — never moved to a status near it. arrow takes a frame. A route's handler returns a response: one that returns another value — json[req.body] parses the text — is refused before the program runs. A handler that stops, or whose response cannot be sent, answers 500 with the failure's id, its reason in the server's log, in both modes. A stream is sent as its feed puts it. stream[feed, a, …] answers at once, and when the response is sent it calls feed[put, a, …] on a thread of its own. Each put[text] sends that chunk to the reader as it is put, and answers whether the reader still listens: false once they have gone, so a long feed can stop early. The arguments after the feed are the values they have when the handler answers, which is how a feed reads the request. A feed puts text — a value is written into text first, put['`row`\n'] — and a put handed anything else is refused before the program runs; the chunks go out in the order they are put, a loop's included. A feed that fails or stops ends the body where it is, and the log says why. The body is text/plain , sent chunked. use web fn numbered[put, n] for i in range[n] if not put['line `i`\n'] return fn flow[req] return stream[numbered, int[req.query.n]] route['/flow', flow] serve[3000] Design Note: a stream's feed. Considered: a feed that returns a list the runtime sends (it holds the whole body, which a stream exists not to); a channel value a handler writes to (a new kind of value for one builtin); send[out, chunk] on a handle (WebSocket's send would name two things); and chunks of any value, sent as JSON lines. Decided: the feed is a named function, as Crow has no lambdas, handed put , a function value the program already knows how to call; stream[feed, a, …] hands it what it needs from the request, as later[f, a, …] does. Text chunks keep one way to write a value (interpolation), and put answering whether the reader listens lets a feed stop with the return it already has. A response is what a route returns. A page shows elements and text, so a view that places one — row[text['3 items']] — is refused in both modes: place the text itself, or p[…] or span[…] . Auth ( use web.auth ) Function Description Example sign[claims, secret] A token — a JSON Web Token signed with HS256 — carrying the claims (a map, or a record), issued now ( iat ) and expiring in an hour ( exp ) unless the claims say when Math: tensors · Web: responses and submodules verify[token, secret] The claims a token carries, as a parsed value ( str[claims.user] ), when it was signed with this secret and has not expired Web: responses and submodules A token is how an API, which has no page session, says who calls it: sign gives one to a client that signed in, and each request carries it back for verify to read. A refusal is an error value of kind 'auth' , its reason saying why: the token has expired , the token's signature does not match , not a token . A secret shorter than 32 characters signs nothing ( a token's secret is 32 characters or more ), as the sign-in cookie's CROW_SECRET keeps the same floor; keep it out of the source, in the environment ( env['TOKEN_SECRET'] ). A page keeps sign_in , which needs no token. Both modes sign and verify through the same functions. (Neither had built them: the compiled program named a type the web runtime did not have, and the interpreter had no such builtins.) They are written in Crow ( src/modules/auth.co ) on the sys layer: the header and the claims as base64url, the signature an HMAC-SHA256 of the two, compared in constant time; the claims reach sign as the JSON text they encode to (Design Note "a builtin written in Crow keeps its row"). Their tests are the module's own ( crow test src/modules/auth.co ), one of them a token another library signed, read with its secret. WebSocket ( use web.ws ) Function Description Example socket[url] A connection to a WebSocket server, ws:// or wss:// Web: responses and submodules send[s, text] Send a text message; answers empty text The standard library's layer: use sys · Web: responses and submodules recv[s] / recv[s, secs] The next message, as text — waiting for it, or at most secs seconds The standard library's layer: use sys · Web: responses and submodules close[s] Close the connection, for every value that holds it The standard library's layer: use sys · Web: responses and submodules A socket is a live feed a program reads — a market's trades, a service's events — in a script, a job, or a handler's background work. Each failure is the call's error value, of kind 'socket' : a server that does not answer is socket 's ( cannot open a socket to … ), a wait that passes its seconds is recv 's ( no message in 5 s ) — one that ends while a message is arriving leaves what came of it for the next recv , which reads the message whole (the message's head had been lost, and the next read took its payload for a frame) — and a server that closed answers closed , after which every call says the socket is closed . A binary message reads as text, and a ping is answered and passed over. A socket is one connection however many values hold it — a function handed it, a loop — and close closes it for all of them. Both modes talk through the same client, which is written in Crow ( src/modules/ws.co ) on the sys layer: the handshake is the protocol's ( sys.upgrade ), and the framing — a message sent masked, the next read whole across its fragments, a ping answered, a close answered and the connection let go — a formula over send , recv , pack and mask . socket and close are its functions, their declaration their own (section 13's opening); send and recv are effects and keep their rows (docs/extending-crow.md, phase 3); the contract above holds in both modes, and its tests are the module's own ( crow test src/modules/ws.co , the RFC's masked example among them), and tests/socket.rs runs it against a server in both modes. use web, web.ws feed = socket['wss://feed.example.com/stocks'] send[feed, '{"action": "subscribe", "params": "T.AAPL"}'] while true m = recv[feed, 30] if not m.ok log['the feed stopped: `m.reason`'] break log[m] Design Note: a socket's name. Considered: connect[url] , the client's first name, which the database's connect already is — one name two ways, told apart by the URL's scheme; and dial , open and ws , which name a mechanism, a verb many things do, or the protocol's initials. Decided: socket , the thing a program holds, as smtp names a mailer and connect a database; send , recv and close act on it. LiveView / Pages Function Description Example page[path, view] Add a LiveView page (server-rendered with live updates via WebSocket); :name in path is a fact in its address (Core, above) Views: the whole element vocabulary · View Blocks · Reactive State and Events · Components · Slow Work and the Live Loop · Testing a Live App · Charts and Styling · The Element Vocabulary · Derivations · Views and Live Updates download[value, name] Hand the reader's browser a file when the handler commits: a frame as CSV, a string as text, a picked file's bytes Reactive State and Events title[text] The page's title, which the browser's tab and history show: a view places it anywhere in the page, reading the page's state like any element ( title['Card card '] ); a render that changes it changes the tab Documentation: use doc · Reactive State and Events meta[name = 'description', content = text] A tag in the page's head: its attributes pass through as HTML ( property = 'og:title' for a link preview) Reactive State and Events A page's head is what its render places. title and meta take no room on the page: a served page carries them in its head from its first render, and a later render that changes them changes the head — the last title the render places is the page's (a layout's placed before the page's own gives way to it), and a page that places none is titled Crow App . In a test they are elements of the render, where elements[a, 'title'] finds them; the layout engine gives them no box. Design Note: a page's address and its head. Considered: a path's names as the view's parameters ( view card[id] ), as Express and Rails hand a route its parameters; and a page's title as an argument of page ( page['/card/:card', card, title = 'Card'] ). Decided: a path's name is a fact. A page's state is its facts and the address already carried facts ( url = […] ), so one rule holds the path and the query string, a handler that changes the fact moves the address, and nothing new reaches a view. A title is an element the render places, so it reads the page's state (a card's own name) and changes with it, where an argument of page would be text fixed when the page is registered. A route keeps req.params : a route's handler is handed its request, and a page is handed none. A page and its session. The page request renders the reader's session once, and the page's socket adopts that session — its facts, its derivations and the render already on screen — so a page loads with one render. A session outlives its connection. When the socket closes — a laptop sleeps, the network drops, a rebuild restarts nothing but the page — the server keeps the session for ten minutes, and the page, which holds the session's token for its tab, resumes it on reconnect: the same facts, a replay still where it was, sent its render at once. A waiting session keeps its facts and its derivations' last values, so it comes back without a flash of loading; at most a thousand sessions wait at once. The token is a credential and is treated as one: it travels only over the socket, it is good once, and every resume replaces it, so a copied token resumes nothing after its tab has. Reloading the tab resumes it too, and so does coming back to it with the browser's back button; a second tab is a session of its own. Following a link opens the session of the address it names, even to the page the tab is on: /?day=2 from /?day=1 starts from day = 2 (the tab's session had been resumed, and the address followed it back to day = 1 ). A socket that brings no live token — a session past its ten minutes, a server that restarted — starts a fresh session from the facts its address carries and is sent its render at once: the page never keeps showing a session the server no longer holds. serve[…, keep = true] keeps sessions across a restart as well: each session's facts are written to .crow/sessions/ as they change, and a tab that comes back to a restarted program finds its session there for the same ten minutes (a kept session had been removed before it was read, and the tab started afresh); a fact whose name or type changed since starts from its declared value, which the log says. The directory ignores itself in version control. While the socket is down the page dims, says reconnecting… and takes no input, so a click is never silently lost. Events that arrive while a render runs are applied together and answered by one render: a slider dragged across its range is one render, not one per step. A render sends what changed, not the page: the server reads the render as the browser builds it — a chart's marks and a table's rows included — compares it with the render the page holds, matching elements by id and then by position as the page does, and sends the changes (a text, an attribute, an element added, gone or replaced) when they are smaller than the page, the whole page when they are not. A moving play-head on a chart is a few attributes, not the drawing again, and a row added to a list whose items carry ids is one row. Each change names the element it expects to find; a page that meets one it cannot place — its shape changed under it — asks for the whole page back, and a field being typed in keeps the reader's draft. Markup the browser would have to repair (a block inside a paragraph, a row outside a table, a tag closed by its parent's end tag) is sent as whole pages, and the server log says which repair, once. Handlers and renders run on worker threads, never on the threads that carry the sockets, so a session's slow work delays only its own page. A clicked element is marked data-crow-busy the moment it is clicked, before the server answers, and the mark clears when the answer to that click arrives — the reader sees the click taken in the same frame, with no program code in the browser. A page sends only what it was offered. A session accepts a click only when a render it sent carried that handler with exactly those arguments ( click = set_speed[10.0] offers set_speed with 10.0 , a table row its key), a bound input or select only when a render drew it — a select, a radio or a tab only with a value it drew among its options — and a form only when a render drew it. A helper no element names, a fact no input binds, and the button of a closed modal or a hidden element are refused — a confirmation's second step is accepted only after its first opened it. A refusal changes nothing and is logged: crow live: refused 'name' — the page did not offer it . The socket opens only from the app's own page (a page on another site is refused before it can send anything), a message on it is at most 4 MB — an event is a click or a field's text, and a file comes by a request of its own, under the uploads limit — so a bigger one closes the socket, which the page opens again (the bound had been 64 MB), and a served app listens on this machine only; set CROW_HOST=0.0.0.0 where the network must reach it — a container, a server behind a proxy. Both modes serve pages. crow run file.co compiles and serves; crow run -i file.co serves from the interpreter at once, with no Rust compile between an edit and the page — the live runtime keeps the sessions (their facts, the commit, the notice, the questions, the address, the reconnects) in both, and only who renders the views and runs the handlers differs. One difference is of timing, not of meaning: the interpreter computes a derivation where it is read, so a page served by it waits for its queries, where the compiled page shows the last value and catches up. crow test --served drives every page in tests/served/ , and every app under examples/ with a main.events script beside its main.co (served from a fresh copy, so its database starts empty in each mode), with the same events in both modes and compares the pages they settle on. Mail ( use web.mail ) Function Description Example smtp[host, port, user, pass] Create an SMTP mailer; its messages come from user The standard library's layer: use sys · Web: responses and submodules · Reactive State and Events mail[mailer, to, subject, body] Send a plain-text message: held to a handler's commit, so a handler that stops sends nothing; r = mail[…] sends at once and r.ok says whether the server took it Reactive State and Events mail is an effect like notice and download : in a handler, or a function a handler calls, a message whose answer is not used waits for the commit, and a stop drops it; used ( sent = mail[…] ), it is sent when asked, and a failure is the answer's reason. Outside a handler it is sent at once. A view or a derivation sends none, itself or through a function it calls, and is refused if it tries: it runs whenever the page needs it. A mailer is made once for the whole program, as a connection is, and prints as its host, never its password. In a test nothing is sent: mails[a] is the list of what the session sent, each a map of to , subject and body , and crow test --compiled records the compiled program's the same way. The sending is written in Crow ( src/modules/mail.co ) on the sys layer, as RFC 5321 says: the greeting, EHLO , the connection secured with STARTTLS where the server offers it (port 465 is TLS from the start; a password travels only encrypted, so a remote server that offers neither is refused — a local relay on the loopback address is not), AUTH PLAIN , the envelope, the message's head ( From , To , a Subject beyond ASCII as an encoded word, Date ) and its body with its dots stuffed (a body beyond ASCII as base64), QUIT . A recipient the server refuses, an address that is none ( name@host ), a server that does not answer or answers anything but what the step wants are the reasons ( mail to bob@example.com failed: the server answered 550 no such user at RCPT TO ). The session layer holds a handler's message to its commit in both modes and hands it to the row's function to send; a script sends it at once. Its tests are the module's own ( crow test src/modules/mail.co ), and tests/smtp_server.rs runs it against a server in both modes. Client ( use web.client ) A program reads a URL with read and load (Files, URLs and S3), sends any other request with request (Requests), and a page pulls remote data with fetch[url] / poll[url, seconds] (reactive, see above). web.client is no module: the client is the language's own, written in Crow. Design Note: one process. Considered: sessions any process can resume from a shared store, and a table's version shared across processes, so that an app could run on several machines as a Phoenix cluster does. Decided (session-layer-design.md §6; measured 2026-10-02): an app is one process — its sessions, its derivations' values and its tables' versions live in it — and how far one goes is measured, not guessed: a connected tab costs about 140 KB while it is open, a parked session a few kilobytes, and a trivial route answers tens of thousands of requests a second on a laptop (the book, Polish and Deployment, "How far one process goes"; tests/capacity.rs measures it on any machine). An app that outgrows one process runs several behind a proxy that keeps each tab on its process, sharing the database; a write one process makes reaches another's derivations by their fresh window, as an external source's does. Sessions across processes wait for an app that needs them. Design Note: what web is. Considered: the modules the web framework had gathered — a task queue ( web.queue , push ), templates ( templates , render ), an embedded SQLite handle ( web.db 's sqlite ), session stores ( sessions[] ), Server-Sent Events and WebSocket servers ( sse , ws ), an LRU cache ( cache ), generated API docs ( web.docs ), and CORS, static files, rate limits and uploads as calls on an app value the language no longer has ( cors[app] , static_dir[app, …] , limit[max, window] , uploads[req] ). Decided (Vijay, 2026-09-30): each was a second way to do what the language already does, or a stand-in the interpreter answered with a placeholder ( render gave [rendered: name] ), and each is gone. Background work is later[f, …] ; a page is a view, not a template; a database is db.connect ; a reader's session is a page's session, with sign_in for who they are; a server reaches a page through its live session and a client through stream ; what a program computes once and reads often is a derivation. use web serves pages and routes, and its modules are web.auth , web.mail and web.ws ; another is refused by name. llm A language model as a connection: conversations, replies, tools as the functions themselves, a reply followed piece by piece, and embeddings, over Anthropic's and the OpenAI-compatible wire formats. Import with use llm . A language model as a connection: one way to ask a model, the same in both modes, over two wire formats — Anthropic's Messages API, and the OpenAI-compatible chat completions that Ollama, vLLM, OpenRouter and LiteLLM serve too — so a program written against a local model runs unchanged against a hosted one. Written in Crow on the sys layer (design rule 20; src/modules/llm.co ), its functions its declaration (section 13's opening: reach , ask , asked , said , told , chat , follow , next , reply , embed , act ); crow test src/modules/llm.co runs its own tests, and tests/llm_server.rs drives it against a server speaking both formats in both modes, the agent loop against runs that server scripts. The design is docs/llm-design.md and, for the loop, docs/agents-design.md. use llm m = reach['anthropic://claude-sonnet-5-5'] talk = ask['What is the capital of Mongolia?'] r = chat[m, talk, system = 'Answer in one word.'] log[r.text] --- Ulaanbaatar log[r.usage.input] --- 21 Function Description Example reach[url] A model as a connection: anthropic://<model> or openai://<host>[:port]/<model> (any server speaking the OpenAI chat completions: Ollama at openai://localhost:11434/llama3.2 , vLLM, OpenRouter, LiteLLM). The key is read from the environment when a call is made — ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY , or the variable ?key=NAME names — and is in no value; a local host ( localhost , 127.0.0.1 ) needs none and is reached over http , any other over https . Answers the model's description, a parsed value: m.provider , m.model , m.base , m.key (the variable's name). An error value of kind 'llm' : a URL of neither scheme, no model named, the key's variable unset for a remote host A language model as a connection: use llm ask[text] A conversation of one user turn: a parsed value, a list of turns A language model as a connection: use llm asked[talk, text] The conversation with another user turn added A language model as a connection: use llm said[talk, reply] The conversation with the model's reply added — its text and its tool calls — as the next request needs it A language model as a connection: use llm told[talk, call, text, failed = false] The conversation with a tool's result added: what the program computed for one of the reply's calls . failed = true marks the result a failure the model is to hear as one: the turn says so, Anthropic's block carries is_error , and the OpenAI-compatible turn its text alone, since that wire has no flag A language model as a connection: use llm chat[m, talk] The model's reply: a parsed value with text , calls (each id , name and args , the arguments as the model wrote them, read as the program's use implies), usage ( input and output tokens) and stop — end , tool (the model waits for its calls' results), length (its tokens reached) or other . By name: system = text , tools = [f, g] (the functions themselves, see below), tokens = n (1024), temperature = t (1.0). An error value of kind 'llm' when no answer came, when the server's status is no success (its message quoted: the model's server answered 401: invalid x-api-key ) or when its answer is no JSON A language model as a connection: use llm follow[m, talk] The same request, the reply followed as the model writes it: a socket the pieces are read from; the same options and errors as chat A language model as a connection: use llm next[s] The next piece of the reply's text, as the model writes it; empty text once the reply has ended. A tool call the model streams is gathered into reply , not shown. An error value of kind 'llm' when the connection breaks A language model as a connection: use llm reply[s] The whole reply the socket has carried so far, in chat 's shape — complete once next has answered empty text A language model as a connection: use llm · The standard library's layer: use sys embed[m, texts] The texts' embeddings: a matrix, a row per text, from an OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint ( openai://host/<embedding model> ); an Anthropic connection is refused, since it serves none A language model as a connection: use llm act[m, talk, tools = [], allow = [], rounds = 8, system = '', tokens = 1024, temperature = 1.0, budget = 0, keep = 0, compact = 0, skills = '', servers = []] The agent loop: the model runs its tools until it answers or a limit stops it. Each reply's calls are answered in order: the program's gates first ( allow = [g, h] , each a function of the call — a parsed value with the call's name , args and id — answering a bool; every one must allow the call, and a gate that takes another count of parameters or answers another kind is refused with why before any model is asked), then the tool of the call's name, applied to its arguments read by each parameter's kind ( apply , sys); a refusal, a name no tool has, an argument missing or of another kind and a tool's own failure are each told to the model as a failed result that says why, so every call is answered. At most rounds model calls and at most budget tokens in all (0 for none): a limit stops the run after the reply's calls are answered, so the conversation ends well-formed and can be continued. keep = n cuts the tool results of rounds older than the last n to a stub naming their size ( [a result of 2400 characters, cut] , the turn marked cut ), compact = n asks the model for a summary once a reply has read n tokens or more and goes on from the summary alone (a step of what compact ), skills = folder names a folder of skills (below), and servers = [s] adds the tools each MCP server offers ( use mcp ), called on the server. Answers a record: text (the model's last words), stop ( end , length , other , rounds , budget ), rounds , usage ( input and output tokens in all, a parsed value as a reply's), talk (the conversation as it ended) and steps , a frame with a row per model call, tool call and compaction — step , what ( chat , tool or compact ), name (the model's or the tool's), input , output , ms , and how (a chat's stop; a tool's ok , failed , arguments , refused or unknown ). An error value of kind 'llm' as chat 's, for rounds below one, for a gate that is none, for a skill that breaks the standard's rules, and for a tool's name two of the lists share A language model as a connection: use llm chat , follow , next , embed and act are effects: a route's handler that calls one runs off the server's threads (Routes), and crow check sees the call. Tools are the functions. tools = [weather, search] hands the functions themselves — a group (Specialization) — and the module writes each one's schema from its description ( describe[t] , sys): its name, its parameters by name with the kinds inference found — an int integer , a float number , text string , a bool boolean , a list an array of its items' kind, a map, a record or a parsed value an object — and, as the description, the comment written above the function. A parameter's kind is what the program's calls of the function hand it, or, where the program never calls it (a tool only the model calls), what its body reads it as: handed to a builtin whose rows take one kind there, upper[city] reads it as text; read by its fields, order.lines and order.id , it is a parsed value — an object in the schema, handed as the model wrote it. (Only a call had typed one, and a tool read in its body was refused with the advice to read it there; the field read came 2026-10-20, when a gate that read the call's fields was refused the same way, its body doing what the advice said.) A function whose parameter nothing types is refused before the program runs, with the fix ( weather's parameter 'city' is typed by nothing — read it in the body, or call weather[…] once with a value of its kind ), and so is a tools that is not a list of functions written. The program makes the calls: the reply's calls name a tool and its arguments, the program dispatches on the name, reads the arguments as its use implies and hands each result back with told . --- the current weather in a city, in °C fn weather[city] r = request['https://wttr.in/`city`?format=j1'] return str[json[r.body].current_condition[0].temp_C] talk = ask['How warm is it in Lisbon right now?'] r = chat[m, talk, tools = [weather]] while r.stop eq 'tool' talk = said[talk, r] for call in r.calls if call.name eq 'weather' talk = told[talk, call, weather[call.args.city]] r = chat[m, talk, tools = [weather]] log[r.text] The loop is the module's. Written by hand, that loop has three gaps every program would close again: no limit, a call the if does not handle left unanswered (the next request is refused), a tool that fails ending the run with nothing told to the model. act[m, talk, tools = [weather]] is the loop written once, in Crow, in the module: the dispatch is apply over the group (sys), which the compiler writes for any list of functions, so every call the model can cause is to a member of the list the program wrote, crow check sees each member called with its effects, and the limits, the failed results and the record of the steps are one code for every program (docs/agents-design.md). A tool's failure, a wrong argument and an unknown name are told to the model, each as a failed result whose text says why, since a model that hears why can try another way; told[…, failed = true] tells one by hand. The program's say between the model's decision and the tool's run is the gate: allow = [g] names functions of the call, each asked before a tool runs, and a call one of them refuses is told to the model as a failed result ( remove is not allowed by the program ) rather than run — the if the hand-written loop had, kept where the loop is the module's. --- the weather may be asked for Lisbon alone fn only_lisbon[call] if str[call.name] ne 'weather' return true return str[call.args.city] eq 'Lisbon' done = act[m, ask['Is it warmer in Lisbon or Porto?'], tools = [weather], allow = [only_lisbon], rounds = 8] log[done.text] --- the answer log[done.stop] --- end, or the limit that stopped the run log[done.steps] --- a frame: every model call and tool call, in order A subagent is a tool that runs the loop. A tool is a function the model calls, and a tool whose body runs act with a tool list of its own is a subagent: the parent model calls research[question] , research runs an inner loop — its own model, prompt, tools, gates and limits — and answers what the inner run found. Nothing of it is new: a function sees no top-level name (Function Scope), so the inner loop reaches its model itself; the loop is copied per tool list (Specialization), the inner copy reached through the outer copy's dispatch of research by name; and the tool's parameter is typed as any tool's is — trim[question] reads the question as text, where ask[question] takes any value and types nothing. The inner run's record is the tool's to read: inner.text answered is what the parent hears, as any tool's result, and a run that failed fails the tool — return inner.text of a failed run answers its failure — so the parent model hears a failed result that says why ( cannot reach the model at … , told as a failure, how failed in the steps), or the tool reads inner.reason and answers in words of its own, failed or not. The parent's steps frame shows the delegation as one tool row named research , its ms covering the whole inner run; the inner run's steps are the tool's own, read from inner.steps and logged or kept where the tool decides (decided 2026-10-20: a subagent needs nothing new, and the delegating run is held in both modes — tests/llm_server.rs, parity 277). --- what a smaller agent finds out about a question, with the weather as --- its only tool fn research[question] small = reach['openai://localhost:11434/llama3.2'] inner = act[small, ask[trim[question]], tools = [weather], rounds = 4] return inner.text done = act[m, ask['Is it warm in Lisbon today?'], tools = [research]] log[done.text] --- what the parent answered, from what research found log[done.steps.name] --- the parent's steps: its model, research, its model Skills are know-how loaded on demand. skills = 'skills/' names a folder in the Agent Skills format (agentskills.io): each skill a folder holding a SKILL.md — YAML frontmatter with its name (1 to 64 characters, lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, neither first nor last, matching the folder) and its description (1 to 1024 characters), then the instructions — and, beside it, the files the instructions refer to. The loop reads every skill's frontmatter once, names each with its description in the system prompt, and offers the model two tools of the module's own: skill[name] answers a skill's instructions, skill_file[name, path] a file inside the skill (a path that leaves it is refused), so a hundred skills cost the model a line each until one is used. A skill that breaks a rule is the call's error value, naming the skill and the rule, before any model is asked; a program's tool named skill or skill_file is refused. Scripts are not run: running one is shell , which waits on the gate. A reply followed is a loop the program writes. A route forwards the pieces as it reads them with the response stream[feed] , a page keeps them in a fact a view shows, a script logs them: s = follow[m, ask['Tell me a story in three sentences.']] piece = next[s] while piece.ok and len[piece] gt 0 log[piece] piece = next[s] whole = reply[s] A conversation is a parsed value — a list of turns, each its role ( user , assistant , tool ) and text , a model's turn with its calls , a tool's with the id of the call it answers — because a map holds one kind and a turn holds several, and JSON is the language's shape for that; the builders keep every turn in the one shape both wire formats are written from, so a conversation started against one provider continues against the other. One reply shape the same way: what one provider answers and the other does not is not there until both mean it. Design Note: a model as a connection, named reach . Considered: the model named on every call, as most SDKs take a model string (rejected: the URL parsed and the key's presence checked at every call, and a program's calls not read as calls on one model); connect , as db makes its handle (rejected: connect is db 's own form, and a program that imports both — an agent that keeps its notes in a database — would write every call qualified); model (rejected: the name most programs give the thing they fit). Decided: reach[url] , a handle made once; the connection holds no secret, since the key is read from the environment as each call is made, so what it holds is description and a parsed value is readable where a handle kind would be opaque ( m.model in a log line), with no kind to thread through the compiler (design rule 21). Design Note: tools are the functions, the schema the compiler's. Considered: a tool written by hand — a name, a description and a schema beside the function (rejected: the signature said twice, and the two drift); the module calling the tool for the program and sending the result back by itself, as agent SDKs do (rejected: a call the program never wrote, an effect crow check could not see, and a model deciding what runs with no if of the program's between); a description handed beside the tool, describe = map[weather = '…'] (rejected: one thing in two places — the comment above the function is the sentence the code already carries). Decided: tools = [f, g] , the compiler writes each schema from the signature it inferred and the function's comment, and the program dispatches. Design Note: who runs the tools. Considered: the program writes the loop, as before (kept, and the only way until 2026-10-20; as the only way rejected: three gaps written again in each program); the lowering expanding act into a loop over hidden rows of llm's, the dispatch written by the compiler per listed tool (rejected: the compiler holds the language and names no module, design rule 24); the module dispatching by name at run time over a table from names to function values (rejected: Crow has no such value — a list of functions is a group whose members are known before the program runs — and the checker could not tell which functions will run). Decided (2026-10-20): the module writes the loop in Crow, and the dispatch is apply over the group, which the compiler writes for any group. It answers this section's objections to a module calling the program's functions: every call the model can cause is to a member of a list the program wrote, the dispatch is over those members alone, and crow check sees each one called, with its effects. A gate the program hands the loop — allow = [g] , functions of the call answering a bool, every one asked before a tool runs — needed one rule of inference, since a gate's parameter is a parsed value its body reads by its fields, which had typed nothing (a parameter was typed by a call of it, or by a single-kind builtin read): a parameter read by its fields that nothing else types is a parsed value (Vijay, 2026-10-20). Considered for the gate: a plain function parameter (rejected: a function taking a function is lowered once, so one act would serve one tool list per program, and no subagent could have tools of its own); a required gate (rejected: a program with tools that reach nothing writes nothing). A run's record is a frame, one row per step, so traces go to ClickHouse and to charts with no conversion; its columns avoid kind , ok , reason and trace , which are every value's own. Design Note: a reply followed is a socket read piece by piece, not a feed. Considered: a function handed to follow and called for each piece, as a response stream[feed] hands its feed a put (rejected: a builtin's row takes no function value — one handed to a row is typed by nothing — and a loop the program writes can stop, show, keep or forward a piece where a callback only receives it). Decided: follow answers a socket, next the pieces, reply the whole; the loop is the program's. Not in this round, each a later note: images and documents in a turn, a conversation the server keeps (prompt caching, stored responses), batches, and embed for a provider that serves no OpenAI-compatible endpoint. A model's answer is kept and replayed as any request's is (Requests: crow check --record-fixtures , crow test --fixtures ), so an agent's test runs without the model. mcp Tools from other programs, and a Crow program as one: the Model Context Protocol over Streamable HTTP — a server named, its tools listed and called, and a route answering as a server over the functions themselves. Import with use mcp . Tools from other programs, and a Crow program as one: the Model Context Protocol, revision 2026-07-28 — stateless, every request carrying its protocol version and the client's capabilities in _meta — over both of its transports: Streamable HTTP, one POST per message, and stdio, a process the program starts and talks to one message per line. Written in Crow on request and the sys layer (design rule 20; src/modules/mcp.co ), its functions its declaration ( server , discover , catalog , tool , answer , listen ); crow test src/modules/mcp.co runs its own tests, and tests/mcp.rs drives a Crow client against a stand-in server, a stand-in client against a Crow server, and a Crow client against a Crow server over stdio, in both modes. The design is docs/agents-design.md. use mcp s = server['http://localhost:8000/mcp'] log[catalog[s][0].name] --- the first tool the server offers log[tool[s, 'weather', map[city = 'Lisbon']]] --- the text its result carries files = server[command = 'npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /tmp'] log[catalog[files][0].name] --- the same calls, the server a process Function Description Example server[url = '', token = '', command = ''] An MCP server as a connection: the URL of its MCP endpoint ( http:// or https:// ), and the bearer token its requests carry, if any — or, by name, the command that runs it over its standard streams (the stdio transport), as shell[cmd] takes a command: server[command = 'npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /tmp'] . A parsed value: s.url , s.token , s.command . An error value of kind 'mcp' for a URL that names no endpoint, for a URL beside a command, for a token with a command (stdio takes its credentials from the environment, as the protocol says), and for nothing named Tools from other programs: use mcp discover[s] What the server says of itself ( server/discover ): supportedVersions , capabilities , its instructions for a model, and who it is under _meta ; a parsed value Tools from other programs: use mcp catalog[s] The tools the server offers ( tools/list ): a parsed value list, each its name , description and inputSchema . A response streamed as events is read to its last message Tools from other programs: use mcp tool[s, name, given] A tool called with its arguments — a map, or a parsed value ( tools/call ) — answering the text its result's content carries. A result the server marks an error ( isError ) is an error value of kind 'mcp' saying what it said, as is a tool the server does not have, a server that answers an error, and one nobody answers (over stdio: a process that ended, or wrote a line that is no message, cannot reach the MCP server /bin/cat: the process ended ) Tools from other programs: use mcp answer[req, tools = [f, g], name = 'crow', instructions = ''] The request a POST route was handed, answered as an MCP server over the functions themselves: server/discover with the versions, the capabilities and the instructions; tools/list with each tool's schema from its description ( describe , sys — the comment above the function, its parameters by name with the kinds inference found); tools/call with the tool of the name applied to its arguments ( apply ), its value's text the result, a wrong argument or the tool's own failure a result marked an error, a name no tool has the protocol's Unknown tool error. A notification is accepted with 202; a body that is no JSON, a request missing its _meta or the headers the transport requires ( MCP-Protocol-Version , Mcp-Method , Mcp-Name ), and one of another protocol version are refused with 400 and the JSON-RPC error the protocol names ( -32700 , -32602 , -32020 , -32022 ); an unknown method with 404 and -32601 Tools from other programs: use mcp · The standard library's layer: use sys | listen[tools = [f, g], name = 'crow', instructions = ''] | The program as an MCP server over its own standard streams: every line of its standard input a message, answered on its standard output exactly as answer answers a route's request — the same server/discover , tools/list and tools/call , the same errors in the message (there is no status and no header over stdio: the body is the source of truth) — a notification answered with nothing, each answer written whole before the next line is read, until the input ends (an empty line ends it too: a message is never empty). Answers empty text. A program serving so writes nothing else to its standard output; its standard error is its own ( log goes to standard output, so a serving program keeps its notes for standard error or a file) | Tools from other programs: use mcp | discover , catalog and tool reach the network through request , or a process through the layer's send and recv , and crow check sees the call. A program becomes an MCP server with one route: use web, mcp --- the current weather in a city, in °C fn weather[city] r = request['https://wttr.in/`trim[city]`?format=j1'] return str[json[r.body].current_condition[0].temp_C] fn served[req] return answer[req, tools = [weather], name = 'weather-server'] route['/mcp', 'POST', served] serve[8000] The stdio transport: a server is a process the program talks to. server[command = 'crow run tools.co'] names a server by the command that runs it. The process starts at the first message — start[command] (sys): sh -c runs the command with its standard input and output piped, as the protocol's client launches its server — and is kept while the thread that started it lives, one process per command on each thread (a served program's handlers, each on a thread of its own, each talk to a process of their own, so no two exchanges interleave), started again at the next message if it ended, as the transport says a client restarts a server that exited. Each request is one line on its input, with the _meta every request carries (the revision mirrors nothing into headers over stdio: there is no header layer), and the response the line on its output carrying the request's id — the ids count up on the process, so a late answer to an earlier request is passed over, as are the notifications a server writes before its response; a line that is no JSON message is refused with its words, since the transport forbids a server anything else on its output. The server's standard error is the program's own: the transport lets a server log there, and a client may forward it, which this one does. Ten minutes is the most a message waits, as over HTTP. A Crow program is such a server with listen[tools = [f, g]] in place of the route: the same answers, the same errors, over its standard streams; a legacy client's initialize is refused naming the revision spoken, as the revision asks of a modern-only server. The client is modern-only: it does not probe with server/discover before another request, and discover is the program's to call (the revision recommends probing to fail deterministically against a legacy server, which here fails with the server's own error instead). use mcp --- the current weather in a city, in °C fn weather[city] r = request['https://wttr.in/`trim[city]`?format=j1'] return str[json[r.body].current_condition[0].temp_C] listen[tools = [weather], name = 'weather-server'] --- crow run weather.co, as a client's command Design Note: a module of its own, stateless as the protocol is. Considered: the client inside use llm , since an agent is who calls a server's tools (rejected: a server needs no model, and use llm stays the one place a program reaches a model); the connection as a handle kind (rejected, as reach 's was: it holds a URL and a token's text, which a parsed value shows); the earlier revisions' initialize handshake and Mcp-Session-Id (rejected: the 2026-07-28 revision removed sessions, and a client sends one request and reads one answer, which is what request does; a legacy server answers 400 with no modern error, which the client names). Decided (2026-10-20): use mcp , the client on request with the headers the transport mirrors from the body, the server a function a POST route calls, the schema writer the same shape use llm writes for a model (a helper is a module's own, so each module writes it). Design Note: a process is a socket, and a server is named by its command. The stdio transport (2026-10-20, docs/agents-design.md) needed a process held open. Considered, for the handle: a handle kind of its own, declared beside sys's rows (rejected: a kind is a Value variant, a Kind , an Arg and an arm in every rule that meets them — a compiler change, where the compiler is frozen — and a process is read and written as bytes, which is what a stream is); a stream ( start[command] answering what open answers, rejected: a message is a line, and what a read takes past the line's end must stay with the process for the next read, which is what a socket holds beside its stream — so a process is a socket, as a WebSocket's connection is: type[p] is socket , send , recv , leftover , unread and close serve it, and nothing was added but start ). Considered, for the surface: the transport inside the URL ( server['stdio: npx …'] , rejected: a parse hidden in text, and a URL that is none); a second export naming a command ( command['npx …'] , rejected: server is the one way to name a server, the transport an option); a program and a list of arguments, as the SDKs' configurations are written ( server[command = 'npx', args = ['-y', …]] , rejected: a second way to write a command beside shell 's, and a list option with a [] default makes a copy of the function whose items have no kind) — decided: server[command = text] , the command as shell takes one, the shell's own quoting. Considered, for the handle's place: a record answered by server , holding the socket (rejected: act reads its servers as their JSON, since a list option's default [] has items of no kind, and a handle is no JSON); a process per message, the protocol being stateless (rejected: a server such as npx … takes seconds to start, and the transport says a client restarts a server only when it exits) — decided: the process is the runtime's, one per command on each thread, found and started by start at every message (per program had let two handlers of a served program write to one process at once and read each other's lines), so server[…] stays a parsed value and the loop's servers = [s] is unchanged. Considered, for when it starts: at server[…] (rejected: server would be an effect for one transport and none for the other, and the shell starts sh -c nosuch as readily as a server, so nothing fails earlier) — decided: at the first message, where crow check sees the call. Its standard error is inherited: the transport lets a server log there and a client forward it, and a server's reason for ending is then where the program's own stops are. What the revision says of stdio (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio, read 2026-10-20): messages are newline-delimited JSON-RPC with no embedded newlines; the server may write anything to standard error and must write nothing but messages to standard output; request metadata is carried in the body's _meta alone, "there is no header layer"; the client ends the server by closing its input, waiting for it to exit, then forcing it, TERM before KILL on POSIX — and a server should exit promptly when its input closes; a client should restart a server that exits unexpectedly; a dual-era client probes with server/discover and falls back to initialize on any error that is not a recognized modern one, and a modern-only server should name the versions it speaks in its answer to initialize . The runtime's close and the restart follow it; the fallback is not built, since the client speaks one revision. sys The standard library's own layer: bytes, and a connection to a host, for the modules written in Crow — a program may not import it. Two operations over functions, for the standard modules (section 7 of docs/extending-crow.md): describe[f] answers a function's description as a parsed value — name , doc (the comment written above it), params (each name , takes — the word errors use for its kind: an int , a number , text , a bool , a list of ints , … — and default , or null ), answers — and apply[f, args] calls the function with its arguments read by name from a parsed value or a map, each by the parameter's kind, and answers the value encoded as text: an argument missing or of another kind is an error value of kind call , the function's own failure its value. Each takes a function written, or one of a group (a list literal of functions: Specialization), and is lowered to what inference knows — a dispatch the compiler writes over every function the value can be — so both modes agree by construction. A parameter nothing types is refused with the fix ( weather's parameter 'city' is typed by nothing — read it in the body, or call weather[…] once with a value of its kind ); one handed a parsed value, or typed by nothing, takes what the body reads it as, or its default's kind; one of a kind no name can hand (a frame, a function, a handle) is refused where it is applied. A program outside the standard library does not call them (sys is the library's own). Design Note: functions as values for native rows, described and called by name. Considered: a tool written by hand beside the function (rejected in llm's note); a list of function values of one signature only, each a function pointer compiled (rejected: a value's name cannot be recovered compiled, so describe could not say what it was handed, and tools of several signatures — the common case — could not share a list); a new expression that chooses by a name at run time (rejected: a dispatch written once by the compiler over the members, which it knows, is the same thing without a construct). Decided (2026-10-19): a native row declares the function it takes with its signature ( Kind::FnOf : any 's predicate over the walked items, later 's deferred work handed the rest, stream 's feed handed put , route 's handler the request, transact 's body the connection, a chart's seek an event), and inference, the checks, the width pass and the classification read the one declaration; a list literal of functions is a group, held by name; describe and apply are sys's, lowered to a dispatch the compiler writes. Import with use sys — only in a module of the standard library. sys is the layer the standard library's own Crow-written modules stand on: bytes, and a connection to a host read and written as bytes. A program may not import it; a program serves with serve[…] , reads with request[…] , read[…] and socket[…] , and connects with connect[…] , which are built on this layer (design rule 20). In a program, use sys is refused before it runs: `sys` is the standard library's own layer — a program serves with serve[…], reads with request[…], read[…] and socket[…], and connects with connect[…] . The book's page shows the layer through the harness's door ( CROW_SYS=1 ), which the tests and the book have and a program has not. Function Description Example bytes[text] The text's UTF-8 as bytes. lines — and its answer read: what exchange does on a connection of its own, and a driver on one it keeps The standard library's layer: use sys exchange[url, method, lines, body, timeout] One HTTP exchange, written in Crow: the request sent to the URL's host with its method, the header lines and the body, its answer read whole — an answer , or an error value of kind 'sys' where none came in timeout seconds (0 as thirty to connect and ten minutes in all) The standard library's layer: use sys redirected[from, location] Where a redirect sends the request: its location , made absolute against the URL it came from The standard library's layer: use sys with_query[url, pairs] The URL with the pairs added, each name and value URL-encoded, after the ? it has or one it is given The standard library's layer: use sys fetch[path, headers, query, timeout] A remote source's answer, written in Crow: a URL got with a reader's options and its redirects followed, or an S3 object got signed — a success, or the reason as an error value of kind 'sys' (the options on a path that is no URL, a timeout below 0, no answer, an answer that is no success) The standard library's layer: use sys · Views: the whole element vocabulary put[path, bytes] The bytes written to an S3 object, signed; a URL is refused — it is read, not written The standard library's layer: use sys · Web: responses and submodules format_of[path] A table's format by its path's extension (a URL's query left out): 'csv' , 'json' , 'parquet' , or '' The standard library's layer: use sys format_sniffed[media, bytes] The format of what a URL with no extension answered: the media type its server named, then the bytes themselves (Parquet's PAR1 , JSON's opening bracket), and CSV otherwise The standard library's layer: use sys A stream is one connection however many values hold it, as a socket is; type[s] is stream . A socket is a stream and what it read past the last message — a WebSocket's connection after its handshake, or a process started under the program ( start ), whose output comes line by line; type[p] is socket , and it shows as <socket /bin/cat> . Every function works identically in both modes ( crow_runtime::sys ). The HTTP protocol is written on this layer, in src/modules/sys.co , as functions of sys itself: a URL taken apart, a connection opened plain or behind TLS, the request line, headers and body sent, the answer's head read to its blank line and its body by its length, by its chunks, or until the server closes ( exchange ), redirects followed and a reader's options applied ( fetch ), an S3 object signed as AWS's Signature Version 4 says and read or written by path at an endpoint ( fetch , put ). On the protocol stand the HTTP client — request (Requests), in src/modules/core.co — and every reader of a URL or an S3 object: read and write (core.co), use io 's csv and lines (io.co), use frame 's load and save (frame.co) and use math 's load (math.co), each a few lines over the layer's parsers ( csv_rows , frame_of_csv , tensor_of_frame ). A program never sees the layer: it sees request and read , effects the session layer holds, whose rows in the builtin table are the contracts the Crow bodies keep until effects are declared on the layer's own rows (math.nn, Design Note "a module written in Crow declares its functions by writing them"; docs/extending-crow.md, phase 3). use sys b = bytes['héllo'] log[len[b]] --- 6 (two bytes for é) log[text[slice[b, 3, 6]]] --- llo log[find[b, bytes['llo']]] --- 3 bad = text[slice[b, 1, 2]] --- half of é: not text log[bad.kind] --- parse s = open['127.0.0.1', 1, false, 0.2] log[s.kind] --- sys: nobody listens on port 1 Design Note: the standard library's layer. Considered: writing the standard library's modules in Rust only, as they were (rejected: a module both backends share is a bug both share, which no parity or fuzz run can see; the week of 2026-10-03 found eleven bugs where the two backends differ and none in the kernels they share, because nothing can look there); giving every program bytes, sockets and threads (rejected: a program would gain the bug classes the language exists to exclude — data races, half-read buffers, protocol state spread over user code — and a second way to serve and connect beside serve and connect ). Decided (Vijay, 2026-10-03): one sys module, the smallest native layer the rest of the library can be written on, importable by the compiler's own modules alone; a program sees one way, and every module written on sys is compiled and run twice, fuzzed, and takes laws. Design Notes — every deliberately rejected feature, with its reason Design Notes about one feature sit next to that feature; the language-wide ones are collected in section 19. 1. Variables and Types Declaration & Assignment Variables are declared by simply assigning a value. No keywords needed. name = 'crow' age = 3 pi = 3.14 active = true Reassignment Variables can be reassigned, but the type cannot change. int and float are compatible with each other. x = 10 x = 20 --- ok, same type x = 3.14 --- ok, int/float compatible x = 'hello' --- error: cannot reassign from int to string A variable whose first value could not fail holds no error. A later value that can fail lands when it is good; when it failed, the assignment refuses it, as a decision refuses one (§10, Errors in Conditions): a function hands the error back to its caller, so a function that can fail this way can fail, as one with such a condition can; a handler stops; a view renders error: reason in its own place; and the top level halts with runtime error: line N: cannot assign an error value to 'x' — <reason> . To keep a failure to look at, give it a name whose first value can fail: r = float[s] , then if not r.ok . x = 1.0 x = float['2.5'] --- 2.5 lands x = float['abc'] --- halts: cannot assign an error value to 'x' — cannot convert 'abc' to float An empty list cannot fail either: xs = [] , then xs = push[xs, float[s]] , holds numbers, and a failed item is refused where it is pushed. Design Note: a plain variable refuses an error. Considered: letting the variable hold the error, its type widening to one that can fail, which the interpreter did while the compiled program returned at the assignment. Decided (Vijay, 2026-09-25): the compiled program's rule, in both modes. A variable's type does not change (above), and an error that silently took the variable's place would surface lines later, far from its cause; refused where it is assigned, it names the line and the variable. A variable that is ever assigned a float is a float for its whole scope. Assigning an int to it stores the float value ( x = 1 above stores 1.0 ), and so does handing an int to a parameter that is a float: half[3] , where fn half[x] is also called with 2.5 , divides 3.0 . (The compiled program handed the function its int and did not build.) So does a record's field that holds floats — P[1, 2] beside P[1, 2.5] holds 2.0 — and a list, a map or a comparison of floats given an int: push[xs, 2] onto floats pushes 2.0 , an item of a list of floats assigned an int holds its float ( xs[0] = 2 stores 2.0 ; compiled, it had not built), and map[lr = 0.01, epochs = 100] holds 100.0 . The other way round too: a list or a map of ints handed a float holds floats from then on — push[range[3], 2.5] is [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 2.5] , set[counts, 'k', 2.5] a map of floats, concat and contains likewise — and a record's float field given an int that can fail holds a float that can fail. (Compiled, those did not build; interpreted, the int was kept among the floats.) (Compiled, those did not build; interpreted, the int was kept, so type[m.epochs] said int beside a float division.) Note for interpreted mode: the widening applies from the first float assignment onward, so an int division performed before any float assignment may differ from compiled mode, where the variable is float from its declaration — don't depend on int division of variables that later hold floats. Types Crow is statically typed with full type inference — you never write type annotations, but every variable has a concrete type determined at compile time. The compiler infers types from usage; if a type cannot be determined, the program is invalid. The built-in types are: Type Example int 42 , -7 , 0 — a whole number of any size float 3.14 , -0.5 decimal decimal['12.30'] , decimal[2, digits = 50] — an exact base-ten number fraction fraction[1, 3] — an exact ratio of two ints str 'hello' , 'crow' bool true , false array [1, 2, 3] , [[1, 2], [3, 4]] map map[home = 78701, office = 78702] Arrays are homogeneous — all elements must be the same type. Use maps for mixed-type named data. [1, 2, 3] --- int array ['a', 'b', 'c'] --- str array [[1, 2], [3, 4]] --- 2D int array [1, 'hello', true] --- error: mixed types Numbers That Keep Every Digit An int is a whole number of any size. Arithmetic on ints gives the exact answer however large it grows: 2 ^ 100 is 1267650600228229401496703205376 , a factorial of a thousand has its 2,568 digits, and an int read from text keeps every digit it was written with — as does one written in the program: 123456789012345678901234567890 is that int (a literal past 64 bits had been refused in Rust's words, number too large to fit in target type ). Nothing is written to ask for it, in either mode. The compiled program keeps an int in 64 bits where it can show the int never grows past them — a loop's counter below its bound, a position in a list, a value taken % n , a sum a loop adds to — and in a form that grows where it cannot, so a program pays for the size only where a number can have it. In showing it, the compiler counts no part of a program as running 2^48 times (days of computing at a billionth of a second a round): a sum taken in a loop, or over a recursion's calls, grows by fewer bits than that past what it adds, and a program that ran longer and grew such a sum past 64 bits would stop with an integer overflow, never with a wrong digit. Where an int past 64 bits is handed to what takes a 64-bit one — a position, a size, a count ( range[n] , xs[i] , repeat[s, n] ), a map's key, a frame's cell, a tensor's number — it is refused where it is handed, with what took it and what it was (its first twenty digits and how many there are, past forty): a whole number past 64 bits where range[] takes an int of 64 bits: 1267650600228229401496703205376 . What shows or holds any value takes one as it is — str , log , text, type , a list's items, a map's values, a record's fields, encode — and so do abs , min , max and sort , and floor , ceil and round of an int are the int itself, every digit; a list or a map of ints handed one past 64 bits ( push[xs, 2 ^ 100] , set[m, k, 2 ^ 100] ) holds it, its ints held as ints that grow from then on (each had stopped, a whole number past 64 bits where an int is held in 64 bits ); float[n] is the nearest float, and int[x] , floor[x] , ceil[x] and round[x] of a float are the whole number it holds, every digit ( int[10.0 ^ 30] is 1000000000000000019884624838656 , the float's own value; of NaN 0 , and of an infinite float a stop). A literal list of whole numbers that holds one growing past 64 bits is a list of ints, as one past 2^53 is (a tensor's numbers are floats). A function handed as a value — to another function, kept in a variable — is called through it as a function of ints of 64 bits: an answer past them is refused where it crosses ( a whole number past 64 bits where a function handed as a value answers an int of 64 bits: … ), while a call of the function by its name keeps every digit (the roadmap holds function values that grow). An int past 64 bits encodes as JSON text of its digits — "123456789012345678901234567890" — as JSON's readers hold numbers in 64 bits or as floats, which would lose them; one within 64 bits is a JSON number. A decimal is an exact base-ten number. decimal['12.30'] holds 12.30 as written, its two places kept ( str shows 12.30 ); decimal[12] and decimal[0.1] hold 12 and 0.1 (a float as the shortest text that reads back as it). + , - and * of decimals are exact and keep their places ( decimal['12.30'] + decimal['1.1'] is 13.40 , decimal['1.10'] * decimal['2.0'] is 2.200 ), so decimal['0.1'] + decimal['0.2'] eq decimal['0.3'] holds, and a sum of money never drifts. / of decimals has 28 significant digits, the last rounded half away from zero, as round rounds, unless a decimal in it holds more: decimal[x, digits = n] is x rounded to n significant digits, and every result it takes part in — + , - , * , / , ^ , and sqrt , exp , ln , sin , cos , tan , atan of it — is rounded to the most digits of the decimals in it. That is the language's big float: sqrt[decimal[2, digits = 50]] is √2 to fifty digits. round[d, places] rounds a decimal to places places after the point, half away from zero ( round[decimal['2.345'], 2] is 2.35 ); round , floor and ceil of a decimal are ints; int[d] cuts toward zero and float[d] is the nearest float. A fraction is an exact ratio of two ints. fraction[1, 3] is one third, held in lowest terms with its sign on the top ( fraction[2, -4] is -1/2 ); fraction[x] of an int or a decimal is that number exactly ( fraction[decimal['0.25']] is 1/4 ). + , - , * , / and ^ of fractions are exact. A fraction shows as n/d , a whole one as its int ( str[fraction[4, 2]] is 2 ); int , float , round , floor and ceil read it as a number; fraction[n, 0] is an error value of kind 'math' , as an int divided by zero is a stop. Kinds meet the exact way. An int meeting a decimal is the decimal it is, and an int or a decimal meeting a fraction is the fraction it is: the answer is the exact one. A float meeting a decimal or a fraction is refused before the program runs, in both modes — a float holds a nearby binary number, and the exact answer would be a guess: price * rate with rate a float is refused with a decimal and a float: decimal[rate] reads the float as the decimal it shows, float[price] reads the decimal as a float . A literal written with a point is the number it writes, so price * 1.1 is price times eleven tenths. Two decimals, two fractions, or a decimal and a fraction compare by value in either order ( decimal['2.50'] eq decimal['2.5'] , fraction[1, 2] eq decimal['0.5'] ), and with an int; with a float, the comparison is refused as arithmetic is. A decimal and a fraction encode as JSON text of what they show — "12.30" , "1/3" — every digit kept, as an int past 64 bits does (JSON's readers hold a number as a float, which would lose digits, and JSON has no ratio); a list, a map or a record holds decimals and fractions as it holds any value, and a fact keeps one as that text. A frame's columns hold ints, floats, text, truths and moments: a column of decimals or fractions is refused where it is made, and a decimal column a database answers is a column of floats (the roadmap holds columns of decimals). Design Note: ints grow. Considered: stopping on overflow (Crow until 2026-10-09: integer overflow: … does not fit in 64 bits ), wrapping (Rust's release build, Java, Go), and a kind of its own the program asks for where it starts a number ( q = big[1] ). Decided (Vijay, 2026-10-09, asked whether Crow could tell by itself which numbers need to be big): the int grows and nothing is written, so the answer is the exact one as Python's is. Whether a number outgrows 64 bits depends on the data and on how long a loop runs, so the compiler cannot know it before the program runs — what it can show before the program runs is the opposite, that an int stays within 64 bits, and there it keeps the 64-bit form, so a loop over positions costs what it did. Design Note: one decimal for exact money and for big floats. Considered: a binary big float beside the decimal (Julia's BigFloat , MPFR), and a precision set for the whole program (Python's getcontext().prec ). Decided (Vijay asked for exact decimals, rationals and big floats, 2026-10-09): one decimal kind, exact where exactness is possible — + , - , * — and rounded to the digits its values ask for where it is not. A precision belongs to the values, never to a mode of the program, so a function rounds the same wherever it is called; a binary big float would be a second way to hold a number with chosen digits, whose digits print in base ten anyway. Design Note: a float meets no exact number silently. Considered: a float meeting a decimal makes a float (C#'s decimal refuses it; Python's Decimal refuses it), or a decimal of the float's exact binary value ( Decimal(0.1) is 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827… ). Decided: refused before the program runs, in both modes, with both conversions named — a computed float is a nearby binary number, and either answer would be a guess the program did not make — while a literal written with a point is the number it writes, which a decimal or a fraction reads exactly. String Escape Sequences Strings support escape sequences with backslash: Escape Character 
 Newline 	 Tab  Carriage return (a line of a wire protocol ends 
 ) \ Literal backslash ' Literal single quote \` Literal backtick (not interpolation) A backslash before any other character is itself, the backslash kept, so a regular expression's escapes are written as they are: '\d+' , '\.' , sub[s, '\|[^|]*\|', '-'] . (Until 2026-10-09 any other character after a backslash was refused as an unknown escape, against strings being inert, and a regex needed [|] for \| .) log['line1
line2'] log['col1	col2'] log['it's here'] log['a \`code span\` in prose'] --- prints: a `code span` in prose Comments and string literals accept any Unicode text. Identifiers are ASCII — a deliberate restriction that keeps the grammar and tooling simple. String Interpolation Backticks delimit an expression inside a string — like a markdown code span. Everything else in a string is inert text: name = 'crow' greeting = 'hello, `name`' result = '1 + 2 = `1 + 2`' li['`item.name` — qty `item.qty`'] log['best: `max[scores]`'] cfg = json['`"a": 1, "hosts": ["x"]`'] --- braces and brackets: plain text m = matches[s, '[a-z]`2,4`'] --- regex: fully raw Rules: `expr` evaluates any Crow expression and splices its value. Its names are read like any others: an undefined one, or a module variable read inside a function, is refused before the program runs. Inside an interpolation you are still inside the string — quotes stay escaped: 'up: upper [ 'hi ' ] ' . An unterminated or empty backtick span is an error (never silent). For repeated formatting, name it: fn money[x] + 'P&L: money [ pnl ] ' (see Formatting). Design Note: Strings Are Inert; Backticks Delimit Code What was considered: brace interpolation {expr} (the original design), \[expr] (Swift-style escape activation), bare `name (marker without terminator). Why paired backticks won: any bare delimiter collides with real text — {} silently corrupted regex quantifiers ( '[0-9]{4}' interpolated the {4} ), bare [] would have destroyed regex character classes and [INFO] -style prose, and bare `name could not delimit ( `names ? `name.csv ?) or express a + b . Pairing the marker gives full expressions, zero termination rules, and one form. Strings become inert by default — JSON, regex, CSS, and prose need no escapes — and interpolation is explicitly activated, unshifted, with the one notation everyone already reads as "this is code". The design lineage (braces → escape-activation → bare marker → paired) is preserved in docs/design-review.md. Multiple Assignment Multiple variables can be assigned in a single line, a value for each name. x, y, z = 1, 2, 3 Values of another count are refused before the program runs, in both modes, and so is one value for several names: Crow takes no list apart into names (Design Note: No Destructuring). c, d = pair[] is refused with the form to write, r = pair[] , then c = r[0] , d = r[1] . (Each had run: one value had been taken apart interpreted and had not built compiled, a value past the names had been dropped, and a name past the values left unset.) Swap a, b = b, a Scope Variables are scoped to the block they are defined in. Inner blocks can access outer variables — but function boundaries are opaque : module variables are not visible inside functions (see Function Scope, section 7). x = 10 if true y = 20 log[x] --- 10 — accessible: blocks see outer variables log[y] --- error — y is not in scope Reading y there is refused before the program runs, in both modes, with what to write instead: set y before the block and assign it inside. Two blocks may each set a variable of the same name, and a name set again after its block has ended is a new variable. They are different variables and may hold different types: if ok x = 1 else x = 'one' --- a different x 2. Comments A comment starts with --- and runs to the end of the line. There is no closing delimiter. --- a comment line x = 5 --- inline comment --- multi-line commentary is just --- consecutive comment lines Design Note: Comments End at the Newline What was replaced: paired --- ... --- comments (open and close delimiters, spanning lines). Why: an unclosed paired comment silently swallowed the following line into code — the comment ran until it found the --- that opened the next comment, and the remainder of that line executed. This failure mode produced real incidents during development (corrupted test files; one bug misdiagnosed as a Unicode issue). End-of-line comments make the failure unrepresentable : every line is locally, independently correct, and commenting out a line is just prepending --- . Migration: old single-line comments ( --- text --- ) still parse — the trailing --- is now inert text — and crow fmt strips these cosmetic closers. Old block comments with bare --- fence lines are no longer supported; write one --- per line. 3. Blocks Blocks are defined by indentation. A new block starts after a statement (e.g. if , fn , for ) and ends when the indentation returns to the previous level. if x gt 5 log['big'] log['done'] next_thing[] Blocks can be nested. if x gt 5 if y gt 10 log['both big'] next_thing[] A line holds one statement: x = 1 y = 2 is refused — the second starts a line of its own (it had run as two). A line is indented only under one that opens a block; one indented under a plain statement is refused, and a block's first line with no indented body under it is too. A line that holds only a comment opens and closes no block, whatever its indentation, as a blank line does. A comment that goes on from a trailing one may be aligned under it, and one at the margin inside a block leaves the block open: fn hello[name] words = 'hi `name`' --- the greeting, as the --- page shows it --- a note at the margin, inside the function return words (Such a line had been refused as indented under a line that opens no block, or had ended the block it sat in.) 4. Operators Arithmetic + - / * % ^ ^ is the power operator (right-associative): 2 ^ 10 --- 1024 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 --- 512 (right-associative: 2^(3^2) = 2^9) 2.0 ^ 0.5 --- 1.4142... -3 ^ 2 --- -9 (the power first: -(3^2)) (-3) ^ 2 --- 9 2.0 ^ -1 --- 0.5 A power binds tighter than a minus sign before it, as in mathematics and in Python, R and Julia: -x ^ 2 is -(x ^ 2) , and an exponent may carry its own sign. (The sign had been part of the base, as in a spreadsheet: -3 ^ 2 was 9, and a Gaussian's exp[-x ^ 2 / 2] grew where it should fall — crow check --self found it, holding its cases to Python's answers.) Division is type-determined — one operator, no ambiguity: 3 / 2 --- 1 (both int → int, rounded toward zero) -7 / 2 --- -3 -7 % 2 --- -1 (the remainder has the sign of the left side; `%` takes ints — a float on either side is refused before the program runs) 3 / 2.0 --- 1.5 (float involved → float) 7 / 3 --- 2 7.0 / 3 --- 2.3333... An int divided by zero stops the program (When a Program Stops, §10); a float divided by zero is infinity. The operands are numbers: text is refused before the program runs, and so is a list of text ( ['1', '2'] + 1 is cannot use '+' with array[str] and int ). (Compiled, a list of text had been parsed as numbers, where the interpreter made each item an error.) Tensor Arithmetic For tensors (numeric arrays), operators follow MATLAB/Julia semantics: Operator Meaning * Matrix multiply (matmul) for tensor×tensor; scalar multiply for tensor×scalar .* Element-wise multiply / Scalar divide (tensor÷scalar only; tensor÷tensor is an error — use ./ ) ./ Element-wise divide ^ Scalar power .^ Element-wise power + , - Element-wise (always) use math W = eye[2] x = ones[2, 1] y = W * x --- matmul a = ones[3] .* full[3, 2] --- element-wise multiply b = ones[3] ./ full[3, 2] --- element-wise divide c = full[3, 2] .^ 3 --- element-wise power d = ones[3] * 2 --- scalar multiply A tensor's shape is in its type. A shape the program states is known before it runs — a literal ( [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]] is 2×2), a constructor given literal sizes ( zeros[2, 3] , ones , full , randn , eye[3] , linspace ), reshape given literal sizes, and what transpose (its last two dimensions swapped), the element-wise operators and * make of them. The type carries the shape where the tensor goes: a reassignment binds the variable anew, as a frame's does (see Frames), so after x = zeros[3, 3] it is 3×3 from that line on; where branches, or a loop's rounds, meet, it has the dimensions they agree on; a function's parameter has the dimensions its calls agree on, and a call has the shape of what the function returns. An operation two known dimensions make certainly wrong is refused before it runs, in both modes: * of tensors that are not both 2-D, or whose inner dimensions differ ( matmul: incompatible shapes [2, 2] × [3, 3] — … ), and an element-wise operation of two shapes that do not broadcast (each pair of dimensions, aligned from the innermost, equal or one of them 1: `+` of tensors of shapes [2, 2] and [2, 3]: dimension 2 is 2 in one and 3 in the other — … ), read in a function with the parameters the tensors were handed as ( (the tensors add[] is handed as `a` and `b`) ). A dimension the program computes ( zeros[n, 3] ), one a function's calls disagree on, and any of a tensor's once a cell or a row of it is assigned ( m[0] = … ) are not known, and nothing about them is refused before the program runs: an operation whose shapes do not meet stops the program where it runs, with the same words, in both modes.
