A chain of element-wise operations is computed in one pass. ` x * 2.0 x . * x - 1.0 reads each element of x ` once and writes one tensor, where each operator would make a tensor of its own — across the machine's cores for a large one. Each element is what the operators compute, in their order and with their formulas, so the answer is the same to the bit, and a shape that does not meet stops with the operator's words at the first operator whose operands do not meet. A chain's operands are what only read — a variable, a fact, a derivation, a number written; one that calls something is computed where the program calls it, and its chain by the operators. The same in both modes. Design Note: a function is one function whatever shapes it is handed. Considered: a copy of a function for each shape its calls hand it, as a frame's columns make one (see Frames), so that each copy's operations are checked against its own shapes. Rejected: a frame's columns are its row type, but a tensor compiles alike whatever its shape, so a copy per shape would grow the build for nothing but earlier refusals inside the function. Decided: a parameter has the dimensions all its calls agree on; a call whose shapes the others do not share is checked where it runs. Scalar-array operations broadcast the scalar: [1, 2, 3] + 10 --- [11, 12, 13] [1, 2, 3] * 2 --- [2, 4, 6] 10 - [1, 2, 3] --- [9, 8, 7] -[1, 2, 3] --- [-1, -2, -3] A list of numbers however it was made — grown by push , read from a file, a mask's truths as 1 and 0 — is a tensor to every operator, as it is to .* : push[push[[], 1], 2] + 10 is [11, 12] , and / of one by a number divides each, [1.5, 0.5] of [3, 1] / 2 . ( + , - , * and / of a list grown by push had been refused, cannot use '+' with array[int] and int , where .* took it — crow check --self found it, holding its cases to Python's answers.) A tensor divided by a number divides each number, as numpy does: [3.0] / 2.5 is [1.2] (it had multiplied by 1 / 2.5 , which rounds twice: 1.2000000000000002 ). Internally, all-numeric arrays use a fast tensor representation for element-wise operations. This is transparent — numeric arrays behave identically to regular arrays for indexing, iteration, comparison and all builtins: two lists of numbers are eq when they hold the same numbers in the same shape, however each was built (a list grown by push and a literal, ints and the same floats, a list of rows and a matrix literal). A list of rows — tensors of one shape, grown by push from a matrix's rows, or lists of numbers of one length — is a matrix wherever a tensor is taken ( transpose[rows] , stack[rows] , tensor[rows] , mean ), as a list of numbers is a vector; stack[rows, 1] stacks its columns. Rows of two shapes stop the program with the reason, in both modes (compiled, a list of rows had been refused where a tensor was taken; a list of lists of numbers had stopped the interpreter and not built compiled). A list of lists whose numbers can fail is no matrix: it is refused before the program runs, and its numbers are read first. A matrix stack makes, or tensor of a list of lists, has a rank the program knows, so its columns walk as rows and each is numbers (its columns had been read as numbers, and mean of one refused). A tensor holds its numbers as floats, and a float holds a whole number exactly only up to 2^53 (9007199254740992): a literal list of ints past it is a list of ints, which holds each as it is (a tensor had held 9007199254740993 as …992 ), and a matrix literal of them is refused, in both modes. A literal list of whole numbers that a function goes on to hold as a list of ints it builds — q = [1] , then q = grow[q, k] with grow pushing ints — is a list of ints from its first line (it had held floats, converted to ints and back at every call and assignment); one used as numbers stays a tensor. Expression Grouping Use () to group expressions and control evaluation order. Parentheses are only for grouping — function calls always use [] . mid = (low + high) / 2 result = (a + b) * (c - d) Comparison No symbols — use words only. Operator Meaning eq equal ne not equal gt greater than lt less than gte greater or equal lte less or equal if x eq 5 log['equal'] if x gt 10 log['big'] eq compares two values whole, in both modes alike: numbers by value (an int beside a float as a float: 1 eq 1.0 ), text by its characters, a list item by item, a map entry by entry, and a record field by field — two records are equal when they are the same struct and every field is ( Point[1, 2] eq Point[1, 2] ). An item or a field that failed equals nothing, not even another failure. contains compares a list's items the same way. A frame's column compared whole — with a column, a list or a tensor — is compared as a list is, cell by cell, a missing cell equal to nothing. A list compared with a single value is a mask instead (see Arrays). (Compiled, comparing two records did not build, and the interpreter answered false for records and maps with equal contents; a column of text with a missing cell had equalled itself, and a column compared with a list had not built.) Two values of two kinds are not compared. Each of the six compares a value with one of its kind: numbers with numbers (an int beside a float as a float), text with text, bools with bools, and lists, maps and records with their own kind. A number is not text, nor a bool either: '1' eq 1 , true eq 1 , a list of text with a list of numbers, a column of text with a number ( df.name eq 2 ), 1 in ['a'] and push[['a'], 1] are refused before the program runs — eq compares values of one kind, not text with a number — and where a kind shows only as the program runs — a parsed value, a cell of a file's column — the comparison stops the program with the same words. A parsed value is compared with a value of its kind ( j.status eq 'ok' ), and JSON's null equals nothing. (Both modes had answered false for a number and text, and contains had too; compiled, 'a' eq 1 had not built; interpreted, a parsed 1 had not equalled 1.0 .) A handle — a database connection, a response, a socket, a mailer — is compared with nothing, another of its kind included: each is its own, equal to no other, and conn eq conn is refused where it is written ( a database connection is not compared: a handle is its own, equal to no other — compare what it holds ; the interpreter had answered false , and the compiled program had not built). str of one is what text shows of it ( <db:sqlite> ), type its kind, and len , encode and every other function that takes something else refuse it in the table's words. gt , lt , gte and lte order numbers with numbers and text with text, by character code — the order sort gives text: 'b' gt 'a' , 'B' lt 'a' , and '10' lt '9' , text and not numbers. Numbers compare exactly, and NaN is equal to nothing and unordered, so of the six only ne holds for it. Bools have no order ( gt compares numbers with numbers or text with text, not a bool with a bool ), nor two lists, and a parsed value is read as the kind the other side says, as arithmetic on one reads it as a number (see JSON). (Compiled, true gt false and 'b' gt 'a' had answered where the interpreter stopped.) Design Note: a number is not text. Considered: answering false for values of two kinds, as Python's == does and as both modes had; converting one side, as JavaScript, R and MySQL do ( '10' < 9 ). Decided (Vijay, 2026-10-01: "a string is not a number"): a comparison of two kinds is the program's mistake, not a question with an answer — an identifier read as text and compared with a number matched nothing, and a filter dropped every row without a word. So all six refuse it where both kinds are known, as a statically typed language does, and stop the program where a kind shows only as it runs. Design Note: text has an order. Considered: refusing an order between texts, as the interpreter had by stopping, so that gt is for numbers alone. Decided (2026-10-01; Vijay: text with text and numbers with numbers are compared): text is ordered by character code, the order sort already gives it — one order for text, not a second — so df[df.day gte '2026-01-01'] keeps the rows of ISO dates written as text from that day on, as the compiled program had. It is not a locale's alphabetical order ( 'B' lt 'a' ); lower first compares without case. Logical and or not if x gt 0 and y lt 10 log['in range'] if not active log['inactive'] if x eq 1 or x eq 2 log['one or two'] and and or decide from the left: the right side is evaluated only where the left does not decide the answer — false and … is false and true or … is true without it. An error on the left is the value, since an error has no truth value (Errors in Conditions); where the right side is evaluated, its error is the value. So a guard reads as it does in nearly every language: if i lt len[xs] and xs[i] gt 0 --- xs[i] is read only when i is in range log['positive'] if r.ok and r.price gt 0 --- r's price is read only when r did not fail log['priced'] A call on the right runs only where the left does not decide. and and or of two lists of truths (masks) join them item by item, and both sides are evaluated. Design Note: and and or Decide From the Left Considered: evaluating both sides, the left first, as every other operator does — the rule from 2026-09-23 to 2026-10-11: an error on either side was the value, and nothing was evaluated conditionally except by if and while . Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-11): the right side is evaluated only where the left does not decide. Evaluating both turned the commonest guard into a stop: i lt len[xs] and xs[i] gt 0 with i past the end stopped the program, because an index outside its list stops rather than failing as a value; inside a while condition the nested if the rule prescribed meant rewriting the loop around a break , and benchmark authors padded their arrays instead (sudoku, n-queens). Measured, the cost of evaluating both was small (n-queens' gap was elsewhere; a brainfuck interpreter about 9%): the reason is the guard, not speed. Both modes decide from the same lowered program — the right side's own refusals wait under the left's decision there — so they cannot part as they did when the compiled program short-circuited on its own. Membership x in xs is true where xs holds x , and x not in xs where it does not — the one way to ask, in words: an item of a list, compared as eq compares; a number in a tensor; a part of text; a key of a map or of a parsed value; and over a frame's column, cell by cell, a mask ( t['AA' in t.sym] ). It binds as a comparison does — tighter than and , or and not , looser than arithmetic — so n + 1 in [3, 4] and n in [2] reads as written. A value of another kind than the items is refused before the program runs, in both modes: 1 in ['a'] is " x in xs takes a list and an item of its kind: its items are text, not a number". if node.tag not in ['button', 'input', 'select', 'summary'] lines = lay_lines[node, inner_w] Design Note: membership is an operator. Considered: keeping contains[xs, x] and has[m, key] as functions (rejected: node.tag ne 'button' and node.tag ne 'input' and … was written in the layout engine where a list would do, because not contains[list, node.tag] reads backwards from how it is said, and has beside contains was two words for one question); adding in beside them (rejected: two ways to write one call). Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-08): in and not in , a pair as eq and ne are, and the functions retired — contains[…] or has[…] written in a program is refused with the operator to write. The parser writes the operator as a call of the row named contains (a map's and a parsed value's rows are has 's functions under that name), so nothing below it knows an operator exists, as with then . Then Chaining then pipes the left value as the first argument to the right function, enabling left-to-right composition instead of nested calls. --- x then f = f[x] s = ' hello ' result = s then trim --- trim[s] --- x then f[a] = f[x, a] result = 'hello world' then split[' '] then join['-'] --- split['hello world', ' '] then join[..., '-'] → 'hello-world' Chains of any length: result = s then trim then split[' '] then join[', '] then binds tighter than comparisons and logical operators, but looser than arithmetic: x + 1 then str --- str[x + 1] x then str eq '5' --- (str[x]) eq '5' Since all builtins are immutable and return new values, then works with every builtin: nums = nums then sort then reverse then slice[0, 3] A chain as lines. An assignment's chain may be written one step a line, each line starting with then , indented under the assignment. A step that is a call takes the value so far as its first argument, as above. A step that names the variable being assigned reads the value so far where it says, as often as it says, so a step may be any expression over it, and the value's kind may change along the way: pr = frame.new[node = keys[m], value = values[m]] then join[pr, table, 'node'] then max[abs[pr.value - pr.pagerank]] pr is the frame through the join and the number at the end. Each step is a statement of its own — a refusal names the step's line, and a step whose value failed hands the failure on, as a call of a failed value does ( n = '42' then int then n + 1 is 43 ; from 'x' it is the error, held by n ). The lines belong to an assignment: a then line under anything else, or under a loop used as a value, is refused before the program runs, in both modes. Style: name a value you use across lines or want to explain, nest a value used once as a first argument, and write then lines for two or more steps. Design Note: a chain's steps name the variable. Considered: a word for the value flowing through — it , self — as Kotlin's scope functions and magrittr's . have (rejected: a keyword on every line of every chain); the dot form, x.f[a] for f[x, a] (rejected: a second way to write every call, and the dot already reads a field — a frame's ok column is unreachable by dot today, and every function name would join it); a pipe symbol (rejected: the shift key, and the same second way); a step continued by indentation alone (rejected: indentation would mean a body under for and a step under a value); bare column names inside a step over a frame, as pandas's eval reads them (rejected: where a name came from would go unsaid, and a variable of a column's name would collide); a dotted statement that replaces its receiver, pr.join[…] (rejected: a statement that changes a variable without = , the confusion push as a statement had). Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-08): the variable being assigned names the value so far, and a step that does not name it is a call that takes it first. One rule, read either way, and a reader can expand the chain into pr = … lines knowing nothing more. The parser does exactly that, each step assigned to a hidden name so the kind may change, which is why nothing below the parser — the lowering, the IR, either backend — knows a chain exists. 5. Control Flow if / else if x gt 5 log['big'] if x gt 5 log['big'] else log['small'] if x gt 5 log['big'] else if x gt 2 log['medium'] else log['small'] A condition is true or false. A number, text or a list decided on — if count , while name — is refused before the program runs: compare it, count gt 0 , len[xs] gt 0 , name ne '' . (A number had reached the compiled program as "the lowered program disagrees with itself", a bug in Crow's words.) A value that can fail is decided on as Errors in Conditions says. Design Note: No Pattern Matching or Sum Types Crow intentionally omits pattern matching ( match ) and sum types (enums with variants). Why no pattern matching? Without sum types, match is syntactic sugar for if/else . It adds a second way to branch, violating "one way to do things." Use if/else instead: if value eq 0 log['zero'] else if value gt 0 and value lt 10 log['small'] else log['big'] Why no sum types? Sum types shine in systems programming and compiler design, where you model distinct variants (e.g. Shape = Circle | Rectangle ). Crow targets data science and practical programming, where data lives in collections, tables, and structs — not algebraic types. Crow's error-value system (section 10) handles the most common sum type use case (success vs failure) without additional syntax. If both were added, they would need to come together. Pattern matching without sum types is pointless sugar. Sum types without pattern matching are unusable. Neither earns its place alone in a language optimized for simplicity and LLM-friendliness. 6. Loops for for loops run their iterations in parallel when nothing the body does can show the order they ran in, and in order when something can (section 14). Results are always collected in the original order. for x in [1, 2, 3] log[x] --- prints 1, 2, 3: output keeps a loop in order A loop walks a list, a tensor (its rows, or its numbers when it has one axis), a frame's column (its cells) or a parsed list. A map, text, a frame or a number has no items, and a loop over one is refused before the program runs, in both modes: walk keys[m] or values[m] , split[s, ''] , or a column of the frame. When a for loop is used as a statement (not assigned to a variable), the results of each iteration are discarded. The loop runs only for its side effects: for x in [1, 2, 3] log[x] --- prints 1, 2, 3; results discarded for as Expression Assign a for loop to a variable to collect results into an array. --- transform each item doubled = for x in [1, 2, 3] x * 2 --- doubled eq [2, 4, 6] --- filter items evens = for x in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] if x % 2 eq 0 x --- evens eq [2, 4] --- filter and transform result = for x in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] if x gt 2 x * 10 --- result eq [30, 40, 50] An item that fails is kept, not dropped: nums = for s in ['1', 'b', '3'] / int[s] is a list of three whose second item is the error, shown by its line and reason — [1, error: line 1: cannot convert 'b' to int, 3] — as a list literal holding a failed value is. The list itself did not fail ( nums.ok is true , see Error Handling); each item's own .ok says which did. Handing a failed value to a function is another matter: push[xs, int['b']] is that error, by auto-propagation. A list whose items can fail, handed whole to a function that takes numbers ( sum[nums] , mean[nums] ), is its numbers, as a column's cells are: a failed item stops the program ( item 1 of the list failed: cannot convert 'b' to int ), in both modes. (Compiled, it did not build.) Compared whole with a tensor or a list of numbers ( nums eq [1, 2] , each item a map's read or a function's answer that can fail) it is its numbers the same way, and the comparison is one truth (the interpreter had compared the items; the compiled program had not built). while while loops run sequentially. They support break and continue . while x gt 0 x = x - 1 break and continue break exits the loop immediately. continue skips to the next iteration. x = 0 while x lt 100 if x eq 10 break x = x + 1 total = 0 i = 0 while i lt 10 i = i + 1 if i eq 5 continue total = total + i In a for loop and outside every loop break and continue are refused before the program runs: a for loop's rounds run at once, in no order, so there is no round after this one to skip to and none before it that stopping would keep — loop with while to stop early or skip in order, skip an item of a for with if , and search with find , any or all . (They had run in a for , the loop quietly made sequential; Vijay, 2026-10-08: "for is parallel, while is for sequential".) Design Note: break and continue are only valid in while loops. for loops are parallel by default (section 14), and break / continue are inherently sequential concepts. Using break in a parallel loop would silently force sequential execution — a hidden performance trap. Use if inside for to skip items, any / all / find for searches that should stop early (they early-exit in parallel — see the Search Builtins Design Note), or while for genuine sequential iteration. 7. Functions Declaration Functions are declared with fn . The last expression in the body is the implicit return value. Use explicit return for early returns. fn add[a, b] a + b --- implicit return fn greet[name] log['hello, `name`'] fn safe_div[a, b] if b eq 0 return 0 --- early return a / b --- implicit return A function answers on every path or on none. One that returns a value somewhere returns one wherever it ends: a return with no value beside it, or a body that can end without one — a loop that finds nothing, an if with no else — is refused in both modes, at the line where the value is missing ( first_big[] returns an int, and its body can end here without returning one ). A while true that only a return leaves ends nowhere else. A function that answers nothing, or only fails ( return error[…] ), may end anywhere. (The interpreter had answered done where the function's value was an int, and the compiled program had not built.) Named Arguments with Defaults Parameters with = value are named arguments with default values. Named arguments must come after all positional arguments. Default values must be literals ( int , float , str , bool ) or an empty collection ( [] , map[] ) — expressions are not allowed, so evaluation order and scope never come into question. A parameter defaulted to [] or map[] is an empty list or map at a call that leaves it out — as a parameter handed [] is — and its items are of the kind the other calls hand it, or, where none does, of the kind the body reads of them: a parameter handed where a builtin takes numbers ( tensor[pred] , mse 's) is a list of numbers, so the call's [] is an empty tensor where the formula computes with it (as the row had read it); chat shows each tool's schema as text ( ' t ' ), so a call naming no tools hands the wire a list of text all the same. fn train[data, lr = 0.01, epochs = 100] for i in range[epochs] update[data, lr] Callers can omit named arguments (uses default), provide them by name, or by position: train[my_data] --- uses defaults train[my_data, lr = 0.001] --- override one train[my_data, 0.001, 50] --- positional also works Named arguments are required for axis parameters in math operations: s = sum[x, axis = 0] --- sum along axis 0 mx = max[x, axis = 1] --- max along axis 1 Named arguments are resolved at compile time (a lowering pass rewrites them to positional form before execution), so they work only when the callee is a directly named function, struct, builtin with named parameters, or ui element. A function received as a value ( fn apply[f, x] calling f[...] ) must be called with positional arguments. Calling Functions are called using [] . greet['crow'] result = add[3, 4] A function answers one kind. Its returns settle what it answers — a value that can fail where a branch answers an error, a float where one return is an int and another a float (§1), a tensor where one return is a list of numbers — and a return of another kind than the others settled is refused before the program runs, naming both: return 'a' beside return x of an int is returns an int where the function answers text — a function answers one kind . A function called with arguments of different kinds is a copy per signature, each answering its own (Named Arguments with Defaults; section 13's opening for the standard modules); the rule holds in each copy. (It had been the IR verifier's internal error, in both modes.) Function Scope A function sees its parameters, its own locals, and the program's vocabulary — other functions, structs, and builtin constants ( pi , e ). Module variables are invisible inside functions. The only way data enters a function is through its parameters; the only way it leaves is through its return value. count = 5 fn build[] return 2 + 3 --- ok: self-contained fn scaled[n] count = n * 2 --- ok: a fresh LOCAL named count — return count --- unrelated to the module variable fn bad[x] --- error: 'count' is a module variable, which a function does not see — --- pass it as a parameter return x + count count = 6 --- ok: top-level code mutates top-level state freely log[scaled[count]] --- 12: pass it in Because module variables were never visible, a local reusing a module name shadows nothing — it is simply a new binding. There are no global declarations and no scope-resolution rules to learn: inside a function, every name is a parameter, a local, or a function/struct/constant. Exception — views and event handlers: in a ui program, top-level assignments become managed reactive state. Only view declarations and event handlers (functions referenced from views or page[] ) access that state — through the state machinery, rewritten to state.get / state.set . Ordinary fn declarations are fully isolated even under use ui . That is the sanctioned mutable-state channel — owned by the runtime and synchronized, like LiveView assigns. Exception — a route's handler reads what the app holds: a function a top-level route[…] answers with reads, by name, a derivation the app holds — one over tables, the clock and facts no session moves (Derivations, A route reads what the app holds). It still sees no module variable, and a function it calls sees no derivation: what a helper needs, the handler hands it. A fact gets one value at the top level. Its top-level assignment declares it, and that value is the one every session starts from; a test runs the declarations and nothing else of the top level, and each declaration's value is computed before the top level's other statements run, in the order written, so a declaration may read a fact or use a connection declared above it ( tripled = base * 3 , made = query[book, 'CREATE TABLE …'] ; compiled, the first had not built and the second had stopped the program as it started, the connection not yet set). A fact holds no error: a declaration whose value can fail — a file loaded, a query, a document parsed — is refused where the facts are set, so the program stops before anything is served, runtime error: line 8: cannot assign an error value to 'trades' — load: No such file or directory (os error 2) , and the fact holds the value itself: trades = load['trades.csv'] is a frame, which a page reads as one. (The interpreter had held the error in the fact, and a compiled program with such a fact had not built: a session's state could not keep it.) So a statement of the top level that changes a fact after its declaration — a second assignment, a loop that pushes into it, cfg['a'] = 2 — would reach only the rest of the top level under crow run , and no session, no test, and no declaration after it ( n = len[xs] after such a loop would be the declared xs 's length). It is refused: 'xs' is state, declared on line 2: it gets one value at the top level, which every session starts from, and handlers move it after that — give it its whole value where it is declared (a function can build it), or derive it . A loop of the top level may bind names of its own, which are not facts (the book's site generator writes its pages in one). A use web program that declares a derivation holds state the same way, for its routes (Derivations): its top-level names are facts, each given one value, which its derivations read — 'xs' is state, declared on line 2: a program with derivations gives each top-level name one value, which its derivations read — … . The state is the file's that imports ui, or that imports web and declares a derivation: an entry file that does neither keeps its top-level variables plain , whatever its parts import, so a script that imports a part — to call its functions over real data — runs its top level in order, as any program does. Design Note: No Ambient Mutability What was considered: letting functions read (and possibly write) module variables, as in Python ( global keyword), Julia, Go, or Lua. Why it was rejected: Same reason closures were rejected. Reading ambient state is capture — a hidden data dependency that makes a function's behavior depend on things not in its signature. Purity detection, auto-testing ( crow check ), and refactoring all rely on parameters telling the whole story. Parallel for requires it. Iterations run concurrently, and the loop rule is sound because every read and write in the body is visible at the call site. An ambient read inside a function would be invisible, so an iteration calling f[] could race with another that writes what f secretly reads. Immutability-by-construction is the only zero-cost fix; the alternatives are interprocedural analysis or locks. The permissive languages document the damage. Python's global / UnboundLocalError is its most-asked scoping question; Julia re-fought its scope rules for two years; JavaScript needed strict mode to stop accidental globals. The concurrency-serious languages — Rust (no unsynchronized mutable statics), Erlang/Elixir (no shared mutable state at all) — sit exactly where Crow now sits. What to use instead: parameters in, return values out. For shared mutable state across events, use the explicit managed channels: ui state , the database, files. First-Class Functions A function name without [] evaluates to the function itself. Functions can be passed as arguments, stored in arrays and maps, and called later with [] . fn double[x] return x * 2 fn apply[f, x] return f[x] result = apply[double, 5] --- 10 ops = [double, square] ops[0][3] --- 6 A function handed as a value is typed by what the parameter it is handed to is applied with — apply[double, 5] types double 's x as an int, by f[x] inside apply — however far it is handed on: through a function that only passes it along to the one that applies it, and to a module's function called qualified ( crossval.crossval[x, y, 3, 1, fit_ridge, score_ridge] in the models package types fit_ridge by the rows crossval fits it to). A function handed as a value that nothing types — one never called directly, handed to a parameter that is only copied into a variable — is refused before the program runs, with the fix: apply it in the function it is handed to, or call it directly once. (Compiled, such a function had been left out of the program, and one handed on had been read as text.) A gradient handed as a value ( bfgs[f, grad[f], x0] ) is a function of what f takes, answering f 's gradient — a tensor, or a float — and f is typed by what the parameter is applied with, through however many hands; a function only a test hands to grad is typed the same way. (Compiled, the parameter's answers had been read as text, and f 's parameters had been guessed floats.) No Lambdas Crow has no anonymous functions. Every function must be declared with fn and a name. To pass behavior, define a named function and pass it. --- correct fn is_big[x] return x gt 100 hit = find[items, is_big] --- not supported hit = find[items, fn[x] x gt 100] --- no anonymous functions This follows Crow's "one way to do things" principle — there is exactly one way to define a function. 8. Collections Arrays hold ordered values of one type — an all-numeric array is a tensor (see Tensor Arithmetic and the math module). Strings index like arrays. Maps are dictionaries: string keys, values of one type. Records with mixed, named fields are structs (section 9); tables are frames (section 13). Arrays Arrays are functions from index to value. Negative indices count from the end: -1 is the last element, -2 is second-to-last, etc. numbers = [1, 2, 3] numbers[0] --- 1 numbers[-1] --- 3 (last) numbers[-2] --- 2 (second-to-last) Negative indices also work for assignment: numbers[-1] = 99 --- sets last element A write lands at one position, and holds the items' kind. The position written is an int (a map's, a key of its keys' kind): a mask picks what is read, never where a write lands, so xs[mask] = v is refused where it is written. The value written is of the items' kind — text into a list of numbers is refused ( an item of 'b' is a number, and the value written to it is text ); a value that can fail is decided where it is written, as one assigned to a variable is; a parsed value is read as the items' kind; and a list or a map of ints written a float holds floats from then on, as a variable does (§1). Text, a frame, a frame's column and a parsed value are not written by position: text is made anew ( concat[slice[s, 0, i], 'x', slice[s, i + 1, len[s]]] ), a column whole, where the frame lies ( df.name = values , see Frames), and what a parsed value holds is made into a map or a list of the program's own to change. (Each had stopped interpreted or been written there, and not built compiled — crow check --self found them.) A value with no positions — a number, a bool, a moment, a record, a sparse matrix (read whole), a response, a database connection, a socket, a mailer, the standard library's bytes (read by byte[b, i] ) and its stream — is refused where it is indexed, and so is [] written and indexed at once. A size has a ceiling. A value holds at most 2^36 items (68,719,476,736 — more numbers than any machine's memory holds): a size past it — range[2 ^ 40] , zeros[n, n] , repeat[s, n] , arange[…] , round[d, places] of a decimal — stops the program where it is asked for, before anything is made, in the same words on every machine ( range: a size too large to hold (… items; at most 68719476736) ). It had panicked in Rust's words, with no line compiled, or grown until the machine's memory ran out. A mask picks. Where the index is a list of bools — what a comparison over a list or a tensor answers — the result is the items where it is true: names[labels eq j] . Of a matrix it is the rows, so mean[x[labels eq j], 0] is the centre of the rows labelled j ; of a vector, the numbers: v[v gt 25.0] ; and of a matrix by a mask of its own shape — what the matrix compared with a number answers — its numbers where it is true, in row order, as a vector: m[m gt 2.0] (numpy's boolean index; a mask of another shape stops). A mask of another length than the items stops. Of a frame it is the rows — df[df.age gt 50] is a frame of every column as it was — and of a frame's column its cells, a column of the same kind with its missing cells kept: df.name[df.age gt 50] ; a column's .ok is a mask too, df[df.age.ok] (see Frames). A frame's index is a mask alone: a column is read as df.name , a cell as df.name[i] . A frame's column of bools is the mask it makes wherever a mask is taken — df[df.active] , where[df.active, a, b] , names[df.active] , and negated or joined, not df.active , df.active and df.age gt 50 — as df.active eq true is, a missing cell false (it had been refused, and eq true written every time; negated it had been one bool, and joined it had not built compiled). Design Note: a mask picks, and counts. Considered: filter[t, mask] for tensors and lists (rejected: a second verb where the index already picks — x[i] one row, x[mask] the rows); any[mask] and all[mask] (rejected: sum[mask] gt 0 and sum[mask] eq len[mask] say it, once a mask counts). Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-08): the index takes a mask, and a mask where numbers are asked is numbers — true 1, false 0 — so sum[v gt 2.0] counts, and math's where[mask, a, b] takes one as it takes numbers. The k-means centre, a loop with an index and a count, is one line. Design Note: a mask picks a frame's rows. Considered: keeping filter[df, mask] , the frame's own verb, beside the index (rejected: two ways to pick rows where the index already picks a list's items and a tensor's rows — the reason filter was rejected for those, above — and a frame's column had been the one collection a mask was refused for); pandas's index, where df[x] is a column, a list of columns or rows by what x is (rejected: a frame's index has one meaning, a mask — a column is df.name , columns select[df, names] ); polars's filter alone, with no index for rows (rejected: every other collection is picked by its index). Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-16): df[mask] picks a frame's rows and df.name[mask] a column's cells, and filter is removed from the language: no builtin has the name, so a program may give it to a function of its own. A mask over the frame's own columns is computed in one pass (see Frames). Out-of-bounds indices (positive or negative) are a runtime error. Multidimensional Arrays Nested brackets create multidimensional arrays. All inner arrays must be the same length. m = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] --- 2x3 array m[0] --- [1, 2, 3] (first row) m[1][2] --- 6 --- creation by shape z = zeros[3, 4] --- 3x4 of zeros r = uniform[0.0, 1.0, 2, 3] --- 2x3 random in [0, 1) --- growing (immutable: returns a new tensor) m2 = push[m, [7, 8, 9]] --- append one row (shape-checked) c = concat[m, m2, 0] --- concatenate along an axis --- errors: shape and type are the tensor's contract push[m, [1, 2]] --- error: row length 2 vs rows of length 3 push[m, 'x'] --- error: arrays are homogeneous [[1, 2], [3]] --- error: all inner arrays must be the same length Iterating a 2-D array yields its rows; comparisons with a scalar broadcast to a boolean mask: totals = for row in m sum[row] --- per-row sums x = [1, 2, 3, 4] mask = x gt 2 --- [false, false, true, true] big = (x gt 1) and (x lt 4) --- masks combine element-wise A tensor's rank is in its type, and a loop over a tensor walks rows or numbers — an index reads a row or a number — as the type decides, so both modes read a value the same way: a literal states its rank by its nesting, a constructor by its sizes, every builtin by what it answers ( relu[m] is shaped like m , sum[m, 1] has one dimension fewer, flatten is a vector, transpose and * a matrix), a parameter by its calls, a record's field by what builds it, a gradient by its parameter. An item of a tensor of floats is a float, whole or not ( type[x] of [2.0, 3.0] 's items is float ; the interpreter had read 2.0 as the int 2 ). Where the rank is not known at a loop or an index — a parameter no call types, a piece of svd read by a position the program computes ( parts[1] has its piece's shape, a vector of singular values; parts[i] has none) — the program is refused before it runs, with the fix: reshape[t, rows, columns] states a matrix, flatten[t] a vector. A tensor is written at the positions that read it, below. A tensor is written where it lies, at the positions that read it. v[i] = x writes a vector's number and m[i][j] = x a matrix's — each position counted from the end when negative, and one past the end stops as reading there does. Fewer positions than axes name a part, as they do when read — m[i] is a matrix's row, c[i] a cube's matrix — and a part is written as a value of exactly its shape: m[i] = [7.0, 8.0] , a list of numbers or a tensor, and c[i][j] = row . A value of another shape is refused before the program runs where both shapes are known, and stops as the program runs where one shows only then, in the same words. A number is no part: m[i] = x on a matrix is refused (and stops where the rank shows only as the program runs) — m[i][j] = x writes a number, m[i] = zeros[n] a row of zeros. A tensor held in a record's field, a list's item or a map's value is written the same way, where it is held: g.cells[i][j] = x , ms[k][i] = row , mats['a'][i] = row . ( m[i] = x had written the matrix's flat number i while m[i] read the row; m[i][j] = x and any write through a field, an item or a key had stopped the interpreter and not built compiled; a row had been refused.) Design Note: a part is written as it is read. Considered: refusing a row, the matrix built anew with concat , stack or reshape (the rule until 2026-10-16 — rejected: a row of the row's own shape has the read's one meaning, and building anew copies the whole matrix for each row written); a number spread over a row, as numpy broadcasts m[i] = 0.0 (rejected: m[i] = x would write a number or a row by the matrix's rank, the trap the flat write had been — m[i] = zeros[n] says it). Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-16): a part is written where its shape matches the place the positions name; a number written at fewer positions than axes is refused. Design Note: rank is in the type. Considered: the interpreter deciding by the value, as it did (rows where the value had two dimensions, a whole number as an int), with the compiled program deciding by the type — the two walked the same matrix differently wherever the type knew no rank, and type[x] differed on a float tensor's items; a dynamic walk in the compiled program (rejected: the loop variable would need a type decided as the program runs, and the body with it); a vector assumed where the rank is unknown (rejected: a guess either way is the same bug with another sign). Decided (Vijay, 2026-10-03): the type decides, every builtin's answer has a rank, and where none is known the loop or index is refused before the program runs; both backends read a tensor through one runtime walk that checks the value's rank against the type's and stops with the reason, so a wrong shape rule can never make the modes differ silently. The rank and the sizes a builtin's answer has are declared on its row (2026-10-19; design rule 24), from a fixed vocabulary — an argument's own shape, the element-wise shape of several, a dimension per size written, each dimension stated, a reduction's axis dropped, a join's axis opened, the last two axes swapped, rows stacked, a decomposition's pieces by position — and read where the call is typed; the compiler holds no shape rule by name. String Access Strings support indexing just like arrays. Each index returns a single-character string. Negative indices count from the end. word = 'hello' word[0] --- 'h' word[-1] --- 'o' word[2] --- 'l' Out-of-bounds indices are a runtime error. len[s] , slice[s, start, end] , and indexing count characters, never bytes, in both execution modes: len['a—b'] is 3 and slice['a—b', 1, 2] is '—' . Maps Maps are created with the map[...] constructor — a variadic call with named arguments. [] is always an empty array. items = [] --- empty array data = map[] --- empty map counts = map[crow = 3, raven = 7] --- map with entries headers = map['content-type' = 'json'] --- quoted keys for special characters by_id = map[1 = 'a', 2 = 'b'] --- keys written as ints key the map by ints A map's keys are one kind: text, or ints. 2 and '2' are different keys, and a map holds one or the other, as it holds values of one kind. The literal's names and quoted keys are text; a key written as an int, map[2 = 'b'] , keys the map by ints; map[keys, values] keys it by what the keys are ( map[[1, 2, 3], ['a', 'b', 'c']] , a tensor of ints too); an empty map[] is open, and its first set decides. A key of the other kind is refused before the program runs, in both modes — m['2'] of a map keyed by ints: "the map's keys are ints, not text: m[2] reads one, '2' is text" — as is a float ( map[[1.5], …] : a map's keys are text or ints, not floats), and the dot form, which names a text key, is refused on a map keyed by ints ( m.a : "a map keyed by ints is read by m[2] "). keys[m] answers the keys as they are, ints in order; in asks for a key of the map's kind. A parsed value's object has text keys, so a map decoded from JSON is keyed by text, and a map keyed by ints encodes its keys as text, as json.dumps does, since JSON's objects have no other kind. scores = map[[7, 3], [0.5, 0.25]] scores[3] --- 0.25 keys[scores] --- [3, 7] 3 in scores --- true scores['3'] --- refused: the map's keys are ints, not text Design Note: a map's keys are typed. Considered: text keys only, a number used as a key read as its text, as JavaScript's objects and JSON do (rejected, Vijay, 2026-10-08: "2 is different from '2'", and a key put in as a number came back as text from keys[m] ); keys of any kind in one map, as Lua's tables (rejected: the map's type would say nothing of its keys, and 2 beside '2' is a bug waiting). Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-08): one key kind per map, text or ints, as Python's dict and Go's map[K]V are used — the map's type carries it ( Ty::Map(Key, value) ), the compiled program's map is BTreeMap<String, _> or BTreeMap<i64, _> by it, the interpreter holds the two apart ( Value::Map , Value::IntMap ), and the eight map rows bridge both by hand, since one function cannot be instantiated twice in one closure. Floats are not keys, as in Go and for the same reason. JSON stays text-keyed both ways. map[key = value, ...] desugars to a chain of set[] calls — it is ordinary Crow, not special syntax. For fully dynamic keys, build with set[] : m = map[] m = set[m, key_var, value] Maps are homogeneous: every value must have the same type. Int and float unify (like arrays), and numbers held as a list unify with numbers held as a tensor: the map holds one form, and a value in the other is converted where it is set — map[a = [1, 2], c = []] holds lists, as a list pushed onto a list of rows is a row (it had stopped the interpreter at the tensor, expected a list, got array , and the compiled program had not built). Mixed named data belongs in a struct — and since the value type can be any type, including structs, the two compose: struct Address [street, city, zip] addresses = map[ home = Address['12 Oak St', 'Austin', 78701], office = Address['500 Main St', 'Austin', 78702] ] addresses.home.city --- 'Austin' addresses = set[addresses, 'work', Address['9 Elm Rd', 'Dallas', 75001]] for label in keys[addresses] a = addresses[label] log['`label`: `a.street`, `a.city`'] Mixed field types live inside the struct; dynamic keys live in the map. Adding a value of a different type is an error in both modes: m = map[a = 1] m = set[m, 'b', 'x'] --- error: a map holds values of one kind: the entry 'b' holds text, and the map's other values are an int — --- a record (struct) holds fields of several kinds Design Note: Maps Are Dictionaries, Not Records What was considered: heterogeneous maps ( map[name = 'crow', age = 3] ) — mixed value types per key, as in Python dicts or Elixir maps. Why it was rejected: sort the use cases by whether keys are known at compile time and whether values are mixed: Homogeneous values Mixed values Keys known in code map or struct — both fine an anonymous struct in disguise Keys are runtime data counts, caches, headers — the true map uses open-schema JSON — the Json type The genuinely map-shaped uses (dynamic keys) are naturally homogeneous; the mixed-value uses have static keys — if every key gets its own type, the keys are code, and a struct gives them typo-checking and native compiled speed. The one dynamic-and-mixed case, open JSON, already has the Json type. Every statically typed language lands here (Go's map[K]V vs struct , Rust's HashMap vs struct ); every dynamic language that conflated them grew record types anyway (Python dataclasses, Ruby's Data.define , Elixir structs), and Julia's Dict{String, Any} shows the performance cliff heterogeneous maps cost a compiled language. Crow makes the idiom the rule: heterogeneity gets its shape from structs; keys get their freedom from maps; compose them. Design Note: No Map Literals What was removed: the bare map literal [name = 'crow'] , which shared the array's delimiters and was distinguished only by the = inside. Why: one bracket form with two meanings created a cascade of special cases — the empty map needed the special form map[] , named arguments were ambiguous against map literals inside call brackets, and UI attribute maps forced double brackets ( button[[click = inc], '+'] ). With the constructor: bare [...] always means an array, name = value inside call brackets always means a named argument, and map[] is just the zero-argument case of the one map constructor. The grammar has one rule per position. Precedent: Go writes map[string]int{...} , Julia uses Dict(...) , Python's dict(k=v) is this exact form. Writing the old literal produces a helpful error: map literals were removed — write map[key = value, ...] instead . Map Access Maps use bare names as keys. Access with dot notation or string key. zips = map[home = 78701, office = 78702] zips.home --- 78701 zips['home'] --- 78701 (string key also works) Bare-name keys are stored as strings internally. Use quoted string keys when the key is dynamic or contains special characters: headers = map['content-type' = 'json'] key = 'home' zips[key] --- dynamic lookup 9. Structs Structs are pure data — no methods. Define with struct , create with [] . What has fields. A record's are its declared fields, a frame's its columns (Frames), a parsed value's whatever it holds, read as the program runs (JSON), a map's its keys ( m.name is m['name'] , and a key the map lacks stops the program), a value that can fail's ok , reason , kind and trace , a tensor's shape , dtype and device , a moment's its calendar fields (Moments), a list's len . A field read of anything else — a number, text, a bool, bytes, a function, a handle — or of a field a tensor or a moment lacks, is refused before the program runs, in both modes, naming the kind and its fields where it has any: text has no field 'provider' , numbers has no field 'id' — its fields are shape, dtype, device . The rule holds in every copy of a function (Calling): a guard that would skip the read as the program runs ( type[c] ne 'map' or not c.id.ok , with c a tensor) does not make it one the program can write. (The interpreter had stopped at the read, or passed it under the guard, where the compiled program had not built.) Declaration struct Bird [name, speed] Creation b = Bird['crow', 50] A field holds one kind, as a variable does — a parsed value given a field of a number, text, a bool or a moment is read as that kind, as one assigned to a variable is: its kind is what the program's records are made with, and a record made with another kind there is refused where it is made ( Box's field 'v' holds a number, and this is text: a field holds one kind, as a variable does ) — an int beside a float is a float, and numbers held as a list or as a tensor are one kind. ( Box[2.5] beside Box['a'] had run interpreted and not built compiled.) A field holds what it is given, a failed value included: Bird['crow', int[s]] is a bird whose speed may be an error, not an error itself, so a list gathered from such records is a list, and b.speed.ok asks the field. Field Access b.name --- 'crow' b.speed --- 50 A Record or None A field may hold a record of its own kind, or 0 where there is none — a tree's children, a chain's next link: struct Node [op, a, b] leaf = Node['leaf', 0, 0] t = Node['+', Node['*', leaf, leaf], leaf] What holds a record or 0 is a record or none : such a field, a variable first given 0 and later a record (or the other way), a function's parameter handed either, and a function's value answering either ( fn child[n, side] answering n.a or n.b ). It passes through all of them as it is, in both modes. Reading a field of none, or handing none to a function that takes a record and reads it, stops the program: cannot access field 'op' on this value . Whether a link holds none is asked by comparing it with the 0 that writes none — t.left eq 0 , cur ne 0 — in both modes; a record always holds one, so leaf eq 0 is false. That is the one comparison of a record with a number: any other is refused, two values of two kinds not compared (Vijay, 2026-10-11: a leaf flag, or type[t] eq 'int' , had been the only ways to tell a leaf). fn size[t] if t eq 0 return 0 return 1 + size[t.a] + size[t.b] type[] of none is int , as of the 0 it is written as, and of a record its name, in both modes (compiled, type[t.left] had said unknown , and of none had panicked). An int handed where a record or none is held — a field only ever given 0 , handed to a function that also takes a record or none — is none when it is 0 ; another int stops the program: a record or 0 (none) is needed here, and this value is 7 (the lowered program had disagreed with itself, an internal error in both modes). A record's field is held the same way where it is made ( Box[3] beside Box[P[1, 2]] stops at the first), and an int that can fail is refused where it is handed there: its failure would be the call's, and the check is made before it. A record or none is shared by every value that holds it, never copied: t.left read, handed on or kept is the same record, so a persistent tree's insert builds only the path to its new leaf, and every version it was stays as it was. A write through it — t.left.key = 3 — is a write to the value written to: the record is copied first where another value still holds it, and that one keeps what it held. (Compiled, a link had been a box copied whole at every read: a treap's split copied every subtree it passed, a thousand times slower than Rust's.) Structs with Functions Structs have no methods. Pass structs to regular functions. struct Bird [name, speed] fn fly[bird] log['`bird.name` flies at `bird.speed`mph'] b = Bird['crow', 50] fly[b] 10. Error Handling Every value in Crow is a result. Fallible operations set ok to false with a reason , kind , and trace . Values auto-unwrap — you use them directly without worrying about the struct. Fallible Builtins These builtins can fail and return an error-value: Builtin When it fails read[path] File doesn't exist or can't be read; a URL or an S3 object that does not answer (Files, URLs and S3) write[path, content] File or S3 object can't be written; a URL, which is read, not written mkdir[path] Directory can't be created ls[path] Path doesn't exist or can't be read rm[path] Path doesn't exist or can't be removed mv[src, dst] Source doesn't exist or move fails cp[src, dst] Source doesn't exist or copy fails env[name] Environment variable not set (no default provided) input[] / input[prompt] Stdin read fails int[string] String can't be parsed as integer float[string] String can't be parsed as float json[string] String is not valid JSON, or value is null load[path] (frame, math) File, URL or S3 object missing or unparsable csv[path] / lines[path] (io) File, URL or S3 object missing or unreadable query[conn, sql] SQL syntax error, or the database refuses the statement insert[conn, table, frame] Bulk insert fails (schema mismatch, connection error) transact[conn, fn] The function failed (its error, the transaction rolled back), or the commit was refused Non-fallible conversions (e.g. int[3.14] , int[true] ) return raw values with ok: true . Every Value Has Status x = 5 log[x] --- 5 x.ok --- true x.reason --- '' x.kind --- '' x.trace --- [] Non-fallible values always have ok of true , reason and kind are '' , and trace is [] — decided before the program runs, from the value's type. What is read for them is still read: loud[4].ok calls loud , and xs[9].ok past a list's end stops, in both modes (compiled, the value read for them had been skipped). A list is a value like any other: names.ok is true for a list that did not fail, whatever it holds, so if not listing.ok guards a listing that failed and nothing else. The one per-row reading is a frame column's: df.age.ok is its cells' validity, false where a cell is missing (see frame). Auto Unwrap content = read['file.txt'] log[content] --- just works, auto-unwraps to the value val = int['42'] doubled = val + val --- auto-unwraps in arithmetic: 84 When an error-value is used in arithmetic, string interpolation, or log[] , the inner value is automatically accessed. A value that failed, shown — logged, in text, in a list — says the line it failed on and why: error: line 4: cannot read 'trades.csv': No such file or directory , the first place its trace names (inside a standard module's function, the line of the program's call). It had shown the reason alone, and a program that logged a failed conversion did not say which line had failed. A frame's missing cell and a parsed JSON null, which no line made, show as error: missing and error: null . Explicit Handling Check .ok only when you want to handle errors yourself. content = read['file.txt'] if not content.ok log['failed: `content.reason`'] log['kind: `content.kind`'] log['trace: `content.trace`'] else log[content] Errors in Conditions An error has no truth value, and no items to walk. A comparison with an error-value operand does not produce true or false — it propagates the error, like every other operator. And a branch cannot be taken on an error, nor a loop run over one: when an if or while condition evaluates to an error-value, or the list a for walks does ( for i in range[len[r]] when r failed), the decision is refused — inside a function : the function immediately returns the error to its caller (auto-propagation, trace appended — a place the trace already ends at is not named twice, as when the refusal is on the line the error came from) — the same rule as error arguments, applied to decisions at top level : the program halts: runtime error: line N: cannot branch on an error value — <reason> , or cannot loop over an error value for a loop A variable whose first value could not fail refuses an error the same way where it is assigned (see Reassignment): cannot assign an error value to 'x' . A value that can fail, dropped by its line, is decided on the same way. A call made for what it does — write[path, text] , query[conn, sql] , rm[path] — or any value that can fail, on a line of its own, answers a value nothing reads: when it failed, a function hands the failure to its caller, a handler stops, and the top level halts: runtime error: line N: cannot drop an error value — cannot write '/x/a.txt': No such file or directory . Assigned, the failure is a value like any other — _kept = rm[tmp] , never read, ignores one on purpose (a name beginning with _ is one crow check asks nothing of; a bare _ is no name) — and what a line hands on is not dropped: a collecting loop's last line, a console cell's, a test's truth. Nor is a mail nothing reads: in a handler it is held for the commit and sent then (Mail), so its failure is the commit's, not its line's; nor a handler's call, or a helper's that writes facts, whose stop is its handler's (Handlers). Design Note: a failure a line drops. Considered: refusing such a line before the program runs, until its value is assigned (rejected: the happy path needs nothing — every write would carry a name); leaving it silent (rejected: it had been, in both modes, and a site generator lost all but two of its pages to a write into a folder that did not exist, every check passing). Decided (2026-10-16): the line is a decision, as a branch on the value is — the failure stops where it was dropped, and the program that means to go on keeps the value. A value that failed has no fields or items to read. A frame's column, a record's field, a map's key or a parsed value's field, read from a value that failed, is refused the same way — a function hands the error back, a handler stops, the top level halts: runtime error: line N: cannot read 'price' of an error value — load: No such file or directory (os error 2) — and so is an item: of a list, a text, a map by its key, a column, a parsed value ( lines[path][0] when the file is not there: cannot read an item of an error value — lines: No such file or directory ; it had been the error, carried on). A position or a key that failed is refused the same way, reading or writing: xs[int[ch]] where ch is no digit is cannot index by an error value — cannot convert 'x' to int (compiled, an index that could fail had not built). A guard (below) makes the read an ordinary one. A record holding a field that failed did not fail itself: p.ok is true, and p.x.ok asks the field (see Structs). (Compiled, the read had found the failed value's placeholder — frame has no property or column 'price' for a load that found no file, JSON's null for text that did not parse — where the interpreter went on with the reason; and a record's .ok had not built.) Design Note: a read refuses a value that failed. Considered: carrying the error through a read as an operator carries it — a field of a failed value the error, an item of a failed list the error. Decided: a read refuses it, as a decision does, field and item alike (Vijay, 2026-10-01: one rule for reading into a value, and failing where the value is first read is safer in production than carrying the error on). A frame's column read from a load that failed would make every column of the frame a result, carried through each mask, sum and join that reads it, where the reason belongs at the line that first reads the frame; and the interpreter's carrying on and the compiled program's placeholder were where the two modes had parted. An operator still computes with an error ( x + 1 of a failed x is that error): it reads no part of it. fn check[s] n = int[s] if n gt 5 --- if n is an error: check returns it here return 'big' return 'small' r = check['abc'] log[r.ok] --- false — the parse error propagated out log[r.reason] --- cannot convert 'abc' to int The same holds when a function hands back an error of another shape — if not b.ok / return b in a function whose value is a number, where b is a frame: the caller receives the error with its reason, kind and trace, and the value is the function's default. A handler has no caller to hand an error to. A handler stops when an error value reaches a decision, a fact, or an effect — an if or while condition, the list a for walks, an assignment to reactive state or to a variable whose first value could not fail, or an argument of an effect held to the handler's commit — the session , db.write and mail kinds: a notice , a database write, a mail (Effects Have Kinds; a read, a request, a query that reads or a command handed a failed argument answers the failure, as any call does) — or of a function that writes facts called for what it writes (a statement, or the handler's last line, whose value nobody reads) — and nothing it did lands: its fact writes are discarded, its database writes are rolled back, its held effects are dropped. The reader is told, as the session's notice, that it stopped and that nothing changed, with an id — apply stopped, and nothing changed — the server's log has why, as 3f9a1c07 — and the served program's log has the reason beside the id ( crow live: apply stopped [3f9a1c07]: cannot convert 'x' to float ): a stop's reason is the runtime's own words, which can name a database's address or a file's path, so it goes no further, as a failed route's does (Vijay, 2026-10-01). Under crow dev the dev panel lists the stopped event with its reason and id. A local whose first value could fail, holding an error and guarded later, computes as it always has: .ok , .reason , .kind and .trace never propagate, so if not r.ok is how a handler does something other than stop. In the harness, click[a, apply] evaluates to that error value and the session's facts are as they were before the click. An event that does not fit the program — no handler of its name, or not the arguments the handler takes ( click[a, apply] where apply takes one) — stops the same way, on a served page and in a test, in both modes. A fact never holds an error: a derivation, which is a belief, may; a fact, which the reader acts on, keeps its last good value. Design Note: a loop over an error is refused. Considered: running such a loop zero times, which the interpreter did for the statement form (the collecting form made a one-item list of the error). Decided (Vijay, 2026-09-23): refused like a condition, so an error never vanishes into an empty loop. A function whose loop walks a list that can fail can fail itself, as one with a condition that can; a guard before the loop narrows (below), so a guarded loop is an ordinary one. The metadata fields .ok , .reason , .kind , .trace never propagate — they are always readable, so the guard idiom is always available and is the one bridge from error-space back to decisions: age = int[input['age: ']] if not age.ok log['invalid: `age.reason`'] else if age gte 18 log['adult'] Checking is optional: the happy path needs nothing, and unguarded errors fail loudly at the decision instead of silently taking a branch. (Frame masks are unrelated: missing cells a mask excludes are validity-bitmap missingness, not error-values.) A guard narrows. After if not x.ok with no else , whose branch always leaves (it ends in return , break or continue ), x is known good for the rest of the block: reading it reads its value, which cannot fail. if not a.ok or not b.ok narrows both. Assigning x again ends it, and so does the end of the block; a loop's body does not inherit a name the body assigns, since an earlier pass through it may have made the value fail again. fn size[path] t = read[path] if not t.ok return 0 return len[t] --- t is known good: len[t] is a number, not a result So a function whose only failures are guarded is not typed as able to fail, and a loop over range[len[t]] after the guard is an ordinary loop. Design Note: Errors Have No Truth Value What was considered: treating error-values as false in comparisons and conditions (SQL NULL / IEEE NaN style: err gte 18 → false). Why it was rejected: fabricating an answer silently misclassifies data — bad input would always take the else branch (an unparseable age becomes a 'minor'). An error cannot be compared with a value; pretending otherwise is the Go zero-value bug with different spelling. Instead: you can compute with an error, but you cannot decide with one. Propagation is implicit through dataflow (like Odin's or_return , applied automatically); the refusal happens at the last moment that doesn't fabricate. A future crow check lint can flag unguarded fallible conditions statically. Creating Errors Use the error[] builtin to create custom error-values. An error made this way has no value, only its reason and kind, so whatever it meets hands it on: error['boom'] gt 0 is that error, in both modes. fn validate[age] if age lt 0 return error['age cannot be negative', 'validation'] return age result = validate[-5] log[result.ok] --- false log[result.reason] --- 'age cannot be negative' log[result.kind] --- 'validation' error[reason] creates an error with an empty kind . error[reason, kind] creates an error with a category. Value Struct Every value has: Field Description ok true or false reason error message (empty on success) kind error category (empty on success or if not specified) trace array of locations the error passed through (empty on success) On failure, the value contains a safe default ( 0 for int, 0.0 for float, '' for string), reason describes what went wrong, kind categorizes the error, and trace records the call chain. Each trace entry uses the format "file.function:line" inside a function or "file:line" at top-level (e.g. "math.divide:5" , "main:3" ). The kinds the language itself produces — branch on .kind when a category matters, not on the text of .reason : kind Produced by 'parse' int[] , float[] , json[] 'io' read , write , mkdir , ls , rm , mv , cp , input , csv , lines 'db' connect , query , insert , transact 'frame' load and save 'load' math.load 'env' env[name] when the variable is not set 'shell' shell[cmd] when the command cannot be started (a non-zero exit is not an error — read .status ) 'time' moment[…] of text that is no moment, of a day that does not exist, or in a zone it does not know; fmt[t, style = …] of a style or a zone it does not know 'http' request[…] when no answer came (a 404 or a 500 is an answer: read .status ) 'socket' web.ws 's socket , send and recv 'auth' web.auth 's sign and verify (a token refused says why) 'mail' web.mail 's mail (a server that refuses the message or does not answer) 'llm' use llm : no answer, a status that is no success, an answer that is no JSON, a stream that breaks; act with rounds below one 'mcp' use mcp : a tool's result the server marks an error, a tool it does not have, a server that answers an error or does not answer 'regex' matches , find , sub with a pattern that is not one 'no_capture' captured[x] on a value that was computed, not read 'conflict' a write refused by a database constraint (see crow-check.md ) '' error[reason] with no kind; find with no match Your own error[reason, kind] values use whatever kind you choose ( 'validation' , 'network' , …). x = int['hello'] log[x.ok] --- false log[x.reason] --- 'cannot convert ...' log[x.kind] --- 'parse' log[x.trace] --- ['main:1'] Auto-Propagation Error-values propagate automatically through function calls. When a function (builtin or user-defined) receives an error-value as an argument, it returns that error immediately without executing. The original error's .reason and .kind are preserved, and the new location is appended to .trace . A call's arguments are all evaluated, left to right, before it is decided: where several failed, the leftmost is the call's value, and an argument after a failed one still runs — so one that stops the program stops it, in both modes (compiled, a failed argument had skipped the ones after it: send[s, j] with s failed refused the socket where the interpreter stopped on reading j ). A parameter is therefore never a value that can fail: its kind is what the calls hand it, and a value that can fail assigned to a parameter inside the body propagates its failure out of the function, as it does from any variable holding a plain value (a parameter typed by its body's reassignment before any call typed it had been a value that can fail, and a call's plain argument was handed bare — the interpreter ran it, the compiled program did not build; 2026-10-20). fn process[x] return x * 2 fn pipeline[x] a = process[x] b = process[a] return b data = int['bad'] --- error-value result = pipeline[data] --- error propagates through pipeline → process log[result.ok] --- false log[result.reason] --- 'cannot convert ...' log[result.trace] --- ['main.validate:5', 'main:6', ...] Exception: log[] does not propagate — it prints error-values directly for debugging. len[] is no exception: the length of an error is the error. Exception: elements, controls and views render what they are given. An error-value handed to an element renders as the text error: the server's log has why, as <id> in place of that child, and one handed to a control ( field , select , slider , checkbox , toggle , radio , tabs , progress , icon ), a chart , a widget 's props or a view renders as that text in place of the control or the view; the tree is never wrapped in a Result. A page with one failed part is still a page. The reader is told an id, not the reason: a reason names what the program reaches — a database's address, a file's path — and a page is read by whoever has it open, as a handler that stopped tells its reader an id (Reactive State, The notice). The server's log has the reason beside the id, once: the id is the same for the same reason, so a page that renders the failure on every tick is stable. A derivation still being computed shows error: loading until its value lands, as before — not a failure, and nothing is logged. Collections: a map[...] built with a fallible value is a fallible map of plain values (the map is built from the unwrapped value or not at all), and encode[] of an array of fallible values writes each ok element's payload and null for each error. Errors also propagate through operators ( + , - , etc.) and unary operations. If either operand of a binary op is an error, the result is that error, its trace unchanged: a call that receives an error, and a branch refused inside a function, are the places a trace records. A trace names the file by its stem ( main.check:14 ), in both modes. Error Messages What is not a program — an undefined name, a builtin's name taken, a call with the wrong number of arguments — is refused before anything runs, every such error at once. Each is printed as the file, line and column of what the program wrote, the message, and the line with that text underlined: ex1.co:1:8: frame.new[] is frame's: add `use frame` 1 │ ours = frame.new[node = keys[m], value = values[m]] │ ^^^^^^^^^ ex1.co:1:30: undefined variable 'm' 1 │ ours = frame.new[node = keys[m], value = values[m]] │ ^ ^ 2 mistakes A refusal is the same in both modes (it is printed before either runs) and in the language server, which underlines the same text and offers the fix. What fails while the program runs stops it with the line it failed on, runtime error: line 7: assertion failed: expected positive (When a Program Stops). A message is held to five rules, which crow test --errors checks over a corpus of wrong programs ( tests/errors/ ), in both modes and in the language server, and crow test --fuzz n --mistakes over programs the fuzzer generates, one mistake planted in each — a slip in a builtin's name, a call written with ( ) , another language's operator, a bracket left open, two statements on a line, an import left out — each refusal held to the line of the mistake and the fix it asks for: It names what the program wrote , or what to write instead — never a form the compiler made. frame.new[…] and map[…] are rewritten before they are checked; a mistake in one is refused as written. It says the fix. A function a module provides that the program does not import, called bare or through the module's name, says what to import ( frame.new[] is frame's: add `use frame` ); one a different module provides says which ( frame has no 'mean' — mean[] is math's: add `use math` ); a name two modules provide names both, with what each answers; a name the core has whose form for this kind of value is a module's says that module ( abs[] of a column is math's: add `use math` ). A name one slip from a name in view — one edit in a name of up to five characters, two in a longer one, a swapped pair counting as one — says which, whether the name is the program's, a keyword or any module's: undefined function 'scroe' — did you mean 'score'? . A use of a module that does not exist is refused. One mistake, one message. A name the program never defines is refused where it is read, once per line however often the line reads it, and what is computed from it is not refused again for being unknown; a module the program lacks is named once, at the first line that needs it, with every name that line calls of it. It points at the mistake : the line and column of the text it is about, not the statement around it or the line after it. It is never the compiler's own. A program refused by Crow is refused as a program; "a bug in Crow" is for Crow's bugs. The parser speaks in the program's words, never its tokens': f(1) says calls use square brackets, a bracket never closed points at where it opened, a line indented under nothing says so, a name one slip from a keyword says which ( esle — did you mean else ?), and the habits of other languages are taught their Crow form where they are met — == , && , ** , ++ , {…} , # , ; , : (after a block's first line, in an index, after lambda ), def , print , None , True , a method call ( df.join(…) is join[df, …] , xs.append(v) is xs = push[xs, v] , xs.includes(v) is v in xs ). A method call names a Crow form only where one exists: a value's method is the function of its name with the value first where the program or a builtin has one that takes a value; a call through a module the program imports is that call in square brackets ( math.sqrt[…] ); a call through another language's module ( datetime.now() , os.getenv(…) ) says how Crow calls and names the builtin of the method's name where there is one, taking what its rows take ( now[] , never now[datetime, …] ); and any other says only that a call is f[x] . ( datetime.now() had been taught as now[datetime, …] , and xs.includes(1) as includes[xs, …] , which Crow does not have.) Some mistakes run quietly unless refused, and are: a builtin that answers a new value of the kind it was handed — push , set , sort , upper , an index by a mask — called as a statement of its own ( push[xs, v] alone answers the longer list and drops it: xs = push[xs, v] keeps it; df[df.age gt 50] alone is named by the form it is written in, `f[mask]` answers a frame, and this line drops it — keep it: df = df[…] , never by the row behind it; a collecting loop's last line and a console cell's hand their value on, and are not dropped), the answer of a call that answers nothing given to a variable, a field or an item — a builtin whose row declares no answer, as log 's, sleep 's and exit 's do, or a function whose every return hands on nothing — ( y = log[3] : log[] answers nothing, which 'y' cannot hold — call it on a line of its own ; it had held done , and after y = 1.0 been an internal error), a return outside every function, view and derivation, break or continue outside a while loop, and a use of a module there is none of. The language server offers each fix the message names (an import added, a slip corrected, a habit in its Crow form) as a quick fix, and crow fix file.co applies them all in place, round after round — a parse error hides the mistakes after it — then lists each change at its line and prints what is left for the author: a name the program never defines, a module two ways out of ( add use frame or use math `` ). One reading of the messages ( diagnostic::fixes ) serves both. When a Program Stops Some failures no value can carry. An index reads an element and an int operation makes an int, and neither an element nor an int can say it failed. These failures stop the program on the line they happen on, with the same words in both modes: runtime error: line N: <reason> on stderr, exit status 1. Inside a function the line is the function's own. In a loop whose iterations run in parallel it is the body's line, for the earliest item that failed, printed once. A handler that meets one stops as it does at a decision: nothing it did lands, and the reader is told so, the reason kept for the server's log.
