a comparison, assert[a eq b] , says both sides: assert failed: eq , then left: … and right: … as they show, in both modes (compiled, it had said only assertion failed ) halt[reason] the reason, as written — a program's own precondition, and a standard module's written in Crow ( math.nn ), on the line of the call in the program a recursive function's calls nested past 10000 deep (the line is the function's first) recursion deeper than 10000 calls — a function that calls itself needs a case that returns without calling a builtin given what it cannot take: a negative size, an axis or a window outside its range, shapes or lengths that do not meet, a frame's column with a missing cell where numbers are taken the builtin's own reason: zeros: a size cannot be negative (got -2) , sma: a window is 1 row or more (got 0) , corr: x and y must be one length, got 3 and 2 a database connection that cannot open (a bad url, a server that does not answer), or whose database does not hold the tables the program declares on it (§13 db, The schema a program declares) the database's reason: unknown database URL scheme: nosuch://x , the database at sqlite://board.db does not hold what the program declares (schema = 'verify'): and each difference (compiled, a connection that could not open had stopped on a Rust unwrap) An int never wraps round and never stops for its size — it grows (Numbers That Keep Every Digit) — and a float never stops: a float divided by zero is IEEE's infinity, and int[] of a float past 64 bits is the whole number it holds. A range that would step past the last int ends there. A check Crow is missing, a panic inside the runtime, stops the program the same way and never crashes it. Design Note: The Failures No Value Carries Stop the Program What was considered: making an index outside its array, or an int divided by zero, an error value, as int['x'] is. Why it was rejected: every xs[i] and a / b would be fallible, so every function that indexes or divides would be typed as able to fail. The two modes had drifted apart instead of choosing. The interpreter answered an error value for a division by zero where the compiled program stopped. It wrapped an overflowing int where crow run stopped and crow build 's binary wrapped. And each mode used its own words for an index out of range. Now each failure is one check in the runtime ( crow_runtime::stops ), called by both modes, so they agree by construction (design rule 12). 11. Core Builtins The functions available in every file without an import. These names are reserved — a definition may not reuse them (see Design Note: Names Are Never Ambiguous). Module functions ( use math , use frame , …) are in section 13. A builtin handed a number of arguments, or a kind of argument, it does not take is refused before the program runs, in both modes, naming what it takes: min['a', 'b'] is min[] takes an int and an int or a number and a number, got text and text . (The interpreter had stopped on the value while the compiled program did not build — or, for min of text, compared it.) A module's function is refused alike: mean['a'] is mean[] takes numbers, got text . A parsed JSON value is read as one type before a builtin computes with it (see JSON). An argument whose kind shows only as the program runs — an item of a list of parsed values, a cell no description typed — is read then, by the same rule. Core Function Description log[value] Print a value to stdout, as it shows: text bare, a number as it displays (a whole float as an int), a list as [1, 'a'] with its text quoted, a map as [key = value] , a record as Point[x = 1, y = 2] (its fields in name order; a module's record by the name it was declared by, as type names it), a value that failed as error: reason — the same in both modes, through one display ( crow_runtime::display ). To a terminal, each line as it is logged; a script whose output goes to a file or a pipe writes it in blocks — before the program sleeps, at least every tenth of a second whatever else it is doing (so a reader watching it sees each line within that), at the end, before a stop is reported, at exit and before input reads (a line at a time had been a write to the system per line); a text of 64 KB or more goes out where it lies, after what is held, never copied into the block (fasta's 125 MB section had been held twice). The search reads the text once at the machine's speed, so counting in a long text costs what reading it does — where len[s] - len[replace[s, part, '']] had made a new text for every count. An empty part is refused translate[s, from, to] Each character of from in s replaced by the character at its place in to , all in one pass — translate[dna, 'ACGT', 'TGCA'] is the complement, where replace in turn needs a stand-in letter to keep one replacement from meeting another's (Unix's tr , Python's str.translate ). from and to have as many characters, or the program stops with both counts upper[s] Convert to uppercase lower[s] Convert to lowercase starts[s, prefix] Check if string starts with prefix ends[s, suffix] Check if string ends with suffix join[arr, sep] Join array elements into string: text as it is, a number as it displays, a bool as true or false ; a frame's column's cells too, where a missing cell stops the program, as it does where numbers are taken; a list whose items can fail (a collecting loop's over a value that can) item by item, a failed item stopping the program with its reason — item 1 of the list failed: cannot convert 'x' to int ; a matrix's items are its rows, which show as no text, and it is refused ( join[flatten[m], sep] joins its numbers) repeat[s, n] Repeat string n times fmt[x, ...] Format a value with named arguments (see Formatting) reverse[s] Reverse a string A value handed to a function is the function's own, and a function that only reads it is lent the caller's. A parameter the body never assigns (nor an item of), never binds anew and never hands on — it is indexed, measured, walked, compared, given to a builtin that reads it, or handed to a function that only reads it in turn — reads the caller's list, map or text where the caller holds it, in both modes; any other parameter gets its own copy, so what the function does to it the caller never sees. (A call had copied every list it was handed: a long list given to a function called once per item was quadratic — revcomp's lines ran 130 times slower than the same loop without the call.) A value read for the last time moves; one read again is copied. A variable's last read — returned, pushed, assigned, handed to a function or a builtin that keeps it — hands its value on without a copy, in both modes, and so does a local of a loop's body, or the loop's variable, at its last read in a round (the next round binds it anew: spec, Scope). A text nothing else holds is changed where it lies: s = replace[s, old, new] of one ASCII character by another, and upper , lower and reverse of a text read for the last time or of another call's answer. Any other read copies, so a name still holds what it held. A value that can fail, held by a name, is read where it lies to be checked and handed on. (A function's return out had copied the list it returned — lines copied every line it read — a loop body's local was copied into the list that kept it, a file's lines held at the top level were copied whole twice by every call they were handed to, and each of twelve replace calls made a new text.) A text read by position costs what is read. A slice, a character and a length count characters, and a text holds UTF-8, where a character is one to four bytes. A text a function reads by position — a parameter, or a local it does not give a new text while the call runs — keeps, in both modes, how far its start is known to be ASCII, checked only as far as a read has needed: within that start a character is a byte, so slice[seq, i, i + k] reads k characters wherever i is, and a loop over a long text's windows is linear (each read had walked the text from its start, and counting k-mers by slices was quadratic). Past the ASCII start, a read walks only from where it ends. A slice compared with a text ( slice[seq, i, i + k] eq pat ) is compared where it lies. Formatting fmt[value, ...] formats numbers and strings using named arguments — plain Crow, no format mini-language: Named argument Meaning Default decimals = n Fixed decimal places (numbers) off commas = true Thousands separators false width = n Minimum width (pads with fill ) off align = 'left'/'right' Alignment within width numbers right, strings left fill = c Pad character ' ' percent = true Multiply by 100, append % (numbers) false fmt[1234.567, decimals = 2] --- 1234.57 fmt[1234.567, decimals = 2, commas = true] --- 1,234.57 fmt[0.123, percent = true, decimals = 1] --- 12.3% fmt[42, width = 8] --- ' 42' fmt[42, width = 5, fill = '0'] --- 00042 fmt['alice', width = 8] --- 'alice ' Name your formats. For repeated formats, define a function once and use it everywhere — shorter and clearer than any per-slot format code: fn money[x] return fmt[x, decimals = 2, commas = true] log['P&L: `money[pnl]`'] decimals / percent on a string is an error. A width is fmt 's to give: pad is no name of the language, so a program may give it to a function of its own. Design Note: No Format Mini-Language What was considered: Python-style format specs inside interpolation ( {pnl:,.2f} ) or as spec strings ( fmt[x, '.2f'] ). Why rejected: format codes are a second grammar — cryptic single-character commands with their own parser, embedded in strings. That violates the no-DSL rule and requires memorization; nobody writes %-+8.2e without a lookup. Named arguments are ordinary Crow: self-documenting, validated at compile time (unknown names and arity are lowering errors), and guessable without docs. The trade: one-off formatting is wordier than {pnl:,.2f} . The sanctioned recovery is the named formatter ( money[x] ), which is shorter than the Python spec at the call site, has a domain name, and keeps every money field in the project formatted identically — the consistency that per-slot codes never provide. Given one list written down, concat[[a, b, c]] , its items joined in order, whatever two of them join — lists, text, tensors, bytes (see Design Note: one word for joining). An empty a takes its items from b ( idx = [] , then idx = concat[idx, [i]] makes a list of ints) concat[a, b, axis] Concatenate two tensors along an axis sort[arr] Return new sorted array: numbers ascending, NaN last; text by character code ( 'B' before 'a' ). A list of anything else — bools, records, lists, a matrix's rows — has no order, and is refused ( sort[flatten[m]] orders a matrix's numbers) reverse[arr] Return new reversed array; text reversed by character contains[arr, value] The row behind value in arr (see Membership; the name is not written): whether an item is value , compared as eq compares (a record field by field), so a value of another kind than the items is refused — a number in a matrix, whose items are rows ( x in flatten[m] asks its numbers); of text, whether it holds the part ( 'ell' in 'hello' ); of a map or a parsed value, whether it has the key any[arr, pred] True if any element passes the predicate (parallel, early exit) all[arr, pred] True if every element passes (parallel, early exit) find[arr, pred] First element passing the predicate; error-value if none slice[arr, start, end] Elements from start to end exclusive, each counted from the end when negative and then clamped to the array — slice[xs, 0, -1] is all but the last, slice[xs, -2, len[xs]] the last two, as xs[-1] is the last — empty when start is not before end ; a string slices by character (a negative end had been taken as 0) Map Operations Function Description keys[m] The map's keys as they are — text, or ints in order values[m] Array of map values has[m, key] The row behind key in m (see Membership; the name is not written) set[m, key, value] Return new map with entry added/updated; a value of another kind than the map's is refused, as is a key of the other kind (an empty map takes its first key's kind) del[m, key] Return new map with entry removed (a key of the other kind is refused) Design Note: one word for joining. Considered: gather[chunks] beside concat[a, b] (rejected: two words, and concat[a, concat[b, concat[c, …]]] eight brackets deep in the Postgres driver where a list of pieces would do). Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-08): concat given one list written down joins its items two at a time, in the first lowering, so every kind two pieces join is joined; a list of bytes held in a variable is concat[chunks] , the row gather was. A list of lists held in a variable is not joined: its items' kind is the lists', which one function over any item kind cannot hold in both modes — write the pieces, or a loop. Design Note: a map from two lists. Considered: a named form, map[keys = ks, values = vs] (rejected: the literal already means a map with a key called keys ); zip (rejected, see No Enumerate or Zip). Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-08): map[keys, values] , positional, the key first as everywhere a key is written — map[k = v] , set[m, key, value] . The loop that set one entry per word, in the retrieval package and twenty-four other places, is one line. A collection builtin walks a tensor as a loop does and an index reads it: a vector's numbers, a matrix's rows. len , slice , reverse , pop and push count and keep rows, so a matrix stays a matrix — slice[m, -1, len[m]] is its last row, reverse[m] its rows backwards, pop[m] all but its last row, and a slice that holds nothing is a matrix of no rows. ( slice , reverse and pop had counted a matrix's numbers: slice[m, -1, 3] of three rows was empty, slice[m, 0, 5] stopped, reverse[m] answered its numbers backwards as one axis, which its type did not say, and the next read of a row stopped; sort[m] had sorted its numbers, 2.0 in m asked them, and join[m, sep] joined them.) A collection builtin takes the kinds its forms above say — a list, a map, text, a tensor — and any other is refused before the program runs, in both modes, naming the forms it takes: 1 in [1, 2] is has[] takes a map and text, got numbers and an int , and len[5] , keys[[1, 2]] and 'a' in m of a map are refused alike. A JSON value's kind shows only as the program runs, so len of one that is a number or a bool stops the program with the same words. (Compiled, those calls did not build, where the interpreter stopped as it ran; and len of a JSON number was 0.) All builtins are immutable. No builtin modifies its arguments. To update a variable, reassign: nums = push[nums, 4] . Both modes turn x = push[x, v] (and pop , sort , reverse , concat , set , del in the same shape) into an in-place update: the collection is moved into the operation, not copied, when the right-hand side reads x exactly once. A value goes after its last read. A variable's last read moves its value where the read can take it — into a call, out of a function — and a variable last read where nothing takes it (indexed, body[0] ; walked by a loop; measured, len[body] ) is let go after the statement that reads it, in both modes, rather than at the end of its block. A collecting loop over a list it reads for the last time takes the list's items into its body, none copied, and a list cut by slice there is cut where it lies, the list it came from let go with what it leaves. So a program that turns a big input into a series of lists holds the lists it still reads: revcomp's 254 MB input had been held beside five of its intermediate lists, each one's last read long past (1.25 GB at the peak, 0.92 GB after), and k-nucleotide's slice of the lines beside every line (645 MB, 356 MB after). Nothing a program prints changes: a value let go is one nothing reads again. I/O Function Description read[path] The text of a file, a URL or an S3 object (error-value on failure; Files, URLs and S3) write[path, content] Write text to a file or an S3 object (error-value on failure) exists[path] Check if file/directory exists (returns bool) mkdir[path] Create directory (and parents). Error-value on failure ls[path] List directory entries as sorted array of strings. Error-value on failure rm[path] Remove file or directory (recursive). Error-value on failure mv[src, dst] Move/rename file or directory. Error-value on failure cp[src, dst] Copy file. Error-value on failure args[] CLI arguments as array of strings: those after the source file when crow runs it, after the program when it runs compiled input[] Read a line from stdin (error-value on failure) input[prompt] Print prompt, then read a line (error-value on failure) A file operation that answers nothing — write , mkdir , rm , mv , cp , and use frame 's save — answers empty text when it succeeds, as its type says, in both modes. (The interpreter had answered done , and the compiled program '' .) What reads the world outside the program — an effect of the kinds files , network , db.read , input , process and shell (Effects Have Kinds): read , ls , exists , shell , env , args , request , a query's answer, the modules' load , csv and lines — is stamped with the moment it was read ( captured[x] ), in both modes, and nothing else is: the compiled program had stamped rm 's answer. Files, URLs and S3 A path is a file on this machine, a URL ( http://… , https://… ), or an S3 object ( s3://bucket/key ) wherever the program reads one — read , use io 's csv and lines , and both modules' load — and a file or an S3 object wherever it writes one ( write , use frame 's save ): bars = load['https://data.example.com/aapl/2026-07-14.parquet'] trades = load['s3://market-archive/2026/07/14/trades.csv'] r = save[bars, 's3://reports/aapl.parquet'] token = env['API_TOKEN'] fills = load['https://api.example.com/fills.json', headers = map[authorization = 'Bearer `token`']] day = load['https://api.example.com/bars.csv', query = map[symbol = 'AAPL', day = '2026-07-14'], timeout = 20] Every reader takes three options for a URL, in both modes: headers = map[…] , sent with its request — an API's key, a token; query = map[…] , its pairs added to the URL, each name and value URL-encoded ( query = map[q = 'crow lang'] asks ?q=crow%20lang , after the URL's own ?… if it has one); and timeout = seconds , how long the read waits for its answer (unless told, thirty seconds to connect and ten minutes in all; 0 is as none). A map's values go as text, each as it shows, so a map of numbers is one too ( query = map[page = 2] ). Without the key a server's refusal is the read's error ( cannot read 'https://…': the server answered 401 Unauthorized ), and so is a server that does not answer in time ( cannot read 'https://…': no answer in 20 s ). A file has none to send and an S3 object is signed with the environment's credentials, so either given an option is refused: cannot read 'trades.csv' with headers, a query or a timeout: they go with an http:// or https:// URL ; a timeout below 0 is refused too ( a timeout is a number of seconds, 0 or more — not -1 ). A table's format is its extension: .csv , .json or .parquet . A URL with none is read as the media type its server names ( application/json , text/csv , Parquet's), and failing that as its bytes show — Parquet's PAR1 , JSON's opening bracket, CSV otherwise. A JSON table is a list of records, a row each, or an object holding exactly one list of records, as an API's answer {"status": "OK", "results": [...]} does; an object holding two is refused, naming them, and json[read[url]] reads it whole. An S3 object is read and written with the environment's credentials — AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID , AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY , AWS_SESSION_TOKEN when there is one, AWS_REGION ( us-east-1 when unset) — signed as AWS's Signature Version 4 says; AWS_ENDPOINT_URL points it at an S3-compatible store (MinIO, R2) by path. Without credentials an object is read unsigned, as a public bucket's is. A URL is read, never written. What goes wrong is the read's error value, as a missing file's is, its reason naming the path: a server that answers an error ( cannot read 'https://…': the server answered 404 Not Found , and S3's own words after it), one that does not answer within 30 seconds (or its timeout ), a transfer longer than ten minutes (or its timeout ), more than 4 GB. A program's own URL, built from what a reader typed, reaches wherever it names: a served program checks it as it checks any input. The readers are written in Crow (design rule 20): the protocol is sys 's own, in src/modules/sys.co — a URL got with the options and its redirects followed, an S3 object signed with the environment's credentials as Signature Version 4 says and reached by path at an endpoint — and each reader is a few lines in its module's source ( src/modules/core.co , io.co , frame.co , math.co ) over the layer's parsers; every row above keeps its contract in both modes. Their tests are their own ( crow test src/modules/sys.co checks the signature against AWS's documented example), and tests/reader_headers.rs and tests/s3_endpoint.rs run them against servers of their own in both modes. Design Note: one load , wherever the data is. Considered: an HTTP client ( get , post ), an s3 module and a parquet module, each with its own readers. Decided: where the data is and what shape it is in are the path's, not the program's, so every reader takes a URL or an S3 object as it takes a file, and the extension names the format — one way, which a new source or format joins without a new name. A key an API asks for is part of where the data is, so a reader sends headers with its URL ( headers = map[…] , Vijay, 2026-10-01), and so is the question a URL asks ( query = map[…] , 2026-10-01); other methods, a body, a form and files are request 's (### Requests). JSON Function Description json[str] Parse JSON string into a Crow value (error-value on failure). Indexing the value reads its elements; a parse that failed, indexed, hands its error on, and an element that is JSON's null — or one the value lacks: past a list's end, a negative position, a key an object does not hold — is an error value of reason null (kind 'parse' ), in both modes encode[value] Encode a Crow value as a JSON string: a record as an object of its fields, a tensor's whole numbers as ints (a float alone keeps its point: encode[2.0] is 2.0 ), a NaN or infinite float as null , an error value as null ; a function, a frame and a sparse matrix have no JSON and are refused. (The interpreter had refused to encode a record, and the compiled program did not build one.) A parsed value is JSON in both modes, held as it was parsed: type says what it holds — map , array , str , int , float , bool , or error for null . It shows as a Crow value of that kind would ( [1, 2.0] shows as [1, 2] ), encodes back as that value would ( [1,2] ), and a parsed object answers keys , values and has , in both modes (compiled, those did not build). A field a parsed object lacks, j.missing , is JSON's null : its .ok is false and its .reason is null . (The interpreter had converted a parsed value to lists, maps and tensors: an item past a parsed list's end, or a field a parsed object lacked, stopped the program where the compiled one read null .) A parsed value is dynamic until the program reads it. In text it shows as the one display shows it — 'name: `j.name`' is name: crow , a list or a map as it prints, JSON's null as error: null — as a dynamic cell of a frame does (compiled, text had shown with JSON's quotes, name: "crow" ). A parsed value is read as the kind its use implies , in both modes: a position ( xs[j.i] ) an int, a key ( m[j.k] ) text, one met in arithmetic or compared in order with a number a float ( j.n + 1 , j.n gt 1 ; % an int), one compared with text text, one decided on, negated or joined with and / or a bool, one met beside a moment a moment, one handed to a builtin the kind its rows take ( upper[j.name] text, abs[j.n] a number, upper[j.names[1]] the item's text), one handed to a collection the kind of its items ( push[ids, j.id] into ints an int, push[names, j.name] into text text, j.id in ids an int; read as the number the push rows take, a list of ints had become floats, and the lowered program disagreed with itself), one assigned to a variable of a kind that kind (a number as a float: the variable widens, as one assigned a float does), and one handed to a function what that function's own body reads of its parameter. Where the value is not that, the program stops with what it holds and the read that asked — a parsed value holds text 'many' where the program reads a number (met in add at line 39) — the same words in both modes; text that reads as a number is one ( j.s + 1 is 8 for "s": "7" ), and a number read as text is its text. int[…] , float[…] , str[…] and moment[…] still read one by hand where the program means the conversion. A parsed whole number is held as it is: a loop walks it and encode writes it with every digit, and int[…] reads it exactly; read as a float — met in arithmetic or compared in order — one past 2^53 stops the program rather than lose digits, as a frame's column of them does at its load (a loop and encode had read whole numbers through a float, and 9007199254740993 became …992 ). A loop walks a parsed list's items ( for x in j.items ), each a parsed value; the builtins that navigate one take it as it is — indexing, .field , len , keys , values , has , encode and type ; and two parsed values compared ( j.a eq j.b , in order too: j.a gt j.b ) compare as the program runs, two numbers or two texts as such and another pair stopping (see Comparison), while two met in arithmetic are both read as numbers. (Until 2026-10-08 each such use was refused until the value was read by hand — upper[] takes text, got a JSON value — a value whose type the program does not know is read as one first — and a parsed value decided on, negated or joined with and had run interpreted and not built compiled.) Parsed JSON is dynamic data — the map homogeneity rule applies to maps you construct, not to values parsed from JSON (open-schema data is exactly what json[] is for). An element that is JSON's null is an error-value with ok: false and reason: 'null' , which auto-propagates through the error-value system (section 10). items = json['[1, 2, 3]'] log[items[0]] --- 1 n = json['null'] log[n.ok] --- false log[n.reason] --- 'null' s = encode[items] log[s] --- [1,2,3] System Function Description rand[] Random float in [ 0, 1) from the program's RNG; seed[n] (math) makes every draw repeatable, in both modes rand[n] Random int between 0 and n-1 (n must be positive) rand[min, max] Random int between min and max (inclusive) sleep[ms] Sleep for ms milliseconds (int) or seconds (float); a negative time stops the program (in both modes it had wrapped to a sleep without end, or panicked) env[name] Get environment variable (error-value if not set) env[name, default] Get environment variable, return default if not set — as text, as the variable is ( env['PORT', 3000] is '3000' when PORT is unset; the interpreter had answered the int); the default is an int, a number, text or a bool, held as a cell is, so an int past 64 bits is refused exit[] Exit with code 0 exit[code] Exit with given code halt[reason] Halt the program with the reason, on the line of the call, as a builtin given what it cannot take does: a program's own precondition (When a Program Stops) Design Note: halt beside assert . Considered: assert[false, reason] for a precondition a program or a standard module written in Crow finds broken (rejected: it says assertion failed: … , an assertion's words, where a module's refusal must read as a builtin's does — crossentropy: target 7 is not a class of 3 (0 to 2) ); exit[1] after log[reason] (rejected: an exit is not a stop — it lands no error, and a handler would not answer 500 with the reason). Decided (2026-10-04, with math.nn written in Crow): one unconditional halt, halt[reason] , the reason as written, on the line of the call; assert remains the check that says it checked. Named as assert 's own description has it ("halt with error"), and not stop : a trading program's stop-loss and a bus's stop are variables a program writes, and a builtin's name is reserved everywhere. Shell Function Description shell[cmd] Run a shell command; returns a record with status , stdout , stderr (error-value with kind 'shell' only if the command cannot start) r = shell['echo hello'] log[r.stdout] --- 'hello' log[r.status] --- 0 Requests Function Description request[url] An HTTP GET; returns a record with status , body and headers (their names in lower case), whatever the status (error-value with kind 'http' only when no answer came) request[url, method] A request without a body: 'DELETE' , 'HEAD' , 'OPTIONS' or 'GET' request[url, method, body] A request with a body, as text: 'POST' , 'PUT' , 'PATCH' or 'DELETE' Each takes these options by name, any of them: Option What it sends headers = map[…] Its headers: an authorization , a content-type naming the body's type query = map[…] Pairs added to the URL, each name and value URL-encoded, as a reader's are (#### Files, URLs and S3) form = map[…] A form, as a browser sends one: application/x-www-form-urlencoded , its fields URL-encoded files = map[field = path] Files with the form, as multipart/form-data : each file's bytes under its field, named by its file name, typed by its extension ( .csv as text/csv , .png as image/png , any other as application/octet-stream ), and the form's fields as text beside them save = path Where a success's bytes go: written to the file as they came — an image, an archive — when the status is a success (2xx), the record's body then '' ; any other answer's body stays in body , saying why, and the file is not written timeout = seconds How long it waits for its answer: unless told, thirty seconds to connect and ten minutes in all ( 0 is as none) order = map[symbol = 'AAPL', side = 'buy'] r = request['https://api.example.com/orders', 'POST', encode[order], headers = map[authorization = 'Bearer k']] if r.status eq 201 log['placed: `r.body`'] found = request['https://api.example.com/search', query = map[q = 'crow lang'], timeout = 5] signed = request['https://example.com/login', 'POST', form = map[user = 'ada', password = pw]] sent = request['https://example.com/upload', 'POST', form = map[title = 'July'], files = map[report = 'july.csv']] got = request['https://example.com/logo.png', save = 'logo.png'] A request is answered, whatever its status: a 404 or a 500 is the record's status , read as shell 's is, and only a request that got no answer is an error value, of kind 'http' — a server that does not answer ( cannot request 'https://…': … ), a URL that is none, a server that does not answer in time ( cannot request 'https://…': no answer in 5 s ), a URL that is none, a method that is not one ( 'FETCH' is not an HTTP method — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS ), a body, a form or files on a method that sends none ( a GET request sends no body — send it with POST, PUT or PATCH ; a form's fields can go as query = map[…] instead), a body beside a form or files ( a request sends a body, or a form and its files — not both ), a timeout below 0, a file to send that cannot be read and one to save that cannot be written. The method is a word in either case ( 'post' is 'POST' ). A body that is JSON — encode[…] , which opens with { or [ — goes as application/json , any other as text, a form and files as their own types say, unless a content-type header names the type. A map's values go as text, each as it shows. A body answered is text — its bytes read as UTF-8, any that are not as � — so bytes that are not text are save d, not held. request is an effect: in a handler, one whose answer is used runs when asked, and one whose answer is not — a webhook told what happened — runs when the handler commits, so a handler that stops sends nothing (A handler is a transaction). A rehearsal ( crow check ) records a request instead of sending it. Both modes send it through the one client the readers use ( crow_runtime::sources ). read and load stay the readers: they want data, so a server's refusal is their error, where a request's record says it. request is written in Crow ( src/modules/core.co ) on the sys layer — the second standard module moved (design rule 20) and the first that reaches the operating system: its row keeps the contract above, in both modes, and its own tests ( crow test src/modules/core.co ) read a URL apart, add a query, name a part's type, decode a chunk's size and spell a timeout; tests/http_request.rs runs it against a server in both modes. The Rust client it replaced ( crow_runtime::sources::request , over ureq ) is gone, and so is ureq : the readers' remote branch ( read[url] , load[url] , S3) moved after it (Files, URLs and S3). A request's answer is kept and replayed as a statement's is ( crow test --fixtures ): crow check --record-fixtures sends the request and keeps what it answered under .crow/fixtures/<hash>.json ( {"kind": "request", "method", "url", "body", "reply": {"status", "headers", "body"}} ), and crow test --fixtures answers the request from that and sends nothing, in both modes — request and every call standing on it ( llm 's chat and embed , a reader of a URL). The fixture is named by the request as made — its method, its URL with the query, and what it sends: a body as written, a form as its encoded pairs, files by their field and path — so a changed prompt is a changed request; its headers are no part of it, and a key sent in one lands in no fixture. A request no fixture holds is, in a replay, the request's error value of kind 'http' ( no fixture holds `POST https://…` — `crow check --record-fixtures` records it where the server is ), which the test run names. In a recording a request already kept is answered from its fixture, as a statement is — delete the file to ask again. A save = path request's fixture holds the answer as the program saw it, its body empty; the file is the recording's. A reply followed piece by piece ( llm 's follow ) is not kept. A rehearsal ( crow check ) answers a request from its fixture too, where a recording kept one, and any other as a request that landed with nothing to say (crow-check.md). The fixture is asked for and kept by request 's own body, through sys 's replaying , recording , rehearsing , replayed and recorded , so the two modes cannot differ on it. Design Note: a request's fixture, keyed by what it sends. Considered: a fixture by the URL alone (rejected: every question to a model would replay the first answer); a name the program gives the request (rejected: a second way to say what the request already says); the fixtures consulted by each backend where it runs the effect (rejected: two places, two chances to differ — the body that both modes run is the one place). Decided (2026-10-11): the method, the URL with its query and what is sent name the fixture, as a statement's text names its own. Design Note: one request , its method named. Considered: a word for each method — get , post , put , delete — as many HTTP clients spell them. Decided: one request with its method as text, as route['/up', 'POST', handler] names the server's (Vijay, 2026-10-01): get would be a second read , put is the name a stream's feed is handed ( fn numbered[put, n] ), and delete would stand beside the map's del ; a method as text reaches PATCH, HEAD and OPTIONS with no more names. Hashing Function Description hash[s, algo] Hash string with algorithm. Supported: 'sha256' , 'sha512' , 'md5' , and 'password' hash[s, stored] Hash s the way the password hash stored was made — its algorithm, cost and salt — so hash[attempt, stored] eq stored checks a password h = hash['hello', 'sha256'] log[h] --- '2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824' hash[pw, 'password'] is for storing a password: a salted, deliberately slow hash (Argon2id), written as one string that carries its algorithm, cost and salt ( $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$… ). Its salt is random, so hashing the same password twice gives two different strings; checking a password therefore hashes the attempt with the stored string in place of the algorithm and compares the two. The fast hashes ( sha256 , sha512 , md5 ) are for fingerprints and checksums, never for passwords: they can be guessed at billions a second. Encodings Function Description encode[text, scheme] Text written so something else can carry it: 'base64' (the standard alphabet, padded with = ), as an authorization: Basic … header or a binary field wants it; 'url' , one component of a URL — every byte but a letter, a digit and - . _ ~ written %XX , so a space is %20 and & , = , / and ? stand for themselves no more decode[text, scheme] The text encode[…, scheme] was given: base64 in the standard or the URL-safe alphabet, padded or not, whitespace between skipped; a URL component's %XX each the byte it stands for (a + stays a + ). Error-value with kind 'parse' when the text is not in the scheme or decodes to bytes that are not text pair = 'ada:secret' coded = encode[pair, 'base64'] log['Basic `coded`'] --- 'Basic YWRhOnNlY3JldA==' log[decode[coded, 'base64']] --- 'ada:secret' log[encode['crow & more', 'url']] --- 'crow%20%26%20more' bad = decode['Zm9v!', 'base64'] log[bad.reason] --- 'Zm9v!' is not base64: '!' is not in its alphabet A scheme neither knows is refused before the program runs when the call writes it ( encode[] knows no scheme 'hex' — base64 or url ); one the program computes stops encode , and is decode 's error value, as text it cannot read is. A query and a form are encoded by request and the readers themselves ( query = map[…] , form = map[…] ), so a program rarely encodes a URL's piece by hand. Design Note: one encode , its scheme named. Considered: a builtin for each encoding — base64 , unbase64 , urlencode — as most libraries spell them. Decided: encode writes a value as text something else carries, and decode reads it back: JSON with no scheme, base64 or a URL's component with one, as hash names its algorithm (2026-10-01, for a Basic authorization). A new scheme joins without a new name. JSON is read back by json[…] , which parses text into a value; decode always takes a scheme, since what it gives back is text. Regex Function Description matches[s, pattern] Check if string matches regex pattern (returns bool); an invalid pattern is an error value of kind 'regex' find[s, pattern] The first match, as a record whose groups holds the whole match followed by each capture group. No match is an error value ( .ok false, reason no match ), as find[arr, pred] answers; an invalid pattern is one with kind 'regex' sub[s, pattern, replacement] Replace all regex matches with replacement string; an invalid pattern is an error value of kind 'regex' . len[sub[s, pattern, replacement]] of text is counted without the text it would make — the characters of s , less each match's, plus each replacement's — in both modes (regex-redux counted nine patterns of a 50 MB sequence so, each count a 50 MB copy) matches['hello', '[a-z]+'] --- true m = find['2024-01-15', '([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)'] log[m.ok] --- true log[m.groups] --- ['2024-01-15', '2024', '01', '15'] log[m.groups[1]] --- 2024 sub['hello world', 'world', 'crow'] --- 'hello crow' Moments A moment is a kind of its own: an instant, and the offset it was written in. It is the same kind in both modes and from every source — now[] , moment[…] , a frame's moment column, a database's — so one vocabulary reads it, moves it, renders it and computes with it, and no program meets a time as a float here and as text there. Function Description now[] The current moment, in UTC — in a live program, the moment the current event began moment[text] , moment[text, tz = zone] A moment read from ISO 8601 text — a date, a date and time, with Z , an offset or neither, a fraction kept to the millisecond; a space may part the date and the time, and seconds may be left out. Text without an offset is UTC's, or the named zone's; an offset in the text wins. Text that is no time is an error value of kind 'time' moment[year, month, day, hour = 0, minute = 0, second = 0, tz = 'UTC'] A moment from its parts in a zone, the zone's offset at that instant kept; a date that does not exist, a time in a DST gap, or a zone it does not know is an error value of kind 'time' moment[t, tz = zone] The same instant in another zone — an IANA name ( 'America/New_York' ), an offset ( '+09:00' ) or 'UTC' ; a zone it does not know is an error value of kind 'time' moment[seconds] , moment[t] The moment seconds after the epoch, in UTC (the reverse of float[t] ); a moment is itself, so moment[x] is the moment of a number, of text or of a moment alike. Seconds past the moments a moment holds (100,000,000 days either side of 1970), or NaN, stop the program, and over a frame's column such a cell is missing (they had been clamped to the last moment, 292278994-08-17T07:12:55.807Z ) t.year , .month , .day , .hour , .minute , .second , .weekday , .offset Its fields, read in its own zone, as ints; weekday 1 is Monday and 7 Sunday; offset the minutes east of UTC it was written in str[t] Its ISO 8601 text — 2026-07-14T13:30:00Z , 2026-07-14T09:30:00-04:00 , a bare date at midnight UTC, a fraction where there is one — which interpolation, log , a CSV and JSON write fmt[t, style = 'iso' | 'date' | 'time' | 'datetime', tz = zone] The moment rendered in a style, in its own zone or in tz ; a style or a zone it does not know is an error value of kind 'time' ( fmt[t] is str[t] ) float[t] , int[t] Seconds since the epoch, as a number — whole for int bucket[t, seconds] The start of the bucket t falls in, seconds wide — bucket[t, 300] the five minutes, bucket[t, 86400] the day — the buckets aligned to midnight in the moment's own offset (a day's bucket starts at the local midnight; from UTC, at the epoch's); a span that is not a positive number stops the program. Over a frame's column, a column of moments (see frame) t + s , t - s The moment s seconds on or back, in its zone ( s an int or a float); a moment lies within 100,000,000 days either side of 1970, as JavaScript's dates do, and one moved past them stops the program on that line ( … + … seconds lies past the moments a moment holds ) t2 - t1 The seconds between two moments, a float t1 lt t2 , eq , ne , gt , gte , lte Compared by instant: two moments of one instant are equal whatever zone each was written in min[a, b] , max[a, b] The earlier of two moments, the later open_bell = moment[2026, 7, 14, hour = 9, minute = 30, tz = 'America/New_York'] log[open_bell] --- 2026-07-14T09:30:00-04:00 log[fmt[open_bell, style = 'datetime']] --- 2026-07-14 09:30:00 log[moment[open_bell, tz = 'UTC'].hour] --- 13 log[open_bell - moment['2026-07-14T13:00:00Z']] --- 1800 --- subtraction is the seconds between; comparison is comparison if print_time lt open_bell - 10.0 log['stale print — not driving price'] A moment multiplied, divided or taken a remainder of, added to a moment, or compared with a number or text is refused before the program runs: a moment adds or subtracts seconds, subtracts a moment, and compares with a moment. A duration is a number of seconds, as sleep , later and every timeout take one; there is no duration kind. A list of moments is a list. A moment written as a column ( df.at = moments ) makes a moment column ( datetime , as .dtypes names it), fill fills one with a moment, a moment column's cell read one at a time is a moment — from a file, a query or a column written alike — and a moment column compares with a moment: df[df.at gt open_bell] . One moment per event. In a script now[] is the clock at the call. In a live program it is the moment the current event began — a click or a change from the page, a render, a refresh tick, a later schedule — everywhere inside it: a handler and every helper it calls, a render and every view and derivation in it. Time advances between events, never inside one, so base, anchor = head, now[] reads one clock twice and gets one answer, and two rows a handler stamps with now[] share a stamp. In the test harness the clock is the test's: it starts at the moment the first app[…] opened and moves only when the test moves it with change[a, 'now', t] . Zones are IANA names ( 'America/New_York' , 'Europe/London' ) or offsets ( '+09:00' , 'UTC' ) and are always explicit — the default everywhere is UTC. Invalid dates, unknown zones, DST gaps and text that is no time are error values of kind 'time' . Design Note: a moment is one kind. Considered: the three moments Crow had grown — the core's, a float of epoch seconds with calendar , parse_time and fmt[t, time = …] ; the frame module's, ISO text with datetime , tz and fields read from the text; and a database column's, a float again — so that df.at[0] was text from a file and a float from a query, and the functions of one refused the other. Decided (Vijay, 2026-10-06): one kind, carrying its instant and the offset it was written in, so t.year is the year it was written in and moment[t, tz = …] moves it; one name for each thing a program does with a moment — now , moment , the fields, str , fmt and the operators — and the rest parameters. So calendar , parse_time , datetime , tz and the duplicate time[] are gone, outright, and fmt 's time = option is style = : the one renderer's option for one more kind, not a renderer per kind. Rejected: a float everywhere, which loses the zone a text was written in; text everywhere, on which nothing computes; a duration kind, where seconds already serve. float[t] and moment[seconds] are the bridges for a program that keeps a time as a number, as finch's simulated clock does. Freshness: captured Values read from the outside world remember when they arrived: Function Description captured[x] The moment x was read from outside (a moment, so ordinary arithmetic applies). A value computed here has no capture moment: the answer is an error value with kind = 'no_capture' px = query[conn, 'SELECT last FROM ticks WHERE symbol = ?', [sym]] if now[] - captured[px] gt 10.0 return error['price is stale — not trading on it', 'stale'] place_order[sym, px.last[0]] Readers stamp: query , read , input , ls , env , shell , csv , lines , load (frame and math), fetch , recv . Only a successful read is stamped — captured[] of a failed read propagates the read's own error. Reading a field of a captured value keeps the capture ( px.last is as old as px ); arithmetic does not — a computed number is a new value, not a remembered one. crow check covers that gap statically: a reader value that flows through computation into a decision without any freshness guard is reported (see crow-check.md ). Design Note: Freshness Lives at the Boundary What was considered: propagating capture time through every operation so a derived value is as old as its oldest input — provenance as a sibling of the error system. Why it was rejected: compiled Crow stores plain numbers as bare machine values with nowhere to keep a header; carrying age through arithmetic would mean boxing every scalar, forfeiting exactly what compiled mode is for. The interpreter could do it (measured: ~4-5% on a scalar-heavy loop), but the two modes must agree, so the feature would have been interpreter-only. Why this design: freshness is tracked where data enters and checked before it is trusted — which is what every system that got burned by stale data already does: HTTP's Age header, ROS message stamps, dbt source freshness, stream-processing watermarks. The flow-through-computation case moves to crow check , which is the same answer compiled languages reached for taint tracking: runtime labels stayed in interpreted languages, while compiled ones (Java's Checker Framework, FlowDroid) moved propagation into static analysis. Deferred: declarative thresholds on the reader itself (dbt's warn_after shape), which would fit a future store declaration. Design Note: Adopting External Ground Truth A remote system's state cannot be made atomic by any language. Observations of it are delayed and transiently wrong — a position row reads flat for a moment while a fill settles, an order looks missing before it appears. The doctrine: never act on an external absence until it has been stably absent. A grace window is freshness inverted — where captured asks "is this recent enough to trust?", adopting an absence asks "has this been true long enough to believe?": if flat[position] and now[] - first_seen_flat gt 15.0 mark_closed[sym] The authoritative source is the external system, not a cached row derived from it: derive closure from order status and fills, not from a position snapshot. No primitive can enforce this — it is a modeling rule, and the reason it is written down here is that every system that skipped it rediscovered it as an incident. Design Note: A Moment Was a Number Superseded on 2026-10-06 by "a moment is one kind" (Moments, above): a moment is a kind of its own, an instant and the offset it was written in. This note is kept for what it decided first and what still holds. What was considered: the design before it — now[] / date[] returning component maps and elapsed[a, b] returning a duration map. It could not express a named timezone, parse a timestamp, add a duration, or compare two moments directly; worse, now[] built its components in machine-local time while date[] timestamped at UTC midnight, so mixed arithmetic was already silently wrong by hours. What it decided: a moment as epoch seconds, so that comparison, subtraction and "ten seconds before the bell" were ordinary arithmetic on floats, with calendars and zones as named-argument functions. What still holds: a duration is a number of seconds, with no duration kind; zones are always explicit and the default is UTC — machine-local time is absent by design, since "correct on my laptop, wrong on the UTC server" is the classic deploy-day bug, and a language that makes the timezone explicit never has it. elapsed , date and today went with the component maps: a moment subtracted from a moment is the seconds between, moment[…] makes a date, and fmt[now[], style = 'date'] is today's. 12. Modules and Imports Importing Use use to import a module. The entire module is imported — no selective imports. Multiple modules can be imported on a single line with commas. use math use views.home use web, ui Dot-separated paths map to directories: use views.home loads views/home.co , and its exports are reached qualified through the last segment — home.render , home.message . Slash paths ( use lib/utils → utils.helper[...] ) work the same way. This is how you import view files, library modules, etc. A module of the program's takes no standard module's name. A use of a standard module's name where a module of the program's of that name lies — a math.co in the project, or a package math under crow_modules/ — would name two modules, and is refused at the import, in both modes, naming the file and the two ways out: 'math' names two modules, the standard library's and math.co in the project — rename math.co and import it by its new name (my_math.co, `use my_math`), or move it out of the project to import the standard one ; what the program calls through the import is that mistake's, and is not refused again (Names Are Never Ambiguous). The standard library's own sources import each other beside their own files, and are not the program's. (The import had reached the standard module silently, and the file's math.double[5] failed only as the program ran, interpreted — examples/multifile's math.co, since renamed arith.co.) Comma-separated imports expand at parse time: use web, ui is equivalent to writing use web and use ui on separate lines. Each file's imports are its own. A file sees the modules it imports and no other: a part's use frame serves the part, not the file that uses the part, so an entry that calls frame.new[…] or join[…] with no use frame of its own is refused for the import ( frame.new[] is frame's: add `use frame` ), whatever its parts import — as every file is when it is checked alone. (The entry had reached a module through a part's import, and lost it when the part's import went; found in October 2026, writing the error corpus.) The program still links every module its parts import; only each file's names resolve against its own imports. What the part declares is reached as before, qualified: helpers.table_of[…] . A part that does not parse is refused by its own file and line ( views/sim.co: line 60, col 5: … ), as a part that fails its checks is; it had been dropped, and the entry told its name was undefined. Aliased Imports: use X as y Any import may take an alias. An aliased import is qualified-only under its alias — exactly Python's import pandas as pd : nothing enters your bare namespace except the alias itself. use math as m sum = 0 --- legal: math's names were never dumped t = m.sum[xs] --- the module is reached through the alias use lib/scene as s --- user modules too: s.mesh[...], s.group[...] For the stdlib this doubles as the opt-out when you want a name the module owns ( sum , mean , e ). For packages and user modules — which are always qualified-only — the alias shortens long prefixes and resolves the otherwise-impossible case of two modules sharing a trailing name ( use alice/stats as astats ). as is contextual: it only has meaning after a use path, so a variable named as stays legal. Accessing After use , all module functions become top-level — no prefix needed. use math result = sqrt[16] --- 4 x = zeros[3, 3] --- 3x3 tensor of zeros Conflict Resolution When two imported modules export the same function name, bare calls are ambiguous. Crow throws an error and requires the module prefix to disambiguate. use math use frame --- ERROR: 'stack' is ambiguous — provided by math and frame t = stack[[a, b], 0] --- Correct: use module prefix t = math.stack[[a, b], 0] both = frame.stack[top, bottom] --- No conflict: only frame exports group g = group[sales, 'region', ['amount', 'sum']] Rules: If only one module exports a name, bare calls work. If multiple modules export the same name, bare calls error with a list of qualified alternatives. Inside a view , an element name is the element: stack[...] is the layout container even with frame and math (which both export stack ) imported. The prefix ( frame.stack[a, b] ) reaches the module function from inside a view. A frame function given something other than a frame is the core builtin of the same name: with use frame , sort[xs] sorts the array and join[parts, sep] joins strings, while sort[df, 'col'] and join[a, b, 'key'] are the frame operations. The first argument decides. The element-wise math functions ( exp ln log2 log10 sign sin cos tan asin acos atan sinh cosh tanh ) take a plain number as well as a tensor and return a number for a number. Module-prefixed calls ( module.fn[args] ) always work regardless of conflicts. One of a name the module does not have is refused before the program runs, in both modes, the nearest of its names offered where one is a slip away ( math has no 'meen' — did you mean 'mean'? ), as every module's is. (A standard module the program imports was among the names its import makes, so that its constants read, and math.double[5] had been let by, typed as nothing known, to fail as the program ran, interpreted.) User Modules: File Structure A source file ends in .co ; no other file is a Crow source. Each file is a module. The file path is the module path, rooted at the project: the nearest directory above the entry file that holds a crowfile , or the entry file's own directory when there is none. So views/sim.co reaches sim/clock.co with use sim.clock whichever file is the entry. A part is validated alone as it is expanded — its own names unprefixed, its imports inlined — so a name the part reserves by what it imports ( derive progress beside use ui ), or a handler nothing in the part wires, is refused whichever file is the entry, under the part's path: crow test part.co and crow run main.co see the same part. Any error found in a part — alone or in the whole program — names the part and its own line ( sim/session.co: line 60: … ), never a line of the entry. In the whole program a part keeps its own names: its facts and derivations carry its path, so a local or parameter of one of its functions, views, handlers or derivations is that body's own, whatever another file holds or imports under the same name — a local ch beside the entry's connection ch , a parameter secs beside the entry's derive secs , a list fills it builds beside the entry's derive fills (a derivation that calls the function reads none of them), a list rsi where another part imports chart bare, a derivation's local c or a handler's local r or parameter s beside the entry's top-level c , r and s . (The expansion gives such a local the part's path as a suffix — c__sim_session — which an error inside the part may show.) Design Note: The Extension Is .co What was considered: .crow (the name, four letters), .cw , .w , .cr , .o , .ro , .caw , .co . Why .co : two letters that say themselves, the head of the name, and no language owns it — its only other users are a few 3D and colour-profile data formats that never meet an editor's language mode or GitHub's detection. .cr is Crystal's, .w is OpenEdge's and CWEB's, .o is every compiled object file on Unix, .cw cannot be said aloud, .ro reads as read-only. .crow was fine and unambiguous; it lost to brevity in a file tree of short part names ( scan.co , nav.co ). The Markdown fence language stays crow , since that names the language, not the file. Decided September 2026, while the tree was one repository and one app. .crow and .crowc were read for a release after the rename, with a note, so a tree could be renamed at leisure; that went in October 2026 (one extension, not two — design rule 1), with the editor association. --- file: myapp/utils.co fn double[x] return x * 2 --- file: main.co use myapp/utils result = utils.double[5] --- 10 A module is a part. It may hold facts, derivations, handlers, views and test blocks, not only functions — the clock of a simulation, its tape, its blotter — and the page that composes them imports each one. The front end expands every module file once, whichever files import it: its names take the module's path as a prefix ( sim/clock.co 's head is sim_clock_head inside the program) and every importer's qualified spelling — clock.head , or an alias's — is rewritten to that name, in code and inside interpolation spans. A module reached through two importers is one copy with one state. A handler in one part may assign another part's fact by its qualified name ( session.day = d ), and it is checked like any fact write. A part's test blocks run with crow test sim/clock.co , with the parts it imports inlined; crow check main.co checks the whole app. A module's top-level statements other than declarations are not part of the program. 13. Standard Library The modules that ship with Crow. Their exports are bare names in files that import them ( use math ), qualified-only under an alias ( use math as m ), and always reachable with the prefix ( math.sum[...] ) — see section 12. A standard module written in Crow ( src/modules/*.co ; design rule 20) declares its functions by writing them: its top-level functions whose names begin with no underscore are its exports, and a function whose name begins with one underscore ( _talk_of ) is a helper, the module's own, which no program reaches. An export is inlined into the program that imports it and typed by its use, as any function of the program is — a copy per signature where programs hand it different kinds — its options are its parameters' defaults ( chat[m, talk, system = '', tools = [], tokens = 1024, temperature = 1.0] ), and a value the program holds crosses to it as itself. A misuse is refused before the program runs where the body first cannot take the kind, the refusal naming the function the program called and the program's line ( in relu: clip[] takes numbers, got an int ); a stop inside one names the program's line too. The builtin table still states the contract of a function the language cannot yet declare in Crow — an effect the session layer holds ( read , write , request , mail , a socket's send and recv , the readers of files and URLs), a rest parameter ( randn[2, 3] , anova[a, b, c] ), a driver's function the database runtime calls — each the subject of a later phase of docs/extending-crow.md. Design Note: what stays native, and why. Considered: the standard library wholly in Crow, Rust kept for the compiler alone. Decided (design rule 20; Vijay, 2026-10-04): native code stays where one of four reasons holds, and every crate the manifests name ( Cargo.toml , crow_runtime/ , crow_web/ , crow_db/ ) is accounted for here — a crate added gets its line, with its reason. A mechanism of the runtime, which no formula can be: the server and its pages (axum, tokio, tower, tokio-stream, futures-util) and what runs inside its request handling — multipart uploads (multer), CORS and static files (tower-http), the signed sign-in cookie and session ids (hmac, sha2, base64, uuid), a live page's fetch[] sources polled by the server (reqwest); the database handles — their pools, a handler's transaction, the race of a query against a stop ( crow_db::driven ); the drivers themselves are written in Crow (docs/db-in-crow-design.md); the seeded process-global random source (rand); the autograd tape; parallel loops (rayon); a record's link to a record of its kind, shared by every value that holds it and copied only where one of them writes through it (triomphe: one count and no weak one, so a node of two links and a flag keeps the 32-byte slot its box took). A validated kernel: TLS (rustls, webpki-roots); the digests, the keyed digests and the password hash (sha2, sha1, md-5, hmac, argon2), randomness from the operating system (getrandom); regular expressions (regex); the byte search the CSV reader splits lines and fields with, vectorised (memchr); the formats a table travels in (arrow, parquet, serde_json, bytes); linear algebra, the FFT, sparse matrices and the GPU (faer, rustfft, sprs, wgpu, pollster, bytemuck — the GPU's linked only by a program that writes gpu[…] ); time zones (chrono, chrono-tz — by the database chrono-tz carries, never the system's local zone, whose lookup links CoreFoundation); markdown (pulldown-cmark); a number written and read exactly (itoa, ryu), erf to the last bit (libm); whole numbers of any size, decimals to any digits with their roots, powers, logarithms and trigonometry correctly rounded, and fractions (dashu-int, dashu-float, dashu-ratio); the distributions drawn by rejection or a ziggurat — Poisson, Bernoulli, gamma, beta and exponential (rand_distr). A C library: SQLite (rusqlite); the memory allocator of the interpreter and of every compiled program (mimalloc): the system allocator on macOS reads the clock in its free and frees a value another thread made slowly, and a program allocates for nearly every text and list it makes — revcomp and k-nucleotide run on every core spent half their time there, interpreted, and compiled binarytrees nine times its CPU. The compiler's own tooling: the Jupyter kernel (zeromq, libc), the REPL (rustyline), the language server (lsp-server, lsp-types), crow check 's SQL facts (sqlparser; the database module's query provider in crow_db reads statements with it too), the kernel's messages and the AST's operators read by their names (serde), the served harness's client (tungstenite, in the compiler alone). Written in Crow on the sys layer, their crates gone: the HTTP client and every reader of a URL or an S3 object (ureq), tokens (jsonwebtoken), msgpack (rmp-serde), the WebSocket client (tungstenite, from the web runtime) and mail (lettre); and, with no crate to drop, the statistics ( math.stats ) and the normal draws ( randn and normal : Box–Muller over uniform draws). The database drivers too (klickhouse; tokio-postgres, deadpool-postgres and crow_db 's tokio), measured first (2026-10-05, on one machine, three columns of a million rows from numbers and generate_series ): the protocol written in Crow with the rows decoded straight into a frame by a kernel matches the native drivers or beats them, in both modes: ClickHouse over its HTTP interface — exchange in Crow, frame_of_rowbinary for the rows — read a million rows in 52 ms against klickhouse's 85 ms (two hundred thousand in 16 ms against 22 ms; five thousand in 2 ms against 1.4 ms, a connection opened per request), every column typed as the server names it; the Postgres wire protocol in Crow — the startup, a simple query, the answer read in large pieces and decoded by frame_of_postgres — read a million rows in 0.25 s against tokio-postgres's 0.24 s, the server's own time. The rows parsed by a parser written in Crow instead took 1.3 s compiled and 3.7 s interpreted (CSV through the frame_of_csv kernel, 77 ms): per-cell work in Crow pays the language's price per operation — a copy, an allocation, a Result — where a kernel pays per byte, which is design rule 20's line. The drivers are called from Rust — the schema modes at connect , a handler's transaction, a derivation's race of a query against a stop, fixture replay, the rehearsal, crow db diff — through a table of calls ( crow_db::driven::Calls ) a compiled program registers at its start and the interpreter answers from a child of its own; the compiler's describe asks a crow db describe process (docs/db-in-crow-design.md). What runs inside the Rust server's request handling moves only once the server can call Crow, or the design changes — a live page's sources polled by the program itself, with request . math The math module is built in — no file needed. It provides tensor creation, element-wise operations, reductions, shape operations, and linear algebra. After use math , all functions are called directly (e.g. zeros[3] , not math.zeros[3] ). Broadcasting Element-wise operations on tensors with different shapes automatically broadcast following NumPy rules: Dimensions are right-aligned Size-1 dimensions expand to match the other tensor Missing dimensions are treated as size 1 use math a = reshape[linspace[1, 3, 3], 3, 1] --- shape [3, 1] b = reshape[linspace[10, 40, 4], 1, 4] --- shape [1, 4] c = a + b --- shape [3, 4] Broadcasting works with all element-wise operators: + , - , .* , ./ , .^ . Incompatible shapes (e.g. [3] + [4] ) are refused before the program runs where both shapes are known (see Tensor Arithmetic), and stop the program where it runs where they are not, with the same words in both modes. The module is inlined into every program that imports it and runs in both modes as the program's own functions do; under grad its formulas are differentiated as any function is, so no rule of their own exists to disagree with them (Automatic Differentiation). Its tests are its own: crow test src/modules/nn.co runs the formulas at known values, their laws over a spread of inputs, and a gradient through every one against central differences. Shapes mse cannot broadcast or linear cannot multiply ( x and w matrices, x 's columns as many as w 's rows), two lengths given to bce , and a crossentropy target that is no class (or not a whole number, or one too few or too many for the rows of logits) stop the program with the reason, on the line of the call in the program (see When a Program Stops): linear: x has 3 columns and w 2 rows — x * w needs them equal , crossentropy: target 7 is not a class of 3 (0 to 2) . Design Note: a module written in Crow declares its functions by writing them. Considered (decided 2026-10-04, undone 2026-10-18): the builtin table stating every builtin's contract whether its body is Rust or Crow — a row per Crow-written function, the arguments read as the row's parameters take them (a list of numbers converted to a tensor), a misuse refused with the row's own words ( relu[] takes numbers, got an int ), a value JSON can hold handed to the function as its JSON text and read back with json[…] . Rejected now: the compiler then names every module's function (design rule 24), a module cannot be written without a row written in Rust beside it, and the row was a second signature that drifted from the function's. Decided (2026-10-18): a module's exported functions are its declaration (section 13's opening) — inlined where the program reaches them, by a bare name, the module's path, an alias, or as a value, and typed by their use, a copy per signature; a helper begins with an underscore. A misuse is refused where the formula first cannot take the kind, the refusal naming the function the program called and the program's line ( in relu: clip[] takes numbers, got an int ); the body's own stops name that line too, never a line of the module's source. A module's function is read in the module's own scope: the program's functions, imports, aliases and elements are invisible in it — the protocol's local lines , indexed lines[0] , stays its local in a program with a lines of its own, and a program names its functions as it likes (parity 162) — and a module's functions are inlined only where the program reaches them: a program that uses math without load carries none of the protocol. A function that reads a value JSON can hold ( sign 's claims, msgpack 's value) takes the value the program holds and reads it as its JSON inside ( json[encode[claims]] ). The rows left (an effect's, a rest parameter's, a driver's) keep the earlier rule until their phases; the IR verifier holds each one's function to its row. use math use math.nn x = linspace[-2, 2, 5] log[relu[x]] --- [0, 0, 0, 1, 2] log[sigmoid[x]] --- [0.119..., 0.269..., 0.5, 0.731..., 0.881...] log[softmax[x]] --- probabilities summing to 1 pred = linspace[0.1, 0.9, 3] target = linspace[0, 1, 3] log[mse[pred, target]] --- 0.00667 input = reshape[linspace[1, 4, 4], 2, 2] w = eye[2] b = ones[2] log[linear[input, w, b]] --- input + bias Constants Constant Description pi π = 3.14159... e Euler's number e = 2.71828... inf Positive infinity nan Not a number Properties Property Description .shape Array of dimension sizes .len Its length, as len[t] gives it: a vector's numbers, a matrix's rows .dtype Data type ( 'float' ) .device Where the tensor lives ( 'cpu' or 'gpu' ) .grad Gradient status ( 'none' if no gradient) use math a = zeros[3, 3] b = eye[3] c = a * b d = det[b] --- 1.0 --- constants log[pi] --- 3.141592653589793 --- properties log[a.shape] --- [3, 3] log[a.dtype] --- float log[a.device] --- cpu io Import with use io . An int's bits and a character's code, for the algorithms that work on them — a set of small numbers held as one int's bits, a hash, a parser that reads character codes. An int is a whole number of any size, read as two's complement with as many bits as it needs (as Python reads one): bitand[n, -1] is n , a negative number's high bits are ones, and a shift right rounds down. Every function works identically in both modes ( crow_runtime::bits ). An int stays in 64 bits where the width rules show it fits (Numbers That Keep Every Digit); a shift left by a count nothing bounds grows, so a mask meant to stay a width is cut to it with bitand after the shift. Each takes a function written, or one of a group (a list literal of functions: Specialization), and is lowered to what inference knows — a dispatch the compiler writes over every function the value can be — so both modes agree by construction. A parameter nothing types is refused with the fix ( weather's parameter 'city' is typed by nothing — read it in the body, or call weather[…] once with a value of its kind ); one handed a parsed value, or typed by nothing, takes what the body reads it as, or its default's kind; one of a kind no name can hand (a frame, a function, a handle) is refused where it is applied. A program outside the standard library does not call them (sys is the library's own). Design Note: functions as values for native rows, described and called by name. Considered: a tool written by hand beside the function (rejected in llm's note); a list of function values of one signature only, each a function pointer compiled (rejected: a value's name cannot be recovered compiled, so describe could not say what it was handed, and tools of several signatures — the common case — could not share a list); a new expression that chooses by a name at run time (rejected: a dispatch written once by the compiler over the members, which it knows, is the same thing without a construct). Decided (2026-10-19): a native row declares the function it takes with its signature ( Kind::FnOf : any 's predicate over the walked items, later 's deferred work handed the rest, stream 's feed handed put , route 's handler the request, transact 's body the connection, a chart's seek an event), and inference, the checks, the width pass and the classification read the one declaration; a list literal of functions is a group, held by name; describe and apply are sys's, lowered to a dispatch the compiler writes. Import with use sys — only in a module of the standard library. sys is the layer the standard library's own Crow-written modules stand on: bytes, and a connection to a host read and written as bytes. A program may not import it; a program serves with serve[…] , reads with request[…] , read[…] and socket[…] , and connects with connect[…] , which are built on this layer (design rule 20). In a program, use sys is refused before it runs: `sys` is the standard library's own layer — a program serves with serve[…], reads with request[…], read[…] and socket[…], and connects with connect[…] . The book's page shows the layer through the harness's door ( CROW_SYS=1 ), which the tests and the book have and a program has not. Function Description bytes[text] The text's UTF-8 as bytes. A bytes value shows as <n bytes> , has a len , and compares with eq and ne to another; type[b] is bytes text[bytes] The text the bytes spell in UTF-8; an error value of kind 'parse' where they spell none slice[bytes, from, to] The bytes from from to to (excluded), counted from the end when negative; a span outside stops find[bytes, needle] Where the needle first occurs, or -1 concat[a, b] The two in order byte[bytes, i] The byte at i as an int, counted from the end when negative; outside stops open[host, port, tls, seconds] A connection to the host's port — each address the host's name resolves to tried in turn ( localhost is ::1 and 127.0.0.1 , and a server may listen on one) — behind TLS when tls is true (the system's roots); each read and write gives up after seconds (none when 0). An error value of kind 'sys' when none can be made: a host that does not resolve, a port nobody listens on, a certificate that does not fit start[command] The process the command names, started under this program — sh -c runs the command, as shell runs one — with its standard input and output piped and its standard error the program's own, as a socket: stream_of[p] is written (the process's input) and read (its output, recv waiting at most its seconds, nothing once the output closed), and the socket keeps what a read took past a message for the next ( leftover , unread ). One process per command on each thread of the program, kept while the thread lives: a start of a command whose process runs on this thread answers the same socket, one whose process ended, or was closed, starts it again — per thread, since a served program's handlers run on threads of their own, and two exchanges with one process would take each other's lines. close[stream_of[p]] ends it as the MCP stdio transport says a client ends its server: the input closed, its exit waited for (1.5 s), then TERM to its process group ( sh and what it runs), then KILL. An error value of kind 'sys' where the command is empty or the shell cannot start; a command the shell does not find starts, says so on standard error and ends — a read then answers nothing, a write the process ended . Made as open makes a connection, no effect of its own: its send and recv are send[stream, bytes] The bytes written, all of them; the count. The HTTP protocol is written on this layer, in src/modules/sys.co , as functions of sys itself: a URL taken apart, a connection opened plain or behind TLS, the request line, headers and body sent, the answer's head read to its blank line and its body by its length, by its chunks, or until the server closes ( exchange ), redirects followed and a reader's options applied ( fetch ), an S3 object signed as AWS's Signature Version 4 says and read or written by path at an endpoint ( fetch , put ). On the protocol stand the HTTP client — request (Requests), in src/modules/core.co — and every reader of a URL or an S3 object: read and write (core.co), use io 's csv and lines (io.co), use frame 's load and save (frame.co) and use math 's load (math.co), each a few lines over the layer's parsers ( csv_rows , frame_of_csv , tensor_of_frame ). A program never sees the layer: it sees request and read , effects the session layer holds, whose rows in the builtin table are the contracts the Crow bodies keep until effects are declared on the layer's own rows (math.nn, Design Note "a module written in Crow declares its functions by writing them"; docs/extending-crow.md, phase 3). use sys b = bytes['héllo'] log[len[b]] --- 6 (two bytes for é) log[text[slice[b, 3, 6]]] --- llo log[find[b, bytes['llo']]] --- 3 bad = text[slice[b, 1, 2]] --- half of é: not text log[bad.kind] --- parse s = open['127.0.0.1', 1, false, 0.2] log[s.kind] --- sys: nobody listens on port 1 Design Note: the standard library's layer. Considered: writing the standard library's modules in Rust only, as they were (rejected: a module both backends share is a bug both share, which no parity or fuzz run can see; the week of 2026-10-03 found eleven bugs where the two backends differ and none in the kernels they share, because nothing can look there); giving every program bytes, sockets and threads (rejected: a program would gain the bug classes the language exists to exclude — data races, half-read buffers, protocol state spread over user code — and a second way to serve and connect beside serve and connect ). Decided (Vijay, 2026-10-03): one sys module, the smallest native layer the rest of the library can be written on, importable by the compiler's own modules alone; a program sees one way, and every module written on sys is compiled and run twice, fuzzed, and takes laws. frame Import with use frame . Column-oriented DataFrames for tabular data. See docs/frame-module.md for design details. Column references: strings for names, expressions for computation. Naming a column is a string; computing on a column is a normal Crow expression over df.col . Every line is plain Crow — there is no special evaluation inside frame calls. Function Description new[] , new[col = values, ...] The empty frame ( frame.new[] , since new reads best qualified), or a frame written down: each named argument a column, in order — frame.new[sym = ['AAPL', 'MSFT'], qty = [100, 50.5]] — its values a list, a tensor or one value repeated, as a column written takes them (each named argument is a column write, df.sym = … , typed column by column; until 2026-10-09 only with could write a frame down) load[path] Load a table → frame, in the format its extension names — CSV, JSON records (columns in name order), Parquet — from a file, a URL or an S3 object (error-value on failure; Files, URLs and S3).
