A CSV column of whole numbers is ints, of numbers floats, of true / false (or True / FALSE , as pandas writes them) bools, of ISO 8601 moments a moment column, anything else text; an empty cell is missing; a cell in quotes may hold a comma or a quote written twice (RFC 4180), though not a line break save[frame, path] Write frame → a file or an S3 object, as CSV, JSON records or Parquet by its extension (CSV otherwise); a text cell holding a comma, a quote or a line break is written in quotes, as load reads it; a failure is an error value of kind 'frame' , as load 's is (compiled, it had stopped the program) select[frame, cols] Pick columns: select[df, ['name', 'age']] an index by a mask, df[mask] The rows where the mask is true, as a list's items are: df[df.age gt 50] ; a column of bools is its own mask: df[df.active] ; a column's cells the same way: df.name[df.age gt 50] sort[frame, col] , sort[frame, [cols]] Sort ascending: sort[df, 'age'] . Descending: sort[df, 'age', desc = true] . By several keys, sort[df, ['symbol', 'qty']] : by the first, ties by the next; desc = true turns every key, desc = [false, true] one each. Stable — rows whose cells are equal keep their order — with a missing cell, or a float that is not a number, last either way group[frame, col, aggs...] Group + aggregate: group[df, 'dept', ['salary', 'mean'], ['age', 'max']] ; by several keys, group[df, ['dept', 'city'], ['salary', 'mean']] — one row per combination of the keys' cells, in the order first seen, each key column as it was (a row with a missing key cell is in no group). Each aggregate is named col_how and is in the kind it has: count the present cells, an int; sum an int over ints or bools and a float over floats, 0 where a group has no present cell; mean a float; min and max a cell of the column's own kind (text by character code, moments by their instant), missing where a group has no present cell. A missing cell is skipped, as SQL's aggregates skip NULL; a sum or mean over text stops the program pivot[frame, rows, cols, values] The long frame made wide: a row per cell of rows , a column per cell of cols — named by the cell's text, in ascending order — holding the values cell of the row that has the pair, and a missing cell where no row does. A pair two rows share stops the program: aggregate with group first window[frame, col, how, n = 0, by = [], span = 0, on = ''] A column computed over each row's partition — the rows sharing the by columns' cells (one name or a list; the whole frame without) — in the frame's order: an aggregate (every word group takes) over the trailing n rows, over every row so far when n is 0, or, with span = seconds and on = column , over the rows whose on cell lies within the span before the row's own (a column of moments, or of numbers in the span's units; the partition in ascending order of it, or the program stops: sort first) — (t - span, t] , as pandas and polars close a time window; a sum , min or max over ints is an int, a mean , median , std , var or percentile a float, a count or distinct an int, first and last the column's own cells; 'lag' and 'lead' the cell n rows back or ahead, missing where there is none; 'rank' the cell's rank in its partition, ascending, equal cells sharing a rank and the next rank skipping (none of the three takes a span). Write it into the frame: df.avg3 = window[df, 'close', 'mean', n = 3, by = 'symbol'] , df.vwap_5m = window[df, 'px', 'mean', span = 300, on = 'at', by = 'symbol'] join[f1, f2, key] , join[f1, f2, [keys]] Join on a key column, or on several: join[df1, df2, 'id'] , join[df1, df2, ['symbol', 'day']] . Its kind: join[df1, df2, 'id', 'left'] — 'inner' (the default), 'left' , 'right' , 'outer' ; 'semi' the left's rows that have a match and 'anti' those that have none, the left's columns alone; 'asof' each left row with the right row whose last key is the latest at or before the left's, the other keys matching exactly — a column of moments, or of numbers — missing where there is none (a left join by time; the right's clock is the frame's own order, sorted as needed) stack[f1, f2] Stack frames vertically head[frame, n] / tail[frame, n] First/last n rows (returns a frame) fill[frame, col, value] , fill[frame, col, how = 'forward' | 'backward'] The column's missing cells given value , of the column's kind; or each given the nearest present cell before it ( 'forward' ) or after it ( 'backward' ), one with none staying missing unique[frame, col] , unique[frame, [cols]] The column's distinct present cells, first seen first, in the column's own kind (an int column's are ints): unique[df, 'symbol'] . With a list of columns, a frame: the first row of each distinct combination of their cells, every column as it was, a missing cell a value of its own rename[frame, old, new] Rename a column: rename[df, 'salary', 'pay'] unpivot[frame, keys, cols] The wide frame made long, the reverse of pivot : a row per key row and column, the key columns (one name or a list, [] for none) repeated, variable the column's name and value its cell — the columns' cells one kind, ints beside floats floats complete[frame] , complete[frame, cols] The rows whose every cell is present, or every cell of the named columns (one name or a list): the rows a mask of .ok over all of them keeps sample[frame, n] n of the rows, drawn without replacement by the seeded generator (see Random Numbers), kept in the frame's order; n beyond the rows stops the program where[mask, a, b] A column that takes a 's cell where the mask is true and b 's elsewhere — each a column, a list or one value for every row, both of one kind (ints beside floats floats); a missing cell stays missing; a column of bools is its own mask. ( math.where is the same word over tensors.) bucket[column, seconds] Each moment's bucket start (see Moments, bucket[t, seconds] ), a column of moments: after df.hour = bucket[df.at, 3600] , group[df, ['symbol', 'hour'], ['px', 'first'], ['px', 'max'], ['px', 'min'], ['px', 'last'], ['qty', 'sum']] is the hourly bars stats[frame] Each numeric column's count, mean, population standard deviation, min, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and max, as text A datetime column holds moments (see Moments): a column written from a list of moments, or one repeated, is one, fill fills one with a moment, a cell read one at a time is a moment, a mask compares the column with a moment, and load reads one from ISO 8601 text and save writes it back as such. Properties: .shape , .columns , .dtypes . Column access: df.age . len[df] returns the row count. Aggregation names for group and window : 'sum' , 'mean' , 'min' , 'max' , 'count' , 'median' , 'std' , 'var' , 'first' , 'last' , 'distinct' and a percentile 'p1' to 'p99' ( 'p90' ). A median and a percentile are interpolated between the two cells they fall between (as pandas, numpy and Julia interpolate), a float; std and var the population's (as stats and std of a tensor answer), floats; first and last the first and the last present cell, in the column's kind; distinct the count of distinct present cells, an int. Join kinds: 'inner' (the default), 'left' , 'right' , 'outer' , 'semi' , 'anti' , 'asof' . A column is written the way it is read. df.qty reads a column, and df.qty = values writes it where the frame lies: a new column, or the column replaced; values a list, a tensor or a column as long as the rows, or one value repeated down them ( df.side = 'buy' ); ints held as a tensor ( [1, 2] ) make a column of ints. Values of another length stop the program ( column 'b' is given 3 values, and the frame has 2 rows ), as a write at a position that is not there does. The frame is whatever holds it — a variable, a record's field ( book.prices.doubled = … ), a list's item — and a function writes the frame it was handed, its caller's copy untouched. A column written through a record's field or a list's item is read as the program runs: the field's type is every record's and the item's every item's, so neither can carry the column, and the frame there is open from that line on (as a frame whose columns show only as it runs is). After a dot, a column's name reads as text does: a backtick inside it is an interpolation, so df.lag_ k = … writes the column named by the text lag_ and k , and df. name = … the column a variable names; read the same three ways ( df.lag_ k , `df.`name ). A name no dot can write — a header with a space, a keyword — is reached through the marks, df. 'in px' , and that is the escape, not the idiom. A computed name is a frame's alone: a record's fields are fixed before the program runs (`.`f of a record is refused), and a map's key is m[key] . Each named argument of frame.new[sym = …, qty = …] is such a write, so the literal and the dot are one mechanism. Design Note: a column is written by the dot. Considered: with[df, 'name', values] , a verb answering a new frame (shipped until 2026-10-20; rejected: a verb for what the dot already reads, the quoted name, the assignment back, and the chains it bred — with[with[frame.new[], 'symbol', syms], 'rsi_3m', vals] ); set[df, name, values] , the map's verb lifted to frames (rejected: the same shape as with ); a method, df.add['name', values] (rejected: a second call shape for one kind, and a method's name reserved on every frame's columns — pandas's df.count ); df[name] = values , the index write (rejected: a frame's index is a mask, by the decision of 2026-10-16, and it would mean a column on the left of = and rows on the right); a then chain of column steps (rejected: a step that mentions the frame changes shape); and no computed name at all, rename after a write under a placeholder (rejected: a loop writing a column per k was two lines of indirection). Decision (Vijay, 2026-10-20): the dot writes, as it reads; after a dot a name reads as text does, a backtick inside it an interpolation; with is removed from the language (an unknown name, as every removed builtin is). The write is the hidden row __set_col and the computed read __col , found by the lowering through their rows' properties ( Prop::ColumnWrite , Prop::ColumnRead ), so the compiler names neither; a refusal names the form as the program writes it. Text, casts and a moment's fields over a column. lower , upper , trim , replace and sub of a frame's column answer a column of text, each present cell as the text function answers it, a missing cell staying missing (a sub pattern that is none stops the program: a cell cannot carry the reason); part in c of a text column (whether each cell holds the part: 'AA' in df.sym ), starts and ends answer a mask, a missing cell false. int , float , str and moment of a column convert every cell as the one-value form does — text read as a number or a moment, a number as seconds, a moment as its seconds, anything as the text it shows — a cell that cannot be converted missing, which the column's .ok says ( int[df.price] cuts toward zero; str[df.day] is text that load would read back as ints). df.at.hour , .year , .month , .day , .minute , .second , .weekday and .offset of a column of moments are a column of ints, each read in its own zone. ( len[df.col] stays the column's length: a cell's length is len[df.col[i]] .) A column the frame lacks, an aggregation or a join it does not know, a mask of another length than the rows, a negative count for head or tail , a fill value of another kind than the column's (an int fills a float column), and a count of arguments the function does not take stop the program with the reason (see When a Program Stops), in both modes, as df.col of a missing column does. A column written from another ( df.b = df.a ) keeps its missing cells. Several keys, pivots and windows. group[df, ['symbol', 'day'], ['qty', 'sum']] has a row per symbol and day, symbol and day as they were and qty_sum an int, as qty is. pivot[df, 'symbol', 'day', 'qty'] lays the days out as columns, one row per symbol, with qty in the cells — the columns are the days' text ( '1' , '2' ), so they show as the program runs and their cells are read as a loaded file's are, with int[…] , float[…] or str[…] ; a symbol and day two rows share stops the program ( pivot: 'b' and '1' appear 2 times — one row per pair: aggregate first, group[frame, ['sym', 'day'], ['qty', 'mean']] ). window[df, 'qty', 'sum', by = 'symbol'] is each row's running total within its symbol, window[df, 'px', 'lag', n = 1, by = 'symbol'] the symbol's previous price, missing on its first row, and window[df, 'px', 'rank'] each price's rank over the whole frame; the trailing forms ( n = 3 ) take the rows there are at a partition's start. A window's cells are typed by what it computes — a sum , min or max in the column's kind, a float for mean , an int for count and rank , the column's own cells for lag and lead , which can be missing — and a column a window or a pivot names that the frame lacks is refused before the program runs, as a key is. A column handed to sum , mean , min or max holds numbers, and a missing cell stops the program as it does where numbers are taken. The same in both modes. Design Note: pivot reshapes, group aggregates. Considered: pivot[df, rows, cols, values, how = 'sum'] , a pivot table that aggregates the rows sharing a pair, as a spreadsheet's does and pandas's pivot_table . Decided (2026-10-02, with the frame work): one way to aggregate — group — and one way to reshape; a pair two rows share stops the program, naming the group that aggregates it. Rows and columns come in ascending order of their cells, where group keeps the order first seen: a pivot is read as a table, and its days and symbols are looked for by their order. Design Note: percentiles are words, keys are lists, and the other names are the old ones. Considered, for a percentile, ['px', 'quantile', 0.9] — a list holds one kind, and 'quantile 0.9' as text — a name with a space in it. Decided: 'p90' , one word for the 90th percentile, as a column is named by it ( px_p90 ); 'median' is 'p50' by its own name. Considered, for a join on several keys with an as-of clock, pandas's and polars's by = beside on = . Decided: one list of keys, the last the clock — join[bars, signals, ['symbol', 'at'], 'asof'] reads as the match it is. Considered, for a conditional column, a new word ( pick , choose ); decided: where , math's word for the same operation over tensors — one name, the kinds picking the row. Considered, for the reverse of pivot , pandas's melt and polars's unpivot ; decided: unpivot , naming its two new columns variable and value as both do, so a program ported from either keeps its names. Considered, for rows without a missing cell, dropna ; decided: complete , the word the masks section already used for them. A bucket's edge is the local midnight of the moment's own offset (a day in New York starts at 04:00Z), where pandas floors a zone-aware moment in UTC: a bar is drawn on the exchange's clock, and a moment carries the offset it was written in for this. A fill by direction is fill[df, col, how = 'forward'] , since fill[df, col, 'forward'] would be the text in a column of text. A text function over a column keeps its name, as the arithmetic operators keep theirs; len of a column stays its row count. Design Note: the frame module is held to pandas. tests/parity/185_frames_held_to_pandas.co computes 59 cases over four tables ( tests/frames/data/ ) and compares each with what pandas 3.0 answered ( tests/frames/expected/ , written once by tests/frames/reference.py ): loading and its kinds, select , six filters, five sorts, head and tail , four groups, a pivot, running, trailing, shifted and ranked windows, the four joins, stack , three fills, unique , rename , a computed column, reductions, moments moved between offsets, and quoted cells read and written back — every column, kind and cell the same, in both modes (2026-10-06); and, since 2026-10-07, the other aggregates (a median, percentiles, the deviation, first and last, distinct), windows of them trailing and running and over a span of six hours, sorts on two and three keys, joins on two keys of every kind, distinct rows, an as-of join, six-hour buckets and the bars over them, text and a moment's fields over a column, an unpivot, fills by direction, complete rows, a conditional column and casts. What that round found: pandas's rolling kernels compile to fused multiply-adds, so a deviation or a percentile agreed to twelve digits and not the last — the runtime's mul_add now computes the same rounding, and a window whose squared sum collapsed is computed afresh as pandas's is. What it found and changed: a CSV column of true / false had loaded as text (so save then load lost the kind) and a quoted cell had been split at its comma; the sort was unstable and a missing int cell sorted as 0 — now stable, missing cells last either way, as pandas sorts them (polars puts them first, Postgres first or last by direction: one rule was needed, and the one that keeps the present cells together was taken); every aggregate of group was a float and a sum over text silently 0; a window's sum over ints was a float; unique answered text for every column, and gave up scanning after a long stretch without a new cell; a right or outer join's unmatched row had lost its key; a sum over floats differed from pandas and numpy in the last digit — a group or window total is now compensated as pandas keeps one (Kahan, with pandas's separate compensations for the cells added and taken off, and its exact answer for a window whose cells are all one value), and sum[t] adds as numpy does, pairwise; and, in the compiled program alone, a moment cell read one at a time was seconds where the interpreter read its text, a field of a moment that can fail ( tz 's answer) did not build, [1, 2] written as a column made a column of floats, a list a function started empty and pushed onto did not build, and a list of a loaded file's cells, read one at a time, did not join . And in crow test alone, window[…, by = …] and request[…, timeout = …] were refused in every test block: the runner desugared the program twice, and the options filled in once were too many arguments the second time. Where pandas has a choice, the spec's is taken, and the script says so: groups in the order first seen ( sort=False ), a trailing window over the rows there are ( min_periods=1 ), rank sharing a rank between equal cells ( method='min' ), the population deviation ( ddof=0 ), a right frame's duplicate column named _right , and a right or outer join compared sorted, since pandas orders those rows by the right frame or by key where Crow keeps the left frame's order and appends the unmatched. Not compared: stats , a display, and fill of a moment column, which neither side needed. Design Note: a window is a frame's, an indicator a series's. Considered: leaving trailing aggregates to the market package's indicators ( sma[bars.c, 3] is a trailing mean over one series), so that a frame has no second way to a moving average. Decided: window computes within a frame's partitions, in its order — one column holding a series per symbol, each windowed on its own — where an indicator takes one series; over one series, sma[df.close, 3] and window[df, 'close', 'mean', n = 3] agree. A trailing window's first rows are the rows there are, as SQL's window frames give them (pandas leaves them empty until the window fills). A frame's type is its columns. A frame built in the program ( frame.new[] , a column written under a name the program writes), a query a database described (see db, Typed cells), and a frame derived from either through select , a mask ( df[mask] ), sort , head , tail , fill , stack , join , rename , group or pivot carries its columns in its type, each with its cells' type (a column written from another keeps its cells' type; a pivot's rows column, and its others as they show). A column written under a name the program computes ( df. name = xs ) leaves the columns the type knows and makes the frame open : a column it cannot name may be there. A column written binds the frame anew: after df.x = xs , df has x from that line on, and before it the frame it was. Where branches, or a loop's rounds, meet, a frame has the columns they all give it; a column only some add may be there, and is read as the program runs. A function handed frames of different columns is a copy per set of columns, so it reads the columns each call hands it. Where a frame's columns are all known, a column it lacks — read as df.x , named where select , sort , fill , rename , group or join takes a column, or named by a table ( key , mark , delta , hide ) or a chart ( candles , lines , bars_y ) — is refused before the program runs, in both modes, with the columns the frame has ( frame has no property or column 'cost' — its columns are 'price' , and, read in a function, the parameter the frame was handed as); the stop above is for a frame whose columns show only as it runs (a file load reads then, a query no database described, a column a variable names). A frame loaded from a file has the columns the program reads. frame.load cannot see a file's columns before the program runs, and neither can the program state them: the reads of the frame's cells say what they are. A cell walked and handed to upper , or to a function that reads it as text, is text; one met as a number — compared with one, added to one, halved — is a number, held as floats whichever the file wrote, so q gt 20 holds for a file's 20.5 and q / 2 of its 7 is 3.5 , as a variable that may hold a float divides (§1); one handed to what takes nothing but an int — a position, xs[q] , or head , repeat , slice — is an int; one decided on is a bool; one met beside a moment is a moment. A function the cell is handed to says what its own body reads the parameter as. The frame is held to that shape where it is bound, before any cell is read: a column missing, or holding another kind — numbers where the program reads text, text where it reads numbers, floats where a position reads ints — stops the program there with the column, what it holds, what the program reads and the read that asked ( column 'slot' holds floats where the program reads ints (a position in labels at line 12) ), the same words in both modes. A column of whole numbers the program reads as numbers is widened to floats at the load, exactly: a whole number beyond 2^53 stops the load there rather than lose digits (read it with int[…] where it is compared). From then on the frame's cells are typed, in both modes, and nothing is read first — each a cell that can be missing, since a file's cell can be empty and a record's field null: read one at a time, a missing one is an error value of reason missing (below; the reads had typed the cells plain, and a missing one had been read as '' or NaN with .ok true, in both modes). A column the program writes on the frame ( df.when = … ) is the program's from then on: what it reads of it after the write — on the frame, on one a verb derives from it, in a function it is handed to — says nothing of the file, which need not have it (a column of moments written and compared had been asked of the file, and the load had stopped: the frame has no column 'when' ). A column no read says anything of stays as it comes, a parsed value read as its use implies where it is used (see JSON). A column read as two kinds — text here, a number there — is refused before the program runs, naming both reads. A page's data source ( fetch[url] , poll[url, seconds] , ui) is such a frame too: its reads say its columns, the fact carries them to the session, and the answer is held to them where it arrives — its records a frame, a column of whole numbers read as numbers floats, an answer of no records the table with no rows yet — before the page shows; what is not what the page reads (no answer, no JSON, a column missing or of another kind) stops the session there, told to the reader as a handler's stop is, the reason in the server's log with the column, what it holds, what the program reads and the read that asked — the same in both modes. fn label[t] return upper[t] df = frame.load['orders.csv'] --- sym is text, qty a number: the reads below say so labels = for t in df.sym label[t] for q in df.qty if q gt 20 log[q] Design Note: a loaded frame's columns are what the program reads, not what it writes. Considered: the program stating a column's type ( columns = map[sym = 'str'] , in the words type answers) or showing it by a sample value ( map[sym = '', qty = 0] ). Rejected: each is a second way of saying what a value already says, and the sample asks the programmer to invent one. Considered: reading every cell first, as a parsed value's (the way until 2026-10-08). Rejected: the program did nothing wrong, and the compiled program had not held a function handed such a cell. Decided: the reads say the columns, the file is held to them where it is loaded, and a column no read types stays as it comes. Considered, and built for a day: a cell compared with an int held as ints, so a file's 20.5 stopped the load where the program wrote q gt 20 . Rejected (Vijay, 2026-10-08: "q gt 20 when q = 20.5 should work. as a human being, it is obvious ... you are comparing two numbers. whether it is a float or int, it does not matter"): the program says a number, which kind the file's are is the file's business, and a program's meaning must not turn on whether the file wrote 7 or 7.0 — the language's own rule, that a variable which may hold a float is a float, says what the column is. Only a use that takes nothing but an int asks the file for ints, and the stop names that use. A page's data source is held the same way where its answer arrives, in the session both modes share (2026-10-08: the interpreter had answered an empty map and registered no source at all, and the compiled program had turned the records into a frame of its own at every render). Design Note: a frame's reassignment is a new binding. Considered: one type per variable, as every other variable has, the frame's columns joined over its assignments — which loses exactly the columns a program adds ( df.x = xs , then df.x ); and a name per shape ( df2 = … for every column added), which asks the program to rename what it changes, and makes a loop that adds columns impossible to write. Decided (Vijay, 2026-09-29): a frame variable's type is its last assignment's — a new binding where its columns change, as a Rust let shadows one — and where ways through meet it has the columns they share. Design Note: a frame operation's misuse stops the program. Considered: error values of kind 'frame' , which the table of kinds listed for filter , sort , group and join , and which the interpreter answered. Rejected: the operations are typed as giving a frame, which cannot fail, and the compiled program stopped — so a program that checked .ok worked in one mode only — and the same column the frame lacks, read as df.col , stops the program. A misuse is the program's mistake, not something it reads: an error value would carry it to wherever a decision first met it. Reading a file, load , stays an error value; a column written with values of another length than the rows stops, as a write at a position that is not there does. Boolean Masks Filtering uses ordinary Crow expressions that evaluate to boolean arrays. These operations are vectorized (element-wise): eq ne gt lt gte lte — column vs scalar → boolean array (the scalar may come first: 50 lt df.age ) 'late' in df.note , starts[df.symbol, 'A'] , ends[df.note, 'k'] — a text column tested cell by cell → boolean array, a missing cell false and / or — two boolean arrays → boolean array; a bool and a boolean array → each item joined with the bool not — boolean array → boolean array A tensor compared with a number is a mask of the tensor's shape, as numpy's is: a vector's is a list of bools, a matrix's its rows of bools — [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]] gt 2.0 is [[false, false], [true, true]] — and deeper for more axes. It keeps that shape through not , and and or (two masks of one shape join truth by truth; of two shapes the program stops), where numbers are taken it is a tensor of that shape — true 1, false 0 — so where[m gt 0.0, m, 0.0 * m] is a matrix and sum[m gt 2.0] counts, and a matrix indexed by a mask of its shape is its numbers where the mask is true, in row order (see Indexing). A tensor whose rank the program does not show — a field given a vector in one place and a matrix in another — compared with a number is refused, naming it: its mask's shape would be decided by nothing ( reshape or flatten it first). (Until 2026-10-18 a matrix's mask had been one flat list of its numbers' answers: where over it answered a vector, and no index of the matrix took it.) use frame df = load['people.csv'] old = df[df.age gt 50] alices = df[df.name eq 'alice'] rich_old = df[df.age gt 50 and df.salary gt 100000] others = df[not (df.name eq 'alice')] Each cell is compared with the value as two values compare (see Comparison): numbers by value, exactly — NaN holds only ne — text by its characters and ordered by character code, bools equal or not, moments by instant. A value of another kind than the cells — df.name eq 2 of a column of text — and an order between kinds with none — gt on a column of bools — are refused where the column's type is known, and stop the program where it shows only as it runs (a file load reads). Missing values compare as false for every operator, ne included — they are excluded by any mask, and not (df.age gt 50) is what keeps them. A list compared with one value is a mask the same way. (Compiled, a missing or NaN cell had been false for ne , eq had been nearness within 2⁻⁵², a column of text had been parsed as numbers and a column of bools had compared as nothing; the interpreter had counted a missing cell as ne and stopped on an order of text; a list of values that can fail, compared with one value, had not built.) A frame's mask is computed in one pass. df[df.age gt 50 and df.name ne 'bob'] — a mask that compares the frame's own columns with values that only read, asks a column's .ok , and combines those with and , or and not — reads no column into a list and makes no mask per comparison: the rows are decided block by block, across the cores for a large frame, each cell as its comparison decides it. The rows kept are the mask's, and a column the frame lacks or an order between kinds with none stops with the operator's words at the first comparison that meets it. The same in both modes. A column's .ok is its rows' validity — true where the cell is present, false where it is missing — so df[df.age.ok] keeps the complete rows. (Every other value's .ok is its own status: a list that did not fail is ok.) A frame shows a missing cell as missing , and a column shown as a list shows it as the error it is read as, error: missing ; a NaN a number column holds is a value, and shows as nan (until 2026-10-08 a missing cell had shown as nan too, in a text column as well). Read one at a time ( df.age[3] ), a cell of a column that can have missing cells is fallible: a missing one is an error value of reason missing , which computes and cannot be decided on (§10), so .ok guards it and a guard narrows it to its value. The columns that can are a loaded file's and a page's data source's, whose columns the program's reads type (A frame loaded from a file, above: an empty cell, a null or absent field), a database column that can hold NULL (see db, Typed cells) and the side of a join a row can have no match on — a left join's right columns, a right join's left ones, all of an outer join's. fill[df, 'age', 0] gives a column a value where it had none, and its cells are plain again, as are a column's that cannot have missing cells. A mask decides every row, so a list of values that can fail — built from such cells — is refused as one, in both modes: fill the column first, or guard each value with .ok . Handed whole to a function that takes numbers — mean[df.age] , median , sma[bars.c, 3] — or used in arithmetic — df.price * 2 , df.a + df.b — a column is its numbers, as a list of numbers is, and the answer is a tensor; a missing cell stops the program ( row 3 of the column is missing — fill the column first: fill[frame, 'column', value] ), and so does a column of text or of bools, in both modes. (Compiled, a missing cell had been read as 0 and a column of text parsed, where the interpreter stopped — or, for df.a + df.b , refused the sum.) A comparison is a mask, as above. A column written from another ( df.b = df.a ) keeps its kind and its missing cells, even when every cell is missing. Design Note: a missing cell is an error, not a placeholder. Considered: reading a missing cell as its column's placeholder in both modes — NaN in a number column, 0 in an int one, false in a bool one, nan in text — as a filter reads it, which both modes did. Honest for a number, since NaN compares as false; for an int or a bool it is a guess the program cannot tell from a value, of the kind §10 refuses elsewhere (an unmatched row's count read as 0 ). Decided (Vijay, 2026-09-25, typed frames decision 3): where the schema says a column can have missing cells its cells are fallible, and where it says it cannot they are plain, so no cell is a guess. Dynamic column names need no special syntax — a string variable works everywhere a column name does: col = 'age' sorted = sort[df, col] Design Note: No Bare-Name Column References What was considered (and originally shipped): Bare identifiers as column names — sort[df, age] , group[df, dept, [salary, mean]] — where an identifier that isn't a defined variable is treated as a column-name string. Why it was removed: Scope-dependent meaning. Adding a local variable named age silently changed sort[df, age] from a column reference into a value argument. Code broke at a distance with no error. Interpreter–transpiler divergence. The interpreter preferred the variable when one existed; the transpiler force-converted certain argument positions to strings regardless. The same program meant different things in the two modes, violating the parity rule. Violates rule 19 (no DSL). A second evaluation rule inside frame calls means a line of Crow can't be read without knowing which builtin it appears in. What to use instead: Strings for column names, expressions for computation — as specified above. One mechanism, no sugar, dynamic columns free. web Import sub-modules with use web.X . Each sub-module enables only its feature — minimal binary, minimal compile time. A sub-module's names are its own: mail and smtp are web.mail's, socket , send , recv and close web.ws's, sign and verify web.auth's — under use web alone each is refused where it is written, with the line that brings it ( smtp[] and mail[] are web.mail's: add `use web.mail` ; the interpreter had stopped as it ran, and the compiled program had not built), and each takes the kinds its rows do ( mail[] handed a column where it takes text is refused). See docs/web-framework.md for full architecture details. View Blocks — the UI Vocabulary Zone UI trees are built in view blocks — a declaration form, sibling of fn : use web, ui count = 0 fn inc[] count = count + 1 view render[] return div[ h1['Count: `count`'], button['+', click = inc] ] serve[3000] page['/', render] Inside a view, the standard HTML element vocabulary is active — plus the vocabulary's own elements: the containers stack , row , grid , overlay , scroll , the layers modal , drawer , toast , and details , summary , dropdown , divider (Revealing and framing, below) — div , span , p , h1 , h2 , h3 , h4 , h5 , h6 , button , ul , ol , li , form , a , nav , header , footer , section , tr , td , th , thead , tbody , option , textarea , label , pre , code , input , img , table — with their exact HTML names. Outside a view, those names don't exist : p = 0.95 , fn add[a, b] , and form = req.body are ordinary code in any ui program, and use ui reserves nothing in your file. Calling an element outside a view is an error that points at the fix. A child that is a list contributes each item. Markup a view or an element made is markup, anything else is text — so rows = for s in sessions over a view, then stack[h2['Sessions'], rows] , renders one row per session. Text is what log writes for the value — a number, a moment, a map, a record or a tensor as it shows, a parsed value as display shows it — and a frame's column contributes each cell, as a list does; a value that failed, a missing cell among them, shows as error: the server's log has why, as <id> with its reason in the log. A function is no child ( log shows none either), refused in both modes. Text is escaped as HTML needs, & , < and > , and an attribute's value its quotes too, by one escape both modes write with; a class joins the element's own ( stack[…, class = 'wide'] is class="stack wide" ), and one that holds no class adds none. A view called outside views — at the top level, by a derivation, handed to doc.document — answers its markup, the HTML a page would draw, in both modes (compiled, log[card[…]] and a name given a view's markup had not built). This is how a page shows many of something with their own controls; table[frame] is for cells that are values. A click can ask first : button['End session', click = end_session, confirm = 'End this session?'] shows the question in a dialog the runtime draws, and runs the handler only when the reader says yes. The server enforces it — the button offers the question, not the handler, and the dialog's own button offers the handler while the dialog is open — so the handler cannot be reached without the answer. On a table the question is a map from action to text: actions = map[Delete = delete_session], confirm = map[Delete = 'Delete this session?'] . A key presses an element : button['Save', click = save, shortcut = 'ctrl+s'] is pressed by Ctrl+S as a click presses it — the same handler with the same arguments, the question first when it asks one — and only while the page draws it and it can be pressed (shown, not disabled, not busy), so a key reaches only what the reader could click. A shortcut names its modifiers, ctrl , alt , shift and meta , then a key: a character ( '?' , '/' , 'g' ) or one of enter , escape , tab , space , backspace , delete , up , down , left , right , home , end , pageup , pagedown and f1 to f12 . Alternatives are separated by a space ( 'ctrl+s meta+s' , for the Mac's Command key), and a character shift makes is written as that character ( '?' , not 'shift+/' ). It is drawn as the browser's aria-keyshortcuts , which a screen reader announces. A key without ctrl , alt or meta is the reader's while they type in a field, Escape excepted, and Enter and Space are the focused control's; of two elements that take the same key, the one in an open dialog is pressed, else the first. The element must do something when pressed — a click , or it is a button or a link — or the program is refused, as a shortcut that names no key is, in both modes. A dialog's Close says shortcut = 'escape' , and the runtime's own question cancels on Escape. A form submits once and never reloads the page : Enter in a field presses the form's first button, and form[field['Name', name], button['Add'], submit = add] runs add when the form is submitted, by its button or by Enter, with the fields' facts already bound. Boolean attributes follow state : button['Start', disabled = starting] writes disabled="" when true and nothing when false, for disabled , hidden , readonly , required , checked , selected , multiple , autofocus . Design Note: keys press elements. Considered: keydown = h on an element or the page, the handler handed the key's name to decide what it means (ui-framework.md, Keyboard Events). Rejected: every shortcut would be an if-chain over key names, in a second kind of handler with arguments of its own, and a key could reach work no button offers, where a session accepts only what a render offered. A key that presses a drawn element keeps one handler, one set of arguments, and the reader's view of what they can do. Views compose: a view calls other views (components) and ordinary functions freely. A module can export views — importers reach them qualified, like any module name: --- cards.co view card[title, body_text] div[h2[title], p[body_text]] --- main.co use cards as c view render[] div[h1['Home'], c.card['Status', 'All good']] This is the JSX/SwiftUI boundary: the lowercase vocabulary is fixed and language-owned; your components are module-exported views. There is no way to add elements or define new vocabulary zones — see the Design Note "Names Are Never Ambiguous". Views and event handlers are the only functions that see reactive state (see Function Scope). crow fmt --fix-views migrates pre-view code ( fn declarations that build ui trees) automatically. The view tree is target-independent. A view describes a tree; what renders it is a build target. Web today; a desktop or mobile shell renders the same tree without a language change. Platforms are build targets, never dialects — there will never be a screen or window vocabulary fork. Reactive Data and Inputs ( use ui ) Top-level variables in a ui program are reactive state (see Function Scope). Three builtins declare state that the runtime keeps current, and bind inputs to it: Function Description fetch[url] A frame loaded once by HTTP GET when the page connects — from a URL, or from a path of this app's own ( fetch['/api/rows'] ) — held where it arrives to the columns the page reads of it (Frames: a frame loaded from a file has the columns the program reads) poll[url, seconds] The same, re-fetched every seconds ; every reader re-renders when it changes field[label, var, type = '', lines = 0] A labeled input two-way bound to reactive variable var (inside a view). type is the input's kind — 'text' , 'number' , 'date' , 'time' , 'password' , 'file' — and defaults to 'number' for an int or float variable; lines = 3 makes it a textarea slider[label, var, min = 0, max = 100, step = 1] A range input bound to a number checkbox[label, var] A checkbox bound to a bool toggle[label, var] A switch bound to a bool — the same binding as checkbox , drawn as a toggle radio[options, var] One of several strings, as radio buttons: radio[['buy', 'sell'], side] tabs[options, var] One of several strings, as a tab strip; the view shows the selected tab's content with if mode eq 'Practice' select[options, var] One of several strings, as a dropdown list progress[value, max = 1.0] A progress bar icon[name, size = 'm', color = ''] An icon from the closed set (below), sized by the type scale, colored by a token Inputs are state: the reader's change lands in the variable, the handlers read it, and the next render draws it. There is no "value of the input" apart from the variable. Files in and out. A file is an input like any other: field['Trades', upload, type = 'file'] binds upload , declared upload = map[] . When the reader picks a file the page sends it to the server, and upload becomes a map of strings — name (the file's name on the reader's computer), type (its media type), size (its bytes, as text) and path , where the server keeps the copy — so a handler reads it as it reads any file: csv[upload.path] , read[upload.path] . The copy is the session's, kept under .crow/uploads/ (a directory that ignores itself in version control) and removed when the session ends; a handler that keeps a file copies it ( cp[upload.path, …] ). A file bigger than the app allows — 10 MB, or serve[…, uploads = 50] in megabytes — is refused before it is sent, and the reader is told the limit. The other way, download[value, name] hands the reader's browser a file: a frame as CSV, a string as text, or a picked file (a map with a path ) as that file's bytes, saved under name . It is an effect held to the handler's commit, as notice is, so a handler that stops sends nothing. In a test, change[a, 'upload', map[name = 'trades.csv', type = 'text/csv', size = '120', path = 'fixtures/trades.csv']] stands for a file the reader picked, and downloads[a] is the list of what the session was handed, each a map of name and text . Derivations — derive Facts are stored; beliefs are derived. A derivation is a value computed from facts and data sources, read like a fact, never assigned, and recomputed only when something it read changed: qty = 100 sym = 'IMRN' derive total return qty * 2 derive trades[fresh = 300] return query[book, 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE symbol = ?', [sym]] view render[] return stack[p['total `total`'], table[trades]] derive name opens a block with a return , like a view; it never takes parameters. The name reads as a variable anywhere a fact can be read — views, handlers, tests, other derivations, and the program's top level, once, as it starts, over the facts as declared (parity 168) — and in a route's handler when the app holds it (below); assigning it is an error that says what to change instead. A derivation writes no fact: only handlers write. What it reads is decided once, from the source , and both execution modes obey the same sets: the facts and derivations it names (transitively through the functions it calls, and inside interpolated strings), now[] if it or a callee reads the clock, and the tables its query literals read. A derivation recomputes, on its next read, when a handler wrote a fact it reads; a derivation it reads recomputed and its value changed — an equal number, string or bool cuts the chain (frames always propagate); a statement in this program wrote a table it reads — an insert , or a query whose statement writes ( INSERT … RETURNING id reads back the row it wrote, and the table is written all the same); it reads now[] and a tick of serve refresh passed — a click's render is not a tick, so a click recomputes only what it moved; it reads a table this program never writes — an external source — and its freshness window elapsed. fresh = N is seconds; the default fresh = 0 means as fresh as the loop : recomputed every tick, which is what a query inside a view did before. Declaring fresh is the relaxation. A derivation that fails — a query error — holds the error value; readers see .ok and .reason , and a view shows the failure in place as an id, its reason in the server's log beside the id. captured[x] on a derivation is the moment it last ran. Derivations live in a program that serves: a use ui program with a page, whose views and handlers read them, or a use web program whose routes read them — derive x needs a program that serves — … in a script, which computes a value where it needs it. In the test harness html[a] is a tick and click[a, h] marks what the handler wrote. Design: derive-design.md . Who holds a derivation is inferred from what it reads. A fact is a top-level variable; a database or socket handle is not one, and neither is a fetch / poll binding. A derivation that reads a fact a session writes — assigned by a handler or a helper a handler calls, bound to an input like field or select , or carried in a page's address (a :name of its path, a name of its url = […] ) — or a data source, whose answers land in each session that asks, or another derivation held per session, is computed per session. One that reads only constants, tables and the clock — the day's universe, the latest bar in a table — is computed once for the app and shared by every session and route, and a table write in any session, or any route, reaches every derivation over that table. (A derivation over a fact of the address, or over a source, had been counted the app's: one session's address, or the source's first answer, served to all.) crow check prints each derivation's read set and who holds it — held by the app , or held by each session (it reads 'picked', which a session writes) . A render never waits for a query it does not need. A derivation that reaches out — its read set includes a table or an external source — is computed off the render in a served page: a render reads its latest value, and when that value is stale the runtime starts a recompute on a worker thread and the render goes ahead with what it has; the page renders again when the new value lands. Staleness has a cause, and the cause decides what waits. A derivation over a table the current event wrote is recomputed before that event's render, so a click's own writes are on the page in its answer — after buy , the blotter shows the trade. One that is stale because time moved, because a fact it reads changed, or because another session wrote its table shows its last value until the recompute lands. A handler that reads a derivation always gets the recomputed value; a derivation over facts and the clock alone is computed where it is read. Before its first value, a derivation whose value can be an error — a query's frame, anything that can fail — reads as an error of kind 'pending' with the reason loading , which a view renders in place like any failed read; one that cannot fail is computed where it is first read. One recompute of a derivation is in flight at a time for each holder — the session, or the app for a shared one, so readers arriving together run a shared query once — and a value whose inputs moved while it was computed is dropped and computed once more with the latest inputs. running[x] is true while a recompute of x is in flight. The root element of a view that read a value still being recomputed carries data-crow-stale while the value is behind something the reader did — it was computed before their last change (a click or an input that moved a fact), or there is none yet — and the default stylesheet dims it after 300 ms, so a fast recompute never flashes. A value behind only the clock is not marked: a query over a playing replay's play-head recomputes each tick and is always one query behind, where marking it dimmed every pane it feeds once a second. In the test harness every event settles before the next line runs: the handler's writes, then every recompute they made stale, so a test reads the page a reader sees once the data is in. A write reaches every reader. When a handler writes a table, every session whose page read a derivation over that table renders again, recomputing it off the render: a reader sees another reader's change without waiting for a refresh tick, and without a line of code to publish it. A route's write is the same: it lands as the route's handler ends — a handler that stops too, since a store without transactions kept what it was given — and the pages over the table render again. A write made outside the program — another service, a person at a SQL prompt — is seen through fresh and the ticks, as above. A route reads what the app holds. A route has no session, so its handler reads, by name, the derivations the app holds — the one value every session reads too — and the cached rows a web service keeps in memory are a derivation: use web, db world_db = connect['postgres://app@127.0.0.1/hello_world'] derive worlds return query[world_db, 'SELECT id, randomnumber FROM world ORDER BY id'] fn cached_h[req] picked = for i in range[20] k = rand[0, len[worlds] - 1] map[id = worlds.id[k], randomNumber = worlds.randomnumber[k]] return json[picked] fn update_h[req] conn = connect['postgres://app@127.0.0.1/hello_world'] query[conn, 'UPDATE world SET randomnumber = ? WHERE id = ?', [rand[1, 10000], rand[1, 10000]]] return text['ok'] route['/cached-queries', cached_h] route['/update', update_h] serve[8080] A route's handler reads each derivation it names once, as its request begins — the app's value, computed then when there is none yet or something it reads moved — and reads that value wherever the body names it after, so a loop over the rows reads them where they lie; the same request reading it twice reads one value. A value is computed once for the requests that arrive together: a burst of requests after a write runs one query, and the rest wait for its answer. The rules above decide when it is computed again, with each request a moment of its own: a derivation over tables this program writes is kept until it writes one — worlds above until /update runs, whose write lands as its handler ends, so the next request reads the new rows — one over the clock, or over a table outside the program at fresh = 0 , is computed for each request that reads it, and fresh = N keeps one over an outside table N seconds. A route that reads a derivation a session holds is refused, with what makes it the session's: 'band' is held by each session, and a route's handler has no session — it reads 'picked', which a session writes: … . Both modes keep the app's values in the one runtime ( crow_web::live ) and read them by the same rule. Design Note: a route's cache is a derivation. Considered: a cache of its own for routes — cache[key, secs, compute] , or a module-level value a route may write — as web frameworks offer beside their database layer, and an external cache (Redis) as part of the language. Rejected: a derivation already says what a value is computed from, so the runtime knows when it is stale — the part a cache by hand gets wrong (a key forgotten at a write, a value served after the row changed). A second form would hold the same rows with the invalidation written out, and a value a route writes would be state a route can move, which routes do not have. A store shared by several processes is a database the program reads, and comes as a driver: what it holds is a table a derivation reads. Decided too: a route's handler reads a derivation once, as its request begins, as a view does, where a page's handler reads it where it uses it — a route writes no fact, so nothing it does moves the value under it, and a loop over the rows reads one value instead of asking the cache each round. Design Note: no channels. Considered: channel.join[name] , channel.send[name, message] and an on_channel handler, so that a route, a job or another process could push to the pages that joined a channel (ui-framework.md, Server Push). Rejected: a write already reaches every reader. The database is the channel, and a page learns of another's change the way it learns of its own, by reading a derivation over the table; a channel would be a second way to say that something changed, and a message pushed past the database could say what the database does not. A process outside the program is seen through fresh . Rows keep their identity through id . The live client patches the page in place: an element with an id is matched to the element with that id in the previous render, so a row rendered from data — p[' s.name ', id = 's- s.id '] — moves when its list is reordered and is dropped when its item is gone, while its neighbours are untouched. Elements without an id match by position. A node that survives a render keeps its focus, caret and scroll, so the field a reader is typing in is never rebuilt under them. The checker teaches the form. A top-level variable assigned from a query and read by a view (a launch-time snapshot) is an error in crow check ; d in the check loop rewrites it into derive x . A query inside a view never gets that far: a view reaches no database (Effects Have Kinds), so it is refused before the program runs, and the query's place is a derive above the view ( derive rows[fresh = 60] for a remote database). Tables over frames A big table pages. table[frame, page = 50] shows fifty rows at a time, says which ( 1–50 of 12000 ) and offers the previous and the next page; the frame stays on the server and only the page shown is drawn, so a hundred thousand rows cost the reader one page. Each paged table keeps its place for its session: new rows arriving keep the reader on their page, and a frame that shrinks brings them to its last one. A table of more than 1,000 rows without page is refused, as a chart over its point budget is — in its place the view shows table: 12000 rows — a table shows at most 1000 at a time: table[frame, page = 50] , never a silent cut. A test sees the first page. table[frame] renders a frame's rows. Numeric columns are typed: their cells carry the class num and the stylesheet right-aligns them with tabular figures. Six named arguments make it interactive and legible: click = handler sends the row's key to the handler when a row is clicked ( fn focus[symbol] ), key = 'col' names the column whose cell is sent (the first column by default; a numeric key travels as a number, a text key as a string), mark = 'col' names a column whose truthy cells put the class marked on their row, tinted by the stylesheet, delta = ['pnl', 'pct'] names columns whose cells are colored by sign ( up / down ), actions = map[Replay = replay, Delete = ask_delete] adds a trailing cell of buttons to every row, each sending the row's key to its handler, and hide = ['id'] keeps columns out of the table that stay in the frame — the key column, a helper. In the test harness click[a, ask_delete[3]] presses a row's button. A reader can sort a table. table[frame, sort = true] makes each header a button: pressing it shows the rows in the order of its column, ascending, and pressing it again, descending. Numbers sort as numbers and text alphabetically; missing cells come last either way, and equal cells keep the frame's order. The session keeps each sorted table's order, as it keeps a paged table's page, and a sorted table that pages pages through the sorted rows. The frame itself is untouched: sort[df, 'col'] orders the program's data, and the table's sort orders only what the reader sees. The sorted header carries aria-sort and an arrow. sort is written true or false , and a test sees the frame's own order. Design Note: no filter on a table. Considered: table[frame, find = true] , a search box that keeps the rows holding the typed text in any shown column (ui-framework.md, Table Features). Rejected: filtering is the program's, over its frame — a field bound to a fact and a derivation that filters by it — which says which columns to search and how to match, where a table's own box would decide both for every table and be a second way to filter a frame. Sorting is the table's because its headers are: nothing in the program draws them. Sliders slider[label, var, min = 0, max = 100, step = 1] is a range input bound to a reactive variable, exactly as field binds a text input. A handler reads the variable when the reader acts (a Seek button beside the scrubber). A bound input keeps its variable's type: text typed into a field bound to an integer becomes an integer (a float is truncated), a float variable gets a float, a bool variable gets a bool, and text that does not parse leaves a number alone. When a handler assigns to a bound variable, every field bound to it shows the new value on the next render; only the input the reader is typing in keeps its draft. Handlers and their helpers A view sees reactive state, a handler moves it, and a function a handler calls that assigns a module-level variable is a handler too — its own part's, or one of a part it uses ( session.picked = symbol in the scanner's part) — it joins the handler class in both renderers, so fn restart[] may call fn rewind_to[t] and the write lands in state. So does one that acts for the session — says a notice , signs the reader in or out, hands a download , sends mail — itself or through a function it calls, so what it does waits for its handler's commit. A pure helper (one that assigns no module variable) keeps its own scope. A helper a handler calls sees what the handler has written so far, and the handler sees what the helper wrote when it returns, in both modes — derivations included: a derivation the handler reads after a write to what it reads, its own or a helper's, is the recomputed one ( clock.jump[t] , then clock.head is t ). A helper that reads state and assigns none is a derivation, not a function: derive band computes the price band from the scanner's config, and the handlers read band . A function reading a derivation is refused with that advice — by crow run , crow test and crow check alike, which pass every program through the same checks before doing anything else. Reactive state may be an array, a map, a record or a list of records, or a frame; the compiled program keeps each fact in a typed field of its own, which its handlers, helpers, views and derivations read and write in place — one copy, so a helper reads what its caller wrote — and writes a fact as JSON only where it leaves the program: the harness, a bound input, the dev panel, a session kept across a restart. A handler is a transaction. It runs on a working copy of the session's facts, sees its own writes at once — as a helper it calls does — and when it ends its writes land as one; a render never sees a handler halfway, and two sessions never see each other's copies. Effects follow one rule, decided from the text: an effect whose answer the handler uses runs when asked; one whose answer it does not use runs when the handler commits, in program order. r = query[…] , n = shell['wc -l x'] and row = query[book, 'INSERT … RETURNING id'] answer at once; notice['saved'] and later[reload] wait for the commit, and a stop drops them. A function's last line is its value, but a handler's value goes to nobody, so an effect on a handler's last line waits for the commit too, as does one a helper returns to a caller that calls it as a statement; a caller that reads the helper's answer ( r = notify[…] ) has it at once. Database writes run in a transaction: the first write a handler makes through a connection begins one on it, every later read and write on that connection is inside it, and it commits when the handler does and rolls back when it stops — RETURNING answers inside it. A handler that writes two databases commits them in program order; the language promises no atomicity across stores, and ClickHouse, which has no transactions, keeps a write the moment it is made. The notice. notice[text] tells the reader something: an effect held to the commit, so a handler that stops never leaves a message saying it succeeded. The session keeps one notice, with the moment it landed; notice reads as a record with text and at , provided by the runtime like a derivation, so a view writes toast[notice.text] . A handler's stop is delivered the same way, as what a reader can act on — skip_symbol stopped, and nothing changed — the server's log has why, as 3f9a1c07 — its reason in the server's log beside the id, never on the page (A handler stops, §10). A page that reads no notice gets the runtime's own toast, which fades after a few seconds; the program keeps no flag and clears nothing. Who the reader is. reader is the page's signed-in reader: a map of strings, empty until someone signs in. A handler signs the reader in with sign_in[record] and out with sign_out[] — effects held to the handler's commit, like notice , so a handler that stops signs nobody in: fn log_in[] found = query[book, 'SELECT id, role, hash FROM people WHERE name = ?', [name]] if len[found] eq 0 notice['no one called `name`'] return if hash[password, found.hash[0]] ne found.hash[0] notice['wrong password'] return sign_in[map[id = str[found.id[0]], name = name, role = found.role[0]]] fn log_out[] sign_out[] Signing in sets reader for the session and gives the browser a cookie, so the reader is signed in on every page and tab they open next — after a restart too — for thirty days, or until they sign out. Signing out clears reader and the cookie, and ends that sign-in everywhere: every session holding it, another tab included, is signed out and redrawn at once, and the cookie is refused if it is ever sent again. A tab already open when someone signs in shows it the next time it opens the page. The program never sees the cookie: the runtime reads it when a page opens and fills reader . Nothing on the page can write reader — no input binds it and no handler assigns it; in a test, change[a, 'reader', record] stands for a reader who signed in. Authorization is ordinary code in the handler that needs it: if reader.role ne 'admin' . A signed-out reader has no role : reading it is an error, and a handler that meets one stops — nothing it did lands, and the reader is told it stopped — so the check fails closed (in a test, click reports the error); 'role' in reader asks first. A derivation that reads reader is computed per session; a plain function is handed the reader as a parameter ( is_admin[reader] ), as it is handed a module variable. The record travels in the cookie, so it stays small: at most 1 KB — an id, a name, a role; look the rest up. The cookie is HttpOnly , SameSite=Lax , and Secure when the page came over https through a proxy ( X-Forwarded-Proto: https ). It is signed with the app's secret: CROW_SECRET (at least 32 characters) when set, otherwise a key the runtime writes to .crow/keys/ on first use, a directory that ignores itself in version control. Changing the secret signs everyone out. Passwords are stored as hash[password, 'password'] and checked with hash[attempt, stored] eq stored (### Hashing). A page for signed-in readers checks reader in its view: view orders[] if 'id' not in reader return sign_in_form[] return stack[ table[open_orders, actions = map[Refund = refund]], button['Log out', click = log_out] ] While the reader is signed out the page draws the sign-in form, and nothing else of the page reaches them: a session accepts only the events a render it sent offered, so refund is refused even in a message written by hand, and a derivation is computed only where it is read, so open_orders is never queried for them. When log_in commits, the same session draws the orders, at the same address, so nothing has to send the reader back. A page for one role checks the role the same way ( reader.role ne 'admin' , after 'role' in reader ). Design Note: no auth on a page. Considered: page['/admin', admin, auth = true] , sending a signed-out reader to a login page and back once they sign in (ui-framework.md, Authentication). Rejected: the view's check already does all of it and fails closed. It draws the sign-in form in place, offers none of the page's handlers and runs none of its queries, and a second way to guard a page would leave two places to look for why a page is shown. The page keeps its address while the reader signs in, so there is nowhere to send them back to. A handler runs off the page's loop. While it runs the page stays live — refresh ticks render and landed values render, from the committed facts — and running[h] , true while a later schedule of h is in flight, is also true while h runs as a handler: every element that offers h renders disabled with aria-busy="true" , so a button shows it is working with no flag in the program. Events are applied one at a time, in arrival order, bound inputs included: a change that arrives while a handler runs waits its turn, and the browser keeps showing what the reader typed. A second click on the handler that is running is dropped: the button already shows it is working. later[f] is the one way to say the session's other clicks need not wait for this work (Design Note: Handlers and later ). Design Note: no debounce. Considered: debounce = ms on an input or a button, holding its events in the browser until the reader pauses (ui-framework.md, Debounce). Rejected: what it guards against is already kept small where it happens. A derivation over a field's fact has one recompute in flight, and a value its inputs moved past is dropped for the latest, so a search typed a key at a time runs at most one query at a time, always for the latest text; a second click on a handler that is running is dropped; and the events that arrive while a render runs are answered by one render. A delay the program chose would slow every reader to spare a server the runtime already spares. Views render wherever they are called A view returns its markup from any call site — a page[] , the test harness, another view, or a program writing pages to disk ( doc.document[title, chapter[...]] ). Text is text. Markup is what a view, an element, a chart, an icon, a bound input, or doc 's markdown , menu and pager make; it stays markup however it travels — held in a local, collected by a for , put in a list, handed to another view as an argument. Every other string is text and is escaped, whatever it holds: a reader who types <img src=x onerror=…> into a field sees those characters on every page that shows them, never an image and never a script. A view given markup in one call and text in another is compiled once for each. Both renderers apply the same rule. Layout — the vocabulary Pages are composed from layout primitives, never styled with CSS. Five containers join the element vocabulary inside views, and a fixed set of layout attributes applies to any element. Each has one written rule; the kernel table ( crow_runtime::layout ) turns it into the CSS a browser lays out with, and the layout engine — written in Crow, shipped inside the compiler — implements the same rule for tests and the desktop shell. Design and rationale: ui-engine-design.md . Container Rule stack[a, b, ...] children top to bottom, each the container's full content width row[a, b, ...] children left to right on one line; overflow is a failure fits[] reports, never a silent wrap ( wrap = true opts in) grid[a, b, ..., columns = 2] cells left-to-right, top-to-bottom, equal columns; columns = '240px fill' names tracks overlay[base, top] top positioned over base by anchor = 'center' | 'top_right' | ... scroll[child, height = '360px'] a fixed-height viewport; the platform scrolls Attribute Values gap , pad ( 'm' or 'm l' ), margin the spacing scale xs s m l xl = 4 8 16 24 32 px align start center end stretch (cross axis) justify start center end between around (main axis) width , height , min_width , max_width '240px' , '50%' (width only), 'fill' for remaining space; aspect = '16/9' size , weight , font the type scale xs s m l xl xxl = 12 14 16 20 24 32 px; regular medium bold ; font = 'mono' sets the monospace face with tabular digits — a figure in a stat tile, a code-like value surface = 'card' , radius , border = true , shadow surfaces: radius none s m l round , shadow s m l color , background a colour token: text muted accent up down surface bg — never a literal colour lines = 2 clamp a wrapping paragraph below = 'phone' | 'tablet' , becomes = 'stack' , columns_then = 1 , hidden_below responsive rules at named widths (phone < 600, tablet < 1024) — no media queries open = true , side = 'left' | 'right' a disclosure's or layer's state (any bool expression) and a drawer's or dropdown's side tip = 'text' , fit = 'cover' | 'contain' , active = '/path' a tooltip on anything; how an img fills its aspect box; the current page of a nav Layout attributes are literals; a wrong value is a compile error naming the scale ( gap = 'huge' is not a spacing step (xs s m l xl) ), the same in both modes. Attributes outside the vocabulary ( class , href , name , ...) pass through as HTML. Labels, headings, buttons, and cells are single-line; only p wraps. Revealing and framing The vocabulary's own elements beyond the containers, each earning its place by a capability a stack of divs cannot compose: Element Renders details[summary[...], ..., open = true] A disclosure: the summary always shows, the rest only when open. open follows a bool — open = show toggles it from state dropdown[summary[...], panel, side = 'right'] A button that opens a floating panel — its second child, usually a stack of buttons or links. side anchors the panel to the button's right edge modal[child, open = var] A dialog layer over a dimmed page while open is true; the child (a stack with a heading, text, and a button['Close', click = close, shortcut = 'escape'] ) is the dialog drawer[..., open = var, side = 'left'] A side panel layer, sliding from the right by default toast[..., open = var] A brief notice at the bottom corner while open is true; it fades on its own, and the program clears the flag divider[] A rule between siblings: horizontal in a stack , vertical in a row nav[a[...], ..., active = path] A navigation row; the link whose href equals active gets aria-current="page" and the stylesheet's active look header[...] The app's bar: a surface with a border holding its name, its nav and a status chip, laid out as a row ( gap , justify , align as on any row) widget[name, props = value, on = map[event = handler]] A piece of the page the program's own JavaScript draws — a map, a rich editor, a calendar: the module widgets/name.js (below) Three attributes any element takes: tip = 'text' is the browser's tooltip, fit = 'cover' (or 'contain' ) sizes an img into its box together with aspect , and open as above. The layers take no room in the flow and are hidden until opened; the layout engine lays an open layer out as a stack where it sits. One way out of the vocabulary: widget . The vocabulary is closed, so a map, a rich-text editor or a calendar is a widget: widget['map', props = map[lat = 51.5, lng = -0.1], on = map[pick = choose]] draws the module widgets/map.js of the program's folder — plain JavaScript that exports mount(el, props, send) and, optionally, update(el, props) . The page loads the module once, calls mount with the element and the props (the value, as JSON), and calls update with the same element whenever a render changes them; the element's contents are the module's, and no render touches them. send('pick', value) runs the handler on names for pick — fn choose[place] receives value — through the offers like any click: a page offers exactly the events its widgets name, and a handler takes a widget's value as it takes a field's, so it checks what it is given. A module name is letters, digits, _ and - ; the server serves only widgets/*.js . In a test a widget is its element, and click[a, choose['Paris']] stands for what it would send. There is no other client code. The icon set , closed like the rest of the vocabulary: check x plus minus chevron_down chevron_up chevron_left chevron_right arrow_up arrow_down arrow_left arrow_right search menu more settings user home calendar clock refresh play pause stop upload download trash edit copy link external info warning error success star filter sort chart table bell mail lock eye eye_off dollar bookmark flag tag circle dot loader . An unknown name is an error that lists them. Icons are inline SVG in the current text color, so color = 'muted' and the theme both apply. Charts — chart[frame, ...] A chart is a view over a frame. chart is an element like table : valid only inside views, it takes a frame plus named arguments that say which columns to draw, and renders server-side as SVG: derive bars return query[conn, 'SELECT ts, o, hi, lo, c, vol FROM bars ORDER BY ts'] view render[] return div[ chart[bars, candles = ['o', 'hi', 'lo', 'c'], bars_y = 'vol', marker = open_bell, tz = 'America/New_York', height = 200] ] Named argument Default Meaning x 'ts' Column of moments for the x axis candles [] Four column names — open, high, low, close — drawn as candlesticks lines [] Column names drawn as line series bars_y '' Column drawn as a volume pane under the chart marker 0 A moment marked with a vertical play-head tz 'UTC' Timezone for the axis ticks height 320 Height in pixels panes [] Lists of column names, each list drawn as its own strip under the volume with its own scale: [['rsi'], ['cvd']] levels 0 Reference lines keyed by column, drawn dashed in the pane that holds the column: map[rsi = [30, 70], cvd = [0]] points 0 A frame of markers on the main pane — columns ts , y , and optionally label and kind ( 'buy' an up triangle in the up color, 'sell' a down triangle in the down color, anything else a dot) seek 0 A handler: every bucket becomes a click target and the handler receives the bucket's moment — seek = jump with fn jump[t] Colors come from the style tokens ( --crow-up , --crow-down , --crow-accent , and --crow-series-2 … --crow-series-6 for the second line onward, counted across the whole chart), so every chart is theme-correct with no color plumbing. Every line series is named in a legend at the top of its pane. The indicators a pane usually draws come from use chart ( ### chart ). An empty frame renders a placeholder rather than an error; a frame over the point budget (1000 points) refuses with an error that says to aggregate first — coarser rows from the query, or head[frame, n] — never a silent downsample. The geometry and the SVG assembly live in crow_runtime::chart , so both modes emit identical markup. Design and roadmap: chart-module-design.md . Styling — the default stylesheet Pages look right with zero CSS: every page shell carries a default stylesheet (light and dark, following the system theme). The whole styling vocabulary is seven classes and eight tokens: classes card stats controls primary up down stale tokens --crow-bg --crow-surface --crow-text --crow-muted --crow-border --crow-accent --crow-up --crow-down Use the classes as ordinary attributes — div[..., class = 'card'] . To restyle, put plain CSS in css/app.css in the project; it is inlined after the defaults, and overriding a token ( :root { --crow-accent: #c60; } ) recolors every element and chart that uses it. crow check flags unknown --crow-* names with a did-you-mean. CSS never appears inside .co files. Design: style-module-design.md . Where this is going — a closed layout vocabulary with an engine written in Crow, so tests can state where things are and what colour they have without a browser — is ui-engine-design.md . Accessibility A page works for a reader on a keyboard or with a screen reader without a line of the program saying so, the same in both modes: A field's label names its input ( aria-label ), as a checkbox's and a radio's label wraps its input. A select is named by a label[...] around it: label['Symbol', select[symbols, sym]] . An element with a click that the browser does not press itself — a div , a card, a table row — is a tab stop with a button's role (a row keeps its own), and Enter and Space press it. A modal is a dialog ( role="dialog" , aria-modal ): when it opens, focus moves into it and Tab stays inside, and when it closes, focus goes back where it was. The runtime's question behaves the same way. A drawer is a dialog that does not hold focus, and a toast is a status a screen reader announces, as the runtime's own notice is. A chart is an image with a name that says what it draws ( a chart of candles, vwap and volume, 390 points ); an icon is hidden from screen readers, since words go beside it. While the page is reconnecting it takes no input from the mouse or the keyboard, and a screen reader is told. A key presses only what a click could (see Keys press elements), and a shortcut is announced ( aria-keyshortcuts ). An img says what it shows, alt = 'the logo' , or that it only decorates, alt = '' ; one that says neither is refused before the program runs, in both modes. The default stylesheet's text meets WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) in both themes, focus is always visible, and a drawer's motion stops for a reader who asks for less ( prefers-reduced-motion ). The page's language is English ( lang="en" ). What stays the program's: headings in order, a main for the page's content, and words on every button — a button that shows only an icon names itself with tip .
