Adding map creates a second way. Naming conflict. map[] already creates an empty map. Overloading the name with a completely different concept (higher-order function application) would be confusing. Requires first-class functions. map[items, fn] needs function references as arguments, which pulls toward lambdas and closures — features Crow intentionally omits. What to use instead: for -as-expression: doubled = for x in items x * 2 No Enumerate or Zip Crow intentionally omits enumerate and zip builtins. Why they were rejected: Mixed-type problem. enumerate[['a','b']] would need to return [[0,'a'], [1,'b']] — arrays mixing int and string. Crow arrays are homogeneous, so this doesn't fit the type system. zip[[1,2], ['a','b']] has the same problem. range[len[arr]] already covers every use case. Index-based iteration with for i in range[len[arr]] handles every scenario that enumerate or zip would address, with no new concepts. No new concepts needed. Adding enumerate or zip would require either tuples, anonymous structs, or mixed-type arrays — none of which exist in Crow. The cost of adding a new type concept outweighs saving one line of code. What to use instead: Numbered output: for i in range[len[players]] log['`i + 1`. `players[i]`'] Find index of something: for i in range[len[scores]] if scores[i] eq max[scores] log['best at index `i`'] Combine parallel arrays (instead of zip): for i in range[len[names]] log['`names[i]`: `scores[i]`'] Dot product (instead of zip + map): products = for i in range[len[a]] a[i] * b[i] total = sum[products] Build a map from two arrays: m = map[] for i in range[len[keys]] m = set[m, keys[i], values[i]] The pattern is always the same: iterate over indices with range[len[arr]] , access elements by index. One pattern, zero new concepts. Search Builtins (any, all, find) — a Reversal Original position: any / all / reduce were rejected ("the loop versions are the same length"), and find was rejected ("finding a position is straightforward with a loop"). Why it was reversed: the recommended flag-loop replacement was worse than the thing it replaced, on three axes at once: it cannot stop early (always O(n)); mutating the flag variable triggers the automatic sequential fallback — the exact "hidden performance trap" the break rejection warns about; and it is more code. Worse, the parallel early-exit search (all cores scanning, all stopping at the first hit) is impossible to express in user code at all — parallel for cannot break, and break -able while cannot parallelize. That is the same "cannot be written cleanly without a builtin" test that justified contains , passed harder. The design: predicates are named functions (no lambdas — name the question): fn over_90[x] return x gt 90 any[scores, over_90] --- true if at least one passes all[scores, over_90] --- true if every one passes hit = find[scores, over_90] --- the first passing ELEMENT if not hit.ok --- error-value when nothing matches log['none found'] find dispatches by argument types: find[str, pattern] is the regex builtin; find[array, function] is the search. Both modes agree; compiled mode runs searches in parallel with deterministic first-match semantics (rayon find_first ). Division of labor: operators and verbs eat most loops; for computes over everything that is left, in parallel; any / all / find ask the questions that deserve to stop early; while handles genuine sequential iteration. reduce stays rejected — the named reductions ( sum , min , max , prod , join ) cover it. No sum, min [ arr ] , max [ arr ] in Core Crow intentionally omits sum[arr] , min[arr] , and max[arr] from core builtins. What was considered: sum[[1, 2, 3]] → 6 , min[[3, 1, 2]] → 1 , max[[3, 1, 2]] → 3 . Why they were removed/rejected: All three are straightforward loops: total = 0 for x in nums total = total + x Including sum but not min[arr] / max[arr] created an inconsistency — all three are the same pattern (reduce an array to a single value). Rather than adding more, we removed sum to keep core honest: if you can write it with a loop, write it with a loop. What to use instead: use math provides sum , min , max , prod , and other tensor/array reductions (see section 13, math). For plain arrays without use math , use a loop. No chars Builtin Crow intentionally has no chars builtin to split a string into an array of characters. Why: split[s, ''] already answers a text's characters — the text split between every two characters, with no empty piece at either end — and s[i] reads one by its place ( s[0] , s[-1] ): letters = split['crow', ''] --- ['c', 'r', 'o', 'w'] Adding a dedicated chars builtin would create a second way to do the same thing. Named Arguments with Defaults (Revised) Crow originally rejected default parameters because greet['alice'] vs greet['alice', 'hi'] created two ways to call the same function. Why the decision was revised: Data science operations like sum[x] vs sum[x, axis = 0] are fundamentally different operations — one sums everything, the other sums along an axis. Forcing separate function names ( sum vs sum_axis ) or requiring the argument every time makes the language worse for its target audience. Every data science language (Python, Julia, MATLAB, R) has this. Rules: Named arguments must come after all positional arguments Named arguments must have defaults — that's what makes them optional Callers can use name or position: sum[x, 0] and sum[x, axis = 0] both work Named arguments without a value at the call site use the default fn train[data, lr = 0.01, epochs = 100] ... train[my_data] --- uses defaults train[my_data, lr = 0.001] --- override one train[my_data, 0.001, 50] --- positional also works No Augmented Assignment Crow intentionally has no += , -= , *= , /= , or any compound assignment operators. Why: x += 1 is syntactic sugar for x = x + 1 . Adding it creates two ways to write the same thing, violating "one way to do things." Every language that supports both spawns style debates about when to use which form. What to use instead: x = x + 1 total = total + item The explicit form is clear, consistent, and only a few characters longer. The compiler can optimize x = x + op patterns into in-place operations automatically — the sugar adds no performance benefit. No Destructuring Crow intentionally has no destructuring assignment from function returns or collections (e.g. a, b = f[] ). What was considered: Allowing a, b = divmod[7, 3] where a function returns an array and multi-assign unpacks it. Why it was rejected: Multi-assign already exists for literal values ( a, b = 1, 2 ). Extending it to destructure arrays would create two ways to access array elements — destructuring and indexing ( result[0] , result[1] ). This violates "one way to do things." What to use instead: Return an array and access elements by index: result = divmod[7, 3] a = result[0] b = result[1] a, b = f[] and a, b = xs are refused before the program runs, in both modes, the message giving this form in the program's own names. No Ternary Expression Crow intentionally has no ternary or inline conditional expression (e.g. x = if val gt 0 then val else -val ). What was considered: An expression-level if/else that returns a value inline. Why it was rejected: Crow already has if/else as a statement. Adding an expression form creates two ways to write conditionals. The statement form is always clear and never ambiguous about precedence. What to use instead: if/else with assignment: x = 0 if val gt 0 x = val else x = -val No Inline Error Fallback Crow intentionally has no inline error recovery syntax (e.g. x = int['bad'] rescue 0 or x = int['bad'] or 0 ). What was considered: A keyword ( rescue , catch , alt , fail , etc.) that silently replaces an error-value with a default, turning a 3-line check into a one-liner. Why it was rejected: Inline fallbacks hide errors. The program continues with a value that may be wrong, and the error's .reason and .trace are silently discarded. This contradicts Crow's error philosophy — errors are values that propagate visibly, carrying context, until you consciously handle them. Crow's errors don't crash the program. They propagate safely through function calls and operators: x = int['bad'] --- error-value, no crash y = x + 10 --- still error-value, no crash log[y.ok] --- false log[y.reason] --- original reason preserved What to use instead: Check errors explicitly. The verbosity is intentional — it forces you to acknowledge the error: x = int[input[]] if not x.ok log['invalid: `x.reason`'] x = 0 This may be revisited in the future if a design emerges that preserves error visibility while reducing verbosity. No Double-Quote Strings Crow uses single quotes for all strings. There is no double-quote alternative. Why: Adding a second string delimiter would create two ways to write the same thing, violating "one way to do things." Every language that supports both '...' and "..." spawns style debates and inconsistency. Nested quotes: Use the ' escape sequence. Most strings don't contain quotes. When they do, ' handles it cleanly: msg = 'he said 'hello' to me' For heavy quoting (SQL, JSON, HTML), use interpolation or load from a file with read[] . No String Concatenation with + Crow does not allow + to concatenate strings. String interpolation is the only way to combine strings. What was considered: 'hello' + ' world' producing 'hello world' . Why it was rejected: + is numeric. For combining pieces, interpolation ( 'hello `name`' ) shows the result's shape; for building from many pieces, collect parts and join[parts, sep] — the O(n) idiom every + -language teaches as best practice anyway; for a rare pairwise merge, concat[a, b] works on strings. Adding + as a fourth way violates "one way to do things". What to use instead: greeting = 'hello `name`' full = '`first` `last`'
